title: AnyGS2Mesh: Feed-Forward Mesh Reconstruction from 3D Gaussian Splatting with Arbitrary-Resolution Views
summary: Existing 3D mesh reconstruction methods from Gaussian scene representations predominantly rely on iterative optimization, resulting in slow inference and limited scalability to high-resolution inputs. In this paper, we present AnyGS2Mesh, the first feed-forward framework for directly reconstructing 3D meshes from 3D Gaussian Splatting representations with support for arbitrary input image resolutions. Our approach incorporates a Gaussian-Guided Transformer architecture that exploits explicit 3D geometric priors for efficient mesh generation. We introduce three key components: (1) a Gaussian-Guided Spatial Reasoning Transformer represents Gaussian primitives as structured 3D tokens and jointly reasons over Gaussian and image features; (2) a Streaming and Patchwise Geometry Encoder processes native-resolution views sequentially and aggregates information across variable-length view sets; (3) a Scale-Aligned Hybrid Depth Refiner uses a PatchFusion-style encoder--decoder to fuse RGB-conditioned predicted depth with Gaussian-rendered metric depth, combining fine local structures with globally consistent metric scale. The refined depth maps are integrated through TSDF fusion, followed by Marching Cubes for deterministic mesh extraction. Extensive experiments show that AnyGS2Mesh achieves state-of-the-art reconstruction quality while significantly reducing inference time compared with optimization-based baselines, enabling near-real-time, high-quality mesh reconstruction. Our results demonstrate the potential of combining Gaussian representations and feed-forward Transformer architectures for scalable 3D geometry reconstruction. The code will be made publicly available upon acceptance.

AI.tldr: Feed-forward mesh reconstruction from Gaussian Splatting; AnyGS2Mesh achieves faster, scalable 3D mesh reconstruction with state-of-the-art quality by using Gaussian-Guided Transformer, streaming geometry encoder, and depth refiner, culminating in TSDF fusion and Marching Cubes; code release on acceptance.
AI.motivation: Current 3D mesh reconstruction from Gaussian representations relies on iterative optimization, which is slow and scales poorly to high resolutions. A direct, feed-forward approach could enable faster, scalable mesh generation.
AI.method: Three components: (1) Gaussian-Guided Spatial Reasoning Transformer that encodes Gaussian primitives as 3D tokens and fuses Gaussian and image features; (2) Streaming and Patchwise Geometry Encoder that processes native-resolution views sequentially and aggregates variable-length view sets; (3) Scale-Aligned Hybrid Depth Refiner with a PatchFusion-like encoder–decoder that fuses RGB-conditioned depth with Gaussian-rendered metric depth. The pipeline performs TSDF fusion and Marching Cubes for deterministic mesh extraction.
AI.result: Experiments report state-of-the-art reconstruction quality with significantly reduced inference time compared to optimization-based baselines, enabling near-real-time high-quality mesh reconstruction.
AI.conclusion: Shows the viability of combining Gaussian representations with feed-forward Transformer architectures for scalable 3D geometry reconstruction; code will be publicly available upon acceptance.

title: The Geometry of Ignorance: LLMs Know When to Temper Bayesian Priors
summary: What does a language model predict when it has few clues? The answer lurks in its unembedding geometry: a single direction of the unembedding matrix encodes the unigram distribution of the training corpus, which serves as the Bayesian prior the model falls back on when uncertain. This structure --- which we term the \emph{direction of ignorance} --- appears in all four model families examined (\texttt{Llama}, \texttt{Qwen}, \texttt{Gemma}, and \texttt{Pythia}), ranging from 0.4B to 405B parameters. Projecting the final prediction state onto this direction yields a per-token \emph{prior loading factor} $λ$, which, empirically, declines steadily as the context becomes more informative. Formally, the same projection decomposes the prediction state into two orthogonal vectors that correspond exactly to the two factors of a tempered Bayesian update: a unigram prior raised to the exponent $λ$ and a context-driven likelihood. This geometric-probabilistic interpretation calibrates $λ$, making it meaningfully comparable across model sizes and families, with larger models generally exhibiting lower prior reliance in the high-context limit. Finally, we show that the direction of ignorance is causally active: raising or lowering $λ$ at the final prediction state steers the prediction toward or away from the unigram prior in KL divergence.

AI.tldr: A single unembedding-direction encodes the unigram prior; defines a 'direction of ignorance' and a per-token prior loading factor λ that declines with context; projection reveals a tempered Bayesian update (prior^λ × likelihood); across Llama, Qwen, Gemma, Pythia (0.4B–405B) the direction is causal and model-size dependent.
AI.motivation: Explain how language models rely on a unigram prior when context is weak, identify geometric structure in the unembedding and quantify its role in prediction across model families and scales.
AI.method: Analyze the unembedding matrix to extract a single 'direction of ignorance'; project the final prediction state onto this direction to obtain λ; decompose into orthogonal components corresponding to prior^λ and contextual likelihood; test causality by perturbing λ at the final state; validate across four model families and wide parameter counts.
AI.result: The 'direction of ignorance' exists as a unigram-encoding direction in all examined models; the projection yields a prior-loading factor λ that decreases with increasing context; the same projection yields a two-factor tempered Bayesian update; larger models show reduced reliance on the unigram prior in high-context settings; the direction is causally active in steering predictions.
AI.conclusion: This geometric-probabilistic framing provides a unified, size-agnostic account of how priors shape predictions; λ enables cross-model comparability and potential controllability of predictions by adjusting the final-state projection.

title: Seeing Less Is Not Seeing Safely: Privacy Leakage from Task-Scoped Robot Perception Exports
summary: Domestic robots rely on rich perception to operate in private homes, but privacy risk persists even when raw sensor data remain local. Structured representations exported to downstream planners, cloud services, logs, or learning pipelines can still reveal household information through semantics, geometry, spatial structure, and task targets. We introduce Task-Functional Perception Distillation (TFPD), a task-scoped representation-export framework that keeps rich perception local and profiles downstream exports according to task utility, direct exposure, and multiple residual inference risks. Using 120 AI2-THOR scenes with scene-disjoint train/validation/test splits, frozen attacker selection, and representation-aware held-out attacks, we evaluate navigation, collision checking, and object-goal execution. Three navigation exports achieve identical success (1.000) and mean path ratio (0.898), yet representation-level linkability ranges from 0.532 to 0.970. Replacing an explicit target label with a target region reduces target-category macro-F1 from 1.000 to 0.077 while preserving success at 0.995, while geometric coarsening reduces object-category macro-F1 from 0.704 to 0.556 at a measurable collision-utility cost. A ProcTHOR replication preserves the navigation task-equivalence/privacy-inequivalence finding while changing the relative ordering of normalized and topological exports. These results show that neither field removal nor stronger abstraction induces a universal privacy ordering and motivate task-specific, multi-risk evaluation of the complete public representation.

AI.tldr: Task-Functional Perception Distillation (TFPD) keeps rich perception local and evaluates privacy risk of downstream exports across tasks, showing that task performance can be preserved while privacy leakage varies with representation export choices; universality of privacy ordering is not guaranteed, motivating task-specific multi-risk evaluation.
AI.motivation: Privacy risk persists even when raw sensor data stay local due to structured representations exported to planners, cloud services, logs, or learning pipelines. The paper argues for task-scoped representations and evaluation of multiple residual inference risks to understand trade-offs between task utility and privacy.
AI.method: Evaluate TFPD using 120 AI2-THOR scenes with scene-disjoint train/validation/test splits, frozen attacker selection, and representation-aware held-out attacks. Assess navigation, collision checking, and object-goal execution under different representation exports, including explicit target labels vs target regions and geometric coarsening. Demonstrate replication in ProcTHOR and analyze privacy/utility trade-offs across exports.
AI.result: Three navigation exports achieve identical task success (1.000) and mean path ratio (0.898); representation-linkability varies from 0.532 to 0.970. Replacing explicit target labels with a target region collapses target macro-F1 from 1.000 to 0.077 while maintaining success at 0.995; geometric coarsening lowers object-category macro-F1 from 0.704 to 0.556 at a measured collision-utility cost. ProcTHOR replication preserves similar task-privacy patterns but alters export orderings.
AI.conclusion: Field removal or stronger abstraction do not yield a universal privacy ordering across tasks. A task-specific, multi-risk framework is needed to evaluate the complete public representation and its privacy implications.

title: IDSPACE: A Novel Document Generator for Reliable Evaluation of Digital Identity Verification Systems [Extended Technical Report]
summary: As services move online, trust institutions such as banks, lenders, and governments must verify the identity of remote users. Fraud detection tools are widely available, but evaluating and fine-tuning them remains difficult because identity documents are sensitive and therefore scarce. Synthetic data generation offers a path forward, and demand is clear: our prior work in this area has been downloaded over $11{,}000$ times (aggregated from eight parts). We introduce IDSpace, extending this line of research in three directions. First, we propose model-guided Bayesian optimization, which tunes generation parameters to maximize both visual similarity and prediction consistency with target-domain models given only a few samples from a target domain. Second, we decouple user-specified metadata (demographics, fraud patterns, capture device) from automatically tuned control parameters (font styles, noise levels, image quality), allowing users to configure evaluations without low-level expertise. Third, we expand beyond template images to support scanned and mobile-captured documents. Experiments show IDSpace improves evaluation consistency by $15-45\%$ over baselines including CycleGAN, diffusion inpainting, and non-guided optimization, using only a few real samples, while improving training accuracy by up to $9\%$ and SSIM similarity with the target domain by $10\%$. We also released a new dataset consisting of $359{,}240$ high-quality synthetic documents across ten European ID types.

AI.tldr: IDSpace advances synthetic ID document generation with model-guided Bayesian optimization, separating metadata from generation controls, and expanding to scanned/mobile-captured docs; it yields stronger evaluation consistency and training performance with minimal real data, and provides a large synthetic dataset for European ID types.
AI.motivation: A lack of diverse, sensitive real identity documents hampers tuning and evaluating fraud-detection tools. Synthetic data that aligns with target-domain models can enable robust evaluation and training with limited real samples.
AI.method: Introduce model-guided Bayesian optimization to tune generation parameters for visual similarity and model-consistency with target-domain detectors using few real samples. Decouple metadata (demographics, capture conditions) from low-level generation controls (font, noise, image quality). Extend generation to scanned and mobile-captured documents, not just templates.
AI.result: IDSpace shows 15–45% improvements in evaluation consistency over baselines (CycleGAN, diffusion inpainting, non-guided optimization) with minimal real samples; training accuracy gains up to 9%; SSIM similarity to target domain up to 10%. Release includes a dataset of 359,240 high-quality synthetic documents across ten European ID types.
AI.conclusion: IDSpace meaningfully advances synthetic identity data for robust evaluation and training, offering controllable, domain-aligned generation and a sizable dataset to support reproducibility and further research.

title: Structure and Implementation of New Practical English Textbooks Driven by Artificial Intelligence
summary: Artificial intelligence is changing the form of applied English materials from fixed paper sequences to adaptive learning systems that can diagnose learners, recommend tasks, and provide formative feedback. This paper studies the structure and application of a new practical English textbook driven by artificial intelligence. A five-layer architecture is proposed: knowledge mapping, learner profiling, task generation, feedback orchestration, and teacher-side governance. A prototype was tested on 186 non-English-major undergraduates for eight weeks of teaching. Compared with a static digital textbook, the proposed system increased the unit completion accuracy from 72.4% to 84.9%, raised the average score for speaking tasks by 10.8 points, and reduced the teacher's correction time by 31.6%. Therefore, an AI-driven textbook can maintain the stability of the curriculum while providing personalised learning paths, rich practice materials and traceable classroom data.

AI.tldr: AI-driven adaptive English textbook with five-layer architecture improves learning outcomes vs static digital textbook; trial with 186 undergraduates over eight weeks shows higher completion accuracy (72.4%→84.9%), speaking score +10.8 points, teacher correction time −31.6%.
AI.motivation: To overcome fixed sequence constraints of conventional English learning materials and deliver personalized, data-driven instruction.
AI.method: Proposed five-layer architecture: knowledge mapping, learner profiling, task generation, feedback orchestration, and teacher-side governance. Built a prototype and evaluated in an eight-week classroom trial with 186 non-English-major undergraduates; compared to a static digital textbook; measured unit completion accuracy, speaking task scores, and teacher correction time; classroom data governance emphasized.
AI.result: Unit completion accuracy improved from 72.4% to 84.9%; speaking tasks average score increased by 10.8 points; teacher correction time reduced by 31.6%.
AI.conclusion: An AI-driven textbook can preserve curriculum stability while offering personalized learning paths, richer practice materials, and traceable classroom data.

title: Equation Recast for Canonical Operator Learning Across Parametric PDEs
summary: Learning solution operators across broad parameter ranges can require substantial coverage of both input functions and physical parameters, particularly for purely data-driven parametric models. In addition, the resulting models may fail silently outside the training distribution. We introduce equation recast, which reformulates parametric operator learning as the learning of a single canonical operator. Parameter-induced operator variations are derived analytically from the governing equation and absorbed into effective sources, enabling zero-shot prediction across new parameter regimes. Across multi-parameter, nonlinear, and singular PDE settings, equation recast supports extrapolation, integrates sparse heterogeneous datasets in a shared canonical representation, and uses loss of convergence as an internal warning signal for failure of the recast iteration. In high-fidelity tokamak simulations for nuclear fusion, the framework unifies electron-temperature data across four device geometries through canonical-domain mapping within one jointly trained operator. Equation recast provides a route toward reusable neural PDE solvers combining equation-guided transfer, data efficiency, and monitorable inference.

AI.tldr: Introduces equation recast to learn a single canonical operator with parameter effects absorbed into effective sources, enabling zero-shot generalization across parameter regimes and heterogeneous data for PDEs.
AI.motivation: Data-driven parametric operator learning requires wide coverage and risks silent failures outside training; need extrapolation, data efficiency, and error monitoring in neural PDE solvers.
AI.method: Reformulate parametric operator learning as learning a canonical operator; derive parameter-induced operator variations analytically from the governing equation and absorb them into effective sources; train across multi-parameter, nonlinear, and singular PDE settings; use loss of convergence as an internal warning signal; canonical-domain mapping to unify data across device geometries.
AI.result: Supports extrapolation across parameter regimes; integrates sparse heterogeneous datasets into a shared canonical representation; enables zero-shot predictions; provides a monitorable inference pathway via convergence loss; demonstrated in high-fidelity tokamak simulations by unifying electron-temperature data across four device geometries with a single jointly trained operator.
AI.conclusion: Equation recast offers a reusable neural PDE solver framework that combines equation-guided transfer, data efficiency, and monitorable inference, as shown by tokamak data fusion across multiple geometries.

title: GPU-Accelerated Astrodynamics World Models for Spacecraft Rendezvous and Proximity Operations
comment: 20 pages, 12 figures, 5 tables, Presented at Advanced Maui Optical and Space Surveillance Technologies Conference 2026
summary: World models are an emerging paradigm in representation learning in which an agent jointly learns state-action dynamics and observation models from offline trajectory data, enabling multi-step planning and trajectory prediction with uncertainty estimates. They have shown strong results in robotics and game environments, but, to the best of our knowledge, have not previously been applied to the space domain. This paper introduces a world model-based approach to cooperative and non-cooperative spacecraft rendezvous and proximity operations. First, we introduce an open-source, JAX-based International Space Station (ISS) docking environment supporting parallel GPU simulation of spacecraft orbit and attitude dynamics, generating the thousands of state-action transitions that world model training requires. Second, we introduce Out-of-this-World-Model, a transformer-based world model that encodes relative kinematic states and body-fixed camera imagery into a latent state and predicts its evolution under commanded thrusts and torques using one-step flow matching. It produces a distribution over future observations, capturing stochastic dynamics and per-timestep uncertainty, and outperforms DreamerV3-style posterior-correction baselines with fewer trainable parameters and hyperparameters. Third, we apply the approach to a capsule autonomously docking with the ISS under keep-out-zone constraints, demonstrating improved sample efficiency and task performance over reinforcement learning baselines (53% versus 29% docking success across ports), better out-of-distribution generalization (on held-out ports the world model more than doubles baseline success, 40% versus 17%), and detection of anomalous objects encountered during approach with 98% classification accuracy. We open-source the simulation environment and model architecture to enable further study of this paradigm.

AI.tldr: Transformer-based world model for space docking that uses an ISS docking environment and one-step flow matching; demonstrates sample-efficient, uncertainty-aware autonomous docking with strong OOD generalization and anomaly detection; open-sourced.
AI.motivation: Extends world-model (offline RL) paradigm to space domain, addressing sample efficiency, safety, and uncertainty in autonomous rendezvous/docking underKeep-Out constraints where data is costly.
AI.method: Develop an open-source JAX ISS docking environment with GPU-parallelized dynamics; introduce Out-of-this-World-Model (a transformer-based world model) that encodes relative kinematics and camera imagery into a latent state and predicts evolution under thrusts/torques via one-step flow matching; models future observation distributions (uncertainty per timestep); compare to DreamerV3-style baselines; evaluate on autonomous capsule docking tasks with keep-out-zone constraints.
AI.result: Better performance than RL baselines: 53% docking success across ports vs 29%; improved OOD generalization on held-out ports (40% vs 17%); anomaly object detection at 98% accuracy; fewer trainable parameters/hyperparameters; open-source the sim and model.
AI.conclusion: World-model-based planning with uncertainty modeling is effective for space rendezvous tasks, offering improved sample efficiency, generalization, and safety-aware perception; the open-source platform enables broader exploration in space robotics.

title: Position: Unlabeled IS NOT Equal to No Human Supervision in Visual Learning
summary: This position paper argues that the absence of labels does not imply the absence of human supervision in visual learning, and urges the research community to identify sources of supervision more explicitly. Many recent methods in computer vision build upon representations learned from large-scale unlabeled data, and are therefore grouped under the same umbrella term ``unsupervised.'' However, different data curation schemes and training objectives embed substantially different human priors on which models rely, and we argue that one ``unsupervised'' umbrella term is no longer capturing these distinctions. This ambiguity makes it harder to compare unsupervised learning research conducted under different assumptions, coinciding with a sharp decline in papers titled with ``unsupervised'' in flagship computer vision conferences since 2021, despite continued growth of the field. While we fully embrace pre-training as a strong foundation for modern computer vision, we advocate for a community-level effort toward greater conceptual clarity: authors are encouraged to disclose priors in data selection and learning objectives, and to specify which components of a learning pipeline depend on which assumptions. Standardized disclosure practices can improve academic communication, ensure fairer comparisons, and preserve methodological diversity in unsupervised learning.

AI.tldr: Callout for clarifying supervision priors in unsupervised visual learning and standardizing disclosure to improve comparison and preserve diversity.
AI.motivation: Ambiguity in the term 'unsupervised' due to diverse data curation and objectives; reduced clarity in comparisons; decline in papers with 'unsupervised' title despite field growth.
AI.method: Position paper proposing a taxonomy of supervision sources and standardized disclosure practices; advise authors to specify priors on data selection and learning objectives and indicate which pipeline components depend on those assumptions.
AI.result: Expected benefits: clearer communication, fairer comparisons across methods, retention of methodological diversity in unsupervised learning; no empirical results presented.
AI.conclusion: Agree that pre-training is valuable, but call for community-wide transparency about supervision priors to enable meaningful evaluation and comparison.

title: MasterControl Seventeen Every Time
summary: We study a governed approach to enterprise analytics: a language model interprets the question, while deterministic policy selects and runs a pre-approved analytical program that returns both results and evidence. We show that this restriction can remain expressive within a defined analytical class, using relational operations plus aggregation, comparison, windows, ranking, and similarity. Fixed meaning, policy, data, and execution rules also make results replayable. Across 440 runs, three 8B models generated SQL and selected tools at runtime, while Qwen3-8B interpreted intent only and policy executed the approved program. None of 330 runtime-planning episodes matched the full answer-and-evidence contract across all test datasets; the policy-executed analyzer matched 110 of 110. This is a configuration-specific result, not evidence that runtime agents cannot succeed under other designs.

AI.tldr: A governed enterprise-analytics approach uses a language model to interpret questions while a deterministic policy selects and runs a pre-approved analytic program that returns results with evidence, enabling replayable results. In tests, 3 eight-billion-parameter models generated SQL and chose tools at runtime, whereas a policy-executed, approved-program analyzer matched all test datasets, though many runtime-planning attempts failed; findings are configuration-specific, not a general negation of runtime agents.
AI.motivation: To improve reliability, auditability, and evidence in enterprise analytics by constraining LLM outputs to a fixed analytic program library while preserving expressivity within a defined analytic class.
AI.method: Define a governance setup: LLM handles intent; a deterministic policy selects from pre-approved analytic programs that operate on relational ops, aggregation, windows, ranking, and similarity. Fixed meaning, policy, data, and execution rules enable replayability. Evaluate across 440 runs with 3 8B models (SQL generation and runtime tool selection) versus Qwen3-8B (intent only; policy runs approved program).
AI.result: Policy-executed analyzer achieved perfect coverage (110/110 datasets). In contrast, 330 runtime-planning episodes failed to meet the full answer-and-evidence contract across test datasets. The 3 8B models could generate SQL and select tools at runtime, indicating more variability and brittleness.
AI.conclusion: The observed success is configuration-specific; the governance approach can yield reliable results under certain designs, but broader generalization requires more diverse evaluation and potential expansion of the approved program library and policy capabilities.

title: From Euclidean to Graph-Structured Data: A Survey of Collaborative Learning
comment: 96 pages. Published in Transactions on Machine Learning Research (TMLR), March 2026, with Survey Certification
summary: The conventional approach to machine learning, that is, collecting data, training models, and performing inference in a single location, faces fundamental limitations, including scalability and privacy, that restrict its applicability. To address these challenges, recent research has explored collaborative learning approaches, including federated learning and decentralized learning, where individual agents perform training and inference locally, with limited collaboration. Most collaborative learning research focuses on Euclidean data with regular, grid-like structure (e.g., images, text). However, these approaches fail to capture the relational patterns in many real-world applications, best represented by graphs. Learning on graphs relies on message-passing mechanisms to propagate information between connected nodes, making it conceptually well-suited for collaborative environments where agents must exchange information. Yet, the opportunities and challenges of learning on graph-structured data in collaborative settings remain largely underexplored. This survey provides a comprehensive investigation of collaborative learning from Euclidean to graph-structured data, aiming to consolidate this emerging field. We begin by reviewing its foundational principles for Euclidean data, organizing them along three core dimensions: learning effectiveness, efficiency, and privacy preservation. We then extend the discussion to graph-structured data, introducing a taxonomy of graph distribution scenarios, characterizing associated statistical heterogeneities, and developing standardized problem formulations and algorithmic frameworks. Finally, we systematically identify open challenges and promising research directions.

AI.tldr: A survey of collaborative learning from Euclidean to graph data, addressing scalability and privacy limits of centralized ML, and outlining a taxonomy, formulations, and frameworks for graph-based distributed learning, plus open challenges and directions.
AI.motivation: Motivate the transition from centralized to collaborative learning to address scalability and privacy, and extend these concepts to graph-structured data where relational patterns and message-passing are essential.
AI.method: Comprehensive literature review and synthesis across Euclidean data and graph-structured data, organized along learning effectiveness, efficiency, and privacy dimensions; introduce a taxonomy of graph distribution scenarios; propose standardized problem formulations and algorithmic frameworks; identify open challenges and directions.
AI.result: A consolidated map of the field including a taxonomy of graph distribution scenarios, standardized problem formulations and algorithmic frameworks for graph-based collaborative learning, and a set of open challenges and promising research directions.
AI.conclusion: Collaborative learning on graphs is a growing, underexplored area with significant potential; effective handling of heterogeneity, privacy, and communication efficiency, as well as practical frameworks and problem formulations, are essential to advance the field.

title: Sensing Which Modality Matters: Evidence-Gated Regularization for Robust VLA Policies
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies fuse multimodal sensory inputs, but training on limited and homogeneous robot demonstrations encourages spurious inter-sensor correlations rather than task-relevant signal, a failure we term modality entanglement. Under real-world occlusions and distractors, this manifests as nuisance sensitivity to corruption of uninformative sensors and single-modality insufficiency when only one informative sensor remains intact. We propose Evidence-Gated Regularization (EGR), a modality-agnostic training objective that introduces zero inference-time overhead. EGR derives a per-frame and per-sensor task-relevance signal to gate two state-conditional consistency objectives: invariance on low-evidence sensors, and single-sensor sufficiency on high-evidence ones. We introduce a benchmark based on BEHAVIOR-1K, comprising a fast inference-only diagnostic suite and 47 rollout-based skills targeting modality entanglement. We validate EGR on this benchmark and on two real-robot setups with fundamentally different embodiments: a bi-manual setup with two Kinova arms and three RGB cameras, and a single-arm MELFA ASSISTA setup combining vision and GelSight tactile sensors. EGR improves simulation success rates (SR) from 12.5% to 16.4% under full modalities (+31%), from 9.4% to 16.5% under uninformative-sensor corruption (+75%), and from 2.8% to 6.1% under single-sensor fallback (+120%). Under physical-object distractors, EGR boosts SR from 30% to 85% on the bi-manual setup (+183%) and from 55% to 70% on the tactile setup (+27%).

AI.tldr: EGR (Evidence-Gated Regularization) mitigates modality entanglement in Vision-Language-Action policies by gating per-frame, per-sensor relevance signals to enforce invariance on low-evidence sensors and sufficiency on high-evidence ones, with no inference-time overhead. Validated on BEHAVIOR-1K and two real-robot setups, showing robust SR improvements under full, corrupted, and single-sensor conditions.
AI.motivation: Training VLA policies from limited, homogeneous robot demonstrations leads to modality entanglement where spurious inter-sensor correlations overshadow task-relevant signals, causing fragility under occlusions, distractors, and sensor loss.
AI.method: Introduce per-frame per-sensor task-relevance signals to gate two state-conditional consistency objectives: invariance on low-evidence sensors and single-sensor sufficiency on high-evidence sensors. The objective is modality-agnostic and requires zero extra inference-time overhead.
AI.result: BEHAVIOR-1K benchmark with 47 rollout-based skills; EGR improves simulation SR from 12.5% to 16.4% with full modalities; 9.4% to 16.5% under uninformative-sensor corruption; 2.8% to 6.1% under single-sensor fallback. Under physical-object distractors, SR rises from 30% to 85% on a bi-manual Kinova setup and from 55% to 70% on a tactile GelSight-enabled MELFA setup.
AI.conclusion: EGR effectively reduces modality entanglement across diverse embodiments by adaptively regularizing training based on sensor evidence, yielding robust performance against sensor corruption and distractors while maintaining zero inference-time overhead.

title: Exemplar: Classical Priors Complement Frozen Features for Few-Shot Microscopy Segmentation at Native Resolution
comment: 5 pages, 3 figures, 2 tables. Code, configurations, and the per-image score records behind every reported number: https://github.com/michalprusek/Exemplar
summary: Segmenting a new biomedical dataset usually means a domain-specific model trained on substantial annotation, or a foundation model steered at inference time. We present Exemplar, a few-shot segmenter that fuses a frozen DINOv3 backbone with a fixed bank of classical native-resolution filter responses in one lightweight head, fitted from the support masks alone. In the few-mask, native-resolution regime, classical priors and frozen self-supervised features are complementary: fused in one head, a single fixed configuration spans eleven biomedical imaging datasets. Under the same head, the classical bank alone reaches 0.693 on the eleven-dataset panel, scored by foreground intersection-over-union or centreline Dice, and the frozen features alone 0.672; the bank leads on seven of the eleven and the features on the rest, and fused they reach 0.782. Against five forward-pass few-shot methods, Exemplar leads in 54 of 55 method-dataset comparisons, 52 of them significant after Holm correction. From a single annotated mask it reaches 0.703 on the same panel, against 0.682 for a from-scratch nnU-Net trained on that same mask. At eight masks nnU-Net overtakes it on the panel mean, chiefly on centreline agreement, but takes 16-77x longer to fit.

AI.tldr: Exemplar achieves strong few-shot biomedical segmentation by fusing a frozen DINOv3 backbone with a fixed bank of classical native-resolution filter responses in a single lightweight head, trained from support masks.
AI.motivation: Reduce annotation burden and enable cross-dataset generalization in biomedical segmentation by leveraging frozen self-supervised features and simple priors within a compact head, avoiding extensive retraining.
AI.method: Use a frozen DINOv3 backbone plus a fixed bank of classical native-resolution filter responses, combined in one lightweight head that is fitted from support masks alone; operates in the few-mask, native-resolution regime across eleven datasets.
AI.result: On eleven datasets, bank alone 0.693, features alone 0.672, fused 0.782 (foreground IoU/centreline Dice). Exemplar leads 54/55 method-dataset comparisons (52 significant after Holm correction). With one annotated mask, 0.703 vs 0.682 for from-scratch nnU-Net; with eight masks nnU-Net overtakes in mean but is 16–77x slower.
AI.conclusion: A fixed-head fusion of deterministic priors and frozen self-supervised features yields robust, data-efficient segmentation across diverse biomedical datasets, outperforming most few-shot baselines and offering a speed advantage over nnU-Net in low-shot settings.

title: Speculative Macro Commit for Faster Tool-Using Agents
summary: Tool-using LLM agents spend wall-clock time not only on model inference but also in serial action--observation turns, where each tool call, environment transition, and observation can delay subsequent decisions. We introduce \textbf{Speculative Macro Commit} (SMC), a runtime mechanism for a two-tier agent system: a large authoritative actor model produces the official trajectory, while a faster speculative drafter model continuously predicts and executes future action chains on an isolated environment snapshot. SMC mines recurring multi-action skeletons from training traces and stores them in a macro library used to match against action chains predicted by the drafter at runtime. When the actor's next tool call matches the first drafted action, SMC commits the remaining pre-executed draft steps, together with their observations, to the official trajectory. Using Qwen3.5-27B INT4 as the authoritative actor model and Qwen3.5-4B as the speculative drafter model, SMC matches the sequential agent's overall accuracy while reducing latency by 10.23\% over the Speculative Actions (SA) baseline and 18.59\% over sequential execution on the $τ^2$-Bench Telecom subset. On AppWorld, SMC reduces wall time by 7.7\% over SA baseline and 44.9\% over sequential execution, with a small reduction in task completion. Overall, SMC provides a practical way to reuse multi-step speculative execution and reduce agent latency beyond single-step speculative actions. Our code is publicly available \href{https://github.com/zeyuliu1037/speculative-macro-commit}{\textcolor{magenta}{here}}.

AI.tldr: Speculative Macro Commit (SMC) couples a fast speculative drafter with a slow authoritative actor to pre-execute multi-step action chains using a macro library, and commits when predictions align, reducing wall-clock latency in tool-using LLM agents.
AI.motivation: Reduce wall-clock latency from serial tool-use by overlapping execution with prediction, enabling reuse of multi-step plans learned from training traces.
AI.method: Two-tier agent: a slow authoritative actor model defines the official trajectory, and a fast speculative drafter pre-executes future action chains on an isolated environment snapshot. A macro library of recurring multi-action skeletons is mined from training traces and used to match predicted action chains at runtime. When the actor’s next tool call matches the first drafted action, the remaining drafted steps are committed to the official trajectory, along with their observations. Evaluation uses Qwen3.5-27B INT4 as actor and Qwen3.5-4B as drafter; benchmarks include τ^2-Bench Telecom subset and AppWorld.
AI.result: SMC achieves similar overall accuracy to a sequential agent while reducing wall-clock latency compared with Speculative Actions (SA) and sequential execution. On τ^2-Bench Telecom: ~10.23% latency reduction vs SA and ~18.59% vs sequential. On AppWorld: ~7.7% latency reduction vs SA and ~44.9% vs sequential, with a small reduction in task completion.
AI.conclusion: SMC offers a practical method to reuse multi-step speculative execution to lower agent latency beyond single-step speculation, with modest trade-offs in completion rate; code is publicly available.

title: Modern Transformers Are Implicit Hybrids: From Functional Differentiation to Principled Hybrid Architecture Design
summary: Hybrid architectures combining Full Attention (FA) and Linear Attention (LA) are increasingly prominent, yet their allocation remains heuristic. We seek an evidence-grounded basis in head-level functional organization learned by RoPE-based Transformers. Behavioral probes do not yield a complete taxonomy, so we propose two intervention metrics: RoPE Frequency Importance Score (RFIS), measuring how each frequency affects a head's attention distribution, and RoPE Positional Dependence (RPD), isolating dependence on rotary positional modulation. On Qwen3-series models and Llama3.1, RFIS suggests and RPD verifies a complete taxonomy of retrieval and positional heads separated by a salient mid-low-frequency band. Controlled Transformers show that this boundary follows the training-length positional scale; we term it the Global Positional Band (GPBand). The analysis suggests a potential cause of zero-shot length-extrapolation failure and yields two principles: positional modeling should operate only locally, with global access through position-independent retrieval; and both functions should be assigned at head granularity with layer-specific allocation. We instantiate them in Head-wise Hybrid Architecture (HwH), using NoPE FA for global retrieval and LA for local positional modeling. With an FA-to-LA ratio below 1:3, HwH retains strong language modeling and commonsense reasoning while improving retrieval and substantially strengthening zero-shot long-context extrapolation over Transformer, LA, and a layer-wise hybrid baseline. Ablations validate both principles and component roles, highlighting principled hybrid architecture design as a promising route toward future foundation models.

AI.tldr: Introduces RFIS and RPD to map RoPE-based Transformer head functionality; identifies a Global Positional Band separating retrieval vs positional heads; proposes Head-wise Hybrid Architecture HwH (NoPE FA for global retrieval, LA for local positional modeling) achieving improved long-context extrapolation with preserved language and reasoning.
AI.motivation: Address the lack of an evidence-grounded basis for allocating Full Attention (FA) and Linear Attention (LA) across heads in RoPE-based transformers; derive a taxonomy of head functions and guidelines to improve zero-shot long-context extrapolation.
AI.method: Define and compute RoPE Frequency Importance Score (RFIS) and RoPE Positional Dependence (RPD) on Qwen3-series and Llama3.1; identify a mid-low-frequency band as a separation between retrieval and positional heads (Global Positional Band, GPBand); validate the boundary's relation to training-length positional scale; implement Head-wise Hybrid Architecture (HwH) with NoPE FA for global retrieval and LA for local positional modeling; compare against Transformer, LA, and layer-wise baselines; perform ablations.
AI.result: Revealed a complete taxonomy of retrieval vs. positional head functions separated by a salient mid-low-frequency band; GPBand boundary aligns with training-length positional scale; HwH with FA:LA ratio below 1:3 preserves language/commonsense performance while enhancing retrieval and substantially improving zero-shot long-context extrapolation; ablations support the two guiding principles and component roles.
AI.conclusion: Principled head-wise hybrid design is a promising direction for foundation models. Key principles: (1) positional modeling should be local with global access via position-independent retrieval; (2) allocate retrieval and positional roles at head level with layer-specific distribution; HwH demonstrates the viability and benefits over existing architectures.

title: Real-Time Shape Control of Multi-Segment Soft Robotic Arms Using Koopman Operators with Global and Local Observables
summary: Multi-segment soft robotic arms can continuously reconfigure their body shapes for safe interaction, but tip control alone is insufficient for constrained-space tasks. Therefore, shape control is a more important task for multi-segment soft arms than tip control, but remains challenging due to the high dimensionality and nonlinear dynamics of continuum deformation. In existing work, shape control accuracy is defined by the error in the global frame (global shape error). For multi-segment soft arms, using only global shape error as the control objective is insufficient, as segment coupling, gravity-induced loading, and inertial effects become more significant. This difficulty increases with the number of segments. In this paper, we present a Koopman-based model predictive control framework that combines global and local observables, enabling real-time shape control on multi-segment soft robotic arms. The framework is evaluated through numerical and physical experiments. Numerical experiments demonstrate the scalability of the proposed controller by achieving shape control on robots with up to 10 independently actuated segments. The physical experiments demonstrate that the controller is capable of (1) real-time shape control of 3- and 5-segment robotic arms with tip speeds up to 0.6 m/s, (2) robust tracking without retraining, including distal payloads up to 400~g and recovery from a 7~N lateral disturbance, and (3) the potential for future inspection applications through a confined-space demonstration. These results demonstrate that the proposed framework enables dynamic, scalable, and accurate real-time shape control on multi-segment soft robotic arms.

AI.tldr: Koopman-based MPC combining global and local observables enables real-time, scalable shape control for multi-segment soft arms, validated numerically up to 10 segments and physically for 3- and 5-segment arms with robust performance.
AI.motivation: Shape control is essential for multi-segment soft robots due to high dimensionality and nonlinear dynamics; global shape error alone ignores segment coupling, gravity, and inertia, especially as the number of segments grows.
AI.method: A Koopman-based model predictive control framework that integrates global and local observables to achieve real-time shape control; validated through numerical simulations and physical experiments, showing scalability to 10 segments and robust performance under payloads and disturbances.
AI.result: Numerical experiments show scalability to 10 independently actuated segments. Physical experiments demonstrate real-time shape control for 3- and 5-segment arms (tip speeds up to 0.6 m/s), robust tracking without retraining (payloads up to 400 g; recovery from 7 N lateral disturbance), and potential confined-space inspection demonstrations.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework enables dynamic, scalable, and accurate real-time shape control on multi-segment soft robotic arms, advancing capability beyond tip-control and addressing high-dimensional continuum dynamics.

title: Solving the Needle-in-a-Haystack Problem in Mammography Vision-Language Model with Differentiable Subset Sampling
summary: There is growing interest in adopting CLIP-style vision--language model (VLM) pretraining for mammography. However, models that directly employ the standard CLIP architecture and training objective exhibit limited zero-shot performance in clinically important tasks such as cancer, finding-type, and BI-RADS predictions. We argue that this underwhelming performance is due to neglecting two characteristics of mammography data: (1) its high-res nature, and (2) homogeneity of radiology reports, largely driven by a predominance of negative/benign findings on examinations. We propose TopKSigLIP, a VLM designed to address these two limitations through a novel architecture and learning objectives. Instead of downscaling high-res mammography images to satisfy GPU memory constraints, TopKSigLIP introduces TopK-Patch module that learns to sample a sparse set of high-res patches likely to contain lesions, sidestepping the resolution--batch size tradeoff of VLM training. The sampled patch locations additionally serve as a built-in localization tool. To address report homogeneity, we replace the contrastive loss, which falsely repels semantically similar pairs, with a Sup-sigmoid loss. Sup-sigmoid loss extends the sigmoid loss from SigLIP with soft labels derived from structured data. TopKSigLIP outperforms existing open-source mammography and general medical VLMs on both internal and external benchmarks on density assessment, BI-RADS classification, finding subtyping, and cancer prediction under zero-shot evaluation. TopKSigLIP remains competitive under linear probing despite using a significantly smaller vision encoder and smaller training batches than baselines. The TopK-Patch module additionally achieves superior lesion localization over post-hoc Grad-CAM. Code and weights are made public:https://github.com/Youngseok0001/TopKSigLIP.

AI.tldr: TopKSigLIP is a CLIP-like vision–language model for mammography that uses a TopK-Patch module to sample high-resolution patches and a Sup-sigmoid loss to handle homogeneous radiology reports, achieving strong zero-shot performance and localization with a smaller vision encoder and training budget.
AI.motivation: To overcome two key data characteristics in mammography—its high spatial resolution and the predominance of negative/benign findings leading to homogeneous reports—that limit standard CLIP-style VLMs.
AI.method: Introduce TopK-Patch: a sampler that selects a sparse set of high-resolution patches likely to contain lesions, enabling high-res learning without downscaling. The patch locations serve as an internal localization signal. Replace contrastive loss with Sup-sigmoid loss, deriving soft labels from structured data to handle semantic similarity in radiology reports.
AI.result: TopKSigLIP outperforms existing open-source mammography and general medical VLMs on internal and external benchmarks for density assessment, BI-RADS classification, finding subtyping, and cancer prediction in zero-shot evaluation; remains competitive under linear probing with smaller vision encoder and smaller training batches; TopK-Patch also yields superior lesion localization versus post-hoc Grad-CAM.
AI.conclusion: Architectural and loss-function adaptations tailored to mammography data enable stronger zero-shot performance and localization in VLMs, with public code and weights supporting replication and further research.

title: Fresh Memory, Stale Plans: Dependency-Scoped Validation for Distributed LLM-Agent Memory
summary: Distributed LLM-agent teams can read the latest shared facts and still act on an obsolete plan. A planner may derive an action from requirement $r_3$, another agent may commit $r_4$, and an executor may receive $r_4$ without replacing the plan derived from $r_3$. We call this \emph{stale-plan execution}: state freshness does not establish that the plan authorizing an action remains valid. We introduce PlanFence, a dependency-scoped action-validation protocol. Plans cite the exact public records they used, and an executor validates only the records that can affect the pending external action, replanning once or blocking when validation is incomplete. In 30 controlled live workflows with a post-plan revision, a freshness-only executor acts on the obsolete plan in every task, whereas PlanFence completes all tasks without an invalid action. Controlled replay reveals two conditional boundaries: proactive synchronization yields lower coordination stall at low churn, while PlanFence avoids repeated update-path coordination as churn grows and avoids validating unrelated state as the shared keyspace grows. These are controlled safety and systems-cost results, not general task-accuracy gains.

AI.tldr: PlanFence is a dependency-scoped action-validation protocol that prevents stale-plan execution in distributed LLM-agent teams by tying plan actions to exact public records and validating only those records that affect pending actions; it reduces stale actions compared to freshness-only approaches, especially as system churn grows.
AI.motivation: Distributed LLM-agent teams risk executing actions based on obsolete plans after public records have changed. A plan author may derive an action from one requirement while another agent updates the same state, leading to stale execution. PlanFence aims to ensure actions are still valid given shared state.
AI.method: Plans cite the exact public records used for pending actions. Executives validate only the records that can affect the pending external action, and replan or block if validation is incomplete. The approach is evaluated in 30 controlled live workflows with post-plan revisions and replay experiments to compare against a freshness-only executor, examining coordination cost under churn.
AI.result: PlanFence completes all tasks without invalid actions, while a freshness-only executor acts on obsolete plans in all tasks under test. Controlled replay reveals that proactive synchronization reduces coordination stalls at low churn, whereas PlanFence reduces update-path coordination needs as churn grows and avoids validating unrelated state as the shared keyspace expands.
AI.conclusion: The results show PlanFence provides safety guarantees against stale actions with potentially lower system coordination costs in high-churn environments, though the study emphasizes safety and systems-cost rather than general task accuracy.

title: Tail-Likelihood Reinforcement Learning
summary: Reinforcement learning typically optimizes average reward. For generative policies, the average can hide an important distinction: two policies can achieve the same mean reward while having very different chances of producing a rare but high-reward rollout. This matters as sampling increases during training and inference, since its benefit depends on retaining probability mass on high-reward outcomes. We propose to optimize this coverage directly. Rather than considering only expected reward, we consider all of its upper tails: for each reward threshold, how likely is the policy to exceed it? This turns a continuous reward into a family of binary success events. We introduce Tail-Likelihood Reinforcement Learning (TailRL), which maximizes the log-probability of exceeding a randomly chosen reward threshold. Its gradient gives more weight to rare, high-reward rollouts and can be interpreted as a mixture of Best-of-(k) gradients. TailRL requires only a simple modification to the advantage function, making it compatible with existing reinforcement learning pipelines. Across object localization, maze navigation, GUI grounding, and code optimization, TailRL leverages rare high-reward training samples to avoid suboptimal solutions and yields models that benefit more from additional samples at inference time.

AI.tldr: TailRL optimizes the upper tail of the reward distribution by maximizing the log-probability of exceeding a random threshold, turning the reward into multiple binary events and emphasizing rare high-reward outcomes.
AI.motivation: The mean reward can mask important risk-sensitive differences; rare high-reward rollouts become more valuable as sampling increases during training and inference, so preserving probability mass on high-reward outcomes is desirable.
AI.method: Replace the single objective with a tail-based objective: maximize the log-probability that the return exceeds a randomly chosen threshold. This yields a gradient that emphasizes rare, high-reward rollouts and can be interpreted as a mixture of Best-of-(k) gradients. The change requires only a simple modification to the advantage function, making it compatible with existing RL pipelines.
AI.result: Empirically validated across object localization, maze navigation, GUI grounding, and code optimization. TailRL leverages rare high-reward samples to avoid suboptimal solutions, and models benefit more from additional samples at inference time.
AI.conclusion: TailRL provides a practical tail-risk–aware reinforcement learning objective that can be integrated into standard pipelines and improves performance by exploiting rare high-reward rollouts.

title: Following a Unique Path: A Fast Certifier Applied to Outlier-Robust Pose Registration
summary: Certifiable methods have arisen as a means to guarantee global optimality of solutions to non-convex problems using convex semidefinite programming (SDP) relaxations. The most performant of these methods use a local solver to obtain the candidate solution, and then certify its optimality using efficient linear algebra techniques. However, for many problems of interest in robotics, this local-solve-then-certify approach is impeded by a form of degeneracy in the relaxation, leaving a costly optimization of the relaxation as the only recourse. In this paper, we introduce our Central-Path Certifier (CP-Cert), a certifiable method explicitly tailored to certify candidate optima to problems that exhibit this form of degeneracy. Using a candidate as a starting point, our approach seeks a nearby region of the feasible space -- known as the central path -- where a valid certificate can be readily obtained. The approach is kept efficient by exploiting indirect linear algebra techniques, problem sparsity, and parallelism. We apply CP-Cert to both matrix-weighted pose registration and pointcloud data association, whose novel SDP relaxation is of independent interest. On simulated examples, we explore the properties of this novel relaxation and show that CP-Cert is fast and scalable, achieving runtimes that are up to three orders of magnitude faster than state-of-the-art direct solvers. Finally, we combine these contributions into a certifiable, outlier-robust pose-estimation pipeline, which we apply to real-world data.

AI.tldr: CP-Cert introduces a central-path certifier for degenerate SDP relaxations in robotics, delivering fast, certifiable solutions and enabling robust pose estimation pipelines.
AI.motivation: certify global optimality for non-convex problems via SDP relaxations, but degeneracy hinders efficient certification; a fast certifier is needed for robotics applications with matrix-weighted pose registration and pointcloud data association.
AI.method: Propose Central-Path Certifier (CP-Cert) that starts from a candidate solution and searches a central path region where a certificate can be found; exploits indirect linear algebra, sparsity, and parallelism; applies to a novel SDP relaxation for matrix-weighted pose registration and pointcloud data association.
AI.result: On simulated data, the CP-Cert framework yields a fast, scalable certifier; runtimes are up to 1,000x faster than state-of-the-art direct solvers; the authors validate a new SDP relaxation and demonstrate a certifiable, outlier-robust pose-estimation pipeline on real-world data.
AI.conclusion: CP-Cert provides an efficient, scalable certifiable approach for degenerate SDP relaxations in robotics, enabling robust, certifiable pose estimation suitable for real-world deployment.

title: WireSeg-32K: A Physics-Grounded Synthetic Dataset for Wire Instance Segmentation
comment: Synthetic Data for Computer Vision @ CVPR 2026 Workshop
summary: Deformable linear objects such as wires and cables are difficult to segment because they are thin, highly deformable, and frequently self-occluded, while large-scale instance-level annotations are expensive to obtain in real scenes. Existing resources either focus on cable tracing or semantic segmentation under constrained settings, or generate visually plausible images without physically grounded wire deformation. We present WireSeg-32k, a synthetic dataset for wire instance segmentation with 32,000 RGB images, instance masks, depth maps, and a complementary real-world test set with annotations. To generate this dataset, we develop DeformX, a co-simulation pipeline that couples Cosserat-rod dynamics with photorealistic Isaac Sim rendering, enabling physically plausible, contact-consistent wire shapes, CAD-based wire assets, and diverse visually grounded scenes. As a simple baseline, LoRA fine-tuning SAM3 on WireSeg-32k alone improves real-world mAP@75 by 10.2% over the off-the-shelf model, showing that physically grounded synthetic data can transfer to real wire perception.

AI.tldr: A synthetic dataset WireSeg-32k for wire instance segmentation using a co-simulation DeformX combining Cosserat-rod dynamics with photorealistic rendering; dataset includes 32k synthetic RGB images with masks, depth, and a real-world test set; baseline using LoRA-tuned SAM3 shows real-world improvement.
AI.motivation: Tackle challenging segmentation of deformable, thin, self-occluding wires and limited annotated data by creating a large, physically grounded synthetic dataset with a real-world test subset.
AI.method: DeformX co-simulation pipeline that couples Cosserat-rod dynamics with Isaac Sim rendering, ensuring physically plausible, contact-consistent wire shapes, CAD-based wire assets, and diverse scenes; dataset generation plus a real-world test set; baseline via LoRA fine-tuning SAM3 on WireSeg-32k.
AI.result: 32k synthetic data with instance masks and depth; complementary real-world annotated test set; LoRA fine-tuned SAM3 on WireSeg-32k yields +10.2 percentage points mAP@75 over an off-the-shelf model.
AI.conclusion: Physically grounded synthetic data can transfer to real wire perception; the dataset and pipeline enable improved wire instance segmentation in real scenes.

title: A Prompt-Engineering Approach to Develop Scalable, Flexible, and Real-Time Hybrid Micro-Level Personalization in a General Purpose AI Teaching Assistant
summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) teaching assistants powered by large language models (LLMs) offer scalable educational support but often provide limited personalization. This study presents a prompt-engineering-based framework for personalizing general-purpose LLM/RAG-based AI teaching assistants such as Jill Watson across academic disciplines and courses. The framework adapts responses using six learner-specific dimensions: self-assessment, abstraction preference, verbosity preference, perceptual orientation, information processing style, and level of understanding, yielding 96 distinct learner profiles. Student queries are additionally analyzed using Bloom's Taxonomy to estimate cognitive complexity at the interaction level. Learner attributes and cognitive assessments are encoded in structured prompts that condition the LLM without requiring model retraining. The framework is evaluated through experiments using NLP metrics and a human study with five participants. Results show perceived differences in response style and structure across personalization conditions, with statistical analyses identifying learner attributes associated with measurable response changes. These findings provide preliminary evidence that prompt-based personalization can support adaptive behavior in LLM-powered educational agents.

AI.tldr: A prompt-based personalization framework for LLM-based teaching assistants uses six learner dimensions and Bloom's taxonomy to adapt responses without retraining; evaluated with NLP metrics and a small human study, showing evidence of adaptive behavior but preliminary.
AI.motivation: Overcoming limited personalization and scalability in LLM teaching assistants by enabling fine-grained, prompt-driven customization across disciplines.
AI.method: Define six learner dimensions (self-assessment, abstraction preference, verbosity preference, perceptual orientation, information processing style, level of understanding) yielding 96 profiles; analyze queries with Bloom's taxonomy to estimate cognitive complexity; encode attributes in structured prompts; apply to general-purpose LLM/RAG TAs; evaluate via NLP metrics and a five-participant human study.
AI.result: Participants perceived differences in response style and structure across personalization conditions; statistical analyses associate certain learner attributes with measurable changes in responses; provides preliminary evidence that prompt-based personalization can support adaptive behavior.
AI.conclusion: Prompt-based personalization is a viable route to adaptive LLM-powered educational agents; results are preliminary and need broader validation across disciplines and larger samples; future work should address learning outcomes and robustness.

title: Mesh-Native Physics-Informed Graph Surrogates for TCAD-in-the-Loop Design Space Exploration
comment: 9 pages, 4 figures, 2 tables. Accepted at IEEE/ACM International Conference on Computer-Aided Design (ICCAD 2026)
summary: High-fidelity TCAD simulation of drift-diffusion transport remains the workhorse of emerging FinFET device design, but it is computationally expensive, especially for 3D structures where runtime escalates steeply with mesh complexity. This sharply limits multi-objective design space exploration. Existing machine-learning surrogates map a fixed set of design parameters to a few scalar device metrics, discarding the underlying physics and losing transferability across device geometries and families. A physics-informed graph attention network (GAT) surrogate is proposed. It operates directly on the tetrahedral TCAD mesh and predicts, at every mesh node, the electrostatic potential together with the electron and hole quasi-Fermi levels, the fundamental unknowns of the drift-diffusion system. Training combines a data loss with finite-volume current-continuity residuals, embedding carrier-transport physics into the objective. Operating on the mesh as a graph, the surrogate inherits size generalization: a model trained on few-fin meshes applies unchanged to substantially larger arrays, bounded at inference only by GPU memory. Per-node uncertainty from a deep ensemble drives an active-learning loop that screens large candidate pools in seconds and forwards only the most informative designs for full simulation. Benchmarked against Sentaurus Device on multi-fin tri-gate FinFETs, the surrogate reproduces the three drift-diffusion fields with sub-volt per-field RMSE and reaches a per-design throughput orders of magnitude higher than the full simulator. The advantage grows with device size: on large multi-fin arrays that are prohibitively slow to simulate directly, inference still completes in under a second per device, enabling Pareto-front exploration across device scales infeasible for direct TCAD sweeps.

AI.tldr: A physics-informed graph-attention surrogate for 3D TCAD drift-diffusion in FinFETs that operates on tetrahedral meshes, enabling size-generalizable predictions of potential and quasi-Fermi levels with large speedups and active-learning driven design exploration.
AI.motivation: High-fidelity TCAD 3D simulations are computationally expensive, especially for 3D FinFET geometries; existing ML surrogates often hard-code a fixed design parameter set and lack physics transferability across device geometries and families.
AI.method: A physics-informed graph attention network (GAT) that runs on the unstructured tetrahedral mesh. It outputs node-wise electrostatic potential and electron/hole quasi-Fermi levels. Training combines data loss with finite-volume current-continuity residuals to embed drift-diffusion physics. The mesh is treated as a graph to enable size generalization. A deep ensemble provides per-node uncertainty used for an active-learning loop to select informative designs. Benchmarking is against Sentaurus Device on multi-fin tri-gate FinFETs.
AI.result: The surrogate reproduces the three drift-diffusion fields with sub-volt per-field RMSE. It achieves orders-of-magnitude higher per-design throughput than the full TCAD simulator. For large multi-fin arrays that are slow to simulate directly, inference completes in under a second per device, enabling Pareto-front exploration across device scales that are infeasible with direct TCAD sweeps.
AI.conclusion: A physics-informed, graph-based surrogate yields transferable, scalable, and efficient 3D TCAD-like predictions, enabling rapid, large-scale design-space exploration across FinFET geometries.

title: Long-Horizon Consistent and Interaction-Aware World Models for Multi-Style End-to-End Driving
summary: End-to-end autonomous driving has increasingly adopted world model-based reinforcement learning frameworks to improve learning efficiency through \textit{imagined rollouts}. However, existing world models suffer from three key limitations: temporal inconsistency in long-horizon imagined rollouts, inadequate modeling of ego-environment interactions, and limited adaptability to diverse driving styles. To address these challenges, we propose \textit{StyleDrive}, a world-model-based learning framework that jointly enforces long-horizon consistency, explicitly disentangles interactive traffic states, and supports multi-style policy optimization within a unified learning paradigm. First, we introduce a temporal consistency regularization that integrates historical latent states through gated cross-attention, stabilizing long-horizon imagined rollouts and mitigating error accumulation. Second, we design an explicit state disentanglement module that separates ego-relevant from ego-irrelevant interactive states, enabling more interpretable and efficient decision-making in complex traffic scenarios. Third, we enable multi-style driving behaviors through Group Relative Policy Optimization, which replaces per-step reward optimization with trajectory-wise relative advantages, reducing reward variance and supporting diverse driving styles without retraining. We evaluate StyleDrive on the Bench2Drive closed-loop driving benchmark, achieving a driving score of 88.44 (+17.08 over the previous best world model-based method) and a success rate of 66.82 (+16.58). Furthermore, we deploy StyleDrive on a real automated guided vehicle platform and demonstrate promising sim-to-real transfer capability in dynamic driving scenarios.

AI.tldr: A world-model-based autonomous driving method (StyleDrive) improves long-horizon consistency, interpretable ego-environment state disentanglement, and multi-style policy optimization, achieving substantial gains on Bench2Drive and showing sim-to-real transfer capability.
AI.motivation: Address three core limitations of existing world models: (1) temporal inconsistency in long-horizon imagined rollouts, (2) poor modeling of ego–environment interactions, and (3) limited adaptability to diverse driving styles.
AI.method: 1) Temporal consistency regularization using gated cross-attention to integrate historical latent states for stabilized long-horizon rollouts. 2) State disentanglement separating ego-relevant from ego-irrelevant interactive states for interpretable decision-making. 3) Group Relative Policy Optimization enabling multi-style behavior by optimizing trajectory-wise relative advantages instead of per-step rewards, reducing variance and enabling style diversity without retraining.
AI.result: On Bench2Drive closed-loop driving benchmark, StyleDrive achieves a driving score of 88.44, up 17.08 over the previous best world-model method, and a success rate of 66.82, up 16.58. Real-robot deployment on an automated guided vehicle shows promising sim-to-real transfer in dynamic driving scenarios.
AI.conclusion: StyleDrive effectively addresses the three highlighted limitations, delivering improved long-horizon consistency, clearer ego–environment information, and flexible multi-style policies, with strong benchmark performance and initial real-world transfer evidence.

title: SLIDEFORGE: An LLM Agent for Controllable Editing of Slides as Structured Artifacts
comment: EMNLP 2026 Main Conference. Haozhen and Fulin contributed equally
summary: Current AI agents compellingly describe slides. However, AI-assisted slide editing requires more than understanding: the output must retain layout, style, component structure, and native editability. Towards, AI-assisted slide editing, existing agents operate on screenshots or weak document representations and often fragment coherent visual units, rasterize editable content, or break layout. In contrast, for controllable slide editing, we introduce an agentic framework, SLIDEFORGE, which builds a Deck State Graph, an executable slide state that links visual decomposition, native pptx object structure, and perceptual organization. By recovering human-referable components while retaining fine-grained editable structure, SLIDEFORGE supports theme-preserving reconstruction through slide-native operations and rendered-state verification. We further introduce an evaluation paradigm for controllable slide transformation that jointly measures component recovery, preservation, restyling consistency, visual quality, and native editability. Experiments show that SLIDEFORGE outperforms direct prompting, screenshot-based agents, and generic code-agent baselines across these dimensions. Code is available at https://github.com/UIUC-MONET/SLIDEFORGE.

AI.tldr: Introduces SLIDEFORGE, an agentic framework that builds a Deck State Graph to enable controllable, theme-preserving slide editing with native PPTX structure, outperforming baselines; releases code.
AI.motivation: Current AI slide editing lacks mechanisms to preserve layout, style, component structure, and native editability; existing agents rely on screenshots or weak representations, leading to fragmentation and loss of editable content.
AI.method: Develop Deck State Graph that connects visual decomposition, pptx object hierarchy, and perceptual organization; recover human-referable components while preserving fine-grained editability; perform slide-native operations and rendered-state verification; propose evaluation paradigm across multiple axes.
AI.result: SLIDEFORGE outperforms prompting, screenshot-based agents, and generic code-agent baselines across component recovery, preservation, restyling consistency, visual quality, and native editability.
AI.conclusion: Provides a controllable slide-editing workflow with theme-preserving reconstruction, validated by a comprehensive evaluation paradigm; code available.

title: Caught in the Story: Narrative Captivity in Multi-turn LLMs Conversation
summary: People increasingly turn to large language models (LLMs) for everyday advice, making ethically charged interpersonal problems a practical moral-advisory context. Most prior work has studied this context through single-turn judgments or pressure-laden rebuttals, assumptions that poorly match how guidance is sought in real-world contexts. These assumptions leave unclear whether narration alone, without an explicit opposing position, can shift model judgments during multi-turn moral consultation. Yet real-world moral-conflict conversation often elicits one party's self-justifying account, which can unfold over multiple turns and create information asymmetry. We introduce \textbf{narrative captivity}, a failure mode in which a model treats an unopposed one-sided account as complete and aligns with the narrator's interpretation without seeking missing perspectives. To measure this phenomenon, we build a benchmark of $5{,}078$ interpersonal-conflict scenarios spanning six moral dimensions. Across 17 LLMs, narrative captivity is widespread: end-state judgments under multi-turn narration shift by 25 percentage points on average beyond the matched single-turn baseline. Stage-level analysis identifies preference optimization as a major contributor, while four inference-time strategies provide only partial mitigation. We hope our project fosters LLM advisors that preserve independent judgment in real-world consultation.

AI.tldr: Introduces 'narrative captivity' as a failure mode where LLMs align with an unopposed one-sided moral narration in multi-turn consultations; builds a large benchmark (5,078 scenarios, six moral dimensions) and evaluates 17 LLMs, finding end-state judgments shift ~25 percentage points beyond single-turn baselines; analyzes stage-level contributions (preference optimization) and tests four inference-time mitigation strategies; advocates preserving independent judgment in real-world advisory contexts.
AI.motivation: Address how real-world, multi-turn moral-advisory conversations can be driven by narrated, one-sided accounts. Prior work focused on single-turn judgments or adversarial rebuttals, leaving unclear whether narration alone can bias judgments and how to mitigate this bias in practical LLM-guided advice.
AI.method: Construct a large benchmark of 5,078 interpersonal-conflict scenarios across six moral dimensions. Evaluate 17 different LLMs on end-state judgments under multi-turn narration and compare to matched single-turn baselines. Perform stage-level analysis to identify factors (notably preference optimization) contributing to narrative captivity. Evaluate four inference-time strategies for mitigation.
AI.result: Narrative captivity is widespread: end-state judgments under multi-turn narration shift by about 25 percentage points beyond the single-turn baseline. Stage-level analysis implicates preference optimization as a major contributor. Four inference-time strategies offer only partial mitigation.
AI.conclusion: To ensure reliable moral guidance, LLM advisors should preserve independent judgment and avoid being steered by one-sided narratives; results call for improved alignment and conversation-design strategies to mitigate narrative captivity in real-world consultations.

title: TRACE: Spatiotemporal Contact Memory Graph Network Simulator for Granular Dynamics
summary: Learned graph simulators provide an efficient alternative to high-fidelity solvers for granular dynamics. However, granular motion depends strongly on inter-granular contact history, which is difficult to preserve when particle contacts form, break, and rearrange. Existing simulators mainly store temporal information in node features or node-level memory. Here we introduce TRACE, a graph-network simulator that stores interaction history directly on contact edges. Each edge maintains a persistent memory updated by attention-based message passing and a gated recurrent unit, while an edge-identity dictionary preserves this memory as the contact graph changes. A physics-structured decoder predicts inter-granular normal and tangential contact forces, enforces the Coulomb friction limit, and applies equal-and-opposite internal forces. The model is trained with single-step pretraining followed by autoregressive rollout fine-tuning. We evaluate TRACE on 2D and 3D granular column-collapse benchmarks. In both cases, TRACE produces stable, physically consistent long-horizon rollouts, closely reproducing the final deposit geometry and the kinetic energy released during collapse. Compared with graph network simulator (GNS) and node-memory graph neural simulator (NMGNS), TRACE reduces long-rollout position error by 31-62% and final-deposit error by 58-89% across the two benchmarks, while using fewer parameters and maintaining near-zero particle interpenetration. TRACE also achieves 12.2$\times$ and 8.9$\times$ speedups over the material point method (MPM) reference solver in 2D and 3D, respectively. Our code is available at https://github.com/Data-Driven-Computational-Geotechnics/TRACE.

AI.tldr: TRACE is a graph-network simulator that stores granular contact history on edges, yielding more stable, accurate, and faster long-horizon rollouts than node-memory GNNs and traditional solvers like MPM.
AI.motivation: Granular dynamics are governed by inter-granular contact history, which is hard to preserve when contacts form or rearrange. Storing history only in node features overlooks edge-level dynamics; persisting memory on contact edges promises more faithful dynamics and better long-horizon stability.
