AI.method: Persistent edge memory updated by attention-based message passing and a gated recurrent unit (GRU); an edge-identity dictionary tracks memory as the contact graph changes; a physics-structured decoder predicts inter-granular normal and tangential forces, enforces Coulomb friction, and applies Newton's third law; training uses single-step pretraining followed by autoregressive rollout fine-tuning.
AI.result: On 2D and 3D granular column-collapse benchmarks, TRACE achieves stable, physically consistent long-horizon rollouts, closely matching final deposit geometry and kinetic energy. It reduces long-rollout positional error by 31-62% and final-deposit error by 58-89% versus GNS and NMGNS, uses fewer parameters, and attains near-zero particle interpenetration. It also delivers 12.2× (2D) and 8.9× (3D) speedups over MPM reference solvers.
AI.conclusion: Edge-based persistent memory with a physics-informed decoder enables more accurate and efficient learned granular simulators, offering a compelling alternative to node-memory GNNs and traditional solvers; code is publicly available.

title: Establishing a Dynamic Multimodal HRI Dataset for Engagement Analysis with a Humanoid Robot
summary: This paper presents an experimental design for constructing a multimodal dataset to analyze user engagement in human-robot interaction (HRI). Prior studies have mainly relied on observable behavioral cues, with limited frameworks integrating physiological signals. We therefore propose a structured data-collection protocol to build a multimodal dataset that includes wearable physiological signals, behavioral data, and self-report measures under different levels of task complexity defined in this experiment.

AI.tldr: Proposes a framework for building a multimodal dataset to study user engagement in human-robot interaction (HRI) by integrating wearable physiological signals, behavioral data, and self-report measures across varying task complexities.
AI.motivation: Addresses the gap that most prior HRI studies rely on observable behavioral cues and lack integrated physiological data; aims to enable richer, multimodal engagement analysis through a structured data-collection protocol.
AI.method: Experimental design that outlines a structured data-collection protocol including wearable physiological signals, behavioral data, and self-report measures, collected under multiple levels of task complexity.
AI.result: This paper presents the design and protocol for a multimodal dataset; no empirical results are reported.
AI.conclusion: The proposed protocol lays groundwork for future data collection, enabling multimodal analysis of user engagement in HRI and potentially improving understanding beyond observable behavior alone.

title: Beyond Small Patches: Black-Box Detection and Purification of Diverse Backdoor Triggers
summary: Deep neural networks (DNNs) are increasingly deployed in real-world vision systems, yet their predictions can be covertly manipulated by backdoor attacks, in which malicious triggers cause targeted misclassification while preserving high clean accuracy. Existing defenses often rely on model internals, training data, or clean validation samples, making them difficult to deploy when only black-box access to a trained model is available. We propose TRIM (Trigger Removal by Identifying Manipulated Regions), a deployment-oriented black-box defense that detects and selectively removes backdoor triggers at inference time without requiring model internals, training data, or clean samples. The key insight behind TRIM is to identify image regions that are responsible for anomalous model behavior and purify only those regions while preserving benign content. TRIM innovates via three key components: (i) region-based segmentation with deep feature representations, (ii) adaptive trigger discovery through inpainting and diffusion-based reconstruction to isolate regions responsible for misclassification---without assumptions about trigger type, shape, or location, and (iii) selective region purification that cleans poisoned regions while retaining benign content. To support practical deployment, TRIM further caches feature embeddings of previously identified triggers, enabling efficient recognition and avoiding redundant detection and purification. Extensive experiments across diverse datasets and backdoor types, including blended, sparse, varying-size, and multiple triggers, show that TRIM consistently outperforms existing black-box defenses, reducing attack success rates (ASR) to as low as 1.16% while preserving clean accuracy of up to 87.87%. These results demonstrate that effective backdoor mitigation is possible at inference time even when the defender has no access to any auxiliary data.

AI.tldr: TRIM: a deployment-friendly black-box defense for backdoor mitigation that detects and purifies triggers at inference time via region-level segmentation using deep features, adaptive trigger discovery through inpainting and diffusion-based reconstruction, and selective region purification, with a cache of trigger embeddings for efficiency; achieves strong robustness across trigger types with ASR as low as 1.16% and clean accuracy up to 87.87%.
AI.motivation: Backdoor attacks pose security risks in vision systems, especially under black-box access where defenders cannot inspect model internals or rely on training data. There is a need for a practical, data-free, model-agnostic defense that operates at inference time without extra data.
AI.method: TRIM deploys three components: (i) region-based segmentation using deep feature representations to identify image regions; (ii) adaptive trigger discovery via inpainting and diffusion-based reconstruction to isolate misclassification-causing regions without assuming trigger type, shape, or location; (iii) selective region purification to clean poisoned regions while preserving benign content. It also caches embeddings of identified triggers to enable efficient future recognition and purification.
AI.result: Extensive experiments across diverse datasets and backdoor types (blended, sparse, varying-size, multiple triggers) show TRIM outperforms existing black-box defenses, reducing ASR to as low as 1.16% while maintaining clean accuracy up to 87.87%. It does not require auxiliary data for deployment.
AI.conclusion: TRIM demonstrates effective backdoor mitigation in a black-box, deployment-oriented setting, enabling inference-time purification without access to model internals or training/validation data.

title: Dude: A Dual-Detection Multi-Agent System for Paper-Code Discrepancy Detection
summary: LLM-empowered paper-code discrepancy detection has received growing concern since the scaling of research submissions exceeds the manual review capability. However, the limited context capacity and one-sided discrepancy detection of existing single-agent LLM paradigms lead to an inferior recall performance in detecting discrepancies. In this paper, we propose Dude, the first Dual-Detection Multi-Agent System for paper-code discrepancy detection. We discover that the granularity asymmetry of the paper-language and code-language introduces over-interpretation and over-reporting challenges in a multi-agent system design for discrepancy detection, resulting in increasing false positives. To address this, we propose a granularity-aligned negotiation and a two-stage salience-filtering mechanism in Dude, which effectively prevents agents from falsely reporting discrepancies. Experimental results in real-world paper-code discrepancy datasets showcase Dude's significant recall and precision improvement by up to 22.8%, increasing F1 score by up to 18.7% compared to baseline methods.

AI.tldr: Dude is a Dual-Detection Multi-Agent System for paper-code discrepancy detection that uses granularity-aligned negotiation and two-stage salience-filtering to address granularity asymmetry, achieving notable gains in recall, precision, and F1 over baselines.
AI.motivation: Escalating paper submissions overwhelm manual reviews; existing single-agent LLM approaches suffer from limited context and one-sided detection, causing missed discrepancies and false positives.
AI.method: Dude employs two agents for paper-language and code-language, with granularity-aligned negotiation to resolve asymmetry and a two-stage salience-filtering mechanism to prevent false reports; evaluated on real-world datasets.
AI.result: Significant improvements in recall and precision by up to 22.8% and F1 by up to 18.7% relative to baselines.
AI.conclusion: Dual-detection with alignment and filtering demonstrates effective improvement in paper-code discrepancy detection in scalable settings.

title: No-Regret Bayesian Optimization with Finite-Library Input-Warped Kernels
summary: Gaussian-process Bayesian optimization (GP-BO) excels at black-box optimization of costly functions, e.g., hyperparameter optimization (HPO) and multi-agent system (MAS) design. Convergence-rate guarantees exist for select methods, notably GP upper confidence bound (GP-UCB), but require a fixed kernel. Critically, the kernel encodes how input proximity affects objective value similarity. When raw coordinates poorly match this geometry - as with log-scaled hyperparameters or localized peaks - input warping can greatly improve sample efficiency, yet known GP-UCB proofs require a fixed kernel. We propose Finite-Library Input-Warped Bayesian Optimization (FLIWBO), which selects warps from a finite library of smooth input maps by any history-dependent rule. It adapts the input geometry to accelerate learning while retaining high-probability convergence guarantees under mild hypotheses, with an explicit $\sqrt(N_\varepsilon)$ library-size cost. Controlled diagnostics show that finite-library warping repairs planted geometry mismatches and identify FLIWBO failure cases. Across four repeated benchmarks - warped synthetic objectives, a confidence-fence trap, and Fashion-MNIST HPO - FLIWBO-UCB beats raw-coordinate GP-UCB under misspecified geometry, escapes traps that defeat even oracle-warp expected improvement, and recovers much of the gain from manual log scaling, while leading the tested methods that admit a matching regret guarantee. A 20-dimensional MAS design study further shows feasibility under costly noisy evaluations. Code for experiments is available: https://github.com/edvin-ketabati/bogp-paper-experiments.

AI.tldr: A finite-library input-warped GP-BO method (FLIWBO) selects from a finite set of input warps to adapt geometry, achieving convergence guarantees and improved performance under misspecified geometry, with practical success on several benchmarks and a 20D MAS study.
AI.motivation: GP-BO performance hinges on input geometry encoded by the kernel; when raw coordinates misalign with objective geometry, input warping can boost sample efficiency, but existing GP-UCB analyses assume a fixed kernel, limiting theoretical guarantees.
AI.method: Introduce FLIWBO: maintain a finite library of smooth input maps (warps) and select among them via a history-dependent rule; provide high-probability convergence guarantees with explicit sqrt(N_epsilon) library-size cost; perform controlled diagnostics on geometry mismatches; validate via four benchmarks (warped objectives, a confidence-fence trap, Fashion-MNIST HPO) and a 20D MAS design study; release code.
AI.result: FLIWBO-UCB outperforms raw-coordinate GP-UCB when geometry is misspecified; it avoids traps that defeat oracle-warped EI; recovers much of log-scaling gains; retains matching regret guarantees; feasible in costly, noisy 20D MAS optimization.
AI.conclusion: Finite-library input warping offers a practical, theoretically grounded mechanism to adapt GP-BO to geometry mismatch, balancing exploration-exploitation with a manageable library-size cost and enabling robust performance gains across diverse tasks.

title: R2S-Eval: Robot Evaluation with Real-to-Sim Calibration via Vision-Language Models
summary: Evaluating robot manipulation policies is becoming increasingly important as generalist models, particularly vision-language-action (VLA) models, are deployed on physical robots. However, conventional real-world evaluation remains labor-intensive, unstable, and insufficiently informative. It requires repeated hardware trials, manual scene resets, and continuous operator monitoring, may produce different policy rankings across repeated evaluations, and primarily relies on success-rate metrics that provide limited information about execution quality. In contrast, humans assess robot performance by observing and comparing complete behaviors rather than relying solely on binary success outcomes. To this end, we propose R2S-Eval, an evaluation pipeline that combines real-to-sim calibration with vision-language model (VLM) preference evaluation. The real-to-sim component efficiently generates rollout videos in a simulator calibrated to the real-world evaluation setting, thereby reducing the need for repeated hardware trials. The VLM evaluator assesses the execution quality of rollout videos and produces pairwise preferences, which are subsequently aggregated into policy rankings. We further introduce a protocol to assess whether the proposed evaluation pipeline yields validated policy conclusions while mitigating the key challenges of conventional real-world evaluation. Experiments in both simulation and real-world settings demonstrate that R2S-Eval produces reliable and stable policy conclusions, achieves agreement with human preferences, substantially reduces repeated hardware-operation effort, and reveals behavior-quality differences that are not captured by binary success labels. In general, R2S-Eval advances robot evaluation from manual success counting toward automated, statistically stable, and quality-aware evaluation of robot behavior. Project page: https://r2s-eval.github.io.

AI.tldr: R2S-Eval combines real-to-sim calibrated rollout videos with vision-language model (VLM) preference evaluation to produce pairwise policy rankings, aiming for reliable, quality-aware robot policy assessment that reduces hardware trials.
AI.motivation: Conventional real-world robot evaluation is labor-intensive, unstable, and overly reliant on binary success metrics, failing to capture execution quality and ranking reliability.
AI.method: Calibrate a simulator to real evaluation settings (real-to-sim) to generate rollout videos; use a VLM to compare video pairs and output pairwise preferences; aggregate preferences into policy rankings; validate that conclusions are stable and human-aligned; test in both simulation and real hardware.
AI.result: R2S-Eval yields reliable and stable policy conclusions, agreement with human preferences, significant reduction in repeated hardware trials, and detection of behavior-quality differences not captured by success labels.
AI.conclusion: R2S-Eval shifts robot evaluation from binary success counting toward automated, statistically stable, quality-aware evaluation of robot behavior, advancing evaluation methodology for VLA models on robots.

title: VeriPhy: Agentic Physical Reasoning for World Model Evaluation and Refinement
summary: Visual fluency in generated video does not imply physical reliability, and a scalar quality score alone is incapable of indicating the obligation a clip violates or the moment it fails. We present VeriPhy, an auditable physical-verification system in which a text-only planner compiles the prompt into typed physical obligations and a statically validated execution plan before any frame is observed. During execution, observations gate and scope only declared calls to frozen low-level experts (e.g., segmentation and tracking, counting, eleven typed physical measurements over the resulting tracks, depth, OCR, and audio-event detection). Each action returns a provenance-carrying evidence record whose payload, when usable, is either a typed measurement or an explicitly tagged learned state. Typed resolvers and fixed composition map usable records to a three-valued state (supported, contradicted, or unknown, surfaced as plausible, implausible, or abstain) with full provenance, so that every verdict is traceable to the evidence that produced it. We anchor evaluation in a 1,500-clip corpus of human-annotated flaw records that localize real generation failures in prompt reference, space, and time. On a 149-clip core carrying 304 such records, VeriPhy accounts for 228, against 164 for a published question-decomposition evaluator given the same clips and the same claims. Recall alone does not separate it from prompting the same backbone monolithically, which reaches 222; what separates them is that each decision retains its evidence record and provenance, making the traces auditable one verdict at a time and usable as the interface through which a critic verdict could be written back into generation.

AI.tldr: VeriPhy provides an auditable physical-verification framework for generated video, using typed physical obligations, provenance-backed evidence, and a three-valued verdict to localize and justify failures, achieving improved flaw detection over a baseline on a curated clip corpus.
AI.motivation: Scalar perceptual quality scores are insufficient to indicate when, where, or why a generated clip violates physical or causal constraints. A traceable, evidence-backed verification system is needed to localize failures and enable accountability and potential feedback into generation.
AI.method: A text-only planner compiles prompts into typed physical obligations and a statically validated execution plan. During execution, observations gate calls to frozen low-level experts (segmentation, tracking, counting, 11 typed physical measurements over tracks, depth, OCR, audio-event detection). Each action returns a provenance-bearing evidence record whose payload is either a typed measurement or a tagged learned state. Typed resolvers and fixed composition map records to a three-valued state (supported, contradicted, or unknown) with full provenance. Evaluation on a 1,500-clip corpus of human-annotated flaw records; core subset (149 clips, 304 records) shows VeriPhy accounting for 228 flaws vs 164 for a published question-decomposition evaluator on the same data; recall alone does not separate from monolithic prompting, but VeriPhy preserves evidence traces for auditable verdicts and potential feedback into generation.
AI.result: VeriPhy yields more flaw-detection accountability than the baseline evaluator on the same data, by producing auditable verdicts with provenance per decision. It localizes failures in time/space and links each verdict to concrete evidence.
AI.conclusion: The approach introduces an auditable physical-verification paradigm for generated video that provides traceable evidence for each verdict, improves flaw localization, and enables a potential feedback channel from critic judgments back into generation.

title: DuplexSpeechBench-IFEval: Evaluating Implicit Instruction Following in Full-Duplex Voice Agents
summary: Full-duplex voice agents must continuously decide when to listen, backchannel, interrupt, handle speech overlaps, take the floor, and yield. Existing benchmarks largely test these behaviors through explicit turn-management instructions, while deployed agents are often configured through roles or personas from which the appropriate conversational behavior must be inferred. We introduce DuplexSpeechBench-IFEval (DSB-IFEval) for evaluating implicit instruction-following in real-time spoken interaction. (DSB-IFEval) comprises 1,038 test cases spanning eight diverse assistant roles and evaluates five conditioning protocols for instruction-following: default behavior, explicit behavioral instructions, persona-implied behavior, combined persona--rule conditioning, and instruction conflict. We measure real-time floor management using a deterministic Instruction Adherence Score (IAS) and persona-consistent content using LLM-judged Persona Adherence Score (PAS). Across six real-time speech systems, we find architecture-dependent trade-offs. Full duplex models like F-Actor and PersonaPlex are more sensitive to whether conversational behavior is stated explicitly or must be inferred from a persona, with adherence dropping by 9.7% and 4.5%, respectively, under persona-only conditioning. In contrast, GPT-Realtime, MiniCPM-o, and Fun-Audio-Chat strongly adhere to persona-consistent content, but their floor behavior does not adapt across explicit and persona-only instructions and remains constrained on several proactive actions. We further find that even if systems reliably follow conflicting directives to their prescribed persona, they still struggle to override them under safety conflict. These results show that inferring the behavior implied by a role, executing it at the appropriate conversational moment, and resolving competing instructions remain distinct challenges for full-duplex voice agents.

AI.tldr: Introduces DuplexSpeechBench-IFEval (DSB-IFEval), a benchmark to evaluate implicit instruction-following in real-time spoken interaction. It uses 1,038 test cases across eight assistant roles and five conditioning protocols, plus two scores (IAS for floor/moment-to-moment adherence and PAS for persona-adherence). Findings show architecture-dependent trade-offs: some models rely more on explicit instructions while others adhere to persona, yet both face challenges in floor control and safety conflicts; inferring role-based behavior, timely execution, and resolving conflicting directives are distinct, hard problems for full-duplex voice agents.
AI.motivation: To move beyond explicit turn-management cues and assess how real-time voice agents infer and enact behavior from personas or implicit cues, measuring both floor management and persona-consistent content under realistic, multi-role conditions.
AI.method: Create DSB-IFEval with 1,038 test cases across eight assistant roles. Evaluate five conditioning protocols: default behavior, explicit behavioral instructions, persona-implied behavior, combined persona–rule conditioning, and instruction conflict. Use deterministic Instruction Adherence Score (IAS) to quantify real-time floor management and LLM-judged Persona Adherence Score (PAS) for persona-consistent content. Compare six real-time speech systems (e.g., F-Actor, PersonaPlex, GPT-Realtime, MiniCPM-o, Fun-Audio-Chat) to reveal architecture-dependent trade-offs.
AI.result: Full-duplex models (F-Actor, PersonaPlex) are sensitive to whether behavior is stated explicitly or inferred from a persona, with adherence dropping 9.7% and 4.5% under persona-only conditioning. Other models (GPT-Realtime, MiniCPM-o, Fun-Audio-Chat) strongly adhere to persona content but show limited adaptation of floor behavior across instruction types and are constrained on proactive actions. Safety-conflict situations show systems struggle to override persona directives. Conclusion: inferring role-based behavior, executing it at the right moments, and resolving competing instructions are distinct challenges for full-duplex voice agents.
AI.conclusion: Inferring and enacting persona-driven behavior in real time, while maintaining flexible floor control and safe override capabilities, remains a key unsolved triad for full-duplex voice agents. The benchmark highlights the need for better integration of persona inference with moment-to-moment floor decisions and conflict resolution mechanisms.

title: Evaluating Graph Neural Networks for Change-Criticality Classification in Maritime Navigation Charts
comment: Accepted at IEEE International Geoscience and Remote Sensing Symposium (IGARSS) 2026
summary: Graph neural networks (GNNs) are a class of neural networks suitable for learning on graph-structured data. Their application to spatial data is a natural extension, however its relatively unclear which message-passing operations, architectural configurations, and graph representation is best suited for classifying changes to objects in electronic navigational charts (ENCs)--geospatial vector datasets used for marine navigation. Maintaining these datasets is a challenge, and categorizing changes to objects in the ENC based on their significance to navigational safety is of particular importance. Here, we propose to represent these vector navigation datasets as a graph structure where the spatial objects serve as nodes and their spatial and semantic relationships form edges. We encode both the old ENC dataset and new ENC dataset into a pair of graphs and frame the task as a graph-pair classification problem. Building on this representation, we investigate the use of GNN architectures to classify whether the encoded graphs constitutes a critical or non-critical risk to navigational safety. We train and evaluate several GNN architectures and model configurations on ENC changes reviewed by maritime experts. Our results demonstrate that graph-based representations improve the classification of ENC updates, providing a scalable approach for automating or improving ENC maintenance workflows.

AI.tldr: Graph-based encoding of ENC changes using graph pairs and GNNs to classify navigational-risk updates; evaluates multiple architectures and configurations; shows improved scalability and performance for ENC maintenance.
AI.motivation: Maintaining electronic navigational charts (ENCs) is critical for maritime safety. Selecting meaningful changes is challenging; graph representations can capture spatial/semantic relations among vector features, enabling automated risk assessment. Framing ENC update changes as a graph-pair classification task leverages GNNs to assess safety impact.
AI.method: Represent old and new ENC datasets as graphs with spatial objects as nodes and spatial/semantic relations as edges. Encode both versions into a graph pair and formulate graph-pair classification to determine if the change is critical to navigational safety. Train and compare several GNN architectures/configurations using ENC changes reviewed by maritime experts.
AI.result: Graph-based representation and graph-pair classification improve the ability to classify ENC updates as critical vs non-critical, with demonstrated scalability and potential to automate or augment ENC maintenance workflows.
AI.conclusion: A graph-pair based GNN approach is effective for ENC change classification and can enhance maintenance workflows. The study supports further exploration of GNN architectures and graph representations for spatial vector data in maritime contexts.

title: ARTiS: An Adaptive Robotic Gripper for Enhanced Tool Manipulation in Disassembly Applications
summary: Grasping and holding tools while using them presents a considerable challenge not only for robots but also for humans. Such a challenge is particularly noticeable in processes involving assembly and disassembly, where efficiency and consistency depend on performing rapidly adaptive tasks. Nonetheless, contemporary robotic grasping technologies that can securely manipulate tools during operation frequently have significant constraints. In this paper, introduce ARTiS (Adaptive Robotic Tool Gripper in Disassembly Systems), a novel gripper that combines the adaptability of soft grippers, the dexterity of anthropomorphic hands, and the robustness of rigid mechanisms with a soft palm and fingertips. This unique combination makes it possible to hold tools securely in a variety of situations through using active jamming in the palm and fin-ray adaptation in fingertips. Furthermore, high finger dexterity is achieved through the seven degrees of freedom design, which enables the fingertips to orient to any surface, both for automated solutions and collaborative tasks. A comprehensive evaluation was conducted using a range of conventional disassembly tools to assess the gripper's compliance, durability, and functional versatility. More information, hardware instructions, and videos at https://romanmykhailyshyn.github.io/artis/

AI.tldr: Hybrid gripper ARTiS combines soft compliance, anthropomorphic dexterity, and rigid robustness to securely grasp tools in disassembly tasks using active palm jamming and fin-ray fingertip adaptation; seven-DOF fingertips enable versatile surface alignment.
AI.motivation: Grasping and holding tools during rapid, adaptive assembly/disassembly is challenging; current robotic grippers struggle with secure, versatile tool manipulation across diverse shapes and contexts; a versatile gripper that integrates compliance, dexterity, and robustness is needed.
AI.method: Design and implement ARTiS with a soft palm and fingertips, active jamming in the palm, fin-ray-inspired adaptive fingertips with seven degrees of freedom; integrate soft, rigid, and flexible components; evaluate with a range of conventional disassembly tools to assess compliance, durability, and versatility; analyze automated and collaborative use cases.
AI.result: The evaluation demonstrated secure tool holding across a variety of tools, high fingertip dexterity enabling orientation to diverse surfaces, and overall compliance, durability, and functional versatility in disassembly tasks.
AI.conclusion: ARTiS provides a robust, adaptable solution for tool manipulation in disassembly contexts, enabling rapid, adaptive grasping in automated and collaborative environments; the approach combines soft tactile adaptability with rigid structure to achieve reliable performance; further details are available at the project site.

title: Who Speaks for the Pruned? Visual Token Pruning as Coverage Optimization
summary: Visual token pruning reduces the inference cost of vision-language models (VLMs), but most methods only ask which tokens to keep. This retained-token view can keep redundant high-scoring tokens while leaving discarded evidence without a close representative. We propose CoverPruner, a training-free pruner that asks the complementary demand-side question: after a token is removed, which surviving original token represents it for the target VLM? CoverPruner formulates pruning as Representational Coverage Maximization (RCM), covering the full projected visual-token set with query-weighted demand. It instantiates RCM with projector-space coverage and a lightweight first-layer attention probe. Across multiple VLM architectures and compression rates, CoverPruner achieves the best average accuracy among all compared methods, with the largest gains usually appearing under aggressive compression.

AI.tldr: CoverPruner is a training-free token pruner for vision-language models that optimizes Representational Coverage Maximization (RCM) to ensure removed tokens are represented by surviving ones, using projector-space coverage and a lightweight first-layer attention probe; achieves state-of-the-art average accuracy across architectures and under aggressive compression.
AI.motivation: Current token pruning mainly selects which tokens to keep, risking redundant high-scoring tokens and missing evidence for removed tokens. A demand-side approach ensuring coverage of removed tokens by survivors is needed.
AI.method: Introduces CoverPruner; formulates pruning as Representational Coverage Maximization (RCM) to cover the projected visual-token space with query-weighted demand; uses projector-space coverage and a lightweight first-layer attention probe; training-free.
AI.result: Empirically, CoverPruner achieves the best average accuracy among compared methods across multiple VLM architectures and compression rates, with the largest gains under aggressive compression.
AI.conclusion: A training-free, demand-driven pruning framework that improves representational coverage and accuracy under compression in vision-language models.

title: Do GUI Agents Know When Not to Act? Enabling Conflict-Aware Termination for Multimodal GUI Agents
summary: Graphical user interface (GUI) agents are increasingly used to execute natural-language instructions on user interfaces, yet real users may issue infeasible instructions due to benign mistakes. A reliable agent should not only know how to act, but also when not to act. In this work, we introduce CONFLICTGUI, a benchmark covering instruction-internal conflicts and instruction-GUI context conflicts to study conflict-aware termination. Our evaluation reveals severe execution-biased overcompliance: agents that perform well on feasible tasks often continue to execute blindly under conflicting instructions. To mitigate this behavior, we propose CONFLICTGUARD, an inference-time framework that aligns an agent's feasibility awareness with its action generation. CONFLICTGUARD contains two coupled components: a feasibility verification protocol that guides the agent to assess instruction logic and GUI-side evidence before acting, and a conditional action modulation mechanism that steers agents from over-compliant execution into termination-oriented behavior. Experiments across five widely-used agents demonstrate that CONFLICTGUARD improves average conflict task success rate significantly, while preserving normal GUI-task performance. These results validate that a lightweight inference-time intervention can substantially boost GUI Agent's competence to identify inappropriate execution scenarios and refrain from unnecessary actions.

AI.tldr: Benchmarks and a lightweight inference-time framework to detect and avoid execution under conflicting instructions in GUI agents, improving conflict success rates while preserving normal task performance.
AI.motivation: GUI agents often receive infeasible or conflicting natural-language instructions. Without termination-aware behavior, agents may overcommit and execute harmful or undesired actions. A benchmark and mechanism to recognize and refuse conflicting guidance is needed.
AI.method: Introduce CONFLICTGUI, a benchmark addressing instruction-internal and GUI-context conflicts to study conflict-aware termination. Evaluate five agents. Propose CONFLICTGUARD, an inference-time framework with two coupled components: (1) a feasibility verification protocol guiding the agent to assess instruction logic and GUI-side evidence before acting, and (2) a conditional action modulation mechanism that shifts from over-compliant execution to termination-oriented behavior.
AI.result: Experiments show a significant increase in average conflict task success rate across agents, with minimal impact on regular GUI tasks, indicating the intervention effectively reduces inappropriate execution while preserving normal performance.
AI.conclusion: Inference-time feasibility checks plus action modulation can substantially curb over-compliance in GUI agents and improve safety by enabling timely termination in conflicting scenarios.

title: Verify Before You Distill: Prompt-Level Teacher Gating for On-Policy Distillation
summary: On-policy distillation (OPD) accelerates post-training by providing dense token-level supervision from a frozen teacher on the student's own rollouts. Vanilla OPD applies this supervision uniformly across prompts, without checking whether the teacher is reliable for each prompt. Because reverse KL is mode-seeking, a confidently wrong teacher can induce a strong yet misleading update. Distributional proxies, such as entropy or teacher-student likelihood agreement, measure uncertainty or agreement but do not directly verify outcome correctness. We introduce Teacher-Gated On-Policy Distillation (TGOPD), built on the principle that teacher reliability should be verified at the prompt level before dense supervision is admitted. TGOPD estimates reliability from a small set of verifier-scored teacher probes and routes each prompt exclusively to dense OPD when the reliability check passes or to verifier-grounded GRPO otherwise. Across 4B and 35B students in mathematics, code, and instruction following, TGOPD outperforms Vanilla OPD in all six single-domain settings and achieves higher seven-benchmark averages at both scales under multi-domain training. By using otherwise-idle teacher capacity for reliability estimation, TGOPD also reduces teacher-side compute waste in asynchronous OPD, increasing teacher-node GPU utilization from 9.8% to 78.9% in the measured 4B single-domain run.

AI.tldr: TGOPD gates dense OPD on a per-prompt reliability check, routing prompts to dense supervision only when a verifier-scored prompt is reliable; otherwise uses verifier-grounded GRPO. This yields better accuracy across 4B/35B models in math/code/instruction domains and greatly improves teacher GPU utilization by using idle capacity.
AI.motivation: Vanilla on-policy distillation (OPD) applies dense supervision uniformly, which can be harmful when the teacher is confidently wrong for certain prompts due to the reverse KL’s mode-seeking tendency. Existing distributional proxies (e.g., entropy, agreement) do not verify outcome correctness, risking misleading updates.
AI.method: Introduce Teacher-Gated On-Policy Distillation (TGOPD). A small verifier evaluates prompts via teacher probes to estimate reliability. Prompts deemed reliable receive dense OPD supervision; prompts failing reliability checks receive verifier-grounded GRPO instead. This gating is applied across single-domain and multi-domain training, across 4B and 35B models, and leverages idle teacher capacity to boost utilization during asynchronous OPD.
AI.result: TGOPD outperforms Vanilla OPD across six single-domain settings and achieves higher seven-benchmark averages under multi-domain training for 4B and 35B students in math, code, and instruction-following. In a measured 4B single-domain run, teacher-node GPU utilization increased from 9.8% to 78.9% by using idle capacity for reliability estimation, reducing wasted compute.
AI.conclusion: Per-prompt reliability gating provides more trustworthy dense supervision, improves performance across domains and scales, and enhances teacher resource utilization by exploiting idle capacity. TGOPD mitigates the risk of misleading updates from confidently wrong teachers while maintaining efficiency gains of OPD.

title: Programming and execution of skill-based human-robot-crane collaborative tasks
comment: 8 pages, 12 figures, accepted for publication in IECON 2026
summary: Highly varying production sets increasing challenges for robotic manufacturing and indoor logistics. New capabilities for agility, flexibility, and robustness are needed. Robot skills, integrating motions, tool operations, and sensor perceptions consistently provide an execution mechanism for a versatile set of tasks with varying parameters. In this paper, easy-to-use CAD-model based programming and execution system for parametrized skills and skill monitors is showcased. The execution control structure is dynamic and parametrized, based on a modified Behavior Tree, where only event based communication is used. A human-robot-crane collaborative skill is shown as a test example, where a human instructs an overhead crane and a manipulator in inserting a heavy object supported by the crane, and guided by the manipulator, into the goal.

AI.tldr: CAD-model based programming for parametrized robot skills with a dynamic, event-driven Behavior Tree; demonstrated via a human-robot-crane collaboration task.
AI.motivation: Address highly variable production sets in robotic manufacturing and indoor logistics, requiring agility, flexibility, and robustness. Emphasizes reusable skills that integrate motions, tool use, and sensing, supported by CAD-based programming and skill monitoring.
AI.method: Develop a CAD-model-based programming and execution system for parametrized skills and skill monitors. Implement a dynamic, parametrized execution control structure based on a modified Behavior Tree with exclusive event-based communication. Demonstrate on a human-robot-crane collaborative task where a human instructs an overhead crane and a manipulator to insert a heavy object supported by the crane into a goal, guided by the manipulator.
AI.result: The approach is showcased with a test scenario illustrating the feasibility of CAD-based parametrized skills, dynamic event-driven execution, and human-robot coordination (crane + manipulator) for a heavy-object insertion task.
AI.conclusion: CAD-model-based parametrized skills with an event-driven, dynamically adaptable Behavior Tree can support agile, robust robotic execution in variable production contexts and enables effective human-robot collaboration for complex assembly tasks.

title: RoboTok: An Internet-Scale Data Engine for Human Demonstration Retrieval and Dexterous Manipulation Learning
summary: Robot learning increasingly depends on broad and diverse demonstrations, yet collecting robot data remains expensive and poorly suited to covering the long tail of real-world tasks. To address this bottleneck, we introduce RoboTok, an internet-scale data engine that, given a query human manipulation video, retrieves manipulation-relevant human demonstrations from web videos for training dexterous robot policies. Specifically, we learn a latent motion space from 3D hand trajectories expressed in estimated actor-centered reference frames. This representation enables manipulation behaviors to be compared across variations in camera viewpoint, scene appearance, and actor occlusions, while remaining compact enough for efficient search and continual indexing over internet-scale video collections. We evaluate RoboTok against existing robot-data retrieval approaches on retrieval benchmarks and downstream robot policy performance. Our results show that RoboTok retrieves more relevant manipulation demonstrations and improves downstream task success, establishing hand-pose trajectory-aware retrieval as a way to make web video a scalable and continuously growing source of supervision for robot learning.

AI.tldr: Introduces RoboTok, an internet-scale data engine that retrieves manipulation-relevant human demonstrations from web videos via a latent hand-trajectory space learned from 3D hand trajectories in actor-centered frames, enabling scalable, robust robot policy learning.
AI.motivation: Robot data collection is expensive and skews toward common tasks; leveraging web videos can provide broad, diverse demonstrations, but requires robust representations to bridge domain gaps and enable scalable search.
AI.method: Learn a latent motion representation from 3D hand trajectories expressed in actor-centered reference frames, making manipulation behaviors comparable across viewpoint, appearance, and occlusion variations; index and search over internet-scale video collections; retrieve demonstrations conditioned on a query video for training dexterous robot policies.
AI.result: RoboTok retrieves more relevant manipulation demonstrations than existing approaches and improves downstream robot policy performance on benchmark tasks, demonstrating the benefit of hand-pose trajectory–aware retrieval for scalable robot learning.
AI.conclusion: Hand-pose trajectory–aware retrieval enables web video to serve as a scalable, continuously growing source of supervision for dexterous robot learning and supports continual indexing over large video collections.

title: Beyond "Made with AI": Visualizing Provenance Density to Mitigate the Transparency Penalty
summary: As generative AI makes polished prose cheap to produce, users can no longer rely on fluency as a proxy for truth. We call this failure mode the Fluency Trap: users trust fluent hallucinations while also discounting accurate content once it is disclosed as AI-generated. Binary ``Made with AI'' labels respond with authorship disclosure, but they do not show what supports a claim. We propose Provenance Density, an evidence-visualization interface that shows the density of verified claims in a text. In a user study with 81 participants, an idealized Provenance Density interface produced a large discernment gap between truth and fabrication ($+4.15$ points, $d=1.82$), whereas participants given no signal showed no detectable discrimination. A technical audit with 200 samples shows that retrieval density alone is insufficient; unexpectedly, the Consistency Veto carries most of the discriminative signal on dynamic queries. As AI-generated content becomes indistinguishable from human writing, effective transparency must move from authorship disclosure toward evidence visualization.

AI.tldr: Provenance Density improves detection of truth vs. fabrication by visualizing evidence density; authorship labels alone are insufficient to convey support for claims.
AI.motivation: To address the Fluency Trap where fluent AI-generated text misleads readers; traditional Made with AI labels fail to disclose what supports a claim, necessitating evidence-centric transparency.
AI.method: 1) User study (n=81) comparing an idealized Provenance Density interface against a signal-free control to measure discrimination between truth and fabrication. 2) Technical audit (n=200 samples) to assess the contributions of retrieval density and the Consistency Veto on dynamic queries.
AI.result: Ideal Provenance Density produced a large discrimination gap between truth and fabrication (+4.15 points, d=1.82); control with no signal showed no detectable discrimination. Retrieval density alone is insufficient; the Consistency Veto provides most discriminative signal for dynamic queries.
AI.conclusion: Transparency should shift from authorship disclosure to evidence visualization; effective verification requires visualizing the density and consistency of verified claims rather than relying on AI-generated labels alone.

title: Causal Foundation Models
summary: Causal inference is the practice of estimating the effect of a treatment or intervention from data. It traditionally requires a bespoke pipeline for every new problem: first proposing a causal mechanism, selecting a compatible estimator, and finally training it. Meanwhile, across diverse settings and modalities, much of machine learning has shifted to the paradigm of foundation models: networks pretrained once at scale and applied to new tasks without fine-tuning. Causal foundation models (CFMs) bring this paradigm to causal inference. CFMs are pretrained neural networks that estimate causal quantities, such as the average treatment effect, on entirely new datasets using in-context learning without requiring model updates. This work provides a practical introduction to this emerging area. We summarize the necessary background in causal inference and machine learning before discussing CFMs. Throughout, we include example code and Jupyter notebooks.

AI.tldr: CFMs apply the foundation-model paradigm to causal inference: pretrained networks estimate causal quantities on new datasets via in-context learning without model updates.
AI.motivation: To replace bespoke, problem-specific causal pipelines with a generalizable, zero-shot/few-shot inference framework across diverse data settings.
AI.method: Survey and exposition of CFMs; discuss causal background, in-context learning for causal estimation (e.g., ATE), and provide example code and Jupyter notebooks to illustrate practical use.
AI.result: Offers a practical introduction and actionable guidance for deploying CFMs on unseen causal tasks, including code/examples to facilitate adoption.
AI.conclusion: CFMs could enable scalable, cross-domain causal inference without fine-tuning, though empirical validation, reliability, and tooling remain important research directions.

title: Air-Ground Collaborative Vision-and-Language Navigation via Shared Bird's-Eye Maps
summary: Air-ground collaborative Vision-and-Language Navigation (VLN) pairs an unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) with a global bird's-eye view and an unmanned ground vehicle (UGV) with a local first-person view, yet the setting remains largely unexplored: existing training-free methods solve single-agent tasks but offer no collaboration mechanism, and a recent CARLA-Air evaluation found no stable cooperative behavior across five state-of-the-art VLA models; naive semantic communication or bidirectional coupling even degrades performance. We establish AGC-VLN (Air-Ground Collaborative VLN), the first training-free baseline for air-ground collaborative VLN. The key insight is that training-free methods decompose navigation into VLM-based semantic reasoning and deterministic geometric execution, exposing a collaboration interface: the UAV's global view, over which it renders the UGV's reported pose and the VLM-anchored target as CAR/GOAL markers with distance labels, yielding a shared bird's-eye map. From this map, the UGV acquires global spatial context its first-person view cannot provide, plans a road-following path with a frozen VLM, and executes it under closed-loop control; in parallel, the UAV runs 3D-SPF, a spatial-search upgrade of SPF that localizes the target in the downward view and flies toward it. On 100 closed-loop episodes in CARLA-Air's Town10HD scene, AGC-VLN reaches a 77.0% joint success rate, a collaboration gain of +27.0% over the weaker individual agent (the UAV, 50.0%), and exceeds the strongest published single-agent baseline (Travel UAV, 53.0%) by 24.0 points, stemming from the complementarity of the UAV's global view and the UGV's road-following execution. Project page: https://github.com/ZSN2024/AGC-VLN.

AI.tldr: Proposes AGC-VLN, a training-free baseline for air-ground collaborative VLN that combines a UAV's global bird's-eye view with a UGV's local first-person view using a shared map; achieves 77.0% joint success in CARLA-Air Town10HD, outperforming single-agent baselines by a sizable margin.
AI.motivation: To address the lack of collaboration mechanisms in training-free multi-agent VLN and the instability observed in CARLA-Air evaluations for cooperative behavior across state-of-the-art models.
AI.method: Decompose navigation into VLM-based semantic reasoning (global) and deterministic geometric execution (local). The UAV renders the UGV-reported pose and VLM-anchored target as CAR/GOAL markers with distance labels on a shared bird's-eye map. The UGV uses a road-following plan with a frozen VLM; the UAV runs 3D-SPF, a spatial-search upgrade of SPF, to localize the target from downward view. Both agents operate in closed-loop, enabling air-ground collaboration without training.
AI.result: Evaluated on 100 closed-loop episodes in CARLA-Air Town10HD. Joint success rate reaches 77.0%, a collaboration gain of +27.0% over the weaker UAV-alone baseline (50.0%), and surpasses the strongest published single-agent Travel UAV baseline (53.0%) by 24.0 points.
AI.conclusion: This work provides the first training-free, air-ground cooperative VLN baseline that leverages complementary global and local sensing via a shared map, yielding substantial performance gains and establishing a new direction for multi-agent VLN without model training.

title: Learning to Zoom Efficiently with a Contrastive Curriculum
summary: Using a zoom-in tool is an important foundational part of modern visual agents, because it allows to efficiently handle tasks involving high-resolution images. Most previous methods need an extensive warm-start supervised fine-tuning phase for teaching models zoom-in. We show that this is not necessary by proposing a new intrinsic reward for learning tool use in MLLMs without the need for additional labels or warm-start SFT. Our InfoNCE-style reward uses a curriculum of increasingly hard negative tool calls as a contrastive training signal. Empirical experiments on $V^*$, HRBench and MME-RealWorld show that our approach is competitive while being more efficient. When used as a drop-in replacement for SFT, we even outperform all baselines. To directly measure the zoom-in ability of models, we further introduce the scalable synthetic Muffin&Chihuahua (M&C) dataset. Each image consists of a grid with every cell either showing a muffin or chihuahua. Leveraging the M&C dataset's unique region of interest labels, we find that recall is the metric that most strongly correlates the zoom-in region with final task performance. Our model and code for reproduction is publicly available under https://github.com/UKPLab/emnlp2026-zoom-in

AI.tldr: Intrinsic reward for learning tool use in multimodal LLMs (zoom-in) via InfoNCE-style curriculum without warm-start SFT; introduces Muffin&Chihuahua (M&C) synthetic dataset to measure zoom-in recall; shows competitive/ superior results on V*, HRBench, MME-RealWorld and as a drop-in SFT replacement.
AI.motivation: Eliminate reliance on extensive warm-start supervised fine-tuning for zoom-in capabilities in visual agents by leveraging self-supervised intrinsic rewards.
AI.method: InfoNCE-style intrinsic reward with a curriculum of increasingly hard negative tool calls; no additional labels or warm-start SFT; evaluation across multiple benchmarks; development of the M&C synthetic dataset with ROI labels to quantify zoom-in ability.
AI.result: Competitive efficiency; outperforms baselines when used as a direct SFT replacement; M&C shows recall strongly correlates with zoom-in region and final task performance; code and model are publicly available.
AI.conclusion: An intrinsic, label-free learning approach can effectively teach zoom-in tool use in MLLMs and provides a scalable dataset (M&C) to evaluate zoom-in ability, with potential to surpass supervised baselines in some setups.

title: AutoGraphForge: Towards Automated Graph Theory Discovery
comment: 17 pages, 1 figure, 3 tables. Submitted to ITAT 2026 (Information Technologies -- Applications and Theory), CEUR Workshop Proceedings. Code: https://github.com/JanPastorek/AutoGraphForge
summary: We report on our ongoing project to develop a computational pipeline, AutoGraphForge, for an automated graph-theoretic conjecturing-refuting-formalizing-proving system. Conjecture generation is counterexample-guided and runs in rounds: a Graffiti3 generator proposes conjectures over a small, evolving snapshot table $T$ (initially a few hundred graphs with their computed invariants) that grows only by counterexamples to its own conjectures. A novelty filter of $559$ classical and folklore relations, closed under transitive composition and linear identity substitution, decides via a linear program whether a candidate is already implied by known results. Surviving candidates are tested against a dataset of about $348,000$ graphs, unioning the complete House of Graphs invariant export, the exhaustive census of all connected graphs on at most nine vertices, several extremal families (strongly regular, minimal Ramsey, Cayley, cages, barbells, lollipops, spiders), and random models. Counterexample-search algorithms then attack the remainder. Run for several rounds on an HPC cluster, the loop yields $6,522$ conjectures that survived the refutation dataset, the novelty filter and every active-search run -- among them nontrivial relations between the annihilation number and the edge-cover number for bipartite and regular graphs, which we prove by hand. A subsequent formalization and proving stage deterministically translates each surviving conjecture into a Lean 4 statement skeleton; every candidate proof is kernel-verified against a pinned mathlib4 and our custom invariant preamble. This stage integrates two neural provers -- DeepSeek-Prover-V2-671B (served with vLLM) and the Lean-specialised OProver-32B -- behind the independent kernel check. It is implemented end-to-end and passes initial sanity checks, with the full pipeline currently running on the cluster.

AI.tldr: An end-to-end AutoGraphForge pipeline automates graph-theoretic conjecturing, refutation, formalization, and proving, yielding thousands of conjectures and hand-proven results, using neural/prover integration on HPC.
AI.motivation: Automate discovery and formal verification of graph-theoretic conjectures by integrating generation, filtering, counterexample search, and formal proof within a single scalable pipeline.
AI.method: Conjecture generation via Graffiti3 over a evolving snapshot table T; novelty filtering using 559 classical/folklore relations closed under transitive composition and linear identity substitution via a linear program; testing against a large invariant-rich dataset (~348k graphs) including House of Graphs, connected graphs up to 9 vertices, extremal families, and random models; counterexample search to prune; multiple rounds on HPC; formalization into Lean 4 skeletons with kernel verification against mathlib4; neural provers (DeepSeek-Prover-V2-671B via vLLM and OProver-32B) integrated behind the kernel check.
AI.result: Accumulation of 6,522 conjectures surviving all stages, including nontrivial relations between annihilation number and edge-cover number for bipartite/regular graphs, some proved by hand; end-to-end pipeline implemented and running on cluster.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates feasibility of a full conjecture–refutation–formalization–proving loop for graph theory, combining data-driven conjecturing with formal verification and neural/prover backends in a scalable HPC workflow.

title: ObserverBench: Testing Mechanistic Estimates for Intervention and Control
comment: 28 pages, 4 figures. Code, benchmark, leaderboards, and submission interface: https://kwisatzh.github.io/observerbench/. Frozen artifact release: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22136091
summary:
Mechanistic interpretability is increasingly used to guide interventions such as activation steering, circuit removal, and safety monitoring. Yet an internal estimate that is accurate on average can still choose a poor action.
  We present ObserverBench, a benchmark framework for testing whether an internal estimator---an observer---is adequate for the intervention, control, or safety task it directs. Each task fixes the model, information boundary, allowed actions, decision rule, held-out cases, and loss. The benchmark reports estimation accuracy separately from the loss caused by the chosen action.
  Theory and experiments show why both are needed. In closed-loop control, observer errors matter at the starting point and along directions the allowed intervention can reach. On circuit-intervention tasks in GPT-2-small and Qwen2.5-7B, pairwise observers predict unseen effects more accurately without always choosing better actions; observers trained on action loss choose lower-loss actions. In safety triage, a score that perfectly separates violations can allocate a fixed intervention budget poorly when violations have different costs. Across Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B-it, and prospectively frozen Qwen3.5-9B APPS tasks, AUROC can rank monitors differently from deployment loss, and the best information source changes across models. Sparse SAE readouts also trail their layer-matched dense controls on the reported Qwen panels, under disclosed activation-density or checkpoint mismatches.
  ObserverBench provides fixed task contracts, runnable baselines, and table-based submissions for evaluating interpretability methods through the actions they enable.

AI.tldr: ObserverBench is a benchmark framework that evaluates whether an internal observer is adequate for intervention/control/safety tasks by decoupling estimation accuracy from action loss, using fixed task contracts and runnable baselines across models.
AI.motivation: To avoid relying on average estimation accuracy as a proxy for safe and effective interventions in mechanistic interpretability; demonstrate that estimation quality does not guarantee optimal actions; provide a standardized evaluation paradigm.
AI.method: Defines fixed task contracts: model, information boundary, allowed actions, decision rule, held-out cases, and loss. Compares observers across tasks (closed-loop control, circuit interventions, safety triage, APPS-style tasks) on estimation accuracy vs deployment loss; includes deployment with sparse readouts vs dense controls; uses AUROC, etc; provides runnable baselines and table submissions.
AI.result: Shows that estimation error matters in starting point/directions; observers predicting unseen effects may not yield better actions; action-loss-optimized observers can choose lower-loss actions; AUROC ranking differs from deployment loss; best information source varies by model; sparse readouts underperform; a benchmark reveals misalignments between internal estimates and downstream actions.
AI.conclusion: ObserverBench offers a fixed, runnable, table-based framework to evaluate interpretability methods through the actions they enable and to identify when estimation quality translates into better interventions; encourages reporting both estimation accuracy and action-based performance.

title: BRIDGE: An Open-Source Humanoid Platform via Morphology-Control Co-Design for Physical AI
summary: Developing humanoid robots capable of leveraging human behavioral data is essential for general-purpose embodiment, yet conventional development remains bottlenecked by a decoupled paradigm that isolates hardware design from whole-body control. This approach leads to suboptimal systems that compromise human-like fluidity and agility. To bridge this gap, we introduce a data-driven morphology-control co-design framework that optimizes humanoid morphology for human-like movement. To quantify morphological fidelity, we also introduce a novel metric that jointly considers kinematic retargeting fidelity to human motion and dynamic tracking performance. Our framework achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance across all metrics compared to baseline humanoids (Bumi, K1, and Toddlerbot). Finally, we realize this design in Bridge, an open-source, 88cm-tall humanoid platform released alongside its control policy. We demonstrate that Bridge captures human motion data with superior fidelity, exhibiting exceptional performance across foundational locomotion, robust balance, and highly dynamic maneuvers. Videos and open-source materials: https://sites.google.com/view/bridgerobot.

AI.tldr: A data-driven morphology–control co-design framework for humanoids that optimizes morphology for human-like movement and introduces a novel fidelity metric combining kinematic retargeting and dynamic tracking; achieves SOTA against Bumi, K1, and Toddlerbot; validates on Bridge (an 88 cm humanoid) with open-source controls and materials.
AI.motivation: Decoupled hardware design and whole-body control limit humanoid performance and fluidity. Leverage human behavioral data through co-design to close the gap between morphology and control for general-purpose embodiment.
AI.method: Proposes a data-driven morphology–control co-design pipeline. Introduces a new morphological fidelity metric that jointly assesses kinematic retargeting fidelity to human motion and dynamic tracking performance. Optimizes morphology for human-like movement and validates on the Bridge humanoid platform with an accompanying control policy and open-source materials.
AI.result: Achieves state-of-the-art performance on all proposed metrics compared to baseline humanoids (Bumi, K1, Toddlerbot). Bridge demonstrates high fidelity in capturing human motion and strong capabilities in foundational locomotion, robust balance, and dynamic maneuvers.
AI.conclusion: The work demonstrates that integrating morphology and control via co-design and a dedicated fidelity metric can substantially advance humanoid performance and accessibility, exemplified by an open-source 88 cm platform (Bridge) and publicly released materials.

title: ProgResViT: Progressive Resolution and Width for Adaptive Vision Transformers
summary: Vision Transformers (ViTs) typically process every image using a fixed input resolution and model width, even though many images can be classified with substantially less computation. We introduce ProgResViT, an input-adaptive ViT that performs inference progressively across multiple rounds. The first round processes a low-resolution image with a narrow subnetwork. Inference terminates when the prediction is sufficiently confident; otherwise, the model reuses the representations produced in the current round and proceeds with a higher-resolution input and a wider subnetwork to refine its prediction. As all rounds share a single backbone, we propose Progress-Conditioned Soft Gating (PSG), which conditions token fusion and layer outputs on the current round, block, and input resolution. On image classification, applying ProgResViT to DeiT yields better accuracy-compute trade-offs than adaptive-width, adaptive-depth, and dynamic-token baselines. With knowledge distillation, a DeiT-based ProgResViT achieves 84.9% top-1 accuracy, slightly exceeding the reported DeiT-III-S accuracy under a comparable evaluation setting. We show that the same design also provides favorable accuracy-compute trade-offs for self-supervised DINO representations and downstream semantic segmentation. Code is available at https://github.com/ds-kiel/ProgResViT.

AI.tldr: ProgResViT enables input-adaptive, progressive inference in ViTs using a single backbone and round-conditioned soft gating, achieving better accuracy-per-compute than various adaptive baselines and generalizing to self-supervised and segmentation tasks; code released.
AI.motivation: Reduce compute for Vision Transformers by making inference conditional on image difficulty and content, avoiding fixed compute across all images.
AI.method: Progressively process images in multiple rounds: start with a low-resolution, narrow subnetwork; terminate when confident, else reuse current representations and upgrade to higher-resolution input and a wider subnetwork. All rounds share a single backbone. Introduce Progress-Conditioned Soft Gating (PSG) to condition token fusion and layer outputs on the current round, block, and input resolution.
AI.result: For classification, ProgResViT with DeiT yields superior accuracy-per-compute versus adaptive-width, adaptive-depth, and dynamic-token baselines. With knowledge distillation, a DeiT-based ProgResViT reaches 84.9% top-1, slightly above DeiT-III-S under a comparable setup. The approach also yields favorable trade-offs for self-supervised DINO representations and downstream semantic segmentation.
AI.conclusion: Progressive, shared-backbone ViTs with round-aware gating offer efficient, accurate inference across supervised, self-supervised, and segmentation tasks, with open-source code.

title: Making Every Tool Call Count: Necessary Tool-Evidence Path Rewards for Agentic Vision-Language Models
summary: Modern vision-language models (VLMs) can directly answer many image-grounded questions, yet they often struggle with complex queries requiring fine-grained visual details or external knowledge. To acquire this missing evidence, agentic VLMs invoke tools such as image cropping, image search, and text search. However, existing training paradigms primarily evaluate tool-use based on final answer correctness, leaving evidence acquisition and utilization insufficiently supervised. This leads to two critical shortcomings: (i) models frequently issue redundant or off-target tool calls that fail to gather necessary evidence, and (ii) even when appropriate tools are called, models often fail to extract the necessary information from the resulting observations. To address these limitations, we introduce the NTEP (Necessary Tool-Evidence Path), a novel annotation scheme that explicitly specifies the essential external evidence and corresponding tool calls for each query. Building upon this, we propose NTEP-R (NTEP Reward), a supervision mechanism ensuring that each tool invocation strictly advances the reasoning process toward the final solution. Specifically, our approach rewards the agent for aligning its pre-call intent with a necessary evidence-seeking goal, and for ensuring the information summarized from the post-call observation aligns with the necessary evidence. Furthermore, we introduce a non-repeated-goal regularizer to penalize redundant calls that revisit satisfied NTEP goals. Extensive evaluations on seven image-grounded benchmarks demonstrate that our 8B-parameter instantiation, NTEP-8B, significantly improves both search-oriented accuracy and tool-use efficiency within a unified three-tool framework. These results highlight the critical value of fine-grained tool-evidence path supervision for training robust agentic VLMs.

AI.tldr: NTEP offers a fine-grained evidence-path supervision framework for agentic VLMs, explicitly annotating necessary external evidence and corresponding tool calls. It uses NTEP-R rewards and a non-repeated-goal regularizer to guide tool use, achieving improved search-oriented accuracy and tool-use efficiency on seven benchmarks with an 8B-parameter model (NTEP-8B).
AI.motivation: Current vision-language models often fail on complex queries that require fine-grained evidence or external knowledge. Standard training emphasizes final answer accuracy, neglecting the evidence acquisition process, which leads to redundant or off-target tool calls and poor information extraction from observations.
AI.method: Introduce NTEP (Necessary Tool-Evidence Path) annotations that specify the essential external evidence and the required tool calls for each query. Develop NTEP-R (NTEP Reward) to reward pre-call intent alignment with necessary evidence-seeking goals and post-call summaries aligned with the necessary evidence. Add a non-repeated-goal regularizer to penalize redundant tool calls. Evaluate within a three-tool framework (image cropping, image search, text search) using an 8B-parameter model (NTEP-8B).
AI.result: Across seven image-grounded benchmarks, NTEP-8B achieves notable gains in search-oriented accuracy and tool-use efficiency, demonstrating that fine-grained tool-evidence path supervision can robustly improve agentic VLM performance.
AI.conclusion: Explicit supervision of tool-evidence paths is valuable for training robust agentic VLMs. NTEP and NTEP-R provide a principled framework to align tool usage with necessary evidence, reduce redundant calls, and improve information extraction from observations, with potential for scaling to more tools and tasks.

title: Learnable composition for neural operators
summary: Neural operators are fast, differentiable surrogates for physical simulation, but their accuracy often degrades when domain geometry, size, or operating conditions differ from training. Supervised adaptation can recover accuracy, but even a small target set requires costly high-fidelity simulations. We therefore ask how pretraining and transfer can be designed together to reduce this deployment cost. LatentDDM first pretrains a neural operator to predict fields on small subdomains. For a new setting, it freezes this operator and trains only a lightweight module that composes the local predictions. We evaluate our method on two complementary problems: steady Darcy flow, where long-range pressure coupling must extend across increasingly large porous domains, and unsteady incompressible flow around a pitching airfoil, where rollout errors compound as target pitching frequencies exceed the training range. Compared with the capacity-matched models that process the full domain at once, LatentDDM's error is 36-56% lower on larger Darcy domains after adaptation with 16 target simulations. It also improves 20-step field rollouts in fast-pitching airfoil flow, both zero-shot and after few-shot calibration. These results identify the co-designed local pretraining and composition-level transfer as a promising design principle for physical foundation models.

AI.tldr: LatentDDM pretrains neural operators on small subdomains and uses a lightweight composition module to adapt to new settings, achieving substantial error reductions in Darcy flow and unsteady flow around a pitching airfoil with limited target simulations.
AI.motivation: Reduce deployment cost of neural operators when domain geometry, size, or operating conditions change; enable effective transfer with few-shot data.
AI.method: Pretrain on small subdomains; freeze operator; train a lightweight module that composes local predictions to produce full-domain outputs.
AI.result: 36-56% error reduction on larger Darcy domains after 16 target simulations; improved 20-step rollouts for fast-pitch airfoil flow, zero-shot and few-shot; two problems demonstrate generality; co-design principle.
AI.conclusion: Local pretraining plus composition-level transfer is a promising design principle for physical foundation models.

title: TRaIL-Odom: Tightly Coupled Continuous Time Radar-IMU-LiDAR Odometry with Adaptive Doppler Weighting
comment: Accepted for publication at the IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters on 23 August, 2026
summary: Existing radar-LiDAR fusion methods rely on fixed residual weights, even though the informativeness of radar Doppler and LiDAR geometry is scan- and direction-dependent, leading to uniform radar weighting that misallocates Doppler information across translational directions. To address this limitation, we propose two degeneracy-aware Doppler reweighting modules within a tightly coupled Radar-IMU-LiDAR odometry framework: per-point radar reweighting and scan-wise radar gain scheduling. Since geometric degeneracy is directional, we first identify weak translational directions from the LiDAR geometry and reweight individual radar Doppler constraints based on their alignment with the weak subspace. We further adjust the overall radar contribution using LiDAR geometric anisotropy such that radar is emphasized when LiDAR observability is poor and suppressed when LiDAR constraints are already reliable. Across 13 evaluated sequences, TRaIL-Odom achieves state-of-the-art overall performance, with clear advantages in geometrically degenerate scenes. In ablation experiments on three degenerate sequences, combining the two adaptive weighting modules reduces RMSE ATE and RTE by 86.0% and 78.5% relative to the fixed-weight baseline. We make our code and an accompanying dataset publicly available at https://github.com/ChiyunNoh/TRaIL-Odom.

AI.tldr: Two degeneracy-aware Doppler reweighting modules integrated into a Radar-IMU-LiDAR odometry system (TRaIL-Odom) to adaptively weight radar Doppler and contributions based on LiDAR observability; achieves state-of-the-art on 13 sequences, with large reductions in degenerate scenes; code/dataset released.
AI.motivation: Current radar-LiDAR fusion relies on fixed residual weights; radar Doppler informativeness is scan- and direction-dependent, causing misallocation of Doppler information across translational directions. Geometric degeneracy is directional, necessitating geometry-aware, adaptive weighting to improve fusion robustness.
AI.method: A tightly coupled Radar-IMU-LiDAR odometry framework augmented with two degeneracy-aware Doppler reweighting modules: (1) per-point radar reweighting, and (2) scan-wise radar gain scheduling. The approach first identifies weak translational directions from LiDAR geometry and reweights individual radar Doppler constraints by their alignment with the weak subspace. It then adjusts overall radar contribution using LiDAR geometric anisotropy to emphasize radar when LiDAR observability is poor and suppress it when LiDAR constraints are reliable. Evaluated on 13 sequences, with ablations on three degenerate sequences.
AI.result: TRaIL-Odom achieves state-of-the-art overall performance across 13 sequences, with clear advantages in geometrically degenerate scenes. In ablation experiments on three degenerate sequences, combining the two adaptive weighting modules reduces RMSE ATE and RTE by 86.0% and 78.5% relative to a fixed-weight baseline.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive, degeneracy-aware radar weighting within a Radar-IMU-LiDAR odometry framework effectively mitigates fixed-weight limitations, yielding robust performance gains in geometrically degenerate environments; the authors also release code and a dataset publicly.

title: Counting Animals in Camera-Traps Image Sequences without Count Labels: Winning Solution to the iWildCam 2021 Challenge
summary: Camera traps have become an essential tool for wildlife monitoring, motivating the development of computer vision methods for the automated extraction of information from these data. While most prior work has focused on species identification, many ecological applications also require estimating the number of unique individuals appearing across short image sequences. This task is particularly challenging because camera traps typically acquire bursts of images at approximately one frame per second, creating large temporal discontinuities that may make conventional multi-object tracking methods unreliable, and because manually collecting individual count annotations is prohibitively expensive. In this work, we describe the winning solution to the iWildCam 2021 Challenge, which introduced a benchmark for counting animals at the sequence level under realistic annotation constraints where count annotations are unavailable for training. Our approach, MaxBoxCount, combines a strong species classification pipeline with a simple yet effective counting heuristic based on MegaDetector detections to estimate the number of unique individuals without requiring count annotations. Code is available at https://github.com/alcunha/iwildcam2021ufam.

AI.tldr: A count-estimation method for camera-trap sequences that imputes unique individuals without per-frame counts, winning iWildCam 2021; MaxBoxCount uses species classifier + MegaDetector-based counting.
AI.motivation: In camera-trap data, counting unique individuals across short image bursts is hard due to temporal discontinuities and lack of count annotations; there is a need for annotation-efficient counting methods.
AI.method: MaxBoxCount: a two-part approach combining a strong species classifier with a counting heuristic based on MegaDetector detections to estimate the number of unique individuals across a sequence without count annotations.
AI.result: Achieved winning solution on the iWildCam 2021 Challenge; code available at GitHub.
AI.conclusion: Shows that simple, detector-based counting, paired with robust species classification, can effectively estimate abundance in camera-trap data under limited supervision.

title: GrowPage: On-Demand KV Budgeting for Efficient LLM Reasoning Serving
summary: Long-output reasoning has made the key--value (KV) cache a critical memory bottleneck for efficient LLM serving. Existing KV compression methods usually rely on a predefined per-request budget and adjust only which KV states are retained, leaving the total capacity fixed throughout decoding. However, reasoning workloads exhibit substantial demand variation: different requests require different KV capacities, and the attention demand of an individual request evolves during generation. We introduce \textbf{GrowPage}, an on-demand KV budgeting framework that treats KV capacity as a runtime resource. GrowPage maintains lightweight dual-timescale query summaries to capture recent and long-term attention behaviors, and uses their relative attention working sets to estimate demand evolution. At each capacity boundary, GrowPage either compresses KV states within the current allocation or acquires an additional physical page when broader demand emerges. By integrating with PagedAttention's page-level memory abstraction, GrowPage preserves continuous batching and prefix caching. Experiments on reasoning benchmarks across multiple models show that GrowPage achieves a superior performance--throughput trade-off over existing approaches.
