AI.tldr: GrowPage enables on-demand KV cache budgeting for LLMs, dynamically resizing KV capacity during decoding using dual-timescale summaries and page-level memory integration to improve throughput under varying reasoning loads.
AI.motivation: KV cache memory is a key bottleneck in scalable LLM serving. Existing KV compression fixes capacity per request, but reasoning workloads exhibit variable demand and evolving attention during generation, necessitating runtime resource reallocation.
AI.method: GrowPage maintains lightweight dual-timescale query summaries to capture recent and long-term attention behavior, uses their relative attention working sets to estimate demand evolution, and at each capacity boundary either compresses KV states within the current allocation or acquires an additional physical page. It integrates with PagedAttention's page-level memory abstraction to preserve continuous batching and prefix caching.
AI.result: Empirical evaluations on reasoning benchmarks across multiple models show a superior performance–throughput trade-off compared with existing approaches.
AI.conclusion: On-demand KV budgeting with a page-level memory abstraction improves efficiency and adaptability for dynamic reasoning workloads in LLM serving.

title: LeanStream: A Speculate-and-Refine Streaming Framework for Efficient on-Device LLM Inference
comment: 6 pages, 13 figures. To appear in the Proceedings of the 32nd Annual International Conference on Mobile Computing and Networking (MobiCom '26)
summary: On-device LLM inference is attractive for privacy and responsiveness, but remains challenging on mobile and embedded devices because model weights far exceed available DRAM. Prior systems exploit activation sparsity and offload weights to SSD or flash storage, but face a fundamental systems trade-off: accurate sparse execution decisions require the latest context, whereas efficient computation-I/O overlap requires early prediction. As a result, existing designs either serialize execution or incur redundant weight fetches, extra computation, and large cache overheads. We present LeanStream, a streaming speculate-and-refine framework for efficient on-device LLM inference. LeanStream progressively refines computation, loading, and cache-retention priorities using partial GPU results, enabling fine-grained overlap between GPU execution and storage I/O. We implement LeanStream on both mobile and embedded platforms. Compared with prior on-device LLM inference systems, LeanStream reduces memory usage by 4.8$\times$ to 7.5$\times$ at the best throughput achieved by prior work, while further improving token generation throughput by 1.6$\times$ to 2.1$\times$.

AI.tldr: LeanStream is a streaming speculate-and-refine framework that enables efficient on-device LLM inference by overlapping GPU execution with I/O and progressively refining computation, loading, and cache retention based on partial results, achieving substantial memory savings and throughput gains on mobile and embedded devices.
AI.motivation: On-device LLM inference is constrained by large model weights that exceed available DRAM in mobile/embedded devices. Activation sparsity and I/O bottlenecks force trade-offs between accurate sparse execution decisions and early prediction, leading to serialized execution or redundant fetches and cache overhead in previous systems.
AI.method: A streaming speculate-and-refine approach that uses partial GPU results to progressively refine computation, loading, and cache-retention priorities, enabling fine-grained overlap between GPU computation and storage I/O. Implemented on both mobile and embedded platforms.
AI.result: Compared to prior on-device LLM inference systems, LeanStream reduces peak memory usage by 4.8×–7.5× at best throughput and increases token generation throughput by 1.6×–2.1×.
AI.conclusion: LeanStream effectively enables memory-efficient, high-throughput on-device LLM inference by enabling speculative, overlapped computation and I/O, with confirmed gains on mobile and embedded platforms.

title: Toward Physically Grounded JEPA World Models for Goal-Conditioned Robotic Planning
comment: 5 pages, 4 figures, 2 tables. Accepted to the IROS 2026 Workshop on Physical World Models for Scaling Embodied AI (PWMS 2026)
summary: Action-conditioned JEPA world models enable planning toward visually specified goals without reconstructing future pixels, yet latent prediction alone does not explicitly encourage the learned representations to retain information relevant to robotic control. We introduce an end-to-end JEPA world model that augments latent prediction with inverse dynamics (IDM) and state alignment (SA). While inverse dynamics discourages latent collapse and makes latent transitions informative of the actions that produced them, state alignment grounds consecutive representations in their associated physical configuration and motion. Across four benchmark tasks, our model attains the highest success rates on TwoRoom (100%), PushT (98%), and OGBench-Cube (87%), while performing comparably to LeWorldModel on Reacher. Our ablation further shows that adding state alignment consistently improves planning success over IDM alone across all four tasks. Although LeWorldModel, our primary baseline, attains higher average straightening on OGBench-Cube, transition-subspace analysis shows that its transition energy is concentrated in a substantially lower-dimensional subspace. Our state-aligned model exhibits a higher effective transition dimension than LeWorldModel and improves planning over IDM alone, supporting state alignment as an effective complement to inverse dynamics for robotic planning.

AI.tldr: An end-to-end JEPA world model augmented with inverse dynamics and state alignment improves planning for robotic control beyond latent prediction alone; SA complements IDM, yielding strong task performance and richer transition dynamics.
AI.motivation: Latent-prediction JEPA models risk latent collapse and loss of control-relevant information. Augmenting with inverse dynamics (to keep transitions informative about actions) and state alignment (to ground representations in physical configuration) aims to preserve control-relevant structure for planning.
AI.method: Extend JEPA with two modules—inverse dynamics model (IDM) and state alignment (SA)—trained end-to-end across four benchmarks (TwoRoom, PushT, OGBench-Cube, Reacher). Compare against LeWorldModel; perform ablations removing IDM or SA; analyze transition properties.
AI.result: Proposed model achieves top-1 success rates: TwoRoom 100%, PushT 98%, OGBench-Cube 87%; Reacher on par with LeWorldModel. Ablation shows SA consistently improves planning over IDM alone. LeWorldModel has higher mean straightening on OGBench-Cube, but transition-energy distribution is focused in a much lower-dimensional subspace; the state-aligned model shows higher effective transition dimension and better planning.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating state alignment with inverse dynamics enhances the informativeness and grounding of latent representations for control, providing a robust complement to IDM that improves planning performance across tasks and yields a richer transition structure than IDM alone.

title: An Ensemble-Based Self-Taught Learning Approach for Parking Space Classification Under Limited Data
summary: Parking spot classification is a fundamental task in intelligent transportation systems, yet most deep learning approaches rely on large amounts of annotated data and exhibit limited generalization across heterogeneous environments. To address these limitations, we investigate a self-taught learning framework based on unsupervised representation learning with convolutional autoencoders. The proposed approach learns transferable visual representations from unlabeled data and reuses the learned encoders as fixed feature extractors for supervised classification with limited annotated samples in the target domain. To further enhance robustness and mitigate architectural bias, an ensemble of heterogeneous autoencoders is employed, with independent classifier heads and prediction fusion at inference time. Experiments conducted on the PKLot and CNRPark benchmarks under cross-dataset evaluation protocols show that the proposed ensemble-based strategy substantially reduces annotation requirements while improving robustness under significant domain shifts, achieving accuracies between 93\% and 96\% in data-constrained scenarios.

AI.tldr: Unsupervised transfer learning via an ensemble of heterogeneous convolutional autoencoders for parking-spot classification, achieving 93–96% accuracy with limited labels across cross-dataset evaluation on PKLot and CNRPark.
AI.motivation: Address data scarcity and significant domain shift in parking-spot classification by learning transferable representations from unlabeled data, reducing annotation burden.
AI.method: Train convolutional autoencoders unsupervisedly to learn encoders; reuse learned encoders as fixed feature extractors for supervised classification with limited annotations; employ an ensemble of heterogeneous autoencoders with independent classifier heads and fuse predictions at inference; evaluate using cross-dataset protocols on PKLot and CNRPark.
AI.result: The ensemble approach reduces annotation requirements and enhances robustness to domain shifts, achieving accuracies between 93% and 96% in data-constrained scenarios on PKLot and CNRPark benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Ensemble self-taught learning with fixed encoders can deliver strong cross-domain performance for parking-spot classification while lowering labeling needs, highlighting the value of representation transfer and architectural diversity.

title: PPO-STGNN: A Proximal Policy Optimization Approach with Spatio-Temporal Graph Neural Networks for DAG Task Scheduling in Cloud-Edge-End Computing
summary: With the rapid development of the Internet of Things, computation intensive directed acyclic graph (DAG) tasks have become increasingly common in cloud-edge-end collaborative environments. However, cloud, edge, and end nodes are highly heterogeneous in computing capacity, network bandwidth, and energy consumption, which makes the efficient scheduling of tasks with complex dependencies an NP-hard problem. Traditional heuristic algorithms and conventional reinforcement-learning methods often fail to capture the spatio-temporal dynamics of system resources. This paper proposes PPO-STGNN, a DAG task-scheduling algorithm that integrates proximal policy optimization (PPO) with spatio-temporal graph neural networks (STGNNs). The method uses an STGNN to extract features from both the DAG task topology and the physical cloud-edge-end resource graph, and then optimizes the scheduling policy through PPO to minimize makespan and schedule length ratio (SLR) while improving CPU and memory load balancing. To accelerate convergence, a multi-teacher behavior-cloning mechanism is introduced for pretraining. Experimental results show that PPO-STGNN significantly improves load balancing while maintaining a low completion time, making it suitable for dynamic and heterogeneous cloud-edge- end DAG scheduling scenarios.

AI.tldr: A PPO-STGNN framework for DAG task scheduling in heterogeneous cloud–edge–end systems, combining spatio-temporal graph networks with proximal policy optimization, plus multi-teacher pretraining; improves load balancing with competitive makespan.
AI.motivation: Scheduling DAG tasks across heterogeneous devices is NP-hard; existing heuristics and RL struggle to capture spatio-temporal resource dynamics; a representation that combines topology and resource graph is needed.
AI.method: Extract features using STGNN from DAG topology and resource graph; optimize scheduling policy with PPO; pretrain with multi-teacher behavior cloning to accelerate convergence.
AI.result: Significant improvement in CPU/memory load balancing and scheduling efficiency; maintains low completion time; effective for dynamic, heterogeneous DAG scheduling.
AI.conclusion: PPO-STGNN offers a capable, scalable approach for cloud–edge–end DAG scheduling by jointly modeling structure and resources; could be extended to other dynamic heterogeneity settings.

title: The Gradient Does Not See Rank: Rank-Indifference in Matrix-CODI on ProsQA
comment: Accepted at the ICML 2026 Mechanistic Interpretability Workshop, https://openreview.net/forum?id=Spof4PusVI. 9 pages. Corrects a data-entry error in the workshop version: the seed-1337 accuracy in the three-seed replication was reported as 80.47% (a control run); the archived value is 78.91%, so the three-seed mean is 81.0 +/- 2.0pp (was 81.5 +/- 1.2pp). All other results are unchanged
summary: Continuous chain-of-thought models compress reasoning into latent tokens. Matrix-valued variants, which route each latent token through a d x d matrix bottleneck, introduce rank as a single-sample structural observable on the latent matrix Z. If matrix latents carry parallel reasoning paths via superposition, rank should track them, and truncating Z to low rank should hurt accuracy on tasks whose solutions plausibly require multiple components. Across four training regimes of a matrix-CODI model (three on ProsQA, one on GSM8K-Aug below the learning threshold), the rank-k projection ablation curve is flat to within 0.6 percentage points. A three-seed replication yields 81.0 +/- 2.0 percentage points accuracy while the final effective rank of Z spans {4, 12, 13}; the loss does not reward any particular rank. To test whether rank-blindness arises from the flatten-then-project readout alone, we trained four readouts: a bilinear reparametrization, a bilinear-plus-GELU readout nonlinear in Z, an SVD-augmented readout feeding singular values through an MLP, and a quadratic readout in Z Z^T. All four rank-k curves remain flat (Spearman p-values 0.63, 0.14, 0.82, 0.46). The flat curves persist for readouts nonlinear in Z. A linear probe on Z underperforms a raw pretrained hidden state at target prediction (AUC 0.673 vs. 0.846). A negative control on vanilla GPT-2 SFT (no matrix bottleneck, no Z, three seeds, n=500) reproduces a flat rank-k curve under the same intervention paradigm with pooled-mean range 0.20pp, and a random-h sensitivity floor lands at the same accuracy: the rank-k ablation alone conflates rank-blindness with position-irrelevance.

AI.tldr: Matrix-valued latent Z in matrix-CODI shows rank-blindness; rank-k truncations do not degrade accuracy; multiple readouts and a linear probe do not reveal rank-based performance differences; a negative control reproduces flat rank curves.
AI.motivation: To test whether rank is a meaningful structural observable for latent matrix representations in continuous chain-of-thought models and whether truncating to low rank harms tasks requiring multiple components.
AI.method: Train matrix-CODI across four regimes (three on ProsQA, one GSM8K-Aug below learning threshold). Apply rank-k projection on Z; three seeds; measure accuracy; test four readout schemes (bilinear, bilinear+GELU, SVD-augmented with MLP, quadratic Z Z^T); test linear probe on Z; perform negative control with vanilla GPT-2 SFT (no matrix bottleneck, no Z, three seeds, n=500); report Spearman p-values for rank-k curves and compare to random-h baseline; datasets/tasks as described.
AI.result: Rank-k ablation curves are flat within ~0.6 percentage points; final effective rank values across regimes span {4,12,13}; no single rank is rewarded; all four readouts maintain flat rank-k curves (Spearman p-values: 0.63, 0.14, 0.82, 0.46); linear probe on Z underperforms raw hidden state (AUC 0.673 vs. 0.846); negative control reproduces flat rank-k curve with pooled mean range 0.20pp; random-h sensitivity floor aligns with the achieved accuracy; rank-blindness conflates with position-irrelevance.
AI.conclusion: The latent Z rank in matrix-CODI does not serve as a reliable proxy for multi-component reasoning; rank-based interventions do not affect performance, indicating that the model utilizes information beyond simple rank-based compression; alternative diagnostics are needed to capture potential parallel reasoning paths.

title: Scaling Bimanual Household Manipulation from 1,500 hours of Demonstrations to On-Policy Corrections
summary: Learning generalist policies for robust bimanual manipulation is bottlenecked by the scarcity of high quality large scale human demonstration data. In this work, we release 1,500 hours of diverse bimanual manipulation demonstrations covering everyday household tasks, and use this comprehensive corpus to train XR-2, a powerful vision-language-action (VLA) model. Enabled by a purpose built high throughput data pipeline and a carefully designed multi stage training paradigm, XR-2 attains strong manipulation performance in our systematic experiments while retaining favorable training efficiency and high data utilization. We further study two critical scaling axes: varying the amount of expert demonstration data, and post training on DAgger correction data from real time human interventions. In both settings, task success rate improves steadily over the data ranges we probe, exhibiting a clear consistent scaling trend at our current data scale. These results validate both the learning capacity of XR-2 and the promising scaling properties of the released dataset, which we open source to support reproducible research on bimanual robot manipulation learning.

AI.tldr: Train XR-2 on 1,500 hours of diverse bimanual demonstrations to learn a robust vision-language-action policy; shows scalable improvements with more data and DAgger corrections; dataset released as open source for reproducible research.
AI.motivation: Address the scarcity of high-quality large-scale human demonstrations for generalist bimanipulation policies and enable scalable, reproducible research.
AI.method: Develop XR-2, a vision-language-action model, trained via a high-throughput data pipeline and a multi-stage training paradigm on a 1,500-hour bimanual dataset; assess scaling along two axes: amount of expert demonstrations and post-training with DAgger corrections from real-time human interventions.
AI.result: XR-2 achieves strong manipulation performance with efficient training and high data utilization; task success rate scales steadily with more data and with DAgger corrections; dataset is open-sourced to support reproducible research.
AI.conclusion: XR-2 demonstrates learning capacity and favorable scaling properties; the released dataset enables reproducible research and further scaling in bimanual manipulation.

title: MedQA-MM: Shortcuts Behind Medical Visual Reasoning
summary: A benchmark score credits final answers, but not the route by which an item can be answered. In medical multimodal multiple-choice questions (MCQs), this distinction matters because a correct answer can be supported by the intended image finding or by benchmark-preserved cues in the wording of answers, non-visual clinical text, visible image text, artificial annotations, or device/context artifacts. We call the resulting score-level overinterpretation reasoning inflation. Here, a route is an observable input path that can support answer selection, not a claim about the model's hidden cognition. Across six medical multimodal MCQ datasets, we separate candidate cues from behavioral evidence through prompt- and image-side audits, modality ablations, and matched repairs that preserve the medical target and answer key. In a 13-configuration open-model panel, full-input accuracy is 62.63%, while text-only and options-only settings achieve 53.96% and 29.71%, respectively. Removing length-gap, absolute/conspicuous, and spatial/prepositional cues lowers accuracy by 6.58, 3.50, and 4.77 percentage points. We also construct MedQA-MM, a 1,000-item shortcut-mitigated subset, where text-only and options-only accuracy fall to 5.21% and 12.33%. This does not imply that models never use images; it shows that medical image-reasoning claims require route-level evidence.

AI.tldr: Benchmarks for medical multimodal MCQs can inflate performance by rewarding shortcut cues rather than true image-based reasoning; authors separate cues from evidence via audits and ablations across six datasets; results show substantial reliance on non-visual cues and need route-level evidence for image reasoning claims.
AI.motivation: To address route-level overinterpretation in multimodal medical AI evaluations and quantify how much current benchmarks rely on non-visual cues.
AI.method: Multi-dataset analysis with prompt- and image-side audits, modality ablations (text-only, options-only, full), and matched repairs; 13-configuration panel; MedQA-MM subset focusing on shortcut mitigation.
AI.result: Full-input accuracy 62.63%; text-only 53.96%; options-only 29.71%. Removing cues reduces accuracy by 6.58, 3.50, 4.77 points. MedQA-MM shows 5.21% text-only and 12.33% options-only. Image reasoning claims require route-level evidence.
AI.conclusion: Benchmark scores alone can misrepresent true multimodal reasoning; need route-level verification and caution in interpreting model capabilities.

title: What Matters for Aggressive Decoding-Time KV Eviction? Temporal Aggregation and Ranking Preservation
summary: Decoding-time KV cache compression research focuses heavily on designing better token scoring functions, while the temporal rule that aggregates scores across decode steps is often treated as an implementation detail. Under aggressive KV compression, we find that exponential-moving-average (EMA) aggregation makes approximately order-preserving scorer modifications largely indistinguishable at the eviction-set level. Value-norm and entropy variants remain highly correlated with attention and produce nearly unchanged retention sets, whereas KeyDiff, key norm, recency, and a learned scorer alter the ranking and degrade substantially. We associate this stability with the evaluated aggregation, which couples layer weighting and temporal retention. Building on this observation, we introduce InertiaKV, an EMA-based decoding-time eviction method, and InertiaKV-Lazy, its periodic-refresh variant, which yields 1.34-1.46x decode throughput relative to full refresh InertiaKV. We also study Score-Free decoding as a separate empirical operating point: it scores the full context once at the first decode step, freezes that ranking, and incurs an average quality change of +0.03 while removing all subsequent scoring. Across six open-weight backbones and the LongBench, LongBench-v2, and RULER benchmarks, the results identify temporal aggregation and ranking preservation as distinct, consequential design factors; they do not imply that scoring quality is irrelevant in general.

AI.tldr: EMA-based decoding-time eviction (InertiaKV) enables efficient KV-cache compression by preserving temporal ranking; Periodic-refresh (InertiaKV-Lazy) yields 1.34–1.46x decode throughput vs full refresh. Score-Free decoding offers another trade-off with small quality loss. Temporal aggregation and ranking preservation emerge as consequential design factors beyond scoring function quality.
AI.motivation: To reassess decoding-time KV-cache compression beyond token-scoring quality, focusing on how temporal aggregation across decode steps and eviction decisions affect performance under aggressive KV compression.
AI.method: Propose InertiaKV, an EMA-based eviction strategy for decoding-time KV cache; add InertiaKV-Lazy with periodic refresh; compare against full-refresh InertiaKV and Score-Free decoding (rank once at step 1, freeze ranking); evaluate on six open-weight backbones across LongBench, LongBench-v2, and RULER benchmarks.
AI.result: Under aggressive KV compression, EMA aggregation makes order-preserving scorer modifications largely indistinguishable at the eviction-set level; value-norm and entropy variants stay highly correlated with attention and retain sets; KeyDiff, key norm, recency, and learned scorers degrade due to altered ranking; InertiaKV achieves 1.34–1.46x throughput relative to full refresh InertiaKV; Score-Free decoding changes quality on average by +0.03 while eliminating subsequent scoring; across six backbones and benchmarks, temporal aggregation and ranking preservation emerge as distinct, consequential factors, though scoring quality remains relevant in general.
AI.conclusion: Temporal aggregation and ranking preservation are key design factors in decoding-time KV cache compression. EMA-based eviction can deliver substantial throughput gains with modest quality impact, while Score-Free decoding offers an alternative operational point. The findings generalize across multiple backbones and benchmarks, underscoring the importance of temporal dynamics alongside scoring quality.

title: Distilling deep optical flow stereo methods to retrieve dense three-dimensional wind fields
summary: Geostationary atmospheric motion vectors (AMVs) provide the dense horizontal wind vectors (u,v) and heights ingested into data assimilation systems. Traditional AMVs track features using window-based cross-correlation and estimate heights via infrared brightness temperatures paired with numerical weather prediction (NWP) background states, creating a circular dependency that yields inaccurate heights, high computational cost, and sparse retrievals. Stereo winds from GEO-GEO and GEO-LEO geometrically resolve heights from parallax shifts across different poses, eliminating NWP dependence and improving accuracy, but they remain computationally heavy with limited coverage. In this work, we replace window-based tracking in stereo matching with deep optical flow for efficient, improved retrieval. Fine-tuning balances a self-supervised geometric residual loss with supervised radiosonde reconstruction. To eliminate multi-satellite overlap requirements, we distill the stereo teacher into a single-satellite student model. Chi-square and height uncertainties from the teacher are emulated by the student for quality assurance. The student generates winds across full-disk GEO imagery globally. Validation compares stereo and student models against radiosondes, operational AMVs, ERA5 reanalysis, and EarthCARE cloud profiles. Results through triple collocation show that stereo winds improve performance beyond operational AMVs for water vapor bands (6.2, 6.9, and 7.3 μm), wit degradation in the long-wave infrared (11.2 μm) band.

AI.tldr: Stereo geostationary wind retrievals replace window-based AMV tracking with deep optical flow in a GEO-GEO/ GEO-LEO setup, enabling height resolution without NWP. A stereo teacher is distilled into a single-satellite student to remove multi-satellite overlap needs. The approach yields globally available winds and improves accuracy in water vapor bands, with some degradation in the 11.2 μm band; validation via triple collocation against radiosondes, operational AMVs, ERA5, and EarthCARE.
AI.motivation: Overcome circular dependencies in traditional AMV height estimation (IR brightness temperatures tied to NWP), address high computational cost and sparse retrievals of stereo winds, and achieve full-disk, high-coverage wind fields with robust height estimates.
AI.method: Replace window-based tracking with deep optical flow for stereo matching. Train with a self-supervised geometric residual loss and supervised radiosonde reconstruction. Distill the stereo teacher into a single-satellite student to remove the need for multi-satellite overlap. The student mimics teacher-provided chi-square and height uncertainties to enable quality assurance and produces winds across the full GEO disk.
AI.result: Validation against radiosondes, operational AMVs, ERA5, and EarthCARE cloud profiles. Triple collocation shows stereo winds outperform operational AMVs for water vapor bands (6.2, 6.9, 7.3 μm); performance degrades for the 11.2 μm long-wave infrared band.
AI.conclusion: Deep-learning–assisted stereo GEO winds can surpass traditional AMVs in accuracy for key infrared bands while offering complete global coverage, made feasible for single-satellite deployment via teacher-student distillation; note band-dependent performance and need for further exploration of coverage and uncertainty handling.

title: FailBench: How Reliable are VLMs at Judging Robot Task Success?
summary: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) are increasingly used to evaluate robot manipulation outcomes, but existing benchmarks offer limited evidence of cross-domain generalization. We introduce FailBench, a benchmark for robot failure detection comprising 2,197 manipulation attempts across 14 public sources (12 real-world, 2 simulated). In FailBench, 75% of failures occur naturally, and six real-world sources come from non-failure-detection datasets. Evaluating 13 VLM-based detectors, we find the best model achieves only 0.77 mean balanced accuracy. Notably, models fine-tuned for failure detection consistently underperform general-purpose VLMs and their own pretrained baselines. Performance depends heavily on required visual evidence: models approach saturation when outcomes depend on observable object motion, but degrade to near-chance (<0.60 balanced accuracy) on contact-intensive assembly tasks. Error analysis reveals a systematic bias toward predicting success under ambiguous evidence, which persists even with increased reasoning effort. Finally, we show that input-level intervention--spatially localizing and cropping outcome-relevant regions--improves the top detector by 2.4 percentage points without extra training.

AI.tldr: FailBench reveals limited cross-domain generalization of VLMs for robot failure detection; best mean balanced accuracy is 0.77 across 13 detectors, with modest gains from input localization; failure-specific fine-tuning underperforms general-purpose VLMs and pretrained baselines; performance varies by evidence type, and the task remains challenging.
AI.motivation: To assess how well vision-language models generalize to fail-detection in robot manipulation across diverse real-world and simulated domains, addressing a gap where existing benchmarks offer limited cross-domain evidence.
AI.method: Construct FailBench with 2,197 manipulation attempts from 14 public sources (12 real-world, 2 simulated); include six real-world sources from non-failure-detection datasets; evaluate 13 VLM-based detectors; measure mean balanced accuracy; analyze error patterns and the effect of input-level interventions by spatially cropping outcome-relevant regions to assess performance gains without additional training.
AI.result: Best detector achieves 0.77 mean balanced accuracy. Failure-focused fine-tuning underperforms general-purpose VLMs and pretrained baselines. Performance hinges on visual evidence: high when observable object motion suffices, but near-chance (<0.60) on contact-intensive assembly tasks. Error analysis shows a bias toward predicting success under ambiguity, persisting with more reasoning. Input-level localization and cropping improves the top detector by 2.4 percentage points without extra training.
AI.conclusion: VLMs exhibit limited cross-domain generalization for robot failure detection; naive fine-tuning for failure detection is ineffective relative to base VLMs; spatially localized input cues can yield small but meaningful performance gains, yet overall the problem remains challenging and highly task-dependent.

title: Tensor-based Brain Surface Modeling and Analysis
summary: We present a unified computational approach to tensor-based morphometry in detecting the brain surface shape differences between two clinical groups based on magnetic resonance images. Our approach is novel in a sense that we combined surface modeling, surface data smoothing and statistical analysis in a coherent unified mathematical framework. The cerebral cortex has the topology of a 2D highly convoluted sheet. Between two different clinical groups, the local surface area and curvature of the cortex may differ. It is highly likely that such surface shape differences are not uniform over the whole cortex. By computing how such surface metrics differ, the regions of the most rapid structural differences can be localized. To increase the signal to noise ratio, diffusion smoothing based on the explicit estimation of Laplace-Beltrami operator has been developed and applied to the surface metrics. As an illustration, we demonstrate how this new tensor-based surface morphometry can be applied in localizing the cortical regions of the gray matter tissue growth and loss in the brain images longitudinally collected in the group of children.

AI.tldr: A unified computational framework for tensor-based surface morphometry detects cortical surface shape differences between two groups from MRI, integrating surface modeling, diffusion smoothing via the Laplace-Beltrami operator, and statistics; illustrated by localizing gray matter growth and loss in longitudinal pediatric data.
AI.motivation: Cortical surface geometry differences are localized and nonuniform; effective detection requires preserving surface topology, enhancing signal-to-noise on surface metrics, and localizing changes rather than averaging over the entire cortex.
AI.method: A unified mathematical framework combining cortex surface modeling, surface data smoothing using diffusion on the Laplace-Beltrami operator, and statistical analysis to compare local surface metrics (area, curvature) between groups; enables localization of regions with rapid shape differences; applied to longitudinal pediatric MRI.
AI.result: Demonstrates localization of cortical regions with gray matter growth and loss in longitudinal brain images of children using the proposed tensor-based surface morphometry approach.
AI.conclusion: The approach provides a cohesive, surface-aware method to detect and localize cortical shape differences between groups, with potential for tracking developmental changes and disease-related morphometry over time.

title: CulturalMenuBench: Probing the Knowledge-Application Gap in Multimodal Culinary Reasoning
comment: Accepted to EMNLP 2026 Findings. Code and data: https://github.com/BobTsang-NLP/CulturalMenuBench
summary: Multimodal language models achieve near-ceiling scores on food recognition benchmarks, yet it remains unclear whether this success reflects genuine cultural understanding or mere visual matching. To probe this distinction, we introduce CulturalMenuBench, a benchmark of 4,870 items in 10 languages across 18 regions; its 10 tasks pair final-dish and step-by-step cooking images with ingredients, procedural text, and regional labels, spanning basic recognition to process-grounded cultural attribution. Evaluating 12 models exposes a substantial knowledge-application gap: models exceeding 94% on standard multiple-choice tasks drop to at most 56% when attributing dishes to Chinese regional cuisines, despite an identical four-way format. Diagnostic analyses explain why: error patterns are consistent with random guessing, accuracy tracks visual distinctiveness rather than cultural structure, and models classify cuisines more accurately from dish names alone than from images (+7-18 points). The knowledge is thus present but cannot be activated through visual input. An ablation confirms these tasks genuinely require procedural evidence: removing sequential cooking images selectively degrades process-grounded tasks while others remain stable. Overall, CulturalMenuBench shows that near-perfect recognition can conceal an inability to apply cultural knowledge, motivating training that explicitly connects perception, procedure, and cultural context. Code and data are publicly available.

AI.tldr: A new benchmark, CulturalMenuBench, reveals a knowledge-application gap in multimodal language models: high recognition accuracy on standard tasks does not translate into cultural attribution or procedural understanding across cuisines.
AI.motivation: To determine whether multimodal models truly understand cultural knowledge or merely perform visual matching, by testing across language and regional dimensions with tasks requiring diet, procedure, and cultural context.
AI.method: Introduce CulturalMenuBench with 4,870 items across 10 languages and 18 regions, 10 tasks pairing final-dish and step-by-step cooking visuals with ingredients, procedural text, and regional labels. Evaluate 12 models; perform ablations to isolate the role of sequential images in process-grounded tasks.
AI.result: Even models scoring >94% on standard MC tasks drop to at most 56% when attributing dishes to Chinese regional cuisines. Error patterns resemble random guessing; accuracy aligns with visual distinctiveness rather than cultural structure; cuisine classification from dish names outperforms image-based classification by 7–18 points. Removing sequential cooking images degrades process-grounded tasks while other tasks remain stable.
AI.conclusion: Knowledge of cuisines exists in models but cannot be activated through visual input alone; training should explicitly connect perception, procedural evidence, and cultural context. Code and data are publicly available to support further research.

title: Scaling Laws, Tabular Data and Actuarial Ratemaking Models
summary: Scaling laws in modern deep learning describe how held-out loss improves as model capacity, training data, and compute increase, often following power-law trends. We investigate whether analogous scaling regularities arise in actuarial ratemaking, where data are tabular, heterogeneous, and noisy, and where classical models such as GLMs remain strong baselines. Using a real-world motor insurance portfolio, we train models from different families across increasing fractions of the training data and multiple random seeds, evaluating out-of-sample Poisson deviance, a likelihood-based loss for Poisson count predictions in which lower values indicate better held-out fit. We find that all model families improve with additional data, but scaling exponents differ substantially: TabM exhibits markedly stronger data scaling than purely supervised tabular Transformers and standard MLP baselines. Transformer variants show weak parameter scaling unless augmented with additional inductive biases (TabM-style adaptation or self-supervision). These results provide quantitative guidance on model selection by data regime and suggest that effective scaling on actuarial tabular tasks depends on architecture and loss function objective design, with simple increases in Transformer size providing limited gains.

AI.tldr: Tabular models show stronger data scaling than Transformers for actuarial tasks; simple Transformer scaling yields limited gains unless inductive biases or self-supervision are used; model choice should consider data regime and loss design.
AI.motivation: Assess whether deep-learning scaling laws generalize to actuarial tabular data and compare model families (TabM, tabular Transformers, MLPs) against GLMs on a real motor insurance portfolio.
AI.method: Train multiple model families on increasing fractions of the training data with multiple seeds; evaluate out-of-sample Poisson deviance for count predictions in a real-world motor insurance dataset.
AI.result: All model families improve with more data; TabM shows markedly stronger data scaling than Transformer or MLP baselines. Transformer variants exhibit weak parameter scaling unless augmented with TabM-style adaptation or self-supervision.
AI.conclusion: Scaling behavior in actuarial tabular tasks depends on architecture and loss design; simple increases in Transformer size yield limited gains; guidance on model choice should account for data regime and bias-inducing mechanisms to achieve effective scaling.

title: QLAUN: A Research-Oriented, Robust, Agile, Modular, and Affordable Torque-Controlled Quadruped Robot
comment: Extended abstract presented at IEEE ICRA@40, Rotterdam, Netherlands, September 2024. 2 pages, 1 figure
summary: QLAUN Bot (Quad-Legged Adaptive Unmanned Navigator Robot) is a torque-controlled quadruped robot that is research-oriented, cost-effective, and aimed at achieving simultaneous robustness and agility while being completely 3D-printed. It is a quadruped robot that is aimed at empowering robotics research at universities and research institutes in Lebanon and the MENA region. Using a novel electronics-free leg design strategy, we present a modular robot with interchangeable and easily replaceable legs. The 15 kg robot possesses 12 DoF (Degrees-of-Freedom) with three per leg, each paired with a completely 3D-printed Quasi-Direct Drive (QDD) actuator that consists of a brushless DC motor and a low-ratio gearbox transmission that is connected to a belt transmission system for significantly increasing the torque outputs at the joints. We present legs that have decoupled hip and knee actuators to improve the overall modularity of the robot. QLAUN is almost completely 3D-printed using polylactic acid (PLA) and assembled using off-the-shelf parts to create a robust, agile, and affordable robot for legged robot locomotion research. The legs possess joints with wide ranges of motion, including a continuous hip flexion-extension joint. A compliant foot, printed using TPU-95A is also implemented for alleviating hard impacts and handling terrain uncertainties. This extended abstract aims to introduce QLAUN, a novel platform for robotics research, emphasizing the design concepts and principles that underpin its development to the academic and research communities in the field of robotics.

AI.tldr: A modular, 3D-printed, torque-controlled quadruped robot (QLAUN) designed for research in Lebanon/MENA, featuring interchangeable legs, quasi-direct-drive actuators, decoupled hip/knee joints, compliant TPU foot, and electronics-free leg design concept for accessibility and rapid prototyping.
AI.motivation: To enable robust and agile legged locomotion research in universities and research institutes in Lebanon and the MENA region with a cost-effective, easily replaceable leg design and a modular, largely 3D-printed platform.
AI.method: A 15 kg quadruped with 12 DoF (3 per leg) employing 3D-printed QDD actuators (brushless motor + low-ratio gearbox + belt transmission) and decoupled hip and knee actuators. Legs are designed to be interchangeable with an electronics-free strategy, constructed mainly from PLA and assembled from off-the-shelf parts. A TPU-printed compliant foot provides impact absorption. The platform emphasizes modularity, wide joint ranges, including a continuous hip flexion-extension joint.
AI.result: Prototype/extended abstract presenting a novel platform for academic robotics research with emphasis on modularity, full 3D-printability, and cost-effectiveness; demonstrates mechanical design concepts and principles rather than full gait-level experimental results.
AI.conclusion: QLAUN offers a low-cost, modular, and largely 3D-printed quadruped platform suited for legged locomotion research in academic settings, highlighting interchangeable legs, decoupled actuators, and compliant contact interfaces as core design principles.

title: Laplacian Frequency Hierarchies for Efficient 3D Gaussian Splatting Training
comment: Accepted to Pacific Graphics 2026 (conference track). Project page: https://sorenzhang574.github.io/Laplacian-GS/
summary: A key bottleneck in 3D Gaussian Splatting training is the continual growth of Gaussian primitives, which increases optimization cost and slows convergence, especially at high resolutions. We propose Laplacian Frequency Hierarchies, a simple yet efficient 3DGS scheme that combines Laplacian image decomposition with coarse-to-fine, frequency-staged training. After fitting lower-frequency structure, we archive the corresponding Gaussian field so that subsequent fields can optimize higher-frequency residuals without carrying the full primitive burden, and we compose the rendered components in the image domain via a Laplacian-style reconstruction at inference time. This design reduces the number of active Gaussians during training, thereby lowering optimization overhead and accelerating training. The proposed scheme is plug-and-play and orthogonal to prior 3DGS accelerations: it can be directly combined with strong backbones such as Taming-3DGS and FastGS to improve training speed with competitive reconstruction quality. It achieves average speedups of 1.73x and 1.21x at 1K setting, and 1.74x and 1.33x at 4K setting on Taming-3DGS and FastGS, with larger gains on more challenging scenes and increasingly pronounced benefits at higher resolutions.

AI.tldr: Laplacian Frequency Hierarchies (LFH) accelerate 3D Gaussian Splatting training by decomposing content into low/high-frequency components, archiving low-frequency Gaussian fields, and training high-frequency residuals with fewer active Gaussians. It is plug-and-play with existing backbones and yields about 1.7x speedups (1K/4K) with competitive quality, especially at higher resolutions.
AI.motivation: The major bottleneck in 3DGS training is the continual growth of Gaussian primitives, which raises optimization cost and slows convergence, particularly for high-resolution scenes. Reducing active primitives without sacrificing quality can accelerate training.
AI.method: Apply Laplacian image decomposition to separate frequency bands and train in a coarse-to-fine, frequency-staged manner. After fitting the low-frequency structure, archive its Gaussian field so subsequent higher-frequency residuals are optimized with fewer active primitives. Reconstruct rendered components in the image domain via a Laplacian-style reconstruction at inference. The scheme is plug-and-play and orthogonal to existing accelerations, compatible with backbones like Taming-3DGS and FastGS.
AI.result: Average speedups of 1.73x and 1.21x at 1K settings, and 1.74x and 1.33x at 4K settings for Taming-3DGS and FastGS, respectively; gains are larger on challenging scenes and increase with higher resolutions.
AI.conclusion: LFH provides a simple, orthogonal acceleration for 3DGS training that reduces optimization overhead by operating on frequency-resolved Gaussian fields, enabling faster training while maintaining competitive reconstruction quality and easy integration with current backbones.

title: NeoRed: A Knowledge-Logic-Alignment Multimodal Large Language Model for Neonatal Respiratory Disease Diagnosis
summary: Neonatal respiratory diseases are a major cause of neonatal morbidity and mortality, posing substantial challenges in clinical practice. Despite recent advances, existing Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) face two key limitations in neonatal diagnosis: (1) domain gap arising from predominantly adult training data; (2) insufficient integration of multidimensional clinical context for accurate diagnosis. To address these challenges, we collect two real-world clinical datasets (NeoCXR and NeoCXR-EV) and propose NeoRed, to the best of our knowledge, the first MLLM tailored for neonatal respiratory disease, filling the gap in neonatal diagnostic reports generation. To enhance joint diagnosis from heterogeneous clinical context and chest X-rays, we design a novel Knowledge-Logic-Alignment (KLA) framework which constrains model behavior from three perspectives: 1) Knowledge Prior Injection (KPI) incorporates neonatologist-inspired diagnostic priors into multimodal representations, guiding disease-specific attention across modalities; 2) Diagnostic Logic Constraint (DLC) aligns the semantics of generated reports with multimodal diagnostic logic; and 3) Visual Semantic Alignment (VSA) establishes semantic correspondence between visual features and imaging conclusions. Extensive experiments demonstrate that NeoRed enables accurate neonatal diagnostic reports generation, achieving ROUGE-L of 53.29% and Clinical Efficacy F1 score of 65.19% on NeoCXR, outperforming existing MLLMs. NeoRed also preserves competitive report generation performance on adult benchmarks (MIMIC-CXR and IU-Xray). Datasets will be available upon application.

AI.tldr: NeoRed introduces a neonatal-specific multimodal LLM for respiratory disease with a Knowledge-Logic-Alignment (KLA) framework. It reports improved diagnostic report generation on NeoCXR (ROUGE-L 53.29%, Clinical Efficacy F1 65.19%), novel datasets NeoCXR and NeoCXR-EV, and maintains performance on adult benchmarks, with datasets available on request.
AI.motivation: Neonatal respiratory diseases are a major cause of morbidity and mortality. Existing MLLMs are domain-shifted toward adults and struggle to integrate multidimensional clinical context for neonatal diagnosis, creating a need for a neonatal-tailored MLLM that can fuse imaging and clinical data for accurate diagnostic reports.
AI.method: Introduce NeoRed and a three-pronged Knowledge-Logic-Alignment (KLA) framework: (1) KPI injects neonatologist priors into multimodal representations to guide disease-specific attention; (2) DLC enforces diagnostic logic alignment so generated reports reflect multimodal reasoning; (3) VSA aligns visual features with imaging conclusions, ensuring semantic consistency across modalities. Build two real-world neonatal datasets (NeoCXR and NeoCXR-EV) and evaluate on them and adult benchmarks.
AI.result: NeoRed achieves ROUGE-L of 53.29% and Clinical Efficacy F1 score of 65.19% on NeoCXR, outperforming existing MLLMs; it maintains competitive report generation performance on adult benchmarks (MIMIC-CXR, IU-Xray). Datasets are available upon application.
AI.conclusion: NeoRed appears to fill a key gap in neonatal diagnostic reporting by tailoring MLLM capabilities to neonatal clinical context and imagery, leveraging KPI, DLC, and VSA to integrate knowledge, logic, and visual-semantic alignment. Further details on dataset sizes, ablations, and external validation are needed for full reproducibility.

title: Kernel Reboot: Breaking the Boundaries of Neural Tangent Kernels for Neural Fields
comment: Published in IEEE TPAMI, vol. 48, no. 9, pp. 10940-10957, Sep. 2026. Author version adds related-work references and biography updates; Figures 12 and 13 were regenerated from the same locked hyperparameter sweep. Tabulated results, reported best points, scientific claims, and conclusions are unchanged
summary: Neural fields (NFs) map continuous coordinates to signals such as color or density, but fast high-quality reconstruction from sparse observations remains difficult. Classical Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) regression gives closed-form fits, yet it is fundamentally linear and cannot accumulate reusable task priors. We develop three algorithms that address these gaps. NTK-KIP learns a distilled support set of coordinates (and optional labels) so that a finite NTK can inpaint large missing regions from little observed data, yielding a compact non-linear representation instead of a raw kernel solve. MetaQuill meta-learns a shared initialization for an INR so that new scenes can be adapted by updating only a small task-specific weight offset, which provides true feature learning and a reusable prior. Finally, MetaQuill-KIP fuses both ideas: it seeds the task with a KIP-style non-linear warm start, then refines only that small offset around the meta-learned initialization. MetaQuill-KIP achieves high-PSNR reconstructions and semantically plausible inpainting under very sparse observations, while requiring only lightweight per-instance adaptation, whereas diffusion-style baselines typically depend on large pretrained generative priors and costly per-image tuning. This shows that NTK-driven neural fields can be made both non-linear and meta-learnable, narrowing the gap between analytic kernels and practical few-shot reconstruction.

AI.tldr: NTK-based neural fields struggle with sparse data but can be improved by non-linear, meta-learning approaches. The paper proposes NTK-KIP (distilled support set for NTK), MetaQuill (shared INR initialization with small per-task offset), and MetaQuill-KIP (combine both). These yield high-PSNR and semantically plausible inpainting with lightweight adaptation, bridging analytic kernels and practical few-shot reconstruction.
AI.motivation: To overcome the linearity and lack of reusable priors in classical NTK regression for neural fields, enabling fast, high-quality reconstructions from sparse observations.
AI.method: Three algorithms: (1) NTK-KIP selects a distilled set of coordinates (and optional labels) to enable a finite NTK to inpaint large regions efficiently; (2) MetaQuill meta-learns a shared INR initialization so new scenes adapt via a small task-specific offset, enabling true feature learning and reusable priors; (3) MetaQuill-KIP seeds the task with a KIP-style non-linear warm start and refines only a small offset around the meta-learned initialization.
AI.result: NTK-KIP, MetaQuill, and MetaQuill-KIP achieve high-PSNR reconstructions and semantically plausible inpainting under sparse observations while requiring lightweight per-instance adaptation, outperforming diffusion-style baselines that rely on large pretrained priors and costly per-image tuning.
AI.conclusion: NTK-driven neural fields can be made non-linear and meta-learnable, narrowing the gap between analytic kernels and practical few-shot reconstruction; the proposed trio of methods demonstrates practical, data-efficient reconstruction with reusable priors.

title: Local Path Planning and Obstacle Avoidance for an Omnicopter Platform
summary: Autonomous unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) increasingly operate in cluttered environments where global planners such as RRT* are not directly deployable at control rates. This paper presents a real-time local planning and obstacle avoidance module for an omnidirectional multirotor (omnicopter) by extending the Dynamic Window Approach to six degrees of freedom (6D-DWA). Our method achieves real-time feasibility through (i) local-map voxelisation, (ii) a compact sphere-based approximation of the vehicle geometry, and (iii) adaptive velocity sampling in the 6D search space. To improve reactivity to unknown obstacles, we introduce a context-aware "Agile Mode" that adjusts scoring weights online to trade-off between goal progress, clearance, and heading/facing constraints during evasive manoeuvres. We evaluate our approach in simulation across computational stress tests, dense-waypoint path tracking, and static/unknown obstacle scenarios. Our planner runs consistently within a 0.2s control loop, tracks waypoint-dense global paths with < 0.1m average cross-track error and 13deg average heading error, and avoids collisions in static environments. For unknown obstacle avoidance, Agile Mode achieves 79.3% success for an off-centre obstacle and 41.4% for a centred obstacle, highlighting both the effectiveness of adaptive weighting and remaining limitations in highly constrained geometries.

AI.tldr: A real-time 6D-DWA local planner for omnidirectional UAVs that enables efficient obstacle avoidance in cluttered environments using voxelized local maps, a spherical vehicle model, and adaptive velocity sampling with an online Agile Mode; achieves 0.2s control loop and low tracking errors, with partial success in unknown obstacle avoidance.
AI.motivation: Global planners like RRT* are often too slow for real-time control in cluttered 6-DOF UAV environments and fail to provide reactive obstacle avoidance at control rates. A real-time local planner is needed to maintain safety and progress toward goals under computational constraints and unknown obstacles.
AI.method: Extend Dynamic Window Approach to 6DoF (6D-DWA) for an omnidirectional multirotor. Key components include local-map voxelisation to reduce state space, a compact sphere-based collision model for the vehicle, and adaptive velocity sampling in the 6D search space. Introduce Agile Mode, an online context-aware weighting scheme that biases the planner toward goal progress, clearance, or heading constraints during evasive maneuvers. Evaluate in simulation with computational stress tests, dense waypoint tracking, and static/unknown obstacle scenarios; the planner runs in a ~0.2 s loop.
AI.result: The approach is feasible in real time, maintaining sub-0.1 m cross-track error and ~13° heading error on dense waypoint paths, and avoiding collisions in static environments. Agile Mode improves unknown obstacle avoidance, achieving 79.3% success for off-centre obstacles and 41.4% for centred obstacles, illustrating the method’s effectiveness and remaining limitations in highly constrained geometries.
AI.conclusion: 6D-DWA with Agile Mode provides a practical, real-time local planning solution for omnidirectional UAVs in clutter, balancing goal progress and safety online. While effective, performance in very constrained or highly uncertain environments is still limited, suggesting avenues for further refinement and more robust unknown-obstacle handling.

title: PointGT: Simultaneous Geometry and Texture Editing for Point-Based Representations
comment: Accepted to ECCV 2026. Project page: https://zvict.github.io/pointgt/
summary: We present PointGT, a point-based 3D representation that enables simultaneous editing of object geometry and appearance. Existing reconstruction and view synthesis techniques produce volumetric 3D representations that are high-quality and photorealistic, but are difficult to edit. In particular, recent efforts to enable texture editing for 3D Gaussian Splatting representations are not compatible with geometry edits and deformations. Our method combines a point-based representation that is well-suited for geometry deformations with a learned UV mapping technique that enables high-resolution texture editing. We show that PointGT enables fine-grained editing of both geometry and texture in point-based neural representations with high rendering quality.

AI.tldr: PointGT enables simultaneous geometry and texture editing for 3D representations by combining a point-based geometry with a learned UV mapping for high-resolution texture editing, addressing editability gaps in volumetric/Gaussian Splatting approaches.
AI.motivation: Editable 3D content is hampered by existing volumetric representations (e.g., neural radiance fields, Gaussian splatting) that trade editing flexibility for rendering quality. A representation that supports geometry deformations alongside texture edits would streamline editing workflows.
AI.method: A point-based neural representation that is easily deformed for geometry editing, augmented with a learned UV mapping to support high-resolution texture editing. Per-point attributes and UV coordinate handling enable synchronized geometry and appearance edits while maintaining rendering quality.
AI.result: Demonstrates fine-grained, simultaneous editing of both geometry and texture with high rendering quality, addressing incompatibilities between geometry edits and texture editing in prior Gaussian Splatting approaches.
AI.conclusion: PointGT offers a practical, editable 3D representation by marrying geometry-friendly point-based structures with learnable texture mappings, enabling end-to-end editing workflows without sacrificing rendering fidelity.

title: Feature Reconfiguration With Visual Prior for Medical Lesion Segmentation
summary: Lesion segmentation in medical images plays a critical role in clinical diagnosis and treatment planning. Despite significant advances, lesion segmentation remains challenging due to two major factors: (1) complex background interference; (2) diverse lesion morphology. Existing encoder-decoder based methods mainly focus on enhancing feature extraction or redesigning decoding strategies. However, they lack early prior guidance and feature reconfiguration during the encoding stage, limiting their effectiveness in handling these challenges. To address these limitations, we propose FreNet, a feature reconfiguration framework with visual priors, which performs pixel-level reconfiguration before encoding and feature-level reconfiguration during encoding for precise medical lesion segmentation. To suppress background responses, we propose an Implicit Prior Neural Network (IPNN), which models a continuous spatial field and leverages visual prior from SAM to reconfigure input image before encoding stage. To better handle diverse lesion morphology, we design a Dual-domain Feature Reconfiguration (DFR) module to progressively reconfigure backbone features during encoding stage. Within DFR, the Frequency Decoupling Module (FDM) decouples backbone features in frequency domain to enhance foreground-background discriminability, while the Spatial Localization Module (SLM) spatially relocates and improving spatial stability after frequency decoupling. Extensive experiments on 9 medical image segmentation benchmarks across three imaging modalities demonstrate that FreNet significantly outperforms state-of-the-art (SOTA) methods. On the challenging ETIS dataset, our method achieves Dice improvements of 5.0% over SOTA method and 7.2% over SAM.

AI.tldr: FreNet introduces an early-prior, dual-domain feature reconfiguration framework for medical lesion segmentation, combining an implicit prior neural network (IPNN) with a dual-domain reconfiguration (FDM + SLM) to improve robustness to background and lesion morphology; achieves state-of-the-art results across 9 benchmarks and notably on ETIS.
AI.motivation: Lesion segmentation is hampered by complex backgrounds and diverse lesion shapes. Existing encoder-decoder methods lack early guidance and feature reconfiguration during encoding, limiting discrimination and localization.
AI.method: FreNet performs pixel-level reconfiguration via IPNN with SAM priors before encoding, and applies Dual-domain Feature Reconfiguration (DFR) during encoding: Frequency Decoupling Module (FDM) in the frequency domain to improve foreground-background discrimination, followed by Spatial Localization Module (SLM) to relocate and stabilize spatial features.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on 9 medical segmentation benchmarks across 3 modalities show FreNet surpasses state-of-the-art methods. On ETIS, Dice improves by 5.0 percentage points over the best prior method and by 7.2 points over SAM.
AI.conclusion: FreNet validates that combining early visual priors with frequency-domain and spatial reconfiguration during encoding yields robust lesion segmentation, addressing both background interference and morphological diversity.

title: Routing Is Not Enough: Diagnosing Intra-Adapter Subspace Contention in MoE+LoRA Fine-Tuning
comment: 13 pages, 1 figure, 16 tables. Accepted to Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026
summary: Multi-domain fine-tuning often combines MoE routing with LoRA, assuming that token-level routing separates domain-specific updates. We test this assumption in MoE+LoRA using Python code paired with biomedical text and mathematical reasoning. Although these domains show near-disjoint expert routing, adding biomedical data substantially increases code perplexity, indicating that routing separation alone may not prevent negative transfer. To localize the failure, we introduce Jaccard routing overlap and adapter-gradient cosine similarity, which measure expert sharing and update compatibility, respectively. These diagnostics indicate that interference arises mostly from nearly orthogonal domain gradients competing within the same low-rank adapter subspace. We address this issue with SpawnLoRA, which dynamically adds gated sub-adapters inside MoE experts when adapter-level contention is detected, while keeping the router fixed. We evaluate SpawnLoRA on Phi-tiny-MoE-instruct and OLMoE-1B-7B across multiple mixture settings and find that it effectively reduces negative transfer compared with standard and rank-adaptive LoRA. These results demonstrate that structural separation inside experts provides benefits beyond routing or rank expansion alone.

AI.tldr: In multi-domain fine-tuning with Mixture of Experts (MoE) and LoRA, routing alone does not prevent negative transfer; the paper introduces diagnostics (Jaccard routing overlap, adapter-gradient cosine similarity) to quantify cross-domain interference and proposes SpawnLoRA, which dynamically adds gated sub-adapters inside MoE experts when contention is detected. Evaluations on Phi-tiny-MoE-instruct and OLMoE-1B-7B show SpawnLoRA reduces negative transfer better than standard and rank-adaptive LoRA, highlighting benefits of intra-expert structural separation.
AI.motivation: Challenge the assumption that token-level routing in MoE with LoRA suffices to isolate domain-specific updates in multi-domain fine-tuning. Demonstrate that routing separation may be insufficient due to gradient interference and explore diagnostic tools and an adaptive architectural solution.
AI.method: Test across Python-based setups with biomedical text and mathematical reasoning domains. Introduce diagnostics: Jaccard routing overlap (shared experts across domains) and adapter-gradient cosine similarity (alignment of domain gradients within the adapter subspace). Propose SpawnLoRA: dynamically insert gated sub-adapters inside MoE experts when adapter contention is detected, while keeping the router fixed. Evaluate on Phi-tiny-MoE-instruct and OLMoE-1B-7B under multiple mixture configurations.
AI.result: Diagnostics reveal that interference mainly comes from nearly orthogonal domain gradients competing within the same low-rank adapter subspace. SpawnLoRA mitigates negative transfer more effectively than standard LoRA or rank-adaptive LoRA across tested mixture settings.
AI.conclusion: Structural separation inside MoE experts—via gated sub-adapters—provides benefits beyond routing or rank expansion alone and is effective at reducing cross-domain interference in multi-domain MoE+LoRA setups.

title: WISE: World-model-guided Imagination Scheduling for Efficient Post-training of Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Post-training VLA policies typically rely on supervised fine-tuning with costly expert demonstrations or reinforcement learning with expensive and potentially unstable real-world exploration. World models offer a promising alternative by evaluating candidate behaviors through imagined futures, yet effective post-training requires more than accurate prediction: imagination must be scheduled where it is useful, bounded within reliable horizons, and translated into trustworthy policy supervision. In robotic manipulation, the value of imagination varies substantially across execution stages, while extended rollouts can accumulate prediction errors and introduce unreliable learning signals. We introduce WISE (World-model-guided Imagination Scheduling for Efficient Post-training of Vision-Language-Action Models), a unified framework that coordinates when and how world-model imagination is used during policy refinement. WISE selectively invokes imagination at interaction-relevant states, performs bounded multi-view rollouts, evaluates candidate futures using progress and completion signals, and uses their relative outcomes to refine actions generated from real interaction contexts. Extensive experiments with both $π_0$ and $π_{0.5}$ demonstrate consistent improvements across diverse manipulation tasks while reducing GPU computation time by approximately 80% compared with full imagination. Real-world evaluations further show substantial gains in robustness and generalization under diverse real-world distribution shifts.

AI.tldr: WISE enables selective, bounded world-model imagination during policy post-training, using interaction-relevant states and progress-based evaluation to refine actions, yielding strong performance gains with far less GPU cost.
AI.motivation: Address the high cost and instability of traditional post-training approaches (supervised demonstrations, RL with real-world exploration) by scheduling imagination to where it is most useful and within reliable horizons, improving robustness under distribution shifts.
AI.method: Wise integrates: (1) selective invocation of imagination at interaction-relevant states, (2) bounded multi-view rollouts to limit error accumulation, (3) evaluation of candidate futures using progress and completion signals, (4) using relative outcomes to refine actions derived from real interaction contexts. Evaluations across π0 and π0.5 show improvements on diverse manipulation tasks with substantial GPU time reduction.
AI.result: Consistent performance improvements across diverse manipulation tasks for both policy variants π0 and π0.5; approximately 80% reduction in GPU computation time compared with full imagination; real-world evaluations show improved robustness and generalization under distribution shifts.
AI.conclusion: WISE provides an effective, efficient framework for post-training of vision-language-action models via world-model imagination scheduling, achieving better performance with substantially reduced computation and improved real-world robustness.

title: P-CORE: Self-Supervised Surface Consistency for Point-Based Neural Editing
comment: Accepted to ECCV 2026. Project Page: https://zvict.github.io/p-core/
summary: Advances in neural rendering have enabled high-fidelity multi-view reconstruction of 3D scenes. However, free-form non-rigid shape editing remains a significant challenge. Point-based neural representations are highly desirable for multi-view reconstruction because they lack fixed connectivity, which does not constrain the learned surface topology to that of the initialization. Yet this same property causes point-based representations to struggle with holes and surface discontinuities under large deformations. To address this, we propose a novel self-supervised method to enable point-based representations to adapt to large deformations without requiring ground truth multi-view images of deformed geometry. The key idea is to generate random deformations and to ensure consistency in the predicted surface before and after deformation. In particular, the surface prediction from the deformed point cloud should be the same as the deformation applied to the surface prediction from the original point cloud. We incorporate our approach into attention-based point representations, which differ from splatting-based point representations in their use of a learned interpolation kernel between points as opposed to a Gaussian kernel around each point. This learned interpolation kernel can learn to adapt to large deformations, without requiring addition or removal of points. We show that our framework significantly enhances its robustness to large deformations. Experiments on synthetic geometry editing benchmarks (Neural Editor, Objaverse) demonstrate that our approach outperforms existing point-based methods in zero-shot editing and significantly reduces artifacts. Furthermore, qualitative results on the DTU and Mip-NeRF 360 datasets demonstrate our method's effectiveness on real-world scenes.

AI.tldr: Self-supervised deformation-consistency for point-based neural rendering enabling large non-rigid edits via random deformations and a learned interpolation kernel in attention-based point representations; improves zero-shot editing and reduces artifacts on synthetic benchmarks and real-world data.
AI.motivation: Point-based representations struggle with holes and surface discontinuities under large deformations; need robust, topology-agnostic editing without ground-truth deformed views.
AI.method: Train with random deformations and enforce that the surface predicted from the deformed point cloud equals the deformation of the surface predicted from the original cloud. Integrate into attention-based point representations using a learned interpolation kernel (not Gaussian splatting); kernel adapts to large deformations without adding/removing points.
AI.result: Notable robustness to large deformations; superior zero-shot editing performance and artifact reduction on Neural Editor and Objaverse; qualitative improvements on DTU and Mip-NeRF 360.
AI.conclusion: The approach enables deformation-tolerant, point-based neural rendering for free-form editing, achieving strong editing performance and generalization to real-world scenes.

title: Dalek: A Constructive Agent Machine
summary:
We present Dalek, a closed machine designed for agents that realizes self-maintenance, self-evolution, self-reproduction, and self-organization on any substrate satisfying a general host contract. The machine is built from three primitives---actors, messages, and channels. Four obligations---a host boundary, a construction language, admissible transitions, and rule heredity---give its boundary, identity, and closure a structural basis.
  Von Neumann's 1948 self-reproducing automaton supplies a hereditary constructional core: a self-description together with a constructor, a copier, and a controller. Dalek combines this core with the four obligations and rederives its medium for a text-and-message agent substrate, adding explicit structures for boundary, identity, history, and growth. A large language model and a compiler occupy the payload position and form a general capability producer. New capabilities are authored, compiled, installed into the description, and inherited by descendants. The same path produces the machine's own organs and even its runtime, closing heredity and evolution within the machine.

AI.tldr: Dalek is a closed self-constructing, self-reproducing agent framework that extends Von Neumann's self-reproducing automaton with four obligations and actor-based primitives to support self-maintenance, evolution, and capability inheritance on adaptable substrates; it uses a payload of a large language model and a compiler to produce capabilities, organs, and runtime, enabling heredity and evolution within the machine.
AI.motivation: To realize autonomous, self-contained agents capable of self-maintenance, growth, and inheritance across descendants on generic substrates, addressing limitations of existing automata and agent architectures.
AI.method: Define primitives (actors, messages, channels) and four obligations (host boundary, construction language, admissible transitions, rule heredity). Integrate Von Neumann's hereditary core (self-description, constructor, copier, controller). Re-derive medium for text-and-message substrates with explicit boundary/identity/history/growth. Position LLMs and compiler as payload to generate capabilities, compiled into the agent description, inherited by descendants; enable self-creation of organs and runtime.
AI.result: A formal design for Dalek that yields self-maintaining, self-evolving, self-reproducing agents that can acquire new capabilities and propagate them through hereditary descent, closing evolution inside the machine.
AI.conclusion: Dalek provides a concrete architecture for closed, hereditary, autonomous agents leveraging a general-capability payload to drive growth and adaptation, integrating a Von Neumann-like core with explicit structural obligations to enable self-description, boundary management, and inheritance.

title: Frontier LLMs are effective batch optimizers: Assessing reasoning models in continuous and discrete settings
summary: Frontier large language models (LLMs) have become attractive priors for optimization due to their large-scale pretraining that enables them to navigate a variety of optimization settings. However, the effectiveness of modern reasoning LLMs in batch optimization settings remains underexplored. Here we investigate the performance of the current generation of frontier LLMs as batch optimizers in both continuous and discrete settings. We find that while LLMs are competitive zero-shot batch optimizers for numerical test functions, their performance is brittle compared to classical non-LLM optimization approaches. However, LLM priors are significantly better in semantically rich settings, indicating that their batch optimization behavior is highly effective when navigating and reasoning over the discrete spaces most similar in structure to their pretraining data.

AI.tldr: Frontier LLMs can serve as priors for batch optimization: competitive zero-shot performance on numerical tests but brittle relative to classical methods, with strong advantages in semantically rich, discrete-like spaces that resemble pretraining data.
AI.motivation: Assess whether current frontier LLMs provide transferable optimization priors in batch optimization across continuous and discrete domains, given their large-scale pretraining.
AI.method: Systematic evaluation of current-generation frontier LLMs as batch optimizers in both continuous and discrete settings, compared to classical non-LLM optimization baselines, focusing on numerical test functions and semantically rich discrete problems to analyze robustness and data-alignment effects.
AI.result: LLMs are competitive zero-shot batch optimizers for numerical test functions but show brittleness compared with classical optimization approaches; priors are significantly more effective in semantically rich settings, especially when discrete spaces resemble the LLMs' pretraining data.
AI.conclusion: LLM priors can be useful for batch optimization in discrete or semantically rich spaces that mirror training data, but robustness and consistency remain challenges; leveraging discrete structure and aligning tasks with pretraining data can enhance performance.

title: Predictive Zonotope Reduction: Precise Runtime Monitoring under Uncertainty
summary: Robots operating in physical environments make control decisions based on uncertain sensor measurements, which can lead to unsafe or suboptimal actions. Runtime monitors that check their behavior against safety specifications must represent this uncertainty soundly. Zonotopes are a widely used representation, but continuously incorporating new measurements grows their order unboundedly, so monitors must periodically apply an over-approximating reduction. The choice of the reduction method substantially affects the zonotope's precision, yet existing approaches typically utilize a fixed method throughout the run, even though the optimal choice depends on the current state. This paper presents a Predictive Zonotope Reduction (PZR) approach, which frames reducer selection as an optimal control problem and solves it using beam-search model predictive control. Policy distillation into a small neural policy further provides substantially higher execution speed than model predictive control while maintaining improved performance, enabling uncertainty-aware runtime monitoring on resource-constrained real-time systems. We implement our approach in the RLola runtime monitoring framework and evaluate it on a 5-degree-of-freedom robotic arm simulated in MuJoCo, with sensor uncertainty modeled according to ISO 5725. Experiments on a Raspberry Pi 5 show that dynamic reduction significantly lowers false-positive rates in monitoring compared with static reduction strategies.

AI.tldr: Dynamic, predictive zonotope reduction (PZR) selects online reduction methods for uncertain safety monitors using beam-search MPC; distills to a compact neural policy for fast execution, enabling uncertainty-aware monitoring on constrained hardware.
AI.motivation: Sensor uncertainty in perception leads to unsafe or suboptimal actions; fixed zonotope reduction methods accumulate error over time; adaptive reduction is needed to balance precision and computation.
