AI.method: Frame reducer selection as an optimal control problem and solve with beam-search model predictive control; distill the policy into a small neural network for fast runtime execution; implement within the RLola runtime monitoring framework; evaluate on a 5-DOF robotic arm in MuJoCo with ISO 5725-based sensor uncertainty; hardware test on Raspberry Pi 5.
AI.result: Dynamic reduction reduces false positives in monitoring compared with static reduction strategies; the distilled policy achieves higher execution speed than MPC while preserving stronger performance.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive, uncertainty-aware runtime monitoring is feasible on resource-constrained systems; the PZR approach provides improved safety-related monitoring accuracy with real-time feasibility and broad applicability.

title: When Depth Hurts: Reliability-Aware Geometry Distillation for Depth-Free RGB-D Salient Object Detection
summary: Depth can resolve appearance ambiguity in RGB-D salient object detection (SOD), yet sensor depth is not uniformly reliable. Missing regions, blurred boundaries, and structural artifacts can propagate through multimodal fusion and make an RGB-D detector less accurate than its RGB-only counterpart. Existing quality-aware approaches regulate observed depth but remain dependent on the same potentially defective modality. We propose \method, a reliability-aware geometry distillation framework developed for RGB-D SOD benchmarks without using dataset-provided depth during training or inference. A frozen Depth Anything V2 model serves only as a training-time teacher, transferring dense relative geometry, hierarchical spatial attention, and boundary structure to a compact edge-aware geometry branch. Pooled bidirectional interaction aligns geometry with appearance, and a pixel-wise reliability estimator selectively injects geometry that is compatible with the current RGB representation. The teacher is removed after training, leaving an RGB-only inference network. Trained on 2,985 RGB-mask pairs, \method{} achieves the best or tied-best result in 26 of 36 metric-dataset comparisons against ten recent RGB-D SOD methods, including a 13.4\% relative MAE reduction on ReDWeb-S. When retrained on DUTS-TR, it also improves the strongest prior $F$-measure by 4.2\% on PASCAL-S, showing that the distilled geometry transfers beyond a particular sensor or dataset domain. Code will be released upon publication.

AI.tldr: RGB-D salient object detection without using depth at inference by distilling geometry from a frozen depth teacher into a compact RGB-only network; strong cross-dataset performance and generalization across sensors.
AI.motivation: Depth signals can improve SOD but are often unreliable due to missing regions, blur, and artifacts. Existing quality-aware methods still depend on depth. The work aims to leverage depth knowledge during training while delivering RGB-only inference, improving robustness and generalization across sensors/datasets.
AI.method: A frozen Depth Anything V2 model serves as a training-time teacher to transfer dense relative geometry, hierarchical spatial attention, and boundary structure to a compact edge-aware geometry branch. Pooled bidirectional interaction aligns geometry with appearance, and a pixel-wise reliability estimator selects geometry compatible with the current RGB. The teacher is removed after training, yielding an RGB-only detector. Trained on 2,985 RGB-mask pairs; evaluated across 36 metric-dataset pairs against 10 RGB-D SOD methods.
AI.result: The proposed method achieves best or tied-best results in 26 of 36 metric-dataset comparisons, including a 13.4% relative MAE reduction on ReDWeb-S. Retraining on DUTS-TR improves the strongest prior F-measure by 4.2% on PASCAL-S, indicating good generalization beyond a single sensor or dataset.
AI.conclusion: Distilling geometry from a depth teacher can yield a robust RGB-only SOD model with strong cross-dataset generalization, reducing reliance on faulty depth inputs while retaining depth-informed geometry guidance. Code will be released.

title: GPS-Bench: A Governance Policy Benchmark for Automating Policy Analysis
summary: Policy analysis requires more than predicting whether a proposal will pass: it requires identifying who will be affected, how those actors respond, and what follows. LLM-based policy simulations model these processes at scale, but their validity is hard to establish when plausible behaviour is never compared with observed outcomes. We introduce GPS-Bench, an evidence-grounded benchmark for governance policy simulation that links policies to relevant actors, actor actions and downstream impacts using legislative records, lobbying disclosures, regulatory documents, corporate filings, economic data and other public evidence. Actors are reconstructed from the dated record rather than prompted as archetypes, so a persona is an evidence object with provenance; a human-annotated pool forms the Gold evaluation set, while cases labelled by a separate LLM from retrieved evidence are treated as Silver supervision and never as test labels. Because every inference mode reads the same grounded state and emits the same schema, GPS-Bench turns "does multi-agent simulation help?" into a controlled comparison: we contrast joint reasoning, independent and communicating actor agents, graph-based methods and weight-level fine-tuning over one policy state. Fine-tuning on the grounded record gives the strongest actor-level impact prediction, and decomposition does not beat it; what decomposition adds is mechanism. Agents hold private, non-identical evidence, each seeing its own exposure clause, and address named partners with concrete joint proposals, what they offer, what they need in return, and why acting together beats acting alone, so the coalitions that form can be checked against the commitments the record holds. GPS-Bench therefore gives a common empirical setting for studying when evidence, actor modelling and multi-agent interaction improve the prediction and interpretation of policy outcomes.

AI.tldr: GPS-Bench provides an evidence-grounded benchmark for governance policy simulation linking policies to actors and outcomes, enabling controlled comparison of multi-agent methods and showing when grounding and fine-tuning improve actor-level predictions.
AI.motivation: Policy analysis requires predicting policy consequences through affected actors and downstream impacts; existing LLM simulations lack grounding in observed evidence and provenance, hindering validation.
AI.method: Construct GPS-Bench by linking policies to actors and actions using legislative records, lobbying disclosures, regulatory documents, corporate filings, and economic data; reconstruct actors from dated records as provenance-rich evidence objects; establish Gold (human-annotated) and Silver (LLM-labeled) evaluation pools; ensure all inference modes read the same grounded state and emit the same schema; compare joint reasoning, independent/communicating agents, graph-based methods, and weight-level fine-tuning across one policy state.
AI.result: Fine-tuning on the grounded record yields the strongest actor-level impact prediction; decomposition does not beat fine-tuning; decomposition adds explanatory mechanism; agents with private evidence form coalitions whose commitments can be checked against the record; GPS-Bench enables controlled empirical studies of when evidence, actor modeling, and multi-agent interaction improve policy outcome predictions.
AI.conclusion: GPS-Bench provides a common empirical setting to study the value of grounding, actor modeling, and multi-agent interaction for predicting and interpreting policy outcomes, with provenance-aware actors and verifiable coalitions.

title: Portable Causal Fairness Across Synthetic Data Generator Families
summary: When a statistical agency or regulator releases synthetic data in place of sensitive records, it chooses the generator that produces the table, and can shape that generator so unfair pathways are absent. DECAF made this concrete on one non-private GAN: three fairness definitions become three sets of edge cuts on the generator's causal graph. Whether the mechanism belongs to DECAF, or to causal factorisation itself, was untested. We port all three definitions to nine generators from three unrelated families (marginals-based, GAN, and diffusion, each with differentially private variants), across three levels of formal privacy guarantee, over 2,520 matched-pair runs on Adult and COMPAS datasets. The mechanism transfers everywhere, and our new causal diffusion backbone yields the fairest release of any family we tested, at fidelity close to the marginals tier. Applying the cut barely moves fidelity, only costs a downstream classifier about $0.07$ to $0.15$ AUC on average, and adding privacy guarantees don't make the data less fair.

AI.tldr: Across nine generator families (marginals, GAN, diffusion) and DP variants, three fairness definitions map to causal-edge cuts; these cuts transfer across mechanisms, with a new causal-diffusion backbone delivering the fairest releases yet preserving fidelity; privacy does not reduce fairness; only small AUC impact (~0.07–0.15) when applying cuts.
AI.motivation: Evaluate whether DECAF-style causal-factorization fairness transfers across diverse data-generating mechanisms and privacy regimes, and whether a causal diffusion backbone improves fair synthetic data release.
AI.method: Port three fairness definitions to nine generators (marginals-based, GAN, diffusion) including DP variants; test across three privacy levels; use 2,520 matched-pair runs on Adult and COMPAS; implement edge-cut fairness on the generator's causal graph; compare fidelity and downstream classifier performance.
AI.result: Fairness mechanisms transfer across generators; the causal-diffusion backbone yields the fairest releases among tested families, with fidelity close to marginals. Edge-cutting minimally impacts fidelity and causes small AUC changes (0.07–0.15) for downstream classifiers. Privacy levels do not reduce fairness.
AI.conclusion: Causal-factorization-based fairness generalizes across generator families; the causal-diffusion approach provides the fairest synthetic data with minimal fidelity loss, and privacy does not inherently undermine fairness in these experiments.

title: Toward an~Integrated Cognitive--Ergonomic Architecture for~Human--Machine Interaction: Combining Cognitive Models with~Human Factors Ergonomics
summary: This paper presents an integrated approach to modeling human competencies by combining the theoretical foundations of cognitive architectures with principles from Human Factors Ergonomics (HFE). Through a comparative analysis of established cognitive models-SOAR, ACT-R, LIDA, and COCOM-we synthesize a tailored architecture designed to address the complexities of human-machine interaction (HMI) in dynamic environments. By contextualizing this model within ergonomic frameworks, we elucidate the mechanisms underlying decision-making, skill acquisition, and adaptive behavior, bridging the gap between cognitive theory and applied system design. Our framework is empirically grounded in industrial robotics applications, where operator expertise, normative knowledge, and real-time feedback loops are critical. The proposed architecture not only enhances the cognitive alignment of HMI systems but also provides a scalable methodology for designing intelligent, human-centered interfaces in high-stakes environments. This work advances both the theoretical understanding of human competencies and the practical implementation of adaptive, ergonomically optimized systems.

AI.tldr: An integrated cognitive-HFE architecture synthesizes SOAR, ACT-R, LIDA, and COCOM to improve human-machine interaction in dynamic environments; grounded in industrial robotics, it promises enhanced decision-making, skill acquisition, and adaptability, with a scalable human-centered interface design.
AI.motivation: Addresses the gap between cognitive architectures and ergonomic, user-centered system design to improve HMI in high-stakes, dynamic contexts, using industrial robotics as a grounding domain.
AI.method: Comparative analysis of cognitive models (SOAR, ACT-R, LIDA, COCOM); synthesis into a unified, HMI-oriented architecture; contextualization within HFE principles; empirical grounding in industrial robotics to validate mechanisms like feedback loops and operator expertise.
AI.result: Proposes an integrated architecture that aligns cognition with HMI requirements and provides a scalable methodology for designing intelligent, human-centered interfaces suitable for high-stakes environments, demonstrated conceptually through industrial robotics applications.
AI.conclusion: Advances both theory and practice by bridging cognitive theory and ergonomically optimized system design, offering a foundation for adaptive HMI architectures in dynamic workflows.

title: FoRIS: Progressive Foreground Refinement for Training-Free In-Context Segmentation
summary: In-Context Segmentation (ICS) aims to precisely segment arbitrary semantic concepts, such as objects or parts, given one or a few annotated visual exemplars. In this paper, we revisit ICS from a more classical segmentation perspective, viewing it as a coarse-to-fine progressive refinement process. Rather than directly predicting the final mask through reference-query matching, we progressively refine the segmentation from coarse and ambiguous foreground responses to precise and complete foreground structures. Building upon this perspective, we propose a training-free in-context segmentation framework, termed FoRIS. Specifically, FoRIS consists of three key stages: Foreground Purification, Foreground Localization, and Foreground Consolidation, which progressively suppress background distractions, localize discriminative target regions, and recover complete foreground structures through semantic aggregation. Experimental results demonstrate that FoRIS achieves SOTA performance across semantic and part segmentation tasks, with average improvements of 4.5 and 4.8 mIoU points over existing approaches in the 1-shot and 5-shot settings, respectively. Code: https://github.com/Xi-Mu-Yu/FoRIS.

AI.tldr: FoRIS is a training-free in-context segmentation framework that refines segmentation in three stages (Foreground Purification, Foreground Localization, Foreground Consolidation) to achieve state-of-the-art results in 1-shot and 5-shot settings.
AI.motivation: Reinterpret ICS as a coarse-to-fine refinement process to reduce reliance on direct reference-query matching and training, mitigating background distractions and incomplete foreground recovery.
AI.method: A three-stage pipeline: Foreground Purification (suppress background distractions), Foreground Localization (localize discriminative regions), Foreground Consolidation (recover complete foreground via semantic aggregation); training-free, relying on progressive refinement instead of end-to-end mask prediction.
AI.result: Achieves state-of-the-art performance on semantic and part segmentation; average improvements of 4.5 mIoU in 1-shot and 4.8 mIoU in 5-shot settings over prior methods; code released.
AI.conclusion: FoRIS shows that a training-free, coarse-to-fine refinement paradigm can surpass prior ICS approaches, highlighting the effectiveness of semantic aggregation for complete foreground recovery.

title: HalluPeer: A Taxonomy-driven Benchmark for Detecting Hallucinations in Scientific Peer Reviews
summary: The growing scale of academic peer review has motivated the use of Large Language Models (LLMs) as review assistants, yet LLMs can generate fluent but unsupported claims that undermine review reliability. Existing hallucination benchmarks are not designed for peer review, where verification requires grounding claims in long, technical papers. We introduce HalluPeer, a benchmark for detecting hallucinations in scientific peer reviews, providing aligned triples of paper content, human-written reviews, and hallucination-injected reviews, annotated for detection, classification, and localization. Our pipeline induces a peer-review-specific hallucination taxonomy, identifies review contexts, and injects hallucinations with automated filtering. Experiments on 12K papers and 38K reviews show that existing detectors struggle to separate hallucinations from legitimate critique, while evaluation on authentic reviews demonstrates that HalluPeer-defined hallucination patterns occur in real peer reviews, highlighting the critical need for source-aware verification. Our project page can be found in https://github.com/Lin-TzuLing/HalluPeer.git

AI.tldr: A benchmark named HalluPeer for detecting hallucinations in scientific peer reviews; aligns paper content, human reviews, and hallucination-injected reviews with taxonomy, contexts, and automated injection; experiments show detectors struggle and real reviews exhibit HalluPeer-like patterns; GitHub project page provided.
AI.motivation: As peer review scales and LLMs are used as review assistants, guaranteeing reliability is critical. Existing hallucination benchmarks are ill-suited for peer review because verification requires grounding in long, technical papers; a source-grounded benchmark is needed to improve detection and verification.
AI.method: Build HalluPeer by creating aligned triples of paper content, human-written reviews, and hallucination-injected reviews; develop a peer-review-specific hallucination taxonomy; identify review contexts; inject hallucinations via automated filtering; evaluate on ~12k papers and ~38k reviews.
AI.result: Detectors trained on existing benchmarks struggle to differentiate hallucinations from legitimate critique; HalluPeer-aligned hallucination patterns occur in authentic reviews, underscoring the need for source-aware verification.
AI.conclusion: HalluPeer provides a dedicated dataset and framework for source-grounded hallucination detection in peer reviews, enabling better verification and detector development; project page: https://github.com/Lin-TzuLing/HalluPeer.git

title: Language-encoded network topology enables large language models to reason about complex networks
summary: Networks describe systems in biology and beyond, from protein interactions and social relationships to power grids and citation records. Reasoning about such systems requires understanding their structure: which elements are central, which connections bridge separate communities, and how it changes when elements are removed. Although large language models (LLMs) excel at natural language, they struggle with such questions when networks are given as edge lists, sentences or measurement tables, because their structural meaning must be inferred. Here we introduce BioGlyph, which compiles network topology into an interpretable and transferable language of structural roles. BioGlyph combines graph partitioning and structural measurements to identify roles such as hubs, community cores and cross-community connectors, and fixed rules to translate them into a universal vocabulary. The representation describes each element through its structural role, supporting evidence and semantic consequences, leaving both the network and the LLM unchanged. Across twenty networks spanning five domains, BioGlyph substantially improves open LLMs' ability to answer structural reasoning questions, outperforming edge-based, numerical and learned representations by up to 26 percentage points in system accuracy. Ablations show that the gain comes from explicitly encoding structural roles in semantically interpretable terms. The gain is more prominent in dense, community-structured networks and diminishes in sparse networks whose topology is more readily inferred from text. In a budding-yeast protein-interaction network, BioGlyph exposes biological organization: cross-community connectors are enriched for essential genes, whereas peripheral proteins are depleted. BioGlyph thus provides an interpretable representation for both language models and scientists to reason about network structure.

AI.tldr: BioGlyph converts network topology into an interpretable structural-role vocabulary to improve LLM-based structural reasoning over networks.
AI.motivation: LLMs struggle to infer structural meaning from network data (edge lists, sentences, measurements); a transferable, human-interpretable representation is needed to support reasoning about centrality, bridges, and topology changes.
AI.method: Combine graph partitioning with structural measurements to identify roles (hubs, community cores, cross-community connectors) and translate them into a universal semantic vocabulary; describe each node by its role, supporting evidence, and semantic consequences without altering the network or LLM.
AI.result: Open LLMs show substantial gains in structural reasoning across 20 networks (up to 26 percentage points) compared to edge-based, numerical, or learned representations; ablations attribute gains to explicit encoding of structural roles; gains are larger in dense, community-structured networks and diminish in sparse networks; biological relevance demonstrated in budding-yeast PPI where cross-community connectors link essential genes.
AI.conclusion: BioGlyph offers an interpretable, transferable representation for network structure that enhances LLM reasoning and yields biological insights, applicable across domains.

title: MINERVA: How Small Can a Manipulation Policy Be and Still Solve LIBERO?
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models with billions of parameters now dominate the LIBERO manipulation benchmark, but the model capacity actually required by the benchmark remains unclear. We introduce MINERVA (MINimal Efficient Robotic Vision-Action policy), a family of deliberately compact visuomotor policies designed to measure this task-specific capacity floor. A 0.54M-parameter policy achieves 95.1% average success over 2,000 rollouts on the four standard LIBERO suites, only 2.4 points below the reported LeRobot $π_{0.5}$ result despite using 7,700$\times$ fewer parameters. Performance saturates near 1M parameters and collapses below 0.25M. Across broad architectural, training, and inference sweeps, only action-chunk length and vision capacity consistently exceed a $\pm$1-point training-seed band. Flow matching provides no detectable advantage over direct L1 regression across three seeds, while regression is up to 3.8$\times$ faster on GPU. A task-ID permutation probe shows that standard LIBERO instruction conditioning primarily selects among memorized tasks: changing only the task-ID mapping reduces success to near chance. The same recipe achieves 94.6% success across 89 LIBERO-90 tasks, while LIBERO-Plus perturbations reduce performance to 46--56%, with near-zero robustness to photometric shifts. The 0.54M policy replans every control step in 5--9 ms per chunk on a laptop CPU, 113$\times$ faster than SmolVLA and 1,400$\times$ faster than $π_{0.5}$, without a GPU. These results establish a first empirical estimate of LIBERO's task-specific capacity floor and motivate capacity-aware design and distillation for deployment-efficient robot policies.

AI.tldr: MINERVA shows that a compact 0.54M-parameter visuomotor policy can nearly saturate LIBERO performance, revealing a task-specific capacity floor and challenging the assumption that billion-parameter models are required for this benchmark.
AI.motivation: Quantify the task-specific capacity required for LIBERO manipulation and assess whether small, deployment-friendly policies can achieve competitive performance while revealing the space of architecture/training choices that influence capacity.
AI.method: Propose MINERVA, a family of compact visuomotor policies (~0.54M parameters) and evaluate across LIBERO suites and LIBERO-90/Plus tasks. Systematically vary architectural elements (vision capacity, action-chunk length), compare regression approaches (L1 regression vs flow matching), perform a task-ID permutation probe to test reliance on memorization, and benchmark inference speed on CPU across multiple seeds and perturbations.
AI.result: A 0.54M-parameter policy achieves 95.1% average success over 2,000 rollouts on LIBERO suites, only 2.4 points below LeRobot π0.5 despite >7,700x fewer parameters. Performance saturates near 1M parameters; collapses below 0.25M. Action-chunk length and vision capacity drive training-seed stability within ±1 point. Flow matching offers no advantage over direct L1 regression (regression is up to 3.8x faster on GPU). A task-ID permutation shows conditioning largely selects memorized tasks; changing only the mapping reduces success to near chance. The same design yields 94.6% on LIBERO-90 tasks; LIBERO-Plus perturbations drop to 46–56% with little robustness to photometric shifts. The 0.54M policy replans every control step in 5–9 ms per chunk on CPU (laptop), 113x faster than SmolVLA and 1,400x faster than π0.5, with no GPU required.
AI.conclusion: This work provides the first empirical estimate of LIBERO’s task-specific capacity floor, highlighting that a small, well-designed policy can achieve near-state performance while exposing the sensitivity to memorization and perturbations. It motivates capacity-aware design and distillation for deployment-efficient robot policies.

title: Exploring the Potential of Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training for Multi-Source Remote Sensing Data
comment: 9 pages, 4 figures, 5 tables. Submitted to AAAI 2027
summary: Contrastive language-image learning (CLIP) has become a key paradigm for remote sensing vision-language understanding. However, existing remote sensing contrastive learning methods are mostly built on RGB-oriented CLIP architectures, making it difficult to exploit heterogeneous sensors such as SAR, multi-spectral imaging (MSI), and hyperspectral imaging (HSI). To address this limitation, we propose OmniRSCLIP, an end-to-end contrastive learning framework that supports multi-source sensor inputs for remote sensing vision-language modeling. The key idea is to extend CLIP beyond its fixed RGB input interface without breaking the pretrained visual knowledge. To this end, OmniRSCLIP introduces Spectral-Spatial Basis Decomposition (SSBD), which formulates arbitrary-channel adaptation as a basis recomposition problem: pretrained CLIP patch embeddings provide transferable spatial bases, while wavelength-conditioned coefficients span sensor-specific embedding kernels within a constrained visual prior space. This design avoids forcing heterogeneous sensors into a fixed-channel input space, while aligning them in a unified image-text semantic space. We further introduce a spectral-context-aware mask-based contrastive learning scheme to suppress modality-specific redundant features and enhance fine-grained image-text alignment. Finally, to support multi-modal training, we construct OmniRS5M, the first large-scale remote sensing image-text corpus covering RGB, SAR, MSI, and HSI. Experiments on retrieval, zero-shot classification, and semantic localization show that OmniRSCLIP preserves strong RGB-domain performance while effectively extending CLIP to heterogeneous remote sensing modalities.

AI.tldr: OmniRSCLIP extends CLIP to multi-source remote sensing sensors (RGB, SAR, MSI, HSI) via Spectral-Spatial Basis Decomposition and spectral-context-aware masking, trained on OmniRS5M, achieving cross-sensor image–text alignment while preserving RGB performance.
AI.motivation: Current remote sensing CLIP methods are RGB-centric, failing to exploit heterogeneous sensors. There is a need to adapt to arbitrary-channel inputs without altering pretrained visual knowledge, enabling a unified cross-modal representation across sensors.
AI.method: Introduce Spectral-Spatial Basis Decomposition (SSBD): treat arbitrary-channel adaptation as basis recomposition where pretrained CLIP patch embeddings provide spatial bases and wavelength-conditioned coefficients generate sensor-specific embedding kernels within a constrained visual-prior space. Add a spectral-context-aware mask-based contrastive learning objective to suppress modality-specific redundancies and sharpen image-text alignment. Train end-to-end on OmniRS5M, a large-scale remote sensing text-image corpus including RGB, SAR, MSI, HSI.
AI.result: Experiments in retrieval, zero-shot classification, and semantic localization show that OmniRSCLIP maintains strong RGB-domain performance while effectively extending CLIP to heterogeneous RS modalities, achieving improved cross-modal alignment across sensors.
AI.conclusion: OmniRSCLIP demonstrates effective, end-to-end vision-language modeling for multi-source remote sensing data, enabling coherent cross-sensor semantic understanding without compromising RGB capabilities; the method introduces SSBD, spectral-context-aware masking, and the OmniRS5M dataset as key contributions.

title: The Attention Triangle in Audio-Video Models
summary: Audio-video diffusion models rely on cross-modal attention to coordinate text, sound, and visual content, yet this same mechanism can introduce subtle and systematic semantic leakage. We study these models by probing and analyzing the ``attention triangle,'' comprising the three cross-attention edges connecting the text, audio, and video streams, and examine how semantic information is routed across modalities during generation. Our analysis reveals that routing along the audio-video edge is bidirectional: audio can influence video generation, while video can influence audio generation. This edge is shaped by biases encoded in the model's parameters and emerges as a major contributor to leakage: when prompts are in tension with learned priors, cross-modal interactions may override the intended conditioning and reroute semantics toward visually canonical but incorrect outcomes. These effects suggest that semantic artifacts arise not merely from attention spreading beyond its intended target, but from structured, bias-driven interactions along specific pathways. Building on this perspective, we extract attention-derived signals that expose how semantics are distributed and grounded across modalities, and use them as a diagnostic tool to both analyze and deliberately incur leakage under controlled conditions. This enables us to probe the internal dynamics of cross-modal routing and isolate the role of individual interactions. We further leverage these signals to guide inference-time interventions that encourage more consistent cross-modal alignment. Extensive experiments support our analysis and demonstrate improved semantic grounding while preserving generation quality.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes cross-modal attention in audio-video diffusion models, revealing a bidirectional audio–video attention edge that can drive semantic leakage; it proposes attention-derived signals as diagnostics and uses inference-time interventions to improve cross-modal grounding while keeping generation quality.
AI.motivation: To understand and diagnose semantic leakage in multi-modal diffusion models, specifically how text, audio, and video semantics are routed through cross-attention, and to develop tools to analyze and mitigate misalignment.
AI.method: Probe the so-called attention triangle (text–audio, text–video, audio–video cross-attention). Analyze routing of semantic information across modalities, extract attention-derived signals to reveal distribution of semantics, deliberately induce leakage under controlled conditions for study, and apply inference-time interventions guided by these signals to improve cross-modal grounding.
AI.result: Found that the audio–video edge supports bidirectional influence: audio can steer video and video can steer audio. Leakage is shaped by learned priors and model biases, especially when prompts clash with priors. Attention-derived signals expose how semantics are grounded, enabling diagnostic use and controlled leakage experiments. Interventions guided by these signals yield improved semantic grounding without sacrificing generation quality.
AI.conclusion: Semantic artifacts arise from structured, bias-driven cross-modal routing rather than indiscriminate attention spread. Attention-based diagnostics allow principled analysis and targeted inference-time remedies to achieve more consistent cross-modal alignment.

title: The 2026 PNPL Competition: Word Classification and Efficient Cross-Subject Generalisation in LibriBrain100
summary:
The ambition of the 2025 PNPL competition (Landau et al., 2025) was to launch a multi-year curriculum for non-invasive speech decoding. Designed to progress from foundational tasks toward the linguistic complexity required for a practical brain-computer interface (BCI), it set the stage with speech detection and phoneme classification tasks. Winning submissions reached F1-macro scores of 95.6% and 73.6% on the respective tasks (Elvers et al., 2026), highly significant advances. This success was built on the LibriBrain dataset (Özdogan et al., 2025), the largest within-subject MEG dataset recorded at the time with ${\sim}50$ hours of data for one subject. However, while within-subject scale drives strong decoding performance, a practical BCI must generalise to new users from minutes of data, not hours.
  The 2026 PNPL competition responds to this challenge with LibriBrain100 (Mantegna et al., 2026), an extended LibriBrain dataset with 32 additional subjects (${\sim}40$ minutes each) plus even more within-subject data (${\sim}80$ hours). Advancing the curriculum of tasks to focus on word classification, two complementary tracks are presented in this competition: the Deep track targets within-subject word classification at scale, aiming at the best possible performance; the Broad track targets cross-subject generalisation, progressively reducing the amount of subject-specific fine-tuning data from ${\sim}40$ to ${\sim}20$ to ${\sim}10$ minutes, a duration that falls within a clinically feasible range and brings us a step closer to a non-invasive BCI capable of restoring communication to people living with profound paralysis.

AI.tldr: PNPL advances from within-subject MEG-based speech decoding to cross-subject generalization for non-invasive BCIs, via LibriBrain/LibriBrain100 datasets and two competition tracks (Deep within-subject word classification and Broad cross-subject generalization with reduced calibration). Reported high F1-macro on early tasks (95.6% and 73.6%) signal strong progress, with calibration down to clinically feasible minutes for broader use.
AI.motivation: To achieve practical non-invasive brain-computer interfaces that generalize to new users with minimal calibration data, addressing the gap between excellent within-subject performance and real-world usability.
AI.method: A multi-year curriculum of tasks starting from speech detection and phoneme classification toward word classification. Foundations built on LibriBrain (large, ~50 h MEG per subject); LibriBrain100 extends data to 32 additional subjects (~40 min each) and ~80 h per subject total data. Two tracks: Deep (within-subject word classification at scale) prioritizing performance, and Broad (cross-subject generalization) progressively reducing subject-specific fine-tuning data from ~40 to ~20 to ~10 minutes.
AI.result: Winning submissions achieved F1-macro scores of 95.6% (speech detection) and 73.6% (phoneme classification). LibriBrain was the largest within-subject MEG dataset at the time (~50 h/subject). LibriBrain100 expands the dataset with 32 new subjects and more within-subject data (~80 h total), enabling cross-subject generalization with minimized calibration.
AI.conclusion: The competition structure and expanded datasets push toward a practical non-invasive BCI capable of restoring communication with minimal per-user calibration. The Deep track targets optimal within-subject performance, while the Broad track confronts the cross-subject generalization challenge essential for real-world deployment.

title: RoughSense: Lightweight Terrain-Induced Rover Vibration Prediction Using Point Clouds and IMU Feedback
summary: Autonomous navigation in space requires reliable terrain assessment for safe operations, especially in underground environments with limited communication, computing resources, and power budget. This paper presents a lightweight method for real-time vibration-aware traversability mapping using a Light Detecting And Ranging (LiDAR) point cloud and Inertial Measurement Unit (IMU) measurements. An initial vibration proxy is estimated from terrain geometry by applying Random sample consensus (RANSAC) to local point-cloud patches produced by a Simultaneous Localisation And Mapping (SLAM) algorithm. In parallel, the IMU provides local observations of the vibration experienced by the rover during traversal. The point-cloud-based prediction is then corrected online using Recursive Least Squares, allowing the system to adapt the geometric estimate to the measured rover response. The approach is evaluated in a lunar analogue environment, an outdoor field, and an underground mine.

AI.tldr: A lightweight, real-time vibration-aware traversability mapping method using LiDAR-based terrain geometry and IMU data, fused online via Recursive Least Squares, validated in lunar analogue, outdoor, and underground mine.
AI.motivation: Autonomous space rover navigation in underground or communication-limited environments requires reliable, real-time terrain assessment that accounts for vibration and rover response within constrained compute and power budgets.
AI.method: 1) Generate local point-cloud patches via SLAM and apply RANSAC to estimate an initial vibration proxy from terrain geometry. 2) In parallel, use IMU measurements to observe rover vibration during traversal. 3) Fuse the geometric estimate with sensor observations online using Recursive Least Squares to adapt the prediction to actual rover response.
AI.result: The method enables online correction of the geometry-based prediction, yielding a lightweight, real-time traversability map. It is evaluated in a lunar analogue environment, an outdoor field, and an underground mine, demonstrating robustness across diverse terrains.
AI.conclusion: The approach provides an efficient, adaptive, vibration-aware traversability mapping framework suitable for resource-constrained, subterranean or space environments, improving safe autonomous navigation.

title: Neural-Collapse-guided Task-Free Continual Anomaly Detection
summary: Recent years have witnessed growing interest in continual anomaly detection for industrial visual inspection. However, real-world manufacturing environments exhibit unpredictable shifts in data distributions, rendering task-dependent continual learning assumptions impractical. To address this limitation, we formulate industrial anomaly detection as a task-free continual learning problem and propose NC-TFAD, a neural-collapse-inspired, geometry-driven framework for learning from non-stationary data streams without task boundaries. NC-TFAD freezes a pretrained backbone and aligns streaming features to a simplex Equiangular Tight Frame (ETF) prototype space to stabilize representation geometry under non-stationary streams. To satisfy the NC-inspired geometric construction in the absence of real anomalies, we generate synthetic anomaly samples as auxiliary anchors during training. Building on this geometry, we further introduce inter- and intra-class regularization together with a Focal Neural Collapse Contrastive (FNCC) loss to suppress representation drift and improve normal-anomaly separability. Finally, a normal-patch-prototype-guided localization branch constructs calibrated patch-wise deviation maps from normal training samples and fuses them with a weak self-attention prior, producing anomaly heatmaps without pixel-level annotations. Extensive experiments on MVTec AD and VisA show that NC-TFAD consistently outperforms representative task-free continual learning methods adapted from general vision, as well as unified anomaly detection baselines, in both image-level detection and pixel-level localization under the task-free continual learning protocol. These results highlight that geometry-driven modeling offers an effective and robust solution for task-free continual anomaly detection in real-world industrial applications.

AI.tldr: NC-TFAD is a task-free continual learning framework for industrial anomaly detection that uses neural-collapse-inspired geometry. It freezes a pretrained backbone and aligns streaming features to a simplex ETF prototype space to stabilize representations under non-stationary data, using synthetic anomalies as anchors, inter-/intra-class regularization and a FNCC loss, plus a normal-patch-prototype-guided localization branch for calibrated anomaly heatmaps. It outperforms task-free continual learning baselines and unified anomaly detectors on MVTec AD and VisA for image-level and pixel-level tasks under task-free CL.
AI.motivation: Industrial anomaly detection operates under non-stationary data streams with unknown task boundaries, making traditional task-specific continual learning ineffective. There is a need for a geometry-driven, task-free approach that maintains stable representations while enabling effective normal–anomaly separation.
AI.method: The approach freezes a pretrained backbone and maps streaming features into a simplex Equiangular Tight Frame (ETF) prototype space to enforce geometric stability. Synthetic anomaly samples serve as auxiliary anchors to satisfy the NC-inspired geometry in the absence of real anomalies. The method introduces inter- and intra-class regularization and a Focal Neural Collapse Contrastive (FNCC) loss to suppress drift and improve separability. A normal-patch-prototype-guided localization branch generates calibrated patch-wise deviation maps from normal samples and fuses them with a weak self-attention prior to produce anomaly heatmaps without pixel-level annotations.
AI.result: Experiments on MVTec AD and VisA show NC-TFAD consistently outperforms representative task-free continual learning methods adapted from general vision, as well as unified anomaly detection baselines, for both image-level detection and pixel-level localization under the task-free CL protocol.
AI.conclusion: Geometry-driven, neural-collapse-inspired modeling provides robust and effective solutions for task-free continual anomaly detection in real-world industrial applications, enabling stable representations and accurate anomaly localization without task boundaries.

title: KC-Bench: A Dynamic Interactive Benchmark for Evaluating Knowledge Conflicts in LLM Agents
summary: As LLMs increasingly act through tools, they must reconcile user instructions, parametric knowledge, and dynamic environmental observations before taking actions. We introduce KC-Bench, a controlled multi-turn benchmark for measuring this capability across world-knowledge conflicts, input inconsistencies, and multi-source temporal conflicts. Its 238 tasks are manually screened from more than 1,000 generated candidates and combine a user simulator, stateful tools, deterministic environment assertions, an open-source natural-language evaluator, and human trajectory verification. Evaluation of nine models, including DeepSeek-V4-Flash, GLM-5.2, and MiniMax-M3, shows substantial cross-domain variation: no model handles factual correction, identity consistency checking, and temporal conflict resolution reliably across all settings. In the simulated environments, missed conflicts can propagate to tool calls or synthetic protected-data flows. KC-Bench isolates this model-level behavior rather than ranking complete agent frameworks, and provides a reproducible diagnostic for developing conflict-aware reasoning and execution safeguards.

AI.tldr: KC-Bench is a controlled, multi-turn benchmark for diagnosing how LLMs reconcile user instructions, world knowledge, and dynamic observations across 238 tasks.
AI.motivation: To measure and diagnose model-level conflict-aware reasoning and safeguards in tool-using LLMs, addressing world-knowledge conflicts, input inconsistencies, and multi-source temporal conflicts that can propagate through tool use.
AI.method: Introduces KC-Bench with 238 manually screened tasks (from >1,000 candidates); combines a user simulator, stateful tools, deterministic environment assertions, an open-source NL evaluator, and human trajectory verification; evaluates nine models including DeepSeek-V4-Flash, GLM-5.2, and MiniMax-M3.
AI.result: Substantial cross-domain variation observed; no model reliably handles factual correction, identity consistency checking, or temporal conflict resolution across all settings; missed conflicts can propagate to tool calls or synthetic protected-data flows in simulated environments.
AI.conclusion: KC-Bench isolates model-level behavior rather than ranking complete agent frameworks, and provides a reproducible diagnostic for developing conflict-aware reasoning and execution safeguards.

title: B2B Customer Conversion Prediction: A Document Representation, Graph Theory, and CatBoost Driven Methodology
comment: 10 pages, 6 figures. Presented at the 2nd Workshop on End-End Customer Journey Optimization at KDD 2023
summary: In the one-time selling B2B context, the buying cycle may last months or even years. During the long process, targeting customers that have a high potential to make purchases and recommending personalized campaigns accordingly are important for effective marketing. For this goal, we study the following problems, B2B customer data aggregation, customer feature generation, and prediction of whether a B2B customer would show interest in making a purchase (i.e., prediction of conversion into sales funnel). We propose an algorithm to aggregate individual contacts to the B2B customer level based on multiple keys. For non-standardized keys such as company names, we propose a novel architecture to cluster them in a domain encompassing irregularities such as spelling mistakes and spelling variants. We then define and generate a set of features and apply the CatBoost model for customer conversion prediction. Our framework achieves 91\% prediction accuracy. Based on the prediction results and analysis of the model, we then discuss personalized campaign recommendations to foster conversion.

AI.tldr: A B2B conversion prediction framework that aggregates contacts to customers across multiple keys, clusters non-standardized keys (e.g., company names) to handle irregularities, generates features, and uses CatBoost for binary prediction, achieving 91% accuracy and enabling personalized campaigns.
AI.motivation: In long B2B sales cycles (months to years), identifying high-potential customers and delivering personalized marketing campaigns is crucial for efficient resource allocation and higher conversion rates.
AI.method: 1) Aggregate individual contacts at the B2B customer level using multiple keys. 2) For non-standardized keys (e.g., company names), use a novel clustering architecture to handle spelling mistakes and variants. 3) Generate a feature set. 4) Apply CatBoost for binary prediction of conversion (interest to purchase).
AI.result: The framework reports 91% prediction accuracy on conversion forecasting. The analysis also discusses personalized campaign recommendations derived from model results to foster conversion.
AI.conclusion: The proposed multi-key aggregation, robust non-standardized-key clustering, and CatBoost-based prediction yield a practical framework for targeting high-potential B2B customers and informing personalized campaigns, with potential for further validation and scalable deployment.

title: A Multi-Vine Soft Robot Enabling Accessible Working Channel and Steering
summary: Soft eversion robots, also known as vine robots, have attracted growing interest for navigation and inspection tasks, including minimally invasive medical applications [1]. A vine robot consists of a thin, flexible, inextensible tube folded inward that everts and grows forward when pressurized. This tip-growth enables navigation with minimal friction, making vine robots well suited for complex environments such as the human colon [2]. While their inherent softness allows passive conforma- tion to curved pathways in confined spaces, navigation performance strongly depends on environmental inter- actions, including contact angle and the length of un- constrained deployed material [3], [4]. Sharp directional changes, such as those in the sigmoid colon, often limit passive growth and necessitate active steering. Existing solutions include distributed artificial muscles [5] or dedicated tip-based steering mechanisms [6]. In addition, many applications require payload delivery, such as sensors and tools [7], [8]. Within the ERC Synergy project EndoTheranostics, this motivates the development of vine robots capable of delivering micro- surgical tools during growth. Prior work has integrated working channels within the vine body [8], [9], but these approaches constrain tool size, introduce friction, and limit access to the environment to the robot tip. In this work, we propose a multi-vine architecture in which two vine robots are coupled to an externally integrated working channel via soft mounting tips [10]. Independent vine actuation enables active tip steering while advancing the working channel without embed- ding it within the vine bodies Figure 1. Experiments demonstrate sharp steering of nearly 90 degrees during growth, highlighting the potential of this architecture for versatile medical and non-medical applications.

AI.tldr: A multi-vine soft robot architecture couples two vine robots to an externally integrated working channel via soft mounting tips, enabling independent tip steering while advancing the channel; demonstrated ~90° steering, enabling micro-tool delivery with reduced friction and external channel deployment.
AI.motivation: To enable onboard delivery of micro-surgical tools during vine robot growth, addressing the constraint of embedding tools inside the vine body and improving steering in constrained environments (e.g., colon).
AI.method: Two vine robots are coupled to an externally integrated working channel through soft mounting tips. Independent vine actuation provides active tip steering while the working channel advances without being embedded in the vine bodies.
AI.result: Experiments demonstrate sharp steering of nearly 90 degrees during growth, validating the feasibility of the proposed architecture for versatile medical and non-medical applications.
AI.conclusion: The architecture offers a viable route for active tip steering with an external tool channel, enabling maneuverability in complex environments and expanding the application space for vine robots, including EndoTheranostics.

title: Mudragen: Geometrically Supervised Generation of Interacting Two-Hand Mudras for Preserving Indian Classical Dance Heritage
comment: Accepted for publication in ACM Journal on Computing and Cultural Heritage (JOCCH) Special Issue on Visual Heritage
summary: Automatic generation of hand gestures is essential for the transmission of Indian classical dance and critical for its preservation. Indian classical dance gesture datasets are inherently low-resource, and the canonical Sanskrit definitions of many mudras lack precise textual descriptions, limiting the effectiveness of conventional text-conditioned image generation models. We present \textbf{MudraGen}, a conditional diffusion framework that synthesizes realistic RGB images of \textit{Samyukta Hasta Mudras} -- interactive two-hand gestures from Bharatanatyam (an Indian classical dance form). Unlike prior work on simple hand signs or single-hand gestures, MudraGen introduces geometry-aware supervision to capture the precise coordination, anatomical validity, and cultural nuance of interacting hands. We formulate three geometry-aware objectives: Keypoint Loss for 3D joint alignment, Joint Offset Loss for inter-hand spatial coherence, and Shape Consistency, which serves as an anatomical regularizer by encouraging consistent hand morphology while allowing independent hand poses. Together, these objectives guide the diffusion model toward anatomically plausible and well-coordinated hand configurations, enabling the synthesis of photorealistic and pose-accurate gesture images. Experimental results show that MudraGen surpasses existing state-of-the-art generative approaches in visual realism, anatomical correctness, and preservation of fine hand-pose structure, enabling faithful reproduction of complex Samyukta Hasta mudras. Beyond quantitative gains, its ability to generate culturally grounded and structurally consistent gestures highlights practical applications in cultural preservation and dance education.

AI.tldr: MudraGen is a diffusion-based model that synthesizes photorealistic, pose-accurate RGB images of two-hand Samyukta Hasta mudras, using geometry-aware supervision to enforce anatomical validity and inter-hand coordination.
AI.motivation: Indian classical dance mudras, especially two-hand configurations, suffer from low-resource datasets and lack precise textual descriptions; existing text-to-image models struggle with anatomical accuracy and cultural nuance in complex gestures.
AI.method: A conditional diffusion framework with three geometry-aware objectives: Keypoint Loss for 3D joint alignment, Joint Offset Loss for inter-hand spatial coherence, and Shape Consistency to regularize hand morphology while permitting independent poses.
AI.result: MudraGen outperforms state-of-the-art generative approaches in visual realism, anatomical correctness, and preservation of fine hand-pose structure, enabling faithful reproduction of Samyukta Hasta mudras.
AI.conclusion: The approach supports cultural preservation and dance education by generating culturally grounded, structurally consistent gestures and offers a viable tool for digitizing and preserving complex traditional gestures.

title: A computable representation of the physical laboratory enables verifiable workflows
summary: Making science computable requires representations of both scientific knowledge and the physical world in which scientific claims are tested. A computable representation of the physical laboratory is established through typed research objects, capability-bound operations and a compositional workflow algebra. It provides the physical-world counterpart to machine-readable knowledge, expressing workflows as programs over evolving laboratory states with explicit dependencies, decisions, iteration and concurrency. The representation was implemented in a modular agentic robotic laboratory by binding formal operations to executable Function Skills. For diverse scientific intents, capability-relative workflows were generated, while stateful simulation propagated object transformations and verified operation preconditions and laboratory constraints before dispatch. The proposed representation and its engineering framework jointly establish a general computational interface between agent reasoning and capability-bound physical transformations, providing a foundation for end-to-end autonomous scientific discovery.

AI.tldr: A computable representation for laboratory workflows using typed objects, capability-bound operations, and a compositional workflow algebra to enable end-to-end autonomous discovery in a modular robotic lab.
AI.motivation: Bridge machine-readable knowledge with physical laboratory processes by providing a general computational interface for agent reasoning and capability-bound physical transformations, enabling programmable, verifiable, and autonomous experimentation.
AI.method: Introduce typed research objects, capability-bound operations, and a compositional workflow algebra. Implement in a modular, agentic robotic laboratory by binding formal operations to executable Function Skills. Generate capability-relative workflows. Use stateful simulation to propagate object transformations and verify preconditions and laboratory constraints before dispatch. Supports dependencies, decisions, iteration, and concurrency.
AI.result: Establishes a general computational interface between agent reasoning and physical transformations; demonstrates end-to-end autonomous laboratory workflows in a modular robotic lab; supports evolving laboratory states, operation preconditions, and constraints; enables diverse scientific intents through capability-relative workflows.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides a foundation for end-to-end autonomous scientific discovery by making laboratory processes computable, verifiable, and adaptable, integrating agent reasoning with capability-bound physical transformations.

title: FlowBalance: Verifier-Grounded Self-Improvement from On-Policy Reasoning Experience
comment: 28 pages, 7 figures, 10 tables. Code and blog available
summary: A reasoning model can improve from its own on-policy experience, but this inner loop is fragile: terminal verifiers provide reliable yet sparse supervision, while dense same-model guidance can reinforce false confidence or overconcentrate learning on a narrow solution mode. We introduce FlowBalance, a verifier-grounded self-improvement method that learns a normalized distribution over complete responses. For each on-policy trajectory, a frozen training-time view of the same policy uses privileged context to produce token-level log-probability gains, which are aggregated into a trajectory-level self-guidance score. FlowBalance calibrates this score with the verifier-derived group advantage: guidance is retained on positive-advantage trajectories, reversed on negative-advantage trajectories, and disabled when the rollout group provides no outcome preference. The resulting energy exponentially reweights a reference policy, and profiled trajectory balance fits the normalized target with one log-partition estimate per rollout group. This realizes outcome-calibrated self-guidance via trajectory balance, without a separate token-level imitation loss. Our analysis establishes within-group contrast preservation, a minimum-change reverse-KL characterization, monotonic verifier control of target reward, and an exact correction against false-positive self-guidance on rejected responses. On mathematical reasoning, FlowBalance improves average performance over FlowRL on both Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B, while also improving training speed and stability, avoiding direct OPSD's response-length collapse, and exhibiting higher correct-strategy diversity in a controlled AIME24 diagnostic.

AI.tldr: FlowBalance is a verifier-grounded self-improvement method that uses a verifier to calibrate trajectory-level self-guidance for on-policy learning, reweighting complete responses via an energy-based formulation to improve reasoning performance and training stability over FlowRL on Qwen models.
AI.motivation: On-policy reasoning models suffer from fragile learning loops: sparse, terminal verifier signals and dense, potentially misleading self-guidance. A mechanism is needed to calibrate self-improvement signals using outcome-aware, group-wise feedback to stabilize learning and improve diversity of correct strategies.
AI.method: For each on-policy trajectory, a frozen training-time view of the same policy uses privileged context to compute token-level log-probability gains. These gains are aggregated into a trajectory-level self-guidance score and calibrated by the verifier-derived group advantage. Guidance is retained on positive-advantage trajectories, reversed on negative-advantage trajectories, and disabled when there is no outcome preference. An energy-based reweighting of a reference policy is performed, with a one-log-partition estimate per rollout group to fit the target distribution. This yields outcome-calibrated self-guidance via trajectory balance without a separate token-level imitation loss.
AI.result: FlowBalance improves average performance over FlowRL on Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B, enhances training speed and stability, avoids OPSD’s response-length collapse, and yields higher correct-strategy diversity on a controlled AIME24 diagnostic.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides within-group contrast preservation, a minimum-change reverse-KL characterization, monotonic verifier control of target reward, and exact correction against false-positive self-guidance on rejected responses, representing a principled, energy-based trajectory-balancing approach to verifier-guided self-improvement.

title: Virtual Testing of Automated Driving Systems through Credible Simulations
summary: Simulation is increasingly used to support safety-related decision-making in road transport, particularly for the assessment and approval of automated driving systems (ADS). The complexity of ADS behavior and size of their operational design domains make exclusive reliance on physical testing impractical, leading to extensive use of virtual testing (VT) during the approval phase. This shift raises critical questions regarding the credibility of modelling and simulation (M&S) results used to support road safety decisions. Current VT accreditation approaches in the ADS domain typically rely on validation-only practices, which have been shown to scale poorly when applied to complex, multi-tool simulation environments. To address this limitation, this paper proposes a risk-based framework for assessing the credibility of simulation toolchains used in ADS safety evaluation, drawing inspiration from established practices in other safety-critical domains, notably NASA's STD-7009 for models and simulations. The framework extends traditional verification and validation (V&V) by explicitly linking credibility requirements to the intended use of simulation outputs and to the safety criticality of the decisions they support within the approval process. It provides a lifecycle-oriented assessment scheme integrating toolchain management, modelling assumptions and limitations, verification, validation, and sensitivity analysis. Credibility acceptance thresholds are defined proportionally, allowing differentiated requirements depending on whether simulation is used for exploratory safety analysis, partial decision support, or as a substitute for physical testing. While demonstrated for ADS, the proposed approach is directly applicable to road safety and simulation studies where VT plays a central role in safety assessment and regulatory decision-making.

AI.tldr: A risk-based credibility framework for ADS simulation toolchains that extends verification and validation (V&V) to account for intended use and safety-criticality, enabling lifecycle assessment of virtual testing (VT) in road safety regulatory decisions.
AI.motivation: Current VT accreditation often relies on validation-only practices, which scale poorly in complex, multi-tool simulation environments. A credible, risk-based approach is needed to link simulation outputs to their intended safety decisions in ADS certification.
AI.method: Proposes a lifecycle-oriented credibility framework that integrates toolchain management, modelling assumptions/limitations, verification, validation, and sensitivity analysis. Defines credibility acceptance thresholds that scale with use-case (exploratory safety analysis, partial decision support, or full substitution for physical testing) and draws on NASA STD-7009 for guidance.
AI.result: A structured, risk-based credibility framework for ADS safety evaluation. Extends V&V by explicitly tying credibility requirements to intended use and safety criticality, providing a lifecycle process for evaluating toolchains and outputs in VT for regulatory decisions.
AI.conclusion: The framework is directly applicable to ADS and road safety VT used in regulatory decision-making and can be applied to other safety-critical simulation studies where VT underpins safety assessments.

title: When Do Frozen VLMs Respond to Image-Free Object-Token Edits? An Answer-Key-Free Protocol and What It Reveals
summary: Answering what-if queries about a scene with a VLM usually means injecting the assumption as text or repainting the scene with a generative model. We instead move the edit to the representation level, before the model input. The image is abstracted into a set of object-level tokens, and the original image never enters the VLM. This design rests on an open question: when do frozen VLMs actually respond to such token edits? We introduce an answer-key-free protocol: no post-edit answer is annotated. It scores edits whose answers are logically determined, and audits itself by reversing each scoreable choice. The protocol reveals three structures. The response is not free: explicit edit teaching, not ordinary VQA training, produces it in dense scenes and multiplies it in sparse ones, on all three operations. Once on, it is governed by token cleanliness and density, with deployable detector+segmenter tokens competitive with the oracle and outperforming it on VRSBench. And reading is a separable axis: the image-free token route preserves 92-96% of a matched patch-token baseline's free-text VQA, and the answers measurably depend on the tokens. The response, cleanliness, and reading structures are sign-preserved across two remote-sensing datasets (iSAID, VRSBench) and three frozen LM backbones. We release the probe generator, records, judge logs, and code.

AI.tldr: Abstracts a scene-editing workflow that operates on object-level tokens before VLM input, avoiding post-editing, and reveals structured behavior (response, cleanliness, reading) that persists across datasets and backbones; introduces an answer-key-free protocol and releases tooling.
AI.motivation: To determine when frozen vision-language models respond to token-level edits and to shift editing from image-space or text prompts into a representation-space, enabling controllable, self-audited VLM interactions without explicit post-edit labels.
AI.method: Represent the image as a set of object-level tokens and perform edits at the token level prior to model input. Introduce an answer-key-free protocol that scores edits based on logically determinate answers, and audits by reversing scoreable choices. Investigate three emergent structures: response, cleanliness, and reading. Compare token-based editing with detector/segmenter tokens, test across dense vs sparse scenes, and evaluate on remote-sensing datasets (iSAID, VRSBench) using multiple frozen LM backbones. Release a probe generator, records, judge logs, and code.
AI.result: Findings show that explicit edit teaching is necessary for strong response behavior in dense scenes and becomes more pronounced in sparse scenes. Token cleanliness and density govern the response, with deployable detector+segmenter tokens performing close to an oracle and outperforming it on VRSBench. Reading is a separable axis where image-free token routes preserve 92-96% of a matched patch-token baseline’s free-text VQA, and answers depend on the tokens. The response, cleanliness, and reading structures generalize across two remote-sensing datasets and three frozen LM backbones. Tools released include probe generator, records, judge logs, and code.
AI.conclusion: Token-level edits at the representation level reveal predictable, audit-able VLM behavior and enable competitive VQA performance without injecting the original image, with robust transfer across datasets and backbones; a reproducible protocol and tooling are provided.

title: Analysis of Prompt Engineering for Drug Toxicity Prediction
summary: Clinical trials in the UK can cost up to £1.3 million, with approximately 90% drug failure rate. Toxicity is a major contributing factor in drug failure. Testing is time and cost intensive. In recent years, the use of artificial intelligence has been increasingly explored to aid in the prediction of drug toxicity, with extensive use of large language models (LLMs). However, LLMs can show considerable variation when minor changes are made to prompts, which raises concerns about their sensitivity to prompt engineering. Prompt engineering is used to optimise a prompt given to an LLM to generate the desired output. This paper proposes a method to analyse prompt engineering for drug toxicity prediction. The aim of the paper is to investigate the importance of prompt phrasing for drug toxicity prediction. LLMs were prompted to identify chemical properties of significance when predicting drug toxicity. Prompts were constructed to investigate; job role, prompt structuring, and rule interpretation. LLMs were then used to generate datasets, using the identified features from initial prompting, which were then passed to machine learning algorithms. The experiments show that the natural variance which occurs in LLMs outweighs any fine-tuning of prompts. There were, however, substantial improvements in model performance when using chemoinformatic code to extract features instead of using LLM-generated values. The proposed analysis methodology is applicable to a wide range of prompt types across different areas of bioinformatics.

AI.tldr: Prompt-engineering analysis for LLM-based drug toxicity prediction; prompts’ phrasing shows limited impact compared with intrinsic LLM variation; chemoinformatic features outperform LLM-derived ones; methodology generalizable to bioinformatics prompts.
AI.motivation: High costs and high failure rates in early clinical trials, with toxicity as a leading cause. LLMs are explored to predict toxicity, but prompt sensitivity raises concerns. A systematic analysis of prompt engineering is needed to assess its impact on model performance.
AI.method: 1) Prompt LLMs to identify chemical properties relevant to toxicity; construct prompts varying job role, structure, and rule interpretation. 2) Use LLM outputs to create datasets. 3) Train conventional ML models on these datasets. 4) Compare with models trained on chemoinformatic features rather than LLM-derived features. 5) Generalize the methodology as applicable to other bioinformatics prompts.
AI.result: Intrinsic variation in LLM outputs dominates the effect of prompt fine-tuning, with natural variance outweighing adjustments to prompts. Using chemoinformatic features yields substantial performance gains over LLM-generated features.
AI.conclusion: The proposed analysis framework is broadly applicable to different prompt types in bioinformatics. Relying solely on prompt engineering for toxicity prediction is insufficient; traditional domain features can provide superior performance. The methodology offers a generalizable approach to evaluating prompt effects across bioinformatics tasks.

title: Selective Hypergraph Refinement for Frozen Graph Clustering
summary: Existing graph-clustering methods typically improve clustering performance by optimizing model parameters and node representations. Effective means of further improving the clustering results of an already trained and frozen model, however, remain limited. We study post-processing for frozen graph clustering. After checkpoint fixation, the procedure uses no labels and updates neither model parameters, node representations, nor the original graph structure. Instead, it exploits an attribute hypergraph to supplement higher-order relations that ordinary graphs cannot readily express, thereby refining existing cluster assignments. Because global hypergraph refinement can yield both performance gains and erroneous updates, we propose Selective Hypergraph Refinement (SHR). The method generates candidate residual directions from the hypergraph and evaluates their reliability using graph structure, node attributes, and matched-null evidence. It updates only nodes with sufficient support and otherwise retains their original assignments. Further analysis shows that whether a node changes cluster is jointly governed by its native assignment gap and the directional strength of the refinement. In a controlled common-suite evaluation, 13 of 15 backbone-dataset cells had a positive mean macro gain, one produced exact no-action, and one was negative. The cell-equal macro gain was 0.066 pp (95% bootstrap CI, [0.030, 0.107] pp), while only 0.209% of hard assignments changed on average. A broader 15-combination native-interface evaluation yielded a macro gain of 0.137 pp at a mean change ratio of 0.375%. These results indicate that frozen clustering outputs retain a limited but measurable refinement space after training. The effect is heterogeneous across backbone-dataset pairs, and broader coverage also increases exposure to negative transfer.

AI.tldr: Post-processing for frozen graph clustering using a hypergraph-based selective refinement (SHR) to adjust cluster assignments without retraining.
AI.motivation: To improve clustering performance after training when models are fixed and no labels are available, by leveraging higher-order relations via an attribute hypergraph.
AI.method: Construct candidate residual directions from the hypergraph, evaluate their reliability using graph structure, node attributes, and matched-null evidence, and selectively update only nodes with sufficient support; gating by native assignment gap and directional strength.
AI.result: Across a controlled suite, 13 of 15 backbone-dataset cells showed positive mean macro gain; one cell had no change, one negative. Cell-equal macro gain ~0.066 pp (CI 0.030–0.107). On average only 0.209% of hard assignments changed. A broader 15-combination native-interface evaluation yielded macro gain ~0.137 pp with mean change ratio ~0.375%.
AI.conclusion: Frozen clustering outputs harbor a small but detectable refinement space; SHR achieves modest gains with low update rate and is sensitive to dataset-backbone heterogeneity, risking negative transfer with broader coverage.

title: Robot Aware Computational Design of Object Specific Passive Grippers for Additive Manufacturing
summary: This paper presents an end-to-end computational pipeline that converts a selected object mesh, a measured object state, and a selected six-axis robot into an object-specific, unactuated, additively manufacturable gripper. The method couples exact-mesh RGB-D/ICP pose registration, deterministic surface-contact sampling, uncertainty-aware wrench screening, selection among six passive capture mechanisms, object-conformal surface synthesis, full-orientation robot inverse kinematics, a swept-volume-aware manufacturing domain, directional fused-deposition finite-element screening, and constrained three-dimensional SIMP topology optimization. Unlike workflows that treat grasp selection, tool geometry, motion, and structural design as separate problems, every exported design is bound to the source mesh, object pose, robot flange, contact set, and insertion hypothesis by a traceable design identifier. We derive the implemented registration, contact, fit-tolerance, finite-element, and density-optimization equations and prove three properties of the numerical construction: nodal load preservation, monotonic compliance sensitivity under SIMP interpolation, and voxel-domain containment after topology post-processing. Four archived object-specific attempts - a rabbit, camera flange, 3DBenchy, and faceted bust - meet the nominal fit, uncertain-wrench, runtime-sweep, and baseline/post-topology FEA gates. A deliberately enlarged +/-3 mm, +/-5 degree pose stress check differentiates the designs, retaining 29-134 of 160 simulated trials. Their reconstructed topologies retain 92.0-97.6% of the FE domain because functional regions are protected. Archived robot photographs show the corresponding printed assemblies qualitatively, while nominal material properties and absent coupon-calibrated, instrumented tests keep all four at digital-screening status rather than operational release.

AI.tldr: End-to-end, object-specific gripper design pipeline that binds a source mesh, pose, and robot to a manufacturable gripper via integrated registration, contact sampling, topology optimization, and FEA; demonstrated in simulation on four objects with traceable design identifiers, but only digital-screening validation.
AI.motivation: To create a fully integrated, traceable design-to-fabrication workflow for unactuated additively manufactured grippers, reducing silos between grasp selection, tool geometry, motion, and structural design and enabling verifiable, repeatable designs bound to source data.
AI.method: 1) Exact-mesh RGB-D/ICP pose registration 2) deterministic surface-contact sampling 3) uncertainty-aware wrench screening 4) selection among six passive capture mechanisms 5) object-conformal surface synthesis 6) full-orientation robot inverse kinematics 7) swept-volume-aware manufacturing domain 8) directional fused-deposition finite-element screening 9) constrained 3D SIMP topology optimization 10) traceable design identifier binding to source mesh, pose, flange, contact set, and insertion hypothesis. The authors derive registration, contact, fit-tolerance, FE, and density-optimization equations and prove: nodal load preservation, monotonic compliance sensitivity under SIMP, voxel-domain containment after post-processing.
AI.result: Four object-specific attempts (rabbit, camera flange, 3DBenchy, faceted bust) achieve nominal fit, uncertain-wrench, runtime-sweep, and baseline/post-topology FEA gates. A stress check of ±3 mm/±5° filters designs to 29–134 of 160 trials. Reconstructed topologies retain 92.0–97.6% of the FE domain, indicating preservation of functional regions. Printed assemblies exist, but due to nominal materials and lack of instrumented tests, all remain at digital-screening status rather than operational release.
AI.conclusion: An integrated, traceable end-to-end design-to-fabrication pipeline is demonstrated, binding design outputs to source data and enabling consistent performance evaluation within a digital screening workflow. Physical validation and instrumented testing remain necessary to transition to operational use, but the approach reduces design fragmentation and enhances manufacturability assurance.

title: OCR-EDR: Rendering-Aware Diagnosis and Repair for Closed-Loop OCR Improvement
summary: Although document OCR systems perform increasingly well on routine documents, complex formulas, structured text, and long-tail formats remain error-prone. OCR predictions may omit fine-grained content or hallucinate unsupported outputs, while equivalent encodings of the same visible content must be accommodated. Existing OCR evaluation methods mostly report aggregate metrics, offering limited support for analyzing case-level errors and improving OCR performance. We propose OCR-EDR (OCR Error Diagnosis and Repair), a rendering-aware framework that advances from fine-grained diagnosis to iterative repair. Given a source image, an editable OCR prediction, and its rendered image, OCR-EDR first jointly assesses whether the prediction and its rendering are consistent with the source, preserving valid predictions, including rendering-equivalent ones, while diagnosing and localizing genuine errors. It then applies executable edits and may request an updated rendering for iterative reassessment. We construct OCRErrBench from diverse real OCR predictions, covering text and formulas, exact and rendering-equivalent positives, and genuine errors, and develop the DocEDR model to execute the diagnosis--repair loop. On OCRErrBench, DocEDR achieves 94.78% diagnostic accuracy.
