It repairs 86.23% of erroneous inputs to visual consistency, raises formula Case-F1 by 30.99 percentage points over DOCR-Inspector-7B on DOCRcaseBench, and improves formula CDM by up to 4.62 percentage points on the identified Bad subsets of four OCR systems on UniMER-Test. These results show that OCR-EDR turns fine-grained OCR analysis into verified corrections and performance gains.

AI.tldr: OCR-EDR introduces a rendering-aware diagnostic-repair loop for OCR, aligning predictions with rendered visuals to diagnose and fix errors, validated on diverse benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Lack of case-level error analysis and misalignment between OCR content and its rendering; enable targeted repairs that preserve valid or rendering-equivalent outputs.
AI.method: Given a source image, an OCR prediction, and its rendering, jointly assess consistency, preserve valid or rendering-equivalent outputs, diagnose genuine errors, apply executable edits, and optionally request updated rendering for iterative reassessment. Build OCRErrBench with diverse predictions and develop DocEDR to execute the loop.
AI.result: DocEDR achieves 94.78% diagnostic accuracy; repairs 86.23% of erroneous inputs to visual consistency; raises formula Case-F1 by 30.99 percentage points over DOCR-Inspector-7B on DOCRcaseBench; improves formula CDM by up to 4.62 percentage points on Bad subsets of four OCR systems on UniMER-Test.
AI.conclusion: Rendering-aware OCR analysis enables verified corrections and measurable performance gains, demonstrating the value of integrating content and rendering in OCR evaluation and repair.

title: Synthetic Semantic Supervision for Contrastive Code Representation Learning in Small Transformers: An Empirical Study
summary: General-purpose code embeddings power tools for code search, classification, and retrieval. Compact transformer encoders for code typically rely on either human-written docstrings (labor-intensive and inconsistent) or mined structural signals such as execution traces (setting-specific and costly to collect). We empirically study an alternative: contrastive pretraining of small encoders with synthetically generated natural-language descriptions emphasizing code functionality and intent, paired with code in a dual-encoder framework at training and discarded at inference. We benchmark this approach against pretraining-based baselines, generalist LLMs, and embedding-specific models on eight retrieval, classification, and generation tasks across C, C++, and Java. Synthetic semantic supervision yields statistically significant gains over pretraining baselines of the same inference-time size on five of eight tasks, with parity on two more; once fine-tuned, it matches or exceeds zero-shot models two orders of magnitude larger on classification, and it stays on par with execution-aware supervision at matched pretraining data, suggesting a scalable, effective alternative to existing code-representation paradigms.

AI.tldr: Synthetic natural-language supervision via contrastive pretraining of small dual-encoder models yields competitive code representations without runtime signals, across eight tasks in C/C++/Java.
AI.motivation: Reduce reliance on labor-intensive human docstrings and costly execution traces by exploring scalable synthetic semantic supervision for small encoders.
AI.method: Pretrain small transformer encoders with contrastive learning using synthetic NL descriptions of code functionality paired to code in a dual-encoder setup (trained together, discarded at inference). Evaluate on eight retrieval, classification, and generation tasks across C, C++, and Java, against pretraining baselines, generalist LLMs, and embedding models.
AI.result: Synthetic supervision provides statistically significant gains over size-matched pretraining baselines on 5 of 8 tasks, parity on 2; with fine-tuning it matches or exceeds zero-shot models two orders of magnitude larger for classification and remains competitive with execution-aware supervision when data is matched.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates a scalable, effective alternative to docstrings or execution traces for code representation: small encoders can achieve strong performance, reducing data collection costs while maintaining broad task coverage.

title: Latent Energy Action Planning with World Models
summary: Latent world models support efficient model predictive control from high-dimensional observations, yet optimizing a single learned latent objective can favor action sequences whose decoder-predicted terminal descriptor does not match the goal descriptor. We introduce Latent Energy Action Planning (LEAP), which treats the complete action horizon as a differentiable variable and optimizes it through a frozen LeWorldModel (LeWM). LEAP couples terminal latent goal matching with a terminal-window state energy. Low energy requires the predicted terminal latent to agree with the goal latent and the decoder-predicted terminal descriptor to agree with the goal descriptor. A frozen goal-conditioned proposal initializes the search, a quasi-Newton solver refines actions through the autoregressive rollout, and post-optimization projection enforces the admissible action range. Across four control domains using the officially released LeWM checkpoints, the complete LEAP planning system raises mean success from 77.5% for LeWM planned with the cross-entropy method (LeWM+CEM) to 94.8% under a matched protocol, a 17.3-percentage-point improvement, while retaining the frozen LeWM representation and predictor.

AI.tldr: LEAP optimizes the full action horizon in a frozen latent world model by jointly minimizing terminal latent goal mismatch and decoder-predicted terminal descriptor energy, improving planning success over LeWM+CEM across four control domains.
AI.motivation: Single latent-objective optimization can drive action sequences whose decoded terminal descriptor mismatches the goal; a joint, differentiable horizon-wide objective can enforce coherence between latent goals and decoded observations while leveraging a frozen world model.
AI.method: Treat the entire action horizon as a differentiable variable within a frozen LeWorldModel. Use a terminal-energy objective combining latent-goal alignment and decoder-terminal-descriptor alignment (plus a terminal-window state energy). Initialize with a frozen, goal-conditioned proposal, refine actions via a quasi-Newton method through autoregressive rollout, and apply a post-optimization projection to satisfy action bounds; preserve the frozen LeWM representation and predictor.
AI.result: Across four control domains using LeWM checkpoints, LEAP raises mean success from 77.5% (LeWM+CEM) to 94.8% under a matched protocol, a 17.3 percentage-point improvement, while retaining the frozen model and predictor.
AI.conclusion: LEAP demonstrates that horizon-wide, energy-based latent planning with a fixed world model and a strong initialization can substantially improve control performance, suggesting the value of jointly regularizing latent goals and decoder outputs in latent-world models.

title: A comparative study on the accuracy & repeatability of mobile robotic platforms for the delivery of precision NDE measurement
summary:
Mobile robotic platforms offer a flexible alternative to fixed manipulators for non-destructive evaluation (NDE) of large aerospace structures, but their base-positioning accuracy and how that accuracy should inform deployment have not been assessed under a common, externally referenced protocol. This work presents a laser tracker-based evaluation workflow (ground truth approximately 6 micrometers) that measures the static and segmented trajectory positioning accuracy of five commercial mobile platforms (KUKA KMP-1500, KUKA KMR, MiR250, Boston Dynamics Spot, Clearpath Husky) under a common protocol. A coupled multi-corner calibration recovers the laser-to-robot transformation and reflector offsets; ordinary least squares over all poses is used, with robust estimation retained only as a blunder check.
  Static positioning accuracy ranged from a median of 8.2 mm (KMP-1500) to 63.5 mm (Spot), with the wheel-odometry-only Husky uncalibratable. Dynamic path following was characterised by cross-track error; the component was insensitive to temporal alignment, which ranged from 6.9 mm (KMP-1500) to 112.1 mm (Spot). Both accuracy and calibratability tracked localisation capability, from the newest LiDAR SLAM platform to map-free visual odometry. No configuration meets the 0.2 to 1.0 mm aerospace NDE tolerance from the base alone; the results are framed as a design input that sizes the supplementary sensing each platform requires: roughly one order of magnitude for the best platform and nearly two for the worst, providing a reproducible basis for platform selection rather than a feasibility claim.

AI.tldr: Laser-tracker-based workflow assesses static and dynamic positioning accuracy of five mobile platforms under a common protocol; none meet aerospace NDE base-position tolerance; results guide platform selection and required supplementary sensing.
AI.motivation: Quantify base-position accuracy of mobile robots for non-destructive evaluation (NDE) of large aerospace structures and establish an externally referenced protocol for cross-platform comparison.
AI.method: Ground-truth positioning via laser tracker (~6 µm) with coupled multi-corner calibration to recover laser-to-robot transform and reflector offsets; ordinary least squares over all poses with robust estimation as blunder check; evaluate static positioning accuracy (median errors) and dynamic path following (cross-track error) across five platforms (KMP-1500, KMR, MiR250, Spot, Husky); analyze calibratability and localisation method influence.
AI.result: Static median position errors: 8.2 mm to 63.5 mm; dynamic cross-track error: 6.9 mm to 112.1 mm; Husky uncalibratable; no platform achieves 0.2–1.0 mm aerospace NDE tolerance; results imply the need for supplementary sensing, roughly one order of magnitude accuracy improvement for the best platform and nearly two for the worst; provide a reproducible basis for platform selection rather than a feasibility claim.
AI.conclusion: The workflow delivers a repeatable, externally referenced benchmark for platform selection and design input in NDE deployments; base-position accuracy alone is insufficient—supplementary sensing must be sized per platform; results frame deployment decisions rather than claiming feasibility.

title: Preserving Knowledge across Space and Time for Continual Video Deepfake Detection
comment: Accepted by ECCV 2025. Code will be available at github.com/rama0126/MSFD
summary: The continuous emergence of high-quality video deepfakes requires detectors that continually adapt to new forgery patterns, yet existing approaches, which are designed for deepfake images, fail to capture video-specific cues. Unlike deepfake images that contain only spatial artifacts, deepfake videos leave distinct evidence along both spatial and temporal axes, necessitating the separate preservation of each modality during sequential model updates. To overcome this limitation, we introduce a continual deepfake video detection framework, Modality-Specific Frequency Distillation (MSFD), that explicitly decomposes video features into spatial, temporal, and spatiotemporal modalities in the frequency domain. This decomposition enables independent preservation of each modality, as different deepfake video types exhibit varying reliance on spatial and temporal cues across tasks. Furthermore, MSFD adopts a cross-modality decorrelation loss that encourages spatiotemporal representations to remain orthogonal to single-modality cues. Extensive experiments show that our framework achieves stronger adaptation and preserves performance more effectively than state-of-the-art methods across diverse continual deepfake video scenarios.

AI.tldr: Proposes Modality-Specific Frequency Distillation (MSFD), a continual deepfake video detector that decomposes features into spatial, temporal, and spatiotemporal modalities in the frequency domain with a cross-modality decorrelation loss to preserve modality-specific cues and improve continual adaptation.
AI.motivation: Video deepfakes evolve; existing detectors trained on images miss video-specific spatial/temporal cues; continual learning demands preserving modality-specific information while adapting.
AI.method: MSFD explicitly decomposes video features into spatial, temporal, and spatiotemporal components in the frequency domain; preserves each modality independently during sequential updates; introduces a cross-modality decorrelation loss to keep spatiotemporal representations orthogonal to single-modality cues.
AI.result: Empirical results show stronger adaptation and better retention of performance across diverse continual deepfake video scenarios, outperforming state-of-the-art methods.
AI.conclusion: Frequency-domain, modality-specific decomposition with decorrelation enables robust continual deepfake video detection, addressing both spatial/temporal cues and catastrophic forgetting in continual learning.

title: Counterfactual Routing Using Integer Programming with Constraint Generation
summary: We present our submission to the IJCAI 2025 'Counterfactual Routing Competition' (CRC 25). The goal of the competition is to find counterfactual explanations for the shortest path problem. This requires deciding what the minimal changes to a road network would make a route chosen by the user the optimal route. This enables explanations such as "Your suggested route would indeed have been optimal, if road X were not a bicycle path." Our solution models the problem as an integer program, iteratively incorporating constraints until an exact solution is found. In the final evaluation on held-out test instances, our method ranked fourth in solution quality and obtained its solution fastest on every instance, with an average runtime of 9.0 seconds compared to 118.8 seconds for the next-fastest submission.

AI.tldr: An IP-based approach to CRC 25 provides exact counterfactual explanations for shortest paths by iteratively adding constraints; it ranks fourth in solution quality but is fastest on all instances (avg 9.0s) compared to 118.8s for the next fastest.
AI.motivation: To provide interpretable explanations for route choice by identifying minimal network changes that would render the user’s route optimal, addressing the need for transparent routing decisions in transportation networks.
AI.method: Formulate the problem as an integer programming model that searches for minimal edge/parameter modifications to the road network. The solver iteratively adds constraints to enforce that the user-specified route becomes the optimal path under the modified network, continuing until an exact solution is found.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation on held-out test instances shows the method achieves fourth place in solution quality while consistently achieving the fastest runtimes, averaging 9.0 seconds per instance (vs 118.8 seconds for the next-fastest submission).
AI.conclusion: An exact, constraint-augmented IP approach yields efficient counterfactual explanations for shortest-path routing, combining correctness with strong practical performance; there is a trade-off between achieving top-quality counterfactuals and maintaining speed.

title: Geometry-Aware Graph Construction via Adaptive Spectral Bandwidth Control
comment: Accepted at IEEE MLSP 2026. 6 pages, 4 figures
summary: Kernelized graph methods - spectral clustering, diffusion maps, and sparse kernel -regression graphs - that use Gaussian kernels depend on the choice of Gaussian bandwidth sigma, which governs the spectral character of the local kernel operator. When sigma is too small, the kernel overestimates local complexity and treats each sample as an independent direction; when sigma is too large, the kernel collapses multiple directions together, the condition number diverges, and all geometric discrimination is lost. We propose a choice of scale to make the spectral complexity of the kernel consistent with the intrinsic complexity of the underlying manifold. We propose a per-node bandwidth criterion that operationalizes this principle by jointly matching the kernel's effective rank to the local intrinsic dimension estimated via minimum spanning tree, anchoring the search in the manifold-consistent log-log scaling regime. We evaluate SSL embeddings from six encoders on CIFAR-100, showing that adaptive bandwidth consistently improves leave-one-out (LOO) classification and label propagation (LP) accuracy over fixed-bandwidth methods and competing adaptive methods.

AI.tldr: Adaptive per-node Gaussian bandwidth for kernelized graph methods aligns spectral complexity with intrinsic manifold complexity, improving SSL embeddings and downstream accuracy on CIFAR-100.
AI.motivation: Gaussian kernels in spectral methods depend on sigma; inappropriate bandwidth leads to over- or under-discrimination and poor geometric separation. A scale that matches intrinsic manifold complexity is needed.
AI.method: Introduce a per-node bandwidth criterion that matches the kernel’s effective rank to the local intrinsic dimension estimated via minimum spanning tree, within a manifold-consistent log-log scaling regime. Evaluate SSL embeddings from six encoders on CIFAR-100 to compare adaptive vs fixed/adaptive baselines.
AI.result: Adaptive bandwidth consistently improves leave-one-out classification and label propagation accuracy over fixed-bandwidth methods and competing adaptive methods.
AI.conclusion: A per-node, MST-informed bandwidth that ties kernel spectral complexity to local intrinsic dimension yields more faithful graph-based SSL representations and better task performance.

title: FWBC-VLA: Force-Aware Whole-Body Compensation for Contact-Rich Loco-Manipulation
summary: Contact-rich loco-manipulation requires a bridge between semantic action generation and physical interaction control. Existing Vision-language-action (VLA) models generate task-level actions from visual and linguistic observations, but cannot interpret the physical interactions induced by those actions. While the whole-body control (WBC) policy can stabilize the robot, it cannot distinguish task-relevant interaction forces from forces induced by external disturbances during manipulation. Although force/torque sensors provide direct measurements of physical interactions, retrofitting them entails additional hardware costs and substantial integration effort, particularly for platforms not designed with sensor integration in mind. To address this problem, we propose FWBC-VLA, a force-aware framework that bridges task-level VLA action generation and low-level whole-body compensation control for wheeled-legged robots. First, we introduce HSR-Force, a sensorless residual-torque estimator for inferring contact strength and its temporal variation. These contact estimates are then encoded as tokens and injected into the VLA action expert during action decoding, enabling the policy to perceive contact onset, sustained loading, and release. For loco-manipulation tasks, all parameters of the pretrained VLA backbone are fine-tuned on our WL\&Arm Dataset, which comprises more than 5,000 episodes. Moreover, the robot's proprioceptive state, the Jacobian-derived body-frame force estimate, and the estimated contact state are jointly fed into a compensation generator to produce corrective actions. The manipulation-centric actions are subsequently combined with the corrective actions and passed to the WBC policy for execution. Real-world experiments on whiteboard wiping and door opening with a door closer demonstrate the effectiveness of our FWBC-VLA in contact-rich loco-manipulation.

AI.tldr: A force-aware framework (FWBC-VLA) connects vision-language action generation with low-level whole-body control for contact-rich loco-manipulation by using a sensorless residual-torque estimator (HSR-Force), tokenizing contact info and injecting it into the VLA decoder, and adding a compensation generator for corrective actions, validated on real tasks.
AI.motivation: To close the gap between semantic action generation and physical interactions in loco-manipulation, and to avoid hardware-intensive force/torque sensors while still distinguishing task-relevant contact forces from disturbances.
AI.method: Introduce HSR-Force to estimate contact strength without sensors; encode contact estimates as tokens for the VLA action decoder; fine-tune the VLA backbone on WL&Arm dataset (>5k episodes); feed proprioception, Jacobian-based body-frame force, and contact state into a compensation generator to produce corrections; combine these corrections with manipulation actions and pass to a WBC policy for execution.
AI.result: Real-world experiments on whiteboard wiping and door opening with a door closer demonstrate the effectiveness of FWBC-VLA in contact-rich loco-manipulation.
AI.conclusion: FWBC-VLA provides an effective bridge between semantic action generation and low-level control for wheeled-legged robots in contact-rich tasks through sensorless contact estimation, token-based context augmentation of the VLA policy, and a corrective action generator that informs a WBC policy.

title: STARS-GS: Structure-Aware Regularized Gaussian Splatting for Large-Scale Aerial Surface Reconstruction
summary: Large-scale 3D surface reconstruction from aerial imagery is fundamental to geospatial mapping and urban modeling. Recent advances in 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) have demonstrated considerable potential for this task. However, existing methods still face three major challenges in large and complex scenes: scene partitioning may split continuous scene elements across independently optimized sub-regions; geometric constraints mainly focus on the attributes of individual Gaussians while overlooking their local organization; and uniform regularization struggles to accommodate heterogeneous geometric structures. To address these issues, we propose STARS-GS, a structure-aware 3DGS framework for large-scale surface reconstruction. First, we introduce a structure-aware scene partitioning strategy that better preserves continuous scene structures during partitioning and reduces cross-region geometric inconsistencies and stitching artifacts through boundary refinement. Second, we develop neighborhood-aware Gaussian organization that extends geometric constraints from individual primitives to their neighborhood organization, encouraging Gaussians to better conform to local surface geometry. Third, we introduce adaptive surface regularization that adjusts the regularization strength according to local geometric characteristics, promoting geometric consistency in structured regions while preserving plausible variations in unstructured regions. Extensive experiments on large-scale aerial photogrammetry benchmarks demonstrate that STARS-GS consistently outperforms the evaluated Gaussian-based methods in surface reconstruction. It increases the average F1-score from 0.640 for the second-best method to 0.698, corresponding to a relative improvement of approximately 9.1\%, demonstrating effective improvements in geometric accuracy and surface completeness.

AI.tldr: STARS-GS proposes a structure-aware 3D Gaussian Splatting framework for large-scale aerial surface reconstruction, addressing partitioning, neighborhood organization, and adaptive regularization to improve geometric accuracy and completeness, achieving ~9.1% relative F1-score gain on benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Large-scale 3DGS struggles with cross-region consistency, local organization of Gaussians, and heterogeneous geometric structures in complex scenes; current methods treat primitives independently and use uniform regularization.
AI.method: Three components: 1) structure-aware scene partitioning with boundary refinement to preserve continuity; 2) neighborhood-aware Gaussian organization guiding Gaussians using local neighborhood constraints; 3) adaptive surface regularization modulating regularization strength by local geometry.
AI.result: On large-scale aerial photogrammetry benchmarks, STARS-GS consistently outperforms Gaussian-based methods, achieving average F1-score 0.698 vs 0.640 (≈9.1% relative improvement).
AI.conclusion: Structure-aware and adaptive constraints yield better geometric accuracy and surface completeness in large-scale reconstructions.

title: Artificial Intelligence for Energy Optimization in Data Centers
summary: Data centers are increasingly optimized by artificial intelligence and, at the same time, increasingly loaded by it. The literature treats these as two unrelated problems: control studies model workload as an exogenous arrival process, while sustainability studies model infrastructure as a fixed multiplier. We screen roughly 194 papers retrieved through a documented protocol, code 63 of them, and report what the coding shows. Of 28 primary control-oriented studies, 18 are validated in simulation alone and 5 reach physical hardware or a production facility; none account for water withdrawal, and none account for embodied carbon. Reported savings intervals across four technique families overlap almost completely, which means the field cannot presently rank its own methods. Ten recurring gaps are scored for consequence and tractability, and we set out CLEAR-DC, a framework coupling a control-policy branch to a workload-demand branch through an explicit elasticity term, reads out net rather than direct benefit, and emits a schema-conformant record covering energy, carbon, water, embodied share and validation venue. The framework is an architectural and methodological proposal, not a trained system; the contribution we defend empirically is the corpus analysis and the reporting schema derived from it. Coding sheet, derived statistics and all result artifacts: https://github.com/Kimalice/AI-for-Energy-Optimization-in-Data-Centers-Closing-the-Optimizer-Load-Loop

AI.tldr: Systematic review of AI-for-energy optimization in data centers; identifies gaps (no water/embodied carbon, simulation-heavy, few hardware validation), and proposes CLEAR-DC for integrated, net-benefit reporting with energy, carbon, water, and embodied metrics.
AI.motivation: Data centers are energy-intensive and increasingly guided by AI, but control and sustainability narratives are treated separately; a unified framework and reporting standard are needed to assess net benefits and environmental impact.
AI.method: Screened ~194 papers via documented protocol; coded 63; 28 control-oriented; validated mostly in simulation; 5 reach hardware; none account for water withdrawal or embodied carbon; mapped savings across four technique families; identified ten gaps; proposed CLEAR-DC architecture coupling control-policy with workload-demand via an explicit elasticity term; emits a schema-conformant record covering energy, carbon, water, embodied share, and validation venue; provided a GitHub repository with artifacts.
AI.result: Most control studies rely on simulation; few touch water or embodied carbon; no studies account for water withdrawal or embodied carbon; savings intervals across technique families overlap (limitation for ranking methods); ten recurring gaps identified and scored for consequence and tractability; CLEAR-DC couples a control-policy branch to a workload-demand branch via elasticity to yield net benefits and a structured reporting schema; the contribution is primarily corpus analysis and the reporting schema, not a deployed system.
AI.conclusion: The field cannot presently rank optimally between methods; CLEAR-DC offers an architectural/methodological path and a standardized reporting approach; emphasis on incorporating water and embodied carbon for comprehensive sustainability assessment; the authors provide data and code artifacts to enable replication and extension.

title: Risk and Anomaly Identification for Distribution Network Optimal Operation Based on Reinforcement Learning and Uncertainty Quantification
summary: Reliable operation of modern distribution networks requires timely identification of operational risks and anomalous events under pervasive uncertainty. In practice, operators must identify risks that are inherent in stochastic yet in-distribution conditions, and anomalies that correspond to out-of-distribution behaviors such as unusual load patterns, extreme weather or cyber-physical attacks. This paper addresses this joint risk and anomaly identification problem for optimal distribution network operation and proposes a deep reinforcement learning framework that is explicitly uncertainty aware. We integrate distributional and Bayesian deep reinforcement learning to realize a second- order uncertainty quantification scheme that decomposes total uncertainty into aleatoric and epistemic components, which are respectively used to characterize inherent risk and out-of- distribution anomalies. The resulting epistemic estimates drive both exploration during training and out-of-distribution detec- tion with fallback control during deployment, whereas aleatoric estimates are used to characterize intrinsic operational risk. Simulation results demonstrate the performance of our DRL agent and the effectiveness of the uncertainty quantification.

AI.tldr: A deep reinforcement learning framework for distribution networks that is uncertainty-aware via a joint distributional and Bayesian approach, decomposing total uncertainty into aleatoric (inherent risk) and epistemic (out-of-distribution anomalies). Epistemic estimates guide exploration and OOD detection with fallback control; aleatoric estimates quantify intrinsic operational risk. Demonstrated via simulations.
AI.motivation: Reliable, safe operation of distribution networks under pervasive uncertainty requires distinguishing inherent risks from anomalies caused by distribution shift (e.g., extreme loads, weather, attacks). A model that quantifies both types of uncertainty can improve decision-making, exploration during training, and safety during deployment.
AI.method: Integrates distributional DRL (to model value distribution) with Bayesian DRL (to quantify epistemic uncertainty). Produces second-order uncertainty quantification that separates aleatoric and epistemic components. Epistemic estimates drive exploration during training and OOD detection with a fallback control during deployment; aleatoric estimates characterize intrinsic operational risk.
AI.result: Simulation results demonstrate the DRL agent's performance and validate the effectiveness of the uncertainty quantification in distinguishing risk from anomalies.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework offers an uncertainty-aware control approach for distribution networks, enabling explicit handling of inherent risks and out-of-distribution anomalies through calibrated exploration, OOD detection, and fallback control, backed by simulation-based validation.

title: A hybrid pipeline for dynamic ontology-based semantic mapping
summary: Semantic mapping plays a crucial role in the ability of a robot to interact with objects, operate and navigate a complex environment. The most common pipeline for semantic mapping consists of geometric mapping and localization (SLAM), perception, semantic fusion and semantic representation. However, more recent works also integrate a form of prior knowledge in their application, most notably knowledge graphs or semantic scene graphs, to improve contextual understanding of the environment. In this paper, we present a hybrid pipeline for semantic mapping. Our system incorporates an external calibrated camera using homography projection for geometric mapping and localization, combined with object detection, persistent object tracking and ontology driven semantic updates to build a dynamic semantic world model. Linear regression models are also used for correction of the estimated values of real world coordinates. The system continuously updates object instances, spatial properties and semantic relations based on real time sensory data. Ontologies are selected as form of knowledge representation due to their hierarchical structure, semantic expressiveness and support for dynamic world modelling.

AI.tldr: Hybrid SLAM + ontology-driven semantic mapping with real-time updates to a dynamic semantic world model.
AI.motivation: To enhance contextual understanding and robustness of semantic mapping by integrating prior knowledge through ontologies/semantic graphs with real-time object-level updates.
AI.method: A hybrid pipeline using an external calibrated camera with homography projection for geometry and localization, combined with object detection, persistent object tracking and ontology-driven semantic updates. The system uses linear regression to correct estimated real-world coordinates and updates object instances, spatial properties, and semantic relations in real time. Ontologies (hierarchical, expressive) are chosen to represent dynamic world knowledge.
AI.result: Demonstrates end-to-end construction of a dynamic semantic world model with real-time updates of objects, spatial properties, and semantic relations, leveraging ontology-driven updates and coordinate corrections.
AI.conclusion: Ontology-based semantic mapping in a hybrid SLAM framework enables dynamic, context-rich representations and improved semantic understanding for robotic perception.

title: Preprocessing Failure and Adversarial Detection in Depthwise-Separable Edge Vision Systems
summary: Preprocessing-based defenses are the standard first-line response to adversarial attacks on edge vision systems, requiring no retraining, no architectural changes, and widely recommended as model-agnostic mitigations. Yet the foundational evaluations of these defenses were conducted on residual or Inception-class architectures, not on the depthwise-separable CNNs that dominate edge deployments. This untested assumption leaves a gap in the security evaluation literature. This paper closes that gap by evaluating six preprocessing defenses against adversarial perturbations across both architecture families. Across all perturbation levels and defenses tested, the two depthwise-separable architectures show consistently poor recovery while the residual architecture shows partial recovery; ablation results are consistent with an architectural rather than parametric explanation, though only three architectures and one attack family are evaluated. Crucially, this failure is not merely a negative result. The same output divergence that disqualifies preprocessing as a recovery mechanism reveals a detection opportunity: preprocessing consistently disrupts clean predictions while leaving adversarial predictions largely unchanged, an asymmetry that is directly measurable without retraining or architectural modification. We further show that standard image quality metrics are unreliable proxies for defense effectiveness, a methodological gap in current evaluation practice. A practitioner decision framework is provided for adversarially resilient edge vision deployment.

AI.tldr: Preprocessing defenses against adversarial perturbations have architecture-dependent effectiveness: depthwise-separable CNNs fail to recover, while residual nets show partial recovery. This reveals an architectural gap in prior security evaluations and uncovers a usable detection signal based on output divergence; standard image quality metrics are poor defense proxies, and a practitioner decision framework is proposed.
AI.motivation: Edge vision systems predominantly use depthwise-separable CNNs; existing security evaluations of preprocessing defenses were conducted on residual/Inception-like architectures, leaving uncertainty about their effectiveness on modern edge models. The work fills this gap by testing defenses across architecture families and examining both recovery and detection aspects.
AI.method: Systematic evaluation of six preprocessing defenses against adversarial perturbations across two architecture families (depthwise-separable vs residual CNNs). Experiments across multiple perturbation levels, ablation studies on architecture mix (three architectures) and one attack family, analysis of output divergence to identify architectural explanations, assessment of image quality metrics as proxies, and formulation of a practitioner decision framework for edge deployment.
AI.result: Across perturbation levels, depthwise-separable architectures exhibit poor recovery to adversarial perturbations; residual architecture shows partial recovery. Ablation supports an architectural rather than parametric explanation. A key detection opportunity arises: preprocessing disrupts clean predictions while leaving adversarial predictions largely intact, enabling post-hoc detection without retraining. Standard image quality metrics are unreliable as proxies for defense effectiveness. A practitioner decision framework for adversarially resilient edge deployment is proposed.
AI.conclusion: Preprocessing defenses are not uniformly effective across modern edge architectures; their value lies in enabling detection of adversarial inputs rather than robust recovery. Architectural characteristics strongly influence defense outcomes. Evaluation practices should account for architecture type, and practitioners should leverage the detected asymmetry between clean and adversarial predictions when deploying edge vision systems.

title: Proactive Service Agents: A Unified Decision Framework, Methods, and Evaluation
summary: Large language model agents can plan, invoke tools, and modify external states, yet most systems still take an explicit user instruction as a fixed starting point. Proactive service moves the decision upstream: an agent must infer service opportunities from incomplete environmental and user signals, choose among remaining silent, asking, assisting, and acting, and account for interruption, misunderstanding, overreach, and privacy costs. This survey gives an operational definition centered on initiative and formulates the problem as a partially observable sequential decision process constrained by authorization and risk. The formulation represents timing, content, and delivery within one structured action, while making explicit the option value of waiting, the decision value of questions, and feedback-induced state changes. On this basis, we organize existing methods along one decision pipeline (state and need estimation, intervention gating, action construction, and feedback adaptation) and describe prescribed, predictive, model based, and return optimizing mechanisms as nonexclusive policy-construction components. We further normalize decision units and three-axis evidence descriptors across streaming dialogue, screen, video, software-engineering, and human-agent collaboration resources, and formalize metrics for triggering, timing, calibration, user burden, safety, and policy value. The synthesis shows why offline classification performance alone does not predict deployment benefit and why long-term memory is not a defining condition of proactivity. Reliable proactive service instead requires calibrated incremental intervention value, verifiable authorization, recoverable execution, and counterfactual evidence.

AI.tldr: A formal, proactive service framework for LLM agents via a constrained, partially observable sequential decision process, with an explicit initiative and a structured action pipeline; deployment depends on calibrated value, authorization, recoverable execution, and counterfactual evidence—not solely offline accuracy.
AI.motivation: To move proactive capabilities upstream, enabling agents to infer opportunities from incomplete signals and choose among silent, asking, assisting, or acting, while managing interruption, misunderstanding, privacy, and risk.
AI.method: Define an operational, initiative-centered framework and cast decision-making as a partially observable sequential process constrained by authorization and risk. Represent timing, content, and delivery within one action; quantify option value of waiting and decision value of questions; develop a four-stage decision pipeline (state/need estimation, intervention gating, action construction, feedback adaptation); survey existing methods as nonexclusive policy-building components; normalize decision units and three-axis evidence descriptors across multiple modalities; formalize metrics for triggering, timing, calibration, user burden, safety, and policy value.
AI.result: A unified formulation and evaluation framework showing that offline classification performance does not guarantee deployment benefit, and long-term memory is not a prerequisite for proactivity. Reliable proactive service requires calibrated incremental intervention value, verifiable authorization, recoverable execution, and counterfactual evidence; provides guidelines for system design and evaluation across modalities.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a concrete operational blueprint for proactive systems, clarifying decision granularity, evidence standards, and success metrics; it emphasizes the need for authorization, recoverable actions, and evidence-based evaluation to ensure real-world usefulness and safety.

title: DE-Venus: A Data-Efficient RLVR Framework for Large Language Models
summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) improves large language model reasoning, but its practical scaling is constrained by expensive on-policy rollouts and the cost of obtaining reliable targets at scale. Existing methods address sample selection, incomplete supervision, or noisy labels separately, often entangling supervision logic with distributed training and hindering controlled comparison and reuse. We present DE-Venus, a unified framework for data-efficient RLVR that treats supervision as evolving state across data preparation and policy optimization. It organizes this lifecycle into three modules: Active Data Selection allocates training and annotation budgets; Weak Supervision Construction derives learning signals from unlabeled examples; and Training-Time Supervision Refinement filters or corrects unreliable supervision. DE-Venus supports seven representative methods and a data-selection pipeline by expressing method-specific decisions as offline dataset transitions or online transformations of targets, rewards, batches, and advantages while preserving verl's distributed execution contracts. Across public benchmarks and three business scenarios, separate configurations preserve or improve model quality with only 10% of labels or as little as 13% of relevant data; selected business configurations also reduce observed convergence steps by 63%--75%. DE-Venus thus reduces annotation and training costs without sacrificing scalable RL execution.

AI.tldr: DE-Venus is a data-efficient RLVR framework that decouples supervision into three lifecycle modules—Active Data Selection, Weak Supervision Construction, and Training-Time Supervision Refinement—enabling multiple RLVR methods with far less labeling/data while preserving distributed training.
AI.motivation: RLVR for LLM reasoning is hampered by expensive on-policy rollouts and unreliable, scale-intensive targets. A unified, data-centric framework can reduce annotation effort, support fair method comparisons, and enable reuse across organizations.
AI.method: DE-Venus organizes supervision as evolving state across data preparation and policy optimization. It defines three modules: Active Data Selection allocates budgets; Weak Supervision Construction derives learning signals from unlabeled data; Training-Time Supervision Refinement filters/corrects unreliable supervision. It expresses method-specific decisions as offline dataset transitions or online transformations of targets, rewards, batches, and advantages, compatible with distributed RL execution and supporting seven representative methods and a data-selection pipeline.
AI.result: Across public benchmarks and three business scenarios, configurations preserve or improve model quality with only 10% of labels or as little as 13% of relevant data; observed convergence steps reduced by 63%–75% in selected configurations.
AI.conclusion: DE-Venus reduces annotation and training costs without sacrificing scalable RL execution and provides a reusable, configurable data-centric approach to RLVR.

title: Revisiting Topological Graphs for Macro Action based Closed-loop Reinforcement Learning of Vision Language Navigation in Continuous Environment
summary: Vision-Language Navigation in Continuous Environments (VLN-CE) requires an agent to follow natural language instructions through unseen environments. Existing imitation learning (IL) pipelines struggle in this closed-loop setting: behavior cloning suffers from distribution shift, and DAgger's expert actions become ambiguous upon trajectory deviation. While Reinforcement Learning (RL) offers a natural paradigm to address this, directly applying RL to micro action spaces is sample-inefficient due to reward sparsity. To overcome this bottleneck, we reformulate VLN-CE as a Hierarchical Markov Decision Process (MDP), explicitly decoupling high-level planning from low-level control. By abstracting the environment into a topological graph, our high-level policy operates on a macro action space of frontier nodes, with a training-free low-level controller acting as its state transition, which significantly compresses the decision horizon and makes closed-loop RL tractable. To support RL optimization on the macro MDP, we propose an action-aware value head to effectively evaluate state values under the dynamic frontier action space, powering a graph-based PPO. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our architecture. Finally, our model achieves state-of-the-art performance on the R2R-CE and RxR-CE benchmarks.

AI.tldr: Hierarchical MDP for VLN-CE using macro frontier actions with a training-free low-level controller and an action-aware value head, enabling graph-based PPO and achieving SOTA on R2R-CE and RxR-CE.
AI.motivation: Overcome IL distribution shift and RL sample inefficiency in continuous VLN-CE by decoupling planning from control and reducing decision horizon.
AI.method: Abstract environment as a topological graph; high-level policy selects frontier nodes (macro actions); a training-free low-level controller performs state transitions; an action-aware value head handles a dynamic frontier action space; optimized with graph-based PPO.
AI.result: Experiments show the approach is effective and achieves state-of-the-art performance on R2R-CE and RxR-CE benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Hierarchical MDP with macro actions and a dedicated value function enables tractable closed-loop RL for VLN-CE, improving sample efficiency and performance.

title: BMCTrack-d: Pig re-identification and tracking via back marks in challenging camera settings
summary: Automated pig monitoring is essential for assessing their health, behaviour, and welfare. To date, most pig monitoring solutions operate on the group-level, because individual-level monitoring requires reliable long-term identification and tracking of each animal. For domesticated pigs this remains challenging because pigs of the same breed often have highly uniform appearances. Moreover, research on pig monitoring is almost exclusively reported in top-down view camera settings, which considerably ease tracking, but are not always an option in practice. In this work, BMCTrack-d is presented, a novel tracking-by-detection approach that leverages unique back marks to enable robust pig re-identification and tracking in a challenging side-view camera setting, afflicted by rapidly moving pigs, severe occlusions and low resolution. The method first predicts the detected pigs' identities using a neural network-based back mark classifier. To improve re-identification reliability over time, two dedicated post-processing stages are introduced: a temporal prediction consistency check, which validates the identity assignments against the recent prediction history, and deduplication, which resolves conflicting identity assignments in each time step. By explicitly prioritising accurate, appearance-based re-identification over continuous tracking, the proposed approach addresses a key limitation of existing trackers for individual-level monitoring scenarios. On a demanding test set BMCTrack-d outperforms two strong baselines, BoT-SORT-ReID and TrackTrack-ReID, by 9.11% and 1.03%, respectively, in higher-order tracking accuracy. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of back mark-based re-identification and tracking for robust individual-level pig monitoring in challenging settings.

AI.tldr: BMCTrack-d uses back marks to enable robust single-pig re-identification and tracking in side-view videos with occlusions and low resolution, achieving improved higher-order tracking accuracy over baselines.
AI.motivation: Enable reliable individual-level pig monitoring in challenging side-view settings where uniform appearance and rapid movement hinder traditional trackers.
AI.method: Tracking-by-detection with a neural network-based back mark classifier, followed by two post-processing stages: (1) temporal prediction consistency check to validate identity history, and (2) deduplication to resolve conflicting identities per frame; prioritizes appearance-based re-identification over continuous tracking.
AI.result: On a demanding test set, BMCTrack-d outperforms BoT-SORT-ReID by 9.11% and TrackTrack-ReID by 1.03% in higher-order tracking accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Back-mark-based re-identification combined with post-processing yields robust, appearance-based individual pig tracking in challenging side-view scenarios, addressing key limitations of existing trackers.

title: SimSkill: A Lifelong Learning AI Agent for Autonomous Mastery of Traffic Simulation
summary: As large language models (LLMs) become increasingly capable, the long-term value of AI systems depends not only on solving individual requests, but also on transforming experience and accumulated knowledge into durable, reusable competence. We introduce SimSkill, a self-evolving agent built around the Simulation of Urban MObility (SUMO) traffic simulator. SimSkill identifies capability gaps, generates and solves environment-grounded tasks, verifies solutions through an action--critic loop, and consolidates experience into episodic, procedural, and semantic memory without updating the backbone model. Through autonomous exploration, it builds a reusable library spanning the traffic-simulation workflow. We evaluate SimSkill on two held-out benchmarks with three backbone LLMs and independent artifact-based verification. SimSkill improves verified completion by up to 25 percentage points, while ablations show complementary contributions from procedural and semantic memory. Its benefits remain backbone- and budget-dependent: memory does not improve every model or uniformly reduce inference cost. More broadly, SimSkill illustrates a design paradigm in which natural language preserves and composes computational capabilities, while executable tools and code provide precise and reproducible execution. All code and experimental data are publicly available at https://github.com/qiliuchn/SimSkill-V1.

AI.tldr: SimSkill is a self-evolving agent built on SUMO that converts experience into reusable competence via episodic, procedural, and semantic memory, improving verified task completion by up to 25 percentage points without updating the backbone model.
AI.motivation: Transform experience and accumulated knowledge into durable, reusable competence for LLM-driven systems, reducing retraining needs and enabling long-term utility across tasks.
AI.method: Construct a SUMO-based agent that (1) identifies capability gaps, (2) generates environment-grounded tasks, (3) solves them via an action--critic loop, (4) consolidates experiences into episodic, procedural, and semantic memory, and (5) autonomously explores to build a reusable traffic-simulation workflow library, without updating the backbone LLM. Evaluation on two held-out benchmarks with three backbone LLMs and artifact-based verification.
AI.result: Up to 25 percentage points improvement in verified completion; ablations show complementary contributions from procedural and semantic memory; benefits depend on backbone model and budget; memory does not uniformly improve all models or reduce inference cost; code and data publicly available.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates a design pattern where natural language preserves and composes computational capabilities while tools and code enable precise, reproducible execution; memory-enabled, self-evolving agents can yield reusable competence but require suitable budgets and models.

title: A Large Open Multi-Energy Corpus of Soil Compaction Tests, with Machine-Learning Baselines
summary: Every engineered fill is specified by a maximum dry density and an optimum moisture content. Each determination needs a full Proctor test. Published correlations rest on one to four hundred specimens, usually from one laboratory at one compactive energy, and are seldom released. This paper releases a corpus without those limits. It holds 2,854 laboratory compaction tests from six public sources, across 162 provenance groups and four Proctor energy levels, with fines from 1.5 to 100%. Every record is audited to the Proctor method its source names, and no energy is inferred. Screening on the zero-air-voids condition removed 11.8% of harmonised records, and 5.7% of those with a measured specific gravity. A material share of published compaction data is physically impossible. The optimum degree of saturation over the corpus is 0.815 at a coefficient of variation of 11%. That is a baseline, not a constant. Both parameters are then estimated from one classification suite and the compaction standard. A tabular foundation model reaches R2 0.824 for density and 0.784 for water content under random folds. It reaches 0.727 and 0.696 with folds drawn around provenance, and 0.520 and 0.614 with a whole source held out. Compactive energy is negligible marginally yet decisive conditionally. Density on the 66 modified-Proctor records is predicted at R2 0.740 with it and -0.651 without. Symbolic regression yields closed forms coupled through a phase relation. No predicted pair can then exceed the zero-air-voids line. The predictions are for screening, not acceptance.

AI.tldr: A large, multi-source, harmonized dataset of 2,854 laboratory Proctor compaction tests across multiple energy levels, audited to the Proctor method, with zero-air-voids screening. A tabular foundation model predicts density and water content with strong cross-validation performance; energy has a conditional, limited effect; symbolic regression yields interpretable closed-form relations, but predictions adhere to the zero-air-voids constraint and are intended for screening, not acceptance.
AI.motivation: To overcome typical limitations of published compaction correlations (small samples, single-lab, unknown energy) by creating a large, auditable corpus from multiple sources, and to investigate the role of compactive energy and the zero-air-voids constraint in predictive modeling.
AI.method: Harmonization of 2,854 proctor tests from six public sources across 162 provenance groups and four proctor energy levels; audit of the Proctor method and avoidance of energy inference; screening of records using the zero-air-voids condition; measurement of specific gravity where available; modeling with a tabular foundation model and symbolic regression; evaluation with random folds, provenance-based folds, and source-held-out folds; assessment on 66 modified-Proctor records.
AI.result: The optimum degree of saturation over the corpus is 0.815 (CV 11%). Random folds yield R2 = 0.824 (density) and 0.784 (water content); provenance folds yield R2 = 0.727 and 0.696; source-held-out folds yield R2 = 0.520 and 0.614. Density on 66 modified-Proctor records reaches R2 = 0.740 with energy and -0.651 without. Symbolic regression provides closed-form relations coupled through a phase relation; no predicted pair exceeds the zero-air-voids line. The work emphasizes screening over acceptance.
AI.conclusion: A large, auditable multi-source corpus supports robust predictive modeling within the zero-air-voids constraint; compactive energy has a marginal but conditional effect; the resulting models are intended for screening purposes rather than acceptance decisions.

title: Toward Unified Robot Learning: Bridging Representation, Vision-Language-Action, and World Models
summary: For robots to operate reliably in real-world environments, they need to perceive their surroundings, act, and reason about the consequences of those actions. Rapid progress in the domains of representation learning, VLA models, and world models has significantly enhanced the capabilities of robot learning systems, enabling robots to work in increasingly complex environments. However, these paradigms are typically developed in isolation, resulting in fragmented systems that struggle with generalization, long-horizon temporal reasoning and planning, and deployment in unstructured environments. In this survey, we present a unified perspective on robot learning by organizing the existing methods along three complementary axes: understanding through representation learning, acting through VLA models, and reasoning through world models. We introduce a structured taxonomy that captures key design choices in environment representation, policy learning, and predictive modeling, and summarize the recent progress in these domains. Beyond classifying the existing works, we analyze how these components interact, discuss common limitations, and highlight emerging trends towards more integrated systems. Through this lens, we identify the challenges in the domain of robot learning, including uncertainty quantification, out-of-distribution generalization, cross-embodiment transfer, long-context understanding, and long-horizon planning. We argue that these challenges arise not only from limitations within individual components but also from the lack of integration across perception, action, and reasoning. Building on this analysis, we outline future directions towards unified, physically grounded, and probabilistic robot learning to develop robust robotic systems that maintain consistent internal representations and support decision making over extended interactions in real-world environments.

AI.tldr: A survey that unifies robot learning along three axes—representation learning (understanding), visual-language-action models (acting), and world models (reasoning)—through a taxonomy of environment representation, policy learning, and predictive modeling; analyzes interactions and limitations, and outlines future directions toward integrated, probabilistic, physically grounded robot learning for robust, long-horizon real-world deployment.
AI.motivation: Robot learning components (perception, control, reasoning) are typically developed in isolation, leading to fragmented systems with poor generalization and limited long-horizon planning in unstructured environments. A unified perspective is needed to improve integration, robustness, and deployment of robots in real-world settings.
AI.method: Propose and apply a structured taxonomy organized around three complementary axes (representation learning for understanding, VLA models for acting, and world models for reasoning). Review and synthesize recent progress across environment representation, policy learning, and predictive modeling; analyze how components interact; identify common limitations; and discuss emerging trends toward more integrated, physically grounded, and probabilistic robot learning.
AI.result: Introduces a unified perspective and taxonomy for robot learning, summarizes progress across perception, action, and reasoning, analyzes component interactions and limitations, and outlines key challenges and directions toward integrated, probabilistic, and physically grounded robot learning for robust real-world operation.
AI.conclusion: There is a need for integrated robot-learning systems that maintain consistent internal representations and support decision making over extended interactions. Future work should emphasize unified, probabilistic, and physically grounded approaches that bridge perception, action, and reasoning to handle uncertainty, long-horizon planning, and generalization in real-world environments.

title: SafeRestore: Detector-Relative Risk Certificates for Selective Industrial Image Restoration
comment: 27 pages, 10 figures, 6 main-text tables, and 17 supplementary tables. Shares the Carinthia-S image identities with arXiv:2607.17401 by the same authors; the overlap and the distinct estimand are stated in Section 2.4 and Table 1
summary: Industrial inspection pipelines often restore a measured image before a detector acts on it, yet restoration can suppress detector-supported defect structure or create clean-region activations. We formulate restoration as a selective action problem over the measured display, five restored candidates, and review. SafeRestore ranks candidates with action-specific fitted scores, chooses a gate on threshold-tuning data, and evaluates the fixed gate on a disjoint certification sample with two one-sided exact binomial bounds: one for the positive-conditional evidence-loss incident rate and one for the all-accepted excess-activation incident rate. The guarantee is marginal for one policy fixed before its certification outcomes are observed, under an image-level i.i.d. working model. In a retrospective split-sample study of 4,591 public Carinthia-S images, the protocol yields auditable risk-coverage behavior. The primary all-action policy passes in one of five training repetitions (12.0% +/- 26.9% pass-gated test coverage when failures count as zero), whereas fixed bicubic and reduced-complexity variants pass more often. On reserved morphologies, evidence-loss incidence rises to 81.1-90.3%, and KolektorSDD lacks both detector competence and enough positive certification images for the stated target. The contribution is therefore an auditable, detector-relative framework for deciding when a transformed image may be returned automatically and when review remains necessary -- not a claim that adaptive routing outperforms simpler policies on the present evidence.

AI.tldr: Treat restoration as a selective action problem among five restored candidates, using gate-based thresholds with certifiable risk bounds to decide when an image can be returned or requires review; demonstrates auditable risk-coverage behavior but no clear superiority of adaptive routing given current data.
AI.motivation: Provide auditable, detector-relative control over automated image restoration in industrial inspection to balance defect detection and avoidance of false positives from restoration.
AI.method: Formulate a five-candidate restoration and review pipeline (SafeRestore). Rank candidates with action-specific scores, apply a threshold gate tuned on data, and certify the gate using a disjoint sample with two one-sided exact binomial bounds for (i) evidence-loss incidents and (ii) excess-activation incidents. Evaluate on retrospective Carinthia-S image set with i.i.d. working model assumptions; report pass rates across training repetitions and compare fixed bicubic/reduced-complexity variants.
AI.result: Auditable risk-coverage behavior achieved. The primary all-action policy passed in 1 of 5 training repetitions (12.0% ± 26.9% pass-gated coverage when failures counted as zero); fixed bicubic and reduced-complexity variants passed more often. On reserved morphologies, evidence-loss incidence rose to 81.1–90.3%, and KolektorSDD showed insufficient detector competence and positive certification imagery for target. The framework yields an auditable, detector-relative basis for deciding when to auto-return transformed images and when review is necessary; it does not claim adaptive routing outperforms simpler policies under current data.
AI.conclusion: The contribution is an auditable, detector-relative framework for safe automated image restoration decisions in industrial inspection, emphasizing certification-guided gating and risk bounds rather than asserting superior adaptive routing.

title: Rethinking World Models for Safety-Critical Embodied Systems
summary: World models have progressed from compact latent dynamics to generative, controllable, and interactive simulators of embodied environments. However, high predictive likelihood and visual fidelity do not necessarily ensure that a model preserves the evidence required for safe decision-making. This perspective identifies three structural mismatches in current world modeling: likelihood versus risk, prediction versus intervention, and finite-horizon prediction versus accumulated consequences. We propose the Risk-Informed World Model (RIWM) as a decision-centric research direction for safety-critical embodied systems. RIWM organizes world modeling around consequences, intervention, epistemic uncertainty, and recoverability, and integrates four interdependent capabilities: decision-relevant representation, counterfactual reasoning, safety-critical episodic memory, and runtime safety assurance. It distinguishes physical, social, and operational consequences while using epistemic uncertainty to qualify the evidence supporting action. We further discuss open challenges in identifying consequential futures, validating counterfactual reasoning, maintaining revisable safety memories, translating learned consequences into executable constraints, and determining when evidence is sufficient to act. This perspective argues that future world models should move beyond predicting likely futures toward identifying which futures matter, revising judgments through experience, and recognizing when to act, revise, sense, defer, or abstain.

AI.tldr: Proposes Risk-Informed World Model (RIWM) to align world modeling with safety-critical decision-making by prioritizing consequences and uncertainty over pure likelihoods, introducing decision-centric representations, counterfactual reasoning, safety memories, and runtime assurance.
AI.motivation: Current world models optimize likelihood and fidelity but may neglect the evidence needed for safe action; there are structural mismatches between prediction objectives and real-world decision requirements in embodied, safety-critical systems.
AI.method: Introduce RIWM as a decision-centric framework that organizes world modeling around consequences, intervention, epistemic uncertainty, and recoverability. It integrates four interdependent capabilities: (1) decision-relevant representation, (2) counterfactual reasoning, (3) safety-critical episodic memory, and (4) runtime safety assurance. It distinguishes physical, social, and operational consequences and uses epistemic uncertainty to qualify evidence supporting action.
AI.result: A conceptual perspective proposing a new research direction; outlines the RIWM architecture and the four capabilities, discusses open challenges such as identifying consequential futures, validating counterfactual reasoning, maintaining revisable safety memories, translating learned consequences into executable constraints, and determining sufficiency of evidence to act.
AI.conclusion: Future world models should focus on which futures matter, revise judgments through experience, and determine appropriate action or restraint by sensing, deferring, or abstaining, rather than solely predicting likely futures.

title: Gradients Know What Outcomes Don't: Unlocking Reinforcement Learning for LLM Reasoning with Gradient-Aligned Rewards
summary: Reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards (RLVR) drives chain-of-thought reasoning in large language models, yet its binary outcome reward cannot distinguish among correct trajectories. Existing dense reward alternatives, from surface heuristics to process reward models, either ignore the expert solutions already present in training corpora or require expensive offline annotation. We propose Gradient-Aligned Reward (GAR), which operates in the policy's own gradient space: truncated backpropagation through the output projection layer extracts a compact gradient vector for each rollout, and cosine similarity with an expert-anchor gradient yields a dense, reasoning-aware reward with less than 9% wall-clock overhead. We prove that this cosine admits a multiplicative decomposition into prediction-error and activation-pattern factors, providing a concrete characterization of what the alignment signal measures. On Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B, GAR consistently improves over GRPO and other baselines on competition-level math benchmarks and transfers to GPQA Diamond and MMLU-Pro without domain-specific data. Code and data are available at https://github.com/LQgdwind/GAR.

AI.tldr: Gradient-Aligned Reward (GAR) uses gradient-space cosine similarity between truncated backpropagation gradients of model outputs and an expert-anchor gradient to produce a dense, reasoning-aware reward for RLHF in LLMs, achieving efficiency and improved math benchmarks with cross-domain transfer.
AI.motivation: Binary RLVR rewards cannot distinguish among correct trajectories; dense rewards based on heuristics or processed rewards either ignore existing expert solutions in training data or require expensive offline annotation.
AI.method: Compute a compact gradient vector by truncated backpropagation through the output projection layer for each rollout; measure cosine similarity to an expert-anchor gradient to derive a dense reward; prove a multiplicative decomposition of this cosine into prediction-error and activation-pattern factors.
AI.result: Empirically, GAR improves over GRPO and baselines on competition-level math benchmarks for Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B; transfers to GPQA Diamond and MMLU-Pro without domain-specific data; wall-clock overhead is under 9%.
AI.conclusion: GAR provides an effective, scalable gradient-space alignment reward for LLM RLHF, capturing reasoning-oriented signals and enabling cross-domain transfer with low computational overhead.

title: Automated Weld Seam Recognition and 3D Mapping for Robotic Post Processing Using Photogrammetry and Semantic Segmentation
comment: Extended abstract not yet published to a conference or journal
summary: Accurate identification of weld seam geometries is essential for automated robotic post processing operations such as grinding, finishing, and inspection. For large workpieces, complete surface scanning using high precision laser scanners or structured light sensors can be time consuming and often generates substantial amount of data that are not relevant. This paper presents an experimental vision based pipeline for the approximate localization of weld seams. This serves as a preliminary stage before high precision measurement. The proposed approach aims to reduce the overall scanning effort and data acquisition efficiency. The proposed method includes capturing images of the workpiece from multiple viewpoints, identifying weld seams from the images using semantic segmentation, reconstructing the workpiece using photogrammetry, and projection of identified weld seams into the reconstructed model.

AI.tldr: Vision-based, multi-view pipeline for approximate weld seam localization to guide high-precision measurements; uses semantic segmentation, photogrammetry, and 3D projection to reduce scanning burden.
AI.motivation: Large workpieces require exhaustive high-precision scans; reducing data volume and scanning time is beneficial for automated post-processing.
AI.method: Capture images from multiple viewpoints; apply semantic segmentation to identify weld regions; reconstruct the object via photogrammetry; project seam locations into the 3D model to localize welds.
AI.result: Not specified; abstract suggests feasibility and efficiency improvements but provides no quantitative evaluation.
AI.conclusion: Provides a practical pre-processing step that enables faster, data-efficient weld seam localization, guiding subsequent high-precision measurements.

title: Tree species mapping in Denmark: A comparison of spectral-temporal features with geospatial foundation model embeddings
comment: Submitted to Remote Sensing of Environment. This preprint presents a national-scale tree species mapping framework for Denmark using Sentinel-1/2 time series, National Forest Inventory data, and EO foundation model embeddings. The resulted national map can be found here: https://zenodo.org/uploads/22108850
summary: We map tree species across Denmark using National Forest Inventory plots and EO data, while evaluating the potential of foundation models for large-scale forest characterization. We compare two alternative input representations for tree species classification: (i) manually engineered spectral-temporal features (STF) derived from multi-temporal Sentinel-1 and Sentinel-2 observations, and (ii) embeddings generated by the EO FMs TESSERA and AlphaEarth. Both representations are complemented with canopy height information. Random forest, XGBoost, and Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) classifiers are evaluated for all input representations, with separate assessments for pure and mixed forest stands. The STF-based MLP achieves the highest classification performance, yielding macro F1 scores of 0.843 and 0.653 for pure and mixed stands, respectively. The MLP trained on TESSERA embeddings delivers competitive performance for pure stands, achieving results within 1.1 percentage points of the best-performing model. TESSERA consistently outperforms STF-based models when fewer than approximately 25% of training plots are available, demonstrating a substantial advantage under limited training data. Multi-year observations systematically improve classification accuracy relative to single-year inputs, while ablation experiments reveal the complementary contributions of Sentinel-1 backscatter, spectral indices, and canopy height data. The best-performing model is subsequently applied at the national scale to generate a 10 m tree species map of Denmark. Area-adjusted validation indicates an overall map accuracy of 79.9%. The resulting map, released as an open-access product, is the first high-resolution national tree species map of Denmark and provides a valuable resource for forest monitoring, ecological research, and land management applications.

AI.tldr: Compared STF-based features and EO foundation-model embeddings (TESSERA, AlphaEarth) for Denmark tree-species mapping using NFI plots + multi-temporal EO data; STF-MLP best for pure stands; TESSERA robust with limited training data; multi-year data boosts accuracy; national 10 m map achieves ~79.9% area-adjusted accuracy; first high-res national map of Denmark released openly.
AI.motivation: Evaluate whether traditional engineered features or modern foundation-model embeddings better support large-scale, high-resolution forest characterization and species mapping, including data-scarce regimes and mixed stands.
AI.method: Combine National Forest Inventory plots with multi-temporal Sentinel-1/2 data to derive spectral-temporal features (STF) and compare with embeddings from foundation models (TESSERA, AlphaEarth); add canopy height; train and evaluate RF, XGBoost, and MLP on pure and mixed stands; conduct ablations to assess contributions of backscatter, indices, and height; assess multi-year vs single-year inputs; apply best model at national scale for a 10 m tree species map; validate with area-adjusted accuracy.
AI.result: STF-MLP achieves macro F1 of 0.843 (pure) and 0.653 (mixed). TESSERA embeddings are competitive for pure stands, within 1.1 percentage points of best model. TESSERA shows superiority over STF-based models when training plots are < ~25% of data. Multi-year inputs systematically improve accuracy over single-year. Ablations show complementary contributions from Sentinel-1 backscatter, spectral indices, and canopy height. The best model yields a 10 m Denmark-wide map with 79.9% area-adjusted accuracy; released as open-access.
AI.conclusion: Foundation-model embeddings can be data-efficient alternatives for forest characterization, but engineered STF features still provide the strongest performance in pure-stand classification. Multi-year EO data enhance accuracy, and the resulting high-resolution national map demonstrates practical utility for monitoring and management.

title: DNative-Twin: Decision Graphs and Digital Twins for Reconstructable Agentic Decisions
summary: AI agents increasingly gather evidence, invoke tools, apply constraints, and produce decisions that people or software may commit to action. A final output alone cannot show which evidence, tool state, rule, authorization, or action path produced it. We present DNative-Twin, a graph-native digital twin that records a committed agentic decision as a typed trajectory and re-executes its decision mechanism under declared conditions. The graph links the state observed by the agent, the path it followed, and the authority behind the resulting action. The twin synchronizes this information, replays the mechanism in isolation, and compares it under controlled changes. We instantiate the framework in enterprise decision processes using three public process logs and controlled replay suites. The experiments identify a specific failure: graph structure localizes represented changes but cannot determine the consequence of an unobserved tool state. In a three-condition controlled experiment with 300 injected instances, unresolved-divergence recall increased from 0 to 0.667 when replay-contract state was added and to 1.0 when verification results were also available; the held-out set contained no critical-class instance. Across 500--5,000 BPI 2020 cases, median end-to-end time increased from 0.794 to 8.889 seconds on the reported platform. These results separate the roles of graph structure, replay context, and verification evidence in reviewing a decision mechanism.

AI.tldr: DNative-Twin introduces a graph-native digital twin to audit agentic decisions by recording a typed trajectory, replaying the decision mechanism under controlled conditions, and comparing outcomes to reveal the roles of observed state, tool state, and verification evidence in decision auditing. It shows that graph structure alone cannot infer unobserved tool states; adding replay-contract state and verification improves divergence recall. End-to-end time scales with replay/verification complexity.
AI.motivation: Enable transparent auditing of AI-agent decisions that are the result of evidence gathering, tool use, and constraints, by capturing the decision path and re-running it under controlled conditions to reveal hidden states and dependencies.
AI.method: Construct DNative-Twin to link observed state, decision path, and authority; synchronize and replay the decision mechanism in isolation under declared conditions; instantiate in enterprise decision processes using three public process logs and controlled replay suites; induce injected instances and measure recall of divergences and timing.
