AI.result: identified a failure where graph structure localizes changes but cannot determine consequences of unobserved tool state; with 300 injected instances in three-condition tests, unresolved-divergence recall rose from 0 to 0.667 when replay-contract state was added and to 1.0 when verification results were available; held-out set contained no critical-class instance. Across 500–5,000 BPI 2020 cases, median end-to-end time increased from 0.794 to 8.889 seconds.
AI.conclusion: Graph structure, replay context, and verification evidence play distinct roles in auditing decision mechanisms; the framework clarifies how to separate these components to review agentic decisions, though unobserved tool states remain a challenge without verification data.

title: From Zero to Hero: An Open LLM Ecosystem for Armenian
comment: 18 pages, 4 figures, 13 tables. Data and model: https://huggingface.co/collections/COPA-AI/armenian-llm-ecosystem. Code: https://github.com/COPATeam/armenian_llm_ecosystem
summary: Pretraining data for Armenian, a morphologically rich and low-resource language, is scarce, and no open Armenian LLM has been released with the data and recipe needed to reproduce it. To address this gap, we curate and release two datasets. ArmWeb is an extensively validated corpus of 4.37M Armenian news documents. ArmSTEM is a parallel English-Armenian collection of 373K math and science problems with step-by-step solutions, translated into Armenian and verified through both answer-preserving LLM judgment and human evaluation. Continued pretraining of Gemma-4-E4B on these datasets yields arm-gemma-e4b, which outperforms every existing open Armenian model as well as its unadapted base, and is the first open Armenian LLM with complete training data and recipe. Our ablations show that news-only continued pretraining improves fluency while eroding knowledge, a pattern we also observe in existing Armenian models, and that a small share of verified translated STEM data reverses the loss. We further find that the largest public Armenian corpora overlap web-derived evaluation panels heavily, including a train/test self-overlap inside FineWeb-2. We openly release all data, models, and code.

AI.tldr: This work curates Armenian data to train an open Armenian LLM, ArmGemma-E4B, by continuing pretraining Gemma-4-E4B on two new datasets (ArmWeb news corpus and ArmSTEM translated problems). It achieves state-of-the-art open Armenian performance with full training data and recipe, and demonstrates tradeoffs between news-domain fluency and knowledge retention, mitigated by a small amount of translation-based STEM data; data, models, and code are openly released.
AI.motivation: Armenian is morphologically rich and low-resource, with no open LLM released alongside accessible data and training recipe. The work addresses data scarcity and reproducibility by curating open datasets and enabling replication of model development.
AI.method: Create ArmWeb: a validated 4.37M Armenian news corpus; ArmSTEM: 373K English-Armenian parallel math/science problems with step-by-step solutions translated into Armenian and validated via LLM judgments and human evaluation. Fine-tune/continue pretrain Gemma-4-E4B on these datasets to obtain arm-gemma-e4b. Conduct ablations: news-only pretraining vs mixed data; assess impact on fluency vs knowledge. Evaluate overlap issues with FineWeb-2 evaluation panels. Release data, models, and code.
AI.result: arm-gemma-e4b outperforms all existing open Armenian models and the base model without adaptation. It is the first open Armenian LLM with complete training data and recipe. Ablations show news-only pretraining boosts fluency but hurts knowledge; adding a small share of verified translated STEM data mitigates this knowledge loss. Large public corpora overlap evaluation panels, highlighting test-train leakage concerns. All data, models, and code are openly released.
AI.conclusion: Targeted data curation combined with mixed-domain continued pretraining can produce a competitive open Armenian LLM, balancing fluency and factual knowledge. The findings emphasize the importance of diversified data (including translated STEM content) to preserve knowledge, while also underscoring potential evaluation leakage from large corpora and the need for transparent training data and recipes.

title: MulDP: Multimodal Diffusion Policy for Autonomous Quadruped Parkour Navigation across Complex Terrains
summary: Quadruped robots have demonstrated impressive agility in parkour locomotion across complex terrains. However, most systems still rely on human intervention for high-level planning, and autonomous parkour navigation remains underexplored. The key challenges include fine-grained velocity regulation, long-horizon anticipatory behaviors, and tight coupling between perception and embodied execution. To address these challenges, we propose a Multimodal Diffusion Policy (MulDP) that integrates visual perception with robot proprioception and goal information to generate temporally coherent and anticipatory navigation velocity commands, tightly coupling perception with embodied control to enable robust autonomous navigation. To support the training of MulDP, we construct the first Quadruped Parkour Navigation Dataset (QPND), a multimodal dataset that encompasses diverse navigation behaviors and complex terrains. Extensive simulation and real-world experiments demonstrate that MulDP enables robust long-horizon autonomous navigation and effective traversal across complex terrains.

AI.tldr: MulDP leverages a multimodal diffusion policy to fuse visual perception, proprioception, and goal information to generate temporally coherent and anticipatory velocity commands for quadruped parkour; supported by QPND dataset; demonstrated robust long-horizon navigation in simulation and real-world tests.
AI.motivation: Autonomous quadruped parkour faces fine-grained velocity regulation, long-horizon anticipation, and tight perception–execution coupling. Lack of large multimodal datasets and models that integrate perception with embodied control hinders autonomous parkour.
AI.method: Introduce MulDP, a diffusion-based policy that combines visual inputs, proprioceptive signals, and goal information to produce velocity commands; train on the Quadruped Parkour Navigation Dataset (QPND); evaluate via extensive simulations and real-world experiments.
AI.result: MulDP achieves robust long-horizon autonomous navigation and effective traversal across complex terrains in both simulation and real-world tests; the QPND dataset covers diverse navigation behaviors and terrains.
AI.conclusion: MulDP and QPND advance autonomous quadruped parkour by deepening perception–action coupling and anticipatory control; future work could address scalability, real-time latency, and sim-to-real transfer.

title: Residual Optimal Transport-Based Experts Collaboration Towards Modality-Aware Infrared-Visible Object Detection
summary: Infrared-visible object detection (IVOD) integrates complementary evidence from visible and infrared sensors for reliable perception in challenging scenes. In practice, sensors may fail or drop frames, leaving one modality unavailable or intermittent. Existing methods for IVOD assume both modalities are always present, and fixed fusion collapses when one stream is missing. Furthermore, it remains a critical challenge to reliably estimate semantic correlation across heterogeneous modalities, especially under spectral distribution discrepancy. We present FlexibleFusion, a unified and adaptive method that flexibly allocates integration pathways and fusion strength, operating seamlessly across complete and missing-modality regimes. At its core, the Modality-Aware Experts Collaboration (MAEC) mechanism selectively activates and aggregates cross-modal or intra-modal expert pathways. It allows cross-modal fusion when full modalities are available and falls back to self-fusion under missing conditions. Additionally, we design Residual Self-Paced Entropic Optimal Transport (RSPEOT) to align heterogeneous feature distributions from a transport perspective. Instead of relying on the fixed sparsity coefficient in standard entropic optimal transport (EOT), RSPEOT introduces a residual-driven self-paced update that prioritizes reliable matches and progressively refines harder ones. This design alleviates the additional optimization burden of standard EOT while preserving reliable semantic alignment. Comprehensive experiments under complete and missing-modality protocols show consistent performance across arbitrary modality configurations. Code will be released upon publication.

AI.tldr: FlexibleFusion is a unified, adaptive infrared–visible object detection framework that gracefully handles complete and missing modalities by using modality-aware experts for cross-modal and intra-modal fusion (MAEC) and a residual self-paced entropic OT alignment (RSPEOT), achieving robust performance across modality configurations with reduced optimization burden.
AI.motivation: IVOD systems often face intermittent or missing modalities in real-world settings. Most existing methods assume both modalities are always present and rely on fixed fusion, which degrades when a modality drops. Spectral distribution discrepancies further hinder cross-modal alignment.
AI.method: Propose MAEC (Modality-Aware Experts Collaboration) to selectively activate and aggregate cross-modal or intra-modal expert pathways, enabling cross-modal fusion when both modalities are available and self-fusion when a modality is missing. Introduce RSPEOT (Residual Self-Paced Entropic Optimal Transport) to align heterogeneous features from a transport perspective with a residual-driven, self-paced update that prioritizes reliable matches and progressively refines harder ones, reducing the optimization burden compared to standard EOT.
AI.result: Comprehensive experiments under both complete and missing-modality protocols show consistent performance across arbitrary modality configurations, demonstrating robustness and adaptability. Code will be released upon publication.
AI.conclusion: FlexibleFusion delivers robust infrared–visible object detection across varying modality availability by dynamically modulating fusion pathways and leveraging an efficient, transport-based alignment mechanism; it outperforms fixed-fusion baselines and is practical for real-world deployments where sensor failure or intermittency occurs.

title: Transfiver: Human-AI Co-Inference through a Shared Editable State
summary:
Long-term human-AI interaction is difficult because the information that guides inference is updated implicitly by the model and is not directly inspectable or controllable by the user. We introduce the TRANSparent Framework for Interactive, Verifiable, Editable Representation (Transfiver), an architecture for human-AI co-inference through a shared editable state. Its central idea is that interaction-specific information is maintained in a single persistent state $(S_t)$ that both the model and the human update.
  Transfiver distinguishes two modes of state evolution. In an implicit stream update, the model interprets ongoing interaction and decides whether new information revises an existing state item or creates a new one. In an explicit directed edit, a human inspects and modifies an addressed item. Both act on the same underlying state, so a human correction changes the state that subsequent computation reads, rather than adding another instruction or separate record.
  The architecture separates shared parameters $(θ)$, learned before ordinary use, from the persistent state $(S_t)$, which evolves during deployment without parameter retraining. Extending Transfiver to rich natural-language, relational, and large-scale shared states remains open.

AI.tldr: Introduces Transfiver: a framework for long-term human-AI co-inference using a single persistent state S_t shared by model and user; separation of parameters θ from state; supports implicit model updates and explicit human edits, enabling verifiability and editability without retraining; open for extension to richer state types.
AI.motivation: To address the challenge of sustaining long-term interaction where guidance information is updated implicitly by the model and becomes hard to inspect or control; a persistent, editable shared state aims to make inference history inspectable, verifiable, and adjustable by both parties.
AI.method: Architectural design with a persistent state S_t updated via two modalities: (1) implicit stream updates by the model interpreting ongoing interaction, revising or creating state items; (2) explicit directed edits by humans inspecting and modifying addressed items. Shared parameters θ are kept separate from the evolving state, enabling deployment-time updates without retraining.
AI.result: A conceptual framework formalizing human-AI co-inference through a persistent shared state; no empirical results reported in the abstract. Highlights include unified state that both model and human read/write, enabling correction to influence subsequent computation. Open questions concern extending to rich natural-language, relational, and large-scale shared states.
AI.conclusion: Open research direction with potential to enhance long-term, verifiable, and editable human-AI interaction; deployment without periodic retraining; requires future work to scale to more complex state representations.

title: Time Without Timesteps: Simulating Coupled Dynamical Systems via Self-Consistency
summary: Numerical simulation of dynamical systems is usually organized as a causal march through time: each state is computed from the previous one. We explore a different formulation for coupled systems. For each subsystem type we train a neural surrogate mapping a full driving trajectory and initial condition directly to a full output trajectory; following classical waveform relaxation, coupled systems are assembled by enforcing self-consistency among these trajectories: simulation becomes a fixed-point problem over complete trajectories rather than a stepwise rollout. On coupled van der Pol oscillators and Hodgkin-Huxley neuron networks, sequential depth becomes the number of solver iterations: 4-10 Newton iterations where the reference integrator takes 1500 steps. The gradient likewise loses its time recursion: it becomes a linear system solved by GMRES at memory independent of solver depth. A single scalar measured from the learned operator, the spectral radius of its Jacobian, predicts in advance where the coupled solve will converge; past that boundary, unrolled backpropagation diverges and a Neumann adjoint fails, while the implicit gradient remains correct to 0.04%. We report where the approach succeeds and where surrogate error degrades it.

AI.tldr: Neural surrogates for full-trajectory coupling via waveform relaxation turn coupled simulations into fixed-point problems; convergence is predicted by Jacobian spectral radius; implicit gradient is robust (0.04%); results on van der Pol and Hodgkin–Huxley networks show when it works and where surrogate error degrades it.
AI.motivation: Replace stepwise time marching with a trajectory-level fixed-point formulation to efficiently solve coupled dynamical systems using learned operators.
AI.method: For each subsystem type, train a neural surrogate mapping the full driving trajectory and initial condition to the full output trajectory. Assemble the coupled system by enforcing self-consistency (waveform relaxation). Solve a fixed-point problem using Newton iterations (4–10) with a reference integrator of ~1500 steps. Backpropagation is replaced by a linear GMRES solve; the gradient depends on all trajectories but memory is independent of solver depth. Use the spectral radius of the Jacobian of the learned operator to predict convergence boundary. Compare unrolled backprop, Neumann adjoint, and implicit gradient.
AI.result: Coupled van der Pol and Hodgkin–Huxley networks converge within 4–10 Newton iterations; gradient memory scales independently of solver depth via GMRES; spectral radius correctly forecasts convergence; beyond the boundary, unrolled backprop diverges and Neumann adjoint fails, while implicit gradients remain correct to ~0.04%.
AI.conclusion: A trajectory-based neural surrogate with waveform-relaxation enables fixed-point coupling with predictable convergence and accurate gradients within a boundary; surrogate error delineates applicability; the spectral radius is a practical predictor for when the method will succeed.

title: Adaptive Vision-Language Grasping via Composable Foundation Priors and Generalizable Grasp Synthesis
summary: This paper proposes AdaRoboVLG, a task-adaptive Vision-Language-Grasp (VLG) framework that supports generalizable grasp synthesis across different robotic hands. Unlike existing VLG methods that tightly couple foundation models with end-to-end grasp policies, AdaRoboVLG learns an efficient generalizable base policy that generates and evaluates physically feasible grasp candidates through explicit kinematic mapping and force-closure-based stability estimation, while offloading task-dependent understanding to specialized foundation-model modules. These modules provide composable priors that are integrated into the grasp synthesis process, enabling contextually adaptive grasp synthesis without retraining the underlying grasp policy. Through extensive simulation and real-world experiments, we demonstrate that (i) the base policy exhibits efficient learning and strong cross-hand generalization, (ii) the framework effectively incorporates spatial, cognitive, and temporal priors to address three representative grasping challenges without compromising grasp synthesis performance compared to state-of-the-art methods, and (iii) these priors can operate jointly to enable functional grasping in cluttered and dynamic environments. These results indicate that decoupling physical grasp synthesis from task-dependent understanding provides a scalable paradigm for robotic grasping, allowing future advances in foundation models to be directly translated into improved grasp capabilities without redesigning or retraining the underlying grasp policy. Supplementary videos are available at https://adarobovlg.github.io/

AI.tldr: AdaRoboVLG decouples task-driven understanding from a general grasp policy to enable cross-hand generalization in vision-language-grasping. A physics-based base policy generates/evaluates grasps via explicit kinematics and force-closure, while foundation-model priors provide task context, enabling adaptive grasping without retraining the base policy.
AI.motivation: Need scalable, cross-hand, task-aware grasping. End-to-end VLG policies with fixed hands struggle to generalize to new hands; foundation models can supply priors but must be integrated without retraining core grasp policy.
AI.method: Train a base grasp policy that uses explicit kinematic mapping and force-closure-based stability to generate and evaluate grasps. Offload task-dependent understanding to modular, composable foundation-model priors that are integrated into the synthesis process. Do not retrain the base policy when adding priors. Validate through extensive simulations and real-world experiments across cluttered/dynamic scenarios and multiple robotic hands.
AI.result: The base policy demonstrates efficient learning and good cross-hand generalization. The priors address spatial, cognitive, and temporal grasping challenges without reducing performance compared to state-of-the-art grasp synthesis methods. When combined, priors enable functional grasping in challenging environments. Supplementary videos are provided.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling physical grasp synthesis from task-dependent understanding provides a scalable framework for robotic grasping, enabling future foundation-model advances to enhance grasp capabilities without retraining the base policy.

title: Neural Video Compression Based on Deformable Temporal Alignment and Difference-aware Fusion
summary: In conditional coding-based neural video compression, the quality of temporal context directly affects compression per- formance. Existing methods mostly construct context from prop- agated reference features, but they are vulnerable to motion esti- mation and local alignment errors in regions with complex mo- tion, occlusion, and high-frequency textures, resulting in inaccu- rate temporal information. To address this issue, this paper pro- poses a method combining deformable temporal alignment and difference-aware spatial selective fusion. A Context-aware Tem- poral Alignment Module is used to generate complementary tem- poral context, while a Difference-aware Spatial Selective Fusion module adaptively selects reliable temporal information and sup- presses misalignment. Experiments show that the proposed method achieves certain rate-distortion performance improve- ment over DCVC-DC.

AI.tldr: A method for neural video compression improves temporal context quality via deformable temporal alignment and difference-aware spatial selective fusion, achieving RD gains over DCVC-DC.
AI.motivation: Temporal context quality is critical for compression efficiency but is hindered by motion estimation errors, misalignment, occlusion, and high-frequency textures in propagated reference features.
AI.method: A Context-aware Temporal Alignment Module generates complementary temporal context, and a Difference-aware Spatial Selective Fusion module adaptively selects reliable temporal information while suppressing misalignment within a conditional coding framework.
AI.result: Experiments report rate-distortion improvements over the DCVC-DC baseline (specific metrics/points not stated).
AI.conclusion: The approach enhances robustness of temporal context in neural video compression, yielding RD gains; further details on datasets, ablations, and complexity are needed for full assessment.

title: Govern the Model, Not Only the Data: Storage, Circulation, and Learning in Creative AI
summary: Federated learning is increasingly presented as a privacy-preserving advance: personal data remain on the device, and only model updates are shared. It borrows the vocabulary of the federated social web, yet inverts its logic, distributing computation while the resulting model stays with whoever convened the training. We argue that federation is not in itself a remedy for extractive AI, because outcomes depend on who governs the data and the model and who has agency over the practices that shape them. We describe three layers at which a creative community can hold its work: storage, circulation, and learning. Examining artist-governed trusts, cooperatives, and consent infrastructures, we show that creator governance is established at storage and circulation but stops at learning: contributors can consent to training, yet have little say over the resulting model or its federation. We map the research space this opens, pairing technical open problems with the human questions from which they unfold. We propose four design principles for a creative data commons that governs models and their federation, not only datasets: govern the model, not only the corpus; make the terms legible at the moment of contribution; design for refusal as a first-class state; and decide stewardship in the open and account for it.

AI.tldr: Federated learning alone does not ensure privacy or prevent extractive AI; governance must address who controls the data, the model, and the federation across storage, circulation, and learning.
AI.motivation: To interrogate how creative communities can govern data and models in federated settings and to prevent governance gaps that allow exploitation of contributed data.
AI.method: Conceptual analysis of three governance layers (storage, circulation, learning) with examples from artist-governed trusts, cooperatives, and consent infrastructures; mapping open technical and human questions and proposing design principles.
AI.result: Found that governance is largely established at storage and circulation but leaves learning under contributor consent, with limited say over the resulting model or its federation; identified a research space linking technical challenges to governance questions.
AI.conclusion: Propose four design principles for a creative data commons: (1) govern the model as well as the corpus, (2) make contribution terms legible at submission, (3) design for refusal as a first-class state, and (4) decide stewardship openly and account for it.

title: SimpleDesign: A Joint Model for Protein Sequence and Structure Codesign
comment: Published in Transactions on Machine Learning Research (TMLR), 2026. https://openreview.net/forum?id=wPfw7GkMns
summary: Proteins are fundamental to biological processes, with their function determined by the complex interplay between the amino acid sequence and the three-dimensional structure. Developing generative models capable of understanding this intrinsically multi-modal relationship is crucial for fields like drug discovery and protein engineering. Existing models often rely on a multi-stage training process where autoencoders that tokenize data into latent representations are trained in a first stage. Secondly, a generative model is trained on the latent representation of the autoencoder(s), i.e., generative modeling in a latent space. We hypothesize that this multi-stage training is not necessary to obtain performant co-design models and thus present SimpleDesign, an effective multi-modal protein design model trained directly in the data space. SimpleDesign leverages a single-stage end-to-end objective that combines discrete cross-entropy for sequences and a regression objective for structures. In order to effectively model the difference in sequence and structure modalities, we develop a Mixture-of-Transformer architecture that allows modality-specific processing while keeping global self-attention over both modalities. We train SimpleDesign on over 2M sequence-structure pairs achieving strong performance across co-design and unconditional sequence/structure generation benchmarks.

AI.tldr: Single-stage, end-to-end multi-modal protein design with a Mixture-of-Transformer, trained on 2M sequence–structure pairs, achieving strong co-design and generation performance without latent-space autoencoders.
AI.motivation: Many existing approaches rely on multi-stage training using autoencoders to tokenize data into latent representations, which may be unnecessary for high-performance co-design; aim to model sequence and structure jointly in data space.
AI.method: Propose SimpleDesign with a Mixture-of-Transformer architecture that processes each modality with modality-specific paths while sharing global self-attention; train with a joint objective combining discrete cross-entropy for sequences and a regression loss for structures, in a single end-to-end stage.
AI.result: Trained on over 2 million sequence–structure pairs; demonstrates strong performance on co-design and unconditional sequence/structure generation benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: End-to-end single-stage learning in data space is effective for multi-modal protein design; latent-space autoencoder-based pipelines may be unnecessary, as evidenced by SimpleDesign's performance.

title: Corner Cases: Headland Coverage Path Planning for Autonomous Driving in Arable Farming
summary: This paper presents a new method for headland coverage path planning for arable fields. Several earlier approaches suggest covering the headland with nested polygons and smooth turns, however, covering the field corners entirely requires manoeuvres with reversing. In the new method, the polygon corners are modified to allow a reversing turn. A comparison to two other methods considering gap, overlap, and crossing the field boundary shows an improvement in the coverage result especially in field corners of around 90 degrees, and 240 degrees and above. Applicability of the new method is shown with several examples of real polygonal field maps.

AI.tldr: Proposes a corner-modified headland coverage path planning method that enables reversing turns to improve corner coverage; evaluated against two baseline methods using gap, overlap, and boundary crossing metrics; demonstrated on real polygonal field maps.
AI.motivation: Address incomplete coverage in headland strategies caused by sharp field corners and the need for reversals by enabling a reversing turn through polygon corner modification.
AI.method: Modify polygon corners to allow a reversing turn during headland traversal; compare the proposed method to two existing approaches using metrics of gap, overlap, and crossing the field boundary; validate with several real polygonal field maps.
AI.result: The method yields improved coverage in challenging corners, notably around 90° and 240° corners and larger, compared to the baselines; demonstrated across multiple real field maps.
AI.conclusion: The corner-modified reversing-turn approach enhances corner coverage and demonstrates practical applicability for real arable fields; suitable for integration in practical field coverage planners and warrants further exploration of trade-offs and scalability.

title: TruncGradGS: Improved 3D Gaussian Splatting via Truncated Gradient Updates
summary: 3D Gaussian Splatting has become a de facto scene representation for novel view synthesis, yet robustly learning 3D Gaussian primitives from visual input remains challenging. Standard optimization relies on gradient-based updates, but a common issue is the gradient vanishing phenomenon: a pixel far from a Gaussian primitive often has diminishing gradient magnitudes to influence primitive attributes, resulting in suboptimal scene reconstruction. In this paper, we propose a method to address gradient vanishing with a piecewise truncated gradient formulation that improves the optimization stability and robustness to initializations. We show that our method consistently improves 3D Gaussian Splatting with random and COLMAP initializations while being generalizable across static and dynamic Gaussian Splatting. As a by-product, we also examine the limitations of current benchmarks for dynamic scenes, and introduce a novel dataset for benchmarking dynamic Gaussian Splatting using synthetic 3D scenes. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in both static and dynamic settings for the public benchmarks and our proposed dataset.

AI.tldr: Proposes a piecewise truncated gradient to mitigate gradient vanishing in learning 3D Gaussian splats for novel view synthesis, yielding more stable optimization and better reconstructions across static/dynamic cases and random/COLMAP initializations, plus a synthetic dynamic Gaussian Splatting dataset and benchmark insights.
AI.motivation: Address gradient vanishing in gradient-based learning of 3D Gaussian primitives from visual input to achieve robust, initialization-insensitive optimization and generalization to dynamic scenes; also critique current benchmarks for dynamic scenes.
AI.method: Introduce a piecewise truncated gradient formulation that prevents vanishing gradients from distant pixels by selectively truncating gradient magnitudes in a piecewise manner, improving optimization stability and robustness.
AI.result: Demonstrates consistent improvements in 3D Gaussian Splatting with random and COLMAP initializations; method generalizes to both static and dynamic Gaussian Splatting; validates on public benchmarks and the authors’ proposed synthetic dynamic dataset.
AI.conclusion: The piecewise truncated gradient improves optimization stability and robustness for learning 3D Gaussian primitives, promotes generalization to static and dynamic scenes and varying initializations, and contributes a synthetic dataset to benchmark dynamic Gaussian Splatting.

title: SVG-Score: Human-Aligned Evaluation of Text-to-SVG Generation
summary: Scalable Vector Graphics (SVG) generation is attracting increasing attention as generative models improve in expressiveness and controllability. Progress, however, is held back by the lack of domain-specific evaluation protocols: current practice relies on metrics designed for natural images, most notably CLIPScore, which was never trained on vector graphics and aligns only partially with human judgment. We introduce \textbf{\ours}, a human-aligned evaluation framework for text-to-SVG generation. Through controlled caption and image perturbations, we first show that CLIP-based scores barely react to the errors SVG generators actually make, such as wrong colors, counts, and spatial relations, and that off-the-shelf Vision-Language Model (VLM) judges, while more sensitive, respond unevenly across error types and SVG styles. We then introduce a human-annotated dataset for \textit{Semantic Alignment}, measuring how faithfully a generated SVG reflects its caption. Building on it, we develop two complementary evaluators: CLIP scorers adapted to vector graphics and then aligned to human preferences, for fast large-scale evaluation, and a VLM judge trained with supervised fine-tuning and reward-shaped reinforcement learning, for more expressive and interpretable assessment. Using both, we benchmark major open-source, commercial, and optimization-based SVG generators on an independent caption set.

AI.tldr: Proposes a human-aligned evaluation framework for text-to-SVG generation, addressing CLIPScore's misalignment with SVG errors, via a semantic-alignment dataset and two evaluators (vector-CLIP adapted and VLM-based), enabling robust benchmarking across generators.
AI.motivation: Current metrics are designed for natural images and fail to capture SVG-specific errors (colors, counts, spatial relations), hindering progress in text-to-SVG generation.
AI.method: 1) Controlled caption and image perturbations showing CLIP's insensitivity; 2) Build a human-annotated Semantic Alignment dataset; 3) Develop two evaluators: vector-graphics-adapted CLIP scores aligned to human preferences; 4) Train a VLM judge with supervised fine-tuning and reward-shaped RL; 5) Benchmark various SVG generators on an independent caption set.
AI.result: CLIP-based scores barely react to SVG errors; VLM judges are more sensitive but uneven; the new evaluators correlate with human preferences and enable fast large-scale evaluation and expressive assessment; independent caption set benchmarking across generators.
AI.conclusion: Provides a domain-specific, human-aligned evaluation framework for text-to-SVG that improves assessment accuracy and benchmarking capability; suggests broader adoption and potential extensions to new SVG styles and perturbations.

title: RecurTrace: Adaptive Latent Reasoning with Loop-Time Memory
summary: Repeating a small block of middle layers increases a language model's effective inference depth without adding parameters or generating extra tokens, and recent work shows that this latent recurrence improves reasoning. However, two design choices limit these gains. Each iteration sees only the previous output and cannot directly access earlier computations. Moreover, a fixed loop count wastes depth on easy inputs while leaving hard ones with too little computation. We introduce RecurTrace, which addresses both limitations using the loop's own trajectory. Specifically, Loop Memory Attention lets each looped layer attend to its own states from previous iterations along the loop-time axis, so the model can revisit earlier computations instead of relying on the latest state alone. A halting head then reads the loop state and predicts whether to continue, with supervision from an oracle that identifies when additional depth still reduces loss. In a controlled MathQA comparison on the same looped backbone, RecurTrace achieves 56.9% accuracy with an average of 2.0 loops, exceeding the best fixed loop depth by 2.2 points at matched compute. By comparison, ACT and PonderNet collapse to one loop, and CALM reaches only 54.1% with 5.6 loops, while the stronger LoopUS-Conf and TaH-Mismatch baselines reach 55.3% at 3.2 loops and 55.7% at 2.1 loops. Finally, RecurTrace improves generation accuracy over same-budget fine-tuned baselines at 0.6B, 1.7B, 4B, and 8B, with the gain growing with model size from 0.6 to 3.4 points.

AI.tldr: RecurTrace enables adaptive, deeper latent recurrence by letting looped layers attend to their own past states and halting control, outperforming fixed-depth loops and several baselines on MathQA and generation tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing latent recurrence methods for parameter-free deepening rely only on the latest loop state and use a fixed number of iterations, wasting compute on easy inputs and limiting reasoning depth.
AI.method: Introduce Loop Memory Attention so each looped layer attends along the loop-time axis to its own earlier states; add a halting head supervised by an oracle to decide when to stop; evaluate on a looped backbone (MathQA comparison) and across generation tasks with varying model sizes.
AI.result: On MathQA, RecurTrace reaches 56.9% accuracy with an average of 2.0 loops, beating fixed-depth baselines by 2.2 points. ACT and PonderNet collapse to one loop; CALM yields 54.1% with 5.6 loops; LoopUS-Conf 55.3% at 3.2 loops; TaH-Mismatch 55.7% at 2.1 loops. In generation, gains over same-budget fine-tuned baselines appear at 0.6B, 1.7B, 4B, and 8B models, increasing with size up to 3.4 points.
AI.conclusion: RecurTrace enables adaptive, stateful loop computation via loop-time attention and principled halting, achieving higher accuracy with similar compute and improving generation quality as model size grows.

title: GIFT: Guided Intermediate Feature Training via Action-Oriented Structural Supervision for Robotic Manipulation
summary: Vision-language pre-training and predictive world modeling provide robot policies with rich semantic and dynamic visual features, but their native action and visual-prediction objectives may omit critical physical and task structure while retaining control-irrelevant visual redundancy. We call this mismatch between visual richness and control utility the action-sufficiency gap. We investigate whether this gap can be bridged by guiding intermediate features to preserve three control-relevant structure in robotic manipulation: geometry governing motion feasibility, affordance encoding instruction-relevant entities, and goals grounding instructions in task-relevant regions. To this end, we present GIFT (Guided Intermediate Feature Training), an architecture-flexible framework for learning intermediate features that translates these structures into training-time constraints through geometry alignment, affordance prediction, and goal-region reconstruction. We instantiate GIFT in a Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policy, a direct-action World-Action Model (WAM), and an inverse-dynamics WAM while retaining each model's action formulation. Under zero-shot transfer to LIBERO-Plus, GIFT-VLA, GIFT-WAM-Fast, and GIFT-WAM-IDM outperform StarVLA-OFT, Fast-WAM, and Fast-WAM-IDM by 4.6, 12.6, and 5.2 points, reaching 79.6%, 72.6%, and 87.8%, respectively. On RoboCasa, the three GIFT variants reach 61.4%, 83.6%, and 82.3%, outperforming their counterparts by 12.6, 9.0, and 8.4 points, respectively. Together, these results establish learning functionally structured intermediate features as a reusable principle across model-specific action formulations, with especially large gains on articulated-object tasks and high-precision real-world manipulation under unseen visual and spatial perturbations. Project page: https://openphoenix-team.github.io/GIFT-pages.

AI.tldr: GIFT introduces intermediate-feature training to bridge the action-sufficiency gap in vision-language-action and world-model policies by enforcing geometry, affordance, and goal-region structures; shows zero-shot gains across LIBERO-Plus and RoboCasa for VLA and WAM variants, suggesting broader utility across action formulations.
AI.motivation: Current vision-language pre-training and predictive world models yield rich visuals but may ignore physics-based and task-relevant structure, creating an action-sufficiency gap that hurts control performance.
AI.method: GIFT framework imposes training-time constraints on intermediate features via three components: geometry alignment (motion-feasibility), affordance prediction (instruction-relevant entities), and goal-region reconstruction (task-region grounding). Implemented flexibly across multiple architectures: Vision-Language-Action policy (VLA), and World-Action Models (WAM) in variants Fast and IDM, preserving their action formulations.
AI.result: Zero-shot transfer gains over baselines: on LIBERO-Plus, GIFT-VLA, GIFT-WAM-Fast, GIFT-WAM-IDM achieve 79.6%, 72.6%, 87.8% respectively (improvements of 4.6, 12.6, and 5.2 points). On RoboCasa, GIFT variants reach 61.4%, 83.6%, 82.3% (improvements of 12.6, 9.0, 8.4 points).
AI.conclusion: Functionally structured intermediate features are reusable across model-specific action formulations, with especially strong gains on articulated-object tasks and high-precision real-world manipulation under unseen perturbations; supports a general principle for integrating physics/task-relevant structure into learned representations.

title: SafeRI: Recognition and Intervention for Token-Level Safety Intervention in Large Vision Language Models
comment: Preprint. 13 pages, 4 figures. Main paper with appendix
summary: Existing safety alignment methods for vision-language models usually modify the model behavior globally: once the safety parameters are trained or loaded, they participate in both unsafe and already-safe generations. This always-on intervention can unnecessarily perturb the model's original reasoning path and degrade general multimodal capabilities. We argue that safety alignment should be an on-demand intervention rather than a permanent modification to every decoding trajectory. To this end, we propose a streaming recognition and gated LoRA framework for intrinsic VLM safety. During autoregressive generation, a lightweight recognizer estimates whether the current pre-token generation state is safe or unsafe. Its output updates the LoRA gate for the following decoding step; otherwise, generation follows the frozen-backbone policy. The LoRA module is trained from unsafe prefixes, transition statements, and safe continuations, so that it learns to redirect unsafe generations back to safe responses after activation. Experiments across multiple safety and general-purpose benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in post-alignment settings.

AI.tldr: Streaming recognizer with a gated LoRA module as an on-demand safety mechanism for vision-language models; avoids global safety changes and preserves general multimodal performance.
AI.motivation: Global safety alignment can impair general reasoning and multimodal capabilities; need on-demand, minimally invasive intervention that can steer dangerous outputs without permanently altering the model.
AI.method: During autoregressive generation, a lightweight recognizer predicts if the current pre-token state is safe or unsafe; its decision gates a LoRA module for the next decoding step; if unsafe, the model follows a frozen-backbone policy while LoRA can redirect unsafe generations to safe continuations. LoRA is trained from unsafe prefixes, transition statements, and safe continuations to learn safe redirection.
AI.result: Demonstrates effectiveness in post-alignment settings across safety and general-purpose benchmarks, showing improved safety behavior with limited impact on general capabilities compared to permanent, global safety modifications.
AI.conclusion: An on-demand streaming safety mechanism using a recognizer and gated LoRA provides intrinsic safety for VLMs without permanently perturbing the backbone, enabling safer interactions with preserved multimodal performance.

title: CauseCollab: Causal Unified and Modality-Agnostic Network for Heterogeneous Collaborative Perception
summary: Collaborative perception enhances environment understanding through multi-agent information sharing, but its performance in real-world scenarios is constrained by heterogeneous sensor modalities and model architectures. Recent protocol-based two-stage methods alleviate this problem by mapping heterogeneous features into a shared protocol space; however, independently trained modality-specific converters often generate modality-specific pseudo-protocol distributions, leading to semantic inconsistency and error accumulation, which is particularly pronounced in scenarios with large modality discrepancies. To address this issue, we propose CauseCollab, a causal unified and modality-agnostic network. CauseCollab formulates representation learning in the protocol space from a causal perspective, explicitly disentangling semantic factors from modality-specific statistical confounders via causal metric learning. Meanwhile, CauseCollab adopts context-guided Unified Converter for heterogeneous modalities to ensure cross-modal semantic consistency. In addition, integrating new modalities only requires training adapters with minimal parameters. Extensive experiments on the OPV2V and DAIR-V2X datasets demonstrate that CauseCollab achieves state-of-the-art performance, with more significant gains in scenarios involving large modality gaps.

AI.tldr: CauseCollab is a causal, modality-agnostic framework for collaborative perception that disentangles semantic factors from modality-specific confounders in a shared protocol space and uses a context-guided Unified Converter plus lightweight adapters, achieving state-of-the-art results, especially when modality gaps are large.
AI.motivation: Heterogeneous sensor modalities and model architectures hinder cross-agent collaboration; existing protocol-based two-stage methods create modality-specific pseudo-protocols that lead to semantic inconsistency and error accumulation, particularly with large modality discrepancies.
AI.method: Learn representations in a protocol space from a causal perspective to disentangle semantic factors from modality-specific confounders via causal metric learning. Use a context-guided Unified Converter to align heterogeneous modalities and ensure cross-modal semantic consistency. Enable easy addition of new modalities via lightweight adapters.
AI.result: Achieves state-of-the-art performance on OPV2V and DAIR-V2X datasets, with larger gains when modality gaps are substantial.
AI.conclusion: CauseCollab effectively addresses semantic inconsistency due to modality heterogeneity, offering scalable integration of new modalities through adapters and showing robustness across larger modality discrepancies.

title: TIGPO: Temporal Instance-Graph Policy Optimization for Long-Horizon LLM Agents
summary: Graph-based policy optimization improves credit assignment for long-horizon LLM agents by organizing rollout trajectories into state-transition graphs. However, existing methods construct graphs independently within each policy update, discarding transitions discovered by earlier policies and limiting advantage estimation to small, batch-local rollout groups. We propose \emph{Temporal Instance-Graph Policy Optimization} (TIGPO), which extends graph-based credit assignment across policy updates. TIGPO maintains a persistent transition graph for each task, allowing valid transitions discovered by different policy versions to jointly determine credit for current rollouts. To actively reconnect current exploration with historical experience, TIGPO allocates a fixed rollout budget between Exploration slots for ordinary task sampling and Revisit slots for delayed reattempts of previously explored tasks. For each revisit, TIGPO pairs the current rollout group with its corresponding earlier Exploration group to construct a cross-temporal reference. The enlarged reference is designed to stabilize relative advantage estimation under small rollout groups, while comparison on the same task directly captures policy improvement across training stages. Historical transitions and scores serve only as structural and detached statistical references and are never replayed in the policy loss. Experiments on ALFWorld and WebShop demonstrate that TIGPO consistently outperforms prior group-based and graph-based policy optimization methods.

AI.tldr: Temporal Instance-Graph Policy Optimization (TIGPO) extends graph-based credit assignment across policy updates by maintaining a persistent task-level transition graph and a fixed rollout budget split between Exploration and Revisit slots, enabling cross-temporal credit estimation and improved stability with small rollout groups.
AI.motivation: Address the limitation that prior graph-based methods build graphs per update, discarding earlier transitions and restricting credit assignment to small local rollouts; leverage historical experience to stabilize advantage estimates and track policy evolution.
AI.method: Maintain a persistent transition graph per task across updates. For each policy update, allocate a fixed rollout budget between Exploration slots (for ordinary task sampling) and Revisit slots (delayed reattempts of previously explored tasks). For each revisit, pair the current rollout group with the corresponding earlier Exploration group to construct a cross-temporal reference. Use historical transitions as structural references; they are not replayed in the policy loss.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation on ALFWorld and WebShop demonstrates that TIGPO consistently outperforms prior group-based and graph-based policy optimization methods.
AI.conclusion: Cross-temporal graph-based credit assignment with persistent graphs and revisit strategy improves stability and credit estimation for long-horizon LLM agents, enabling better policy improvement across training.

title: WIDE: Wildcard Inference with Dynamic Expansion for Cross-Modal Generative Retrieval
comment: Accepted to the 34th ACM International Conference on Multimedia (ACM MM 2026). 10 pages, 5 figures
summary: Generative retrieval has demonstrated significant success by unifying representation learning and search into a single sequence-to-sequence generation task. However, extending this paradigm to cross-modal retrieval reveals a critical challenge arising from the inherent information asymmetry across different modalities, such as the gap between concise text queries and dense visual candidates. This structural mismatch causes the autoregressive decoder to suffer from forced hallucination when generating identifiers via standard trie-constrained beam search, where the model is severely penalized for failing to guess fine-grained details absent from the query, allowing irrelevant candidates to hijack top rankings. To address this issue, we propose Wildcard Inference with Dynamic Expansion (WIDE). WIDE employs Adaptive Entropy Thresholding (AET) to calibrate layer-specific uncertainty boundaries offline. During the decoding generation phase, Asymmetry-aware Wildcard Decoding (AWD) detects semantic blind spots and emits wildcards instead of forced deterministic identifiers, dynamically expanding the search space without incurring log-probability penalties. Finally, Blind-Spot Re-ranking (BSR) evaluates the expanded candidate pool using a hybrid scoring mechanism that combines discrete generation confidence with continuous semantic similarity. Extensive experiments on the M-BEIR benchmark demonstrate that WIDE outperforms state-of-the-art generative retrieval methods, effectively suppressing forced hallucination while maintaining compact index structures.

AI.tldr: Proposes WIDE, a cross-modal generative retrieval framework that uses adaptive entropy thresholding, wildcard decoding, and blind-spot re-ranking to mitigate information asymmetry and reduce hallucination during decoding, achieving state-of-the-art on M-BEIR.
AI.motivation: Cross-modal retrieval faces an information asymmetry between concise text queries and dense visual candidates, causing forced hallucination in autoregressive decoding under trie constraints; existing generative retrievers struggle to align modalities while preserving compact indices.
AI.method: Three components: Adaptive Entropy Thresholding (AET) for offline layer-wise uncertainty calibration; Asymmetry-aware Wildcard Decoding (AWD) emitting wildcards during decoding to expand search space without log-probability penalties; Blind-Spot Re-ranking (BSR) uses a hybrid score combining discrete generation confidence and continuous semantic similarity to re-rank expanded candidates.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation on the M-BEIR benchmark shows WIDE outperforms state-of-the-art generative retrieval methods, reducing hallucination while maintaining compact index structures.
AI.conclusion: Wildcard-based expansion with adaptive uncertainty and hybrid re-ranking provides a robust solution to cross-modal generative retrieval asymmetry, enabling accurate retrieval without excessive index growth.

title: Semantic Bayesian World Models
summary: Knowledge graphs describe reality in crisp assertions, while the systems now consuming them, foundation models and autonomous agents, reason natively in probabilities. We argue that this mismatch is why the integration of language models and knowledge graphs remains a data-feeding pipeline rather than a unified reasoning architecture. We envision Semantic Bayesian World Models (SBWMs): a Web that describes the world not as a database of facts but as a shared, evolving fabric of beliefs over knowledge graphs, where ontological axioms constrain priors, observations update beliefs by Bayesian conditioning, and actions intervene upon the world. We work through what an agent gains from such a model: a home-security agent deciding whether the figure at the gate is a courier or a burglar, an actuarial estimate aggregated by entailment rather than by string frequency, a planning task that language models reliably fail, and the estimation of quantities that no document has ever stated. We then set out what the community must build to make them possible: belief annotation over RDF~1.2, probabilistic entailment regimes, semantic calibration layers, and protocols by which agents that have never met can exchange, and disagree over, calibrated beliefs.

AI.tldr: Proposes Semantic Bayesian World Models (SBWMs) that embed probabilistic reasoning over knowledge graphs, enabling unified inference and action; outlines required infrastructure and use cases.
AI.motivation: Knowledge graphs provide crisp facts, while foundation models and autonomous agents reason probabilistically. This mismatch hinders unified reasoning and integration; SBWMs aim to bridge this gap.
AI.method: Conceptual framework introducing SBWMs: belief annotations over RDF 1.2, ontological axioms constraining priors, Bayesian conditioning for observations, and actions that intervene in the world. Analyzes gains via four exemplar tasks and delineates the necessary building blocks (probabilistic entailment, semantic calibration, and exchange protocols).
AI.result: Articulates concrete benefits for agents (e.g., improved decision-making, entailment-based actuarial estimates, robust planning) and outlines a roadmap for implementation; no empirical results are provided, but a detailed blueprint is laid out.
AI.conclusion: Calls for concrete infrastructure to realize SBWMs: belief annotation over RDF 1.2, probabilistic entailment regimes, semantic calibration layers, and interoperable belief-exchange protocols among agents.

title: Inferred Generative-Process Diversity Predicts Correlated Failure Across Language Models
summary: Diversity is a widely observed factor in the resilient function of collective systems, yet the type of diversity that matters depends on the properties and failure modes of the system. This distinction is important for systems composed of multiple language models. Different models may be treated as independent components even when their behaviour and failures remain strongly correlated. Assessments of language-model populations using semantic similarity demonstrate limited semantic diversity, but this captures only differences in the meaning of observed outputs. We argue that a more fundamental notion of model diversity is generative-process diversity, the differences between processes capable of generating the observed outputs. Drawing from Algorithmic Information Theory, we use Normalised Compression Distance between raw model outputs, residualised against a permutation control, as a measure of inferred generative-process diversity. Across 38 language models, this measure identifies population structure missed by semantic similarity and predicts cross-task variation in chance-corrected correlated failure among model pairs across ten disjoint benchmark families, beyond semantic similarity and model-pair capability. The cross-benchmark partial rank association is $-0.216$ with a 95% interval of $[-0.309,-0.122]$, and the estimate is negative on all ten benchmarks. These results indicate that increased generative-process diversity is associated with reduced correlated failure in model pairs that is not attributable to semantic similarity or capability. Inferred generative-process diversity offers a novel and practical approach for investigating diversity of multi-model systems in safety-relevant contexts.

AI.tldr: Introduces generative-process diversity for language-model ensembles using Normalised Compression Distance on raw outputs (residualised against a permutation control). It uncovers population structure beyond semantic similarity and links to reduced correlated failures across benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Diversity's role in the resilience of multi-model systems is contingent on the failure modes and generative processes; semantic similarity alone underestimates true diversity when models share failure modes despite output differences.
AI.method: Compute Normalised Compression Distance between raw model outputs, residualised against a permutation control, across 38 language models. Evaluate on ten disjoint benchmark families, examining cross-task variation in chance-corrected correlated failure, and compare against semantic similarity and model-pair capability.
AI.result: Generative-process diversity reveals population structure not captured by semantic similarity and predicts variation in cross-task correlated failures. The cross-benchmark partial rank association is -0.216 (95% CI [-0.309, -0.122]), negative on all ten benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Inferred generative-process diversity provides a novel, practical framework for studying diversity in multi-model systems, with implications for safety-relevant contexts.

title: SV-WAM: An Efficient Surround-View World-Action Model for End-to-End Autonomous Driving
summary: World models (WMs) have demonstrated strong potential for end-to-end autonomous driving by learning predictive representations of future scene dynamics. However, generating future videos during inference introduces substantial computational overhead, leading many recent driving WMs to adopt a single front camera as input for efficient deployment. This design restricts spatial coverage in safety-critical maneuvers such as lane changes, merges, and turns. To address this limitation, we propose SV-WAM, a surround-view world-action model (WAM) that preserves full six-camera observations while maintaining efficient inference. SV-WAM leverages future-video prediction as dense training supervision for action learning within a shared generative model, rather than as an inference-time output. At the core of this design is an action-centered causal mask that prevents action tokens from attending to future-video tokens during joint action-video denoising. Consequently, the video branch can be discarded at deployment, enabling efficient action-only planning. Furthermore, we introduce a differentiable drivable-area compliance regularizer that penalizes vehicle-footprint corners approaching or crossing drivable boundaries, improving planning safety and boundary awareness. Extensive experiments on the closed-loop NAVSIMv2 benchmark and the open-loop nuScenes benchmark demonstrate that SV-WAM achieves state-of-the-art planning performance with low inference latency and competitive zero-shot transfer capability.

AI.tldr: SV-WAM is a surround-view world-action model that uses future video prediction as training supervision while enabling action-only planning at deployment through an action-centered causal mask, achieving state-of-the-art planning with low latency on NAVSIMv2 and nuScenes.
AI.motivation: Existing world models for autonomous driving often rely on a single front camera due to the heavy cost of predicting future videos, which limits spatial coverage and safety in maneuvers like lane changes. There is a need to preserve full surround-view input while maintaining efficient inference.
AI.method: Train a joint action-video denoising model with an action-centered causal mask that prevents action tokens from attending to future-video tokens during training. The video branch is used for supervision during training but can be discarded at deployment, leaving an action-only planner. Introduce a differentiable drivable-area compliance regularizer that penalizes vehicle footprint proximity to drivable boundaries.
AI.result: SV-WAM achieves state-of-the-art planning performance with low inference latency on NAVSIMv2 (closed-loop) and nuScenes (open-loop), with competitive zero-shot transfer.
AI.conclusion: By decoupling training-time video prediction from deployment-time action planning through an action-focused mask and surround-view inputs, SV-WAM delivers safe, efficient planning without incurring the inference cost of video generation.

title: Building Pretraining Data for World Models: An Unreal Engine-Based Pipeline for Action-Conditioned Video Generation
summary: Action-conditioned video models require large-scale visual data paired with control signals that are temporally aligned with the resulting scene transitions. Such supervision is difficult to obtain from ordinary real-world video because the actions that caused each visual change are typically unknown. We present a large-scale synthetic data production pipeline built on Unreal Engine for generating action-conditioned, multi-view video. To accommodate the different execution requirements of real-time physics and high-quality offline rendering, the pipeline executes trajectory generation and final rendering in two stages: Stage I runs real physics in PIE and records per-frame character states, control inputs, and camera states into an intermediate trajectory representation; Stage II replays those trajectories in a new engine process and renders them offline with Movie Render Queue (MRQ). Around this core, we develop a distributed production system with cache-aware task partitioning, node-local slot scheduling, automated scene screening, aesthetic and luminance filtering, partial-output recovery, asynchronous upload, and continuous cluster health monitoring. The production cluster contains 25 servers with eight NVIDIA RTX 5090 GPUs per server. From 2,384 asset packs, 429 levels were retained for production together with a pool of 40 humanoid characters. The pipeline has produced 2,691 hours of 1080p video and 6,076 hours of 720p video. We describe the system architecture, the implementation decisions that emerged from production failures, and the limitations of using perceptual quality proxies for world-model data curation. The pipeline described in this report constitutes the Unreal Engine synthetic-data production component used in EchoWM.

AI.tldr: A two-stage Unreal Engine synthetic-data pipeline generates action-conditioned, multi-view video at scale, with Stage I capturing physics-driven trajectories and Stage II offline rendering, supported by a distributed cluster; it enables large-scale data curation for EchoWM while highlighting limitations of perceptual proxies.
AI.motivation: Action-conditioned video models require large-scale, temporally aligned supervision. Real-world videos lack known action signals, making it difficult to obtain suitable training data. Synthetic generation can provide controlled, labeled data with precise control signals and camera viewpoints.
AI.method: Stage I runs real-time physics in PIE, recording per-frame character states, control inputs, and camera states into an intermediate trajectory representation. Stage II replays trajectories in a separate engine process and renders offline with Movie Render Queue (MRQ). A distributed production system handles cache-aware task partitioning, node-local scheduling, automated scene screening, aesthetic and luminance filtering, partial-output recovery, asynchronous upload, and cluster health monitoring. The deployment spans 25 servers with eight RTX 5090 GPUs each, using 2,384 asset packs, 429 levels, and 40 humanoid characters; producing 2,691 hours of 1080p and 6,076 hours of 720p video.
AI.result: Demonstrates scalable synthetic data production for action-conditioned video, enabling large volumes of multi-view video with aligned control signals. Provides architectural decisions, production-failure lessons, and notes on limitations of perceptual proxies for world-model data curation.
AI.conclusion: The pipeline is the Unreal Engine synthetic-data production component used by EchoWM. It demonstrates feasibility and scalability for large-scale action-conditioned video data, while also acknowledging limitations in relying on perceptual proxies for world-model data curation.

title: Adapting to Evolving Requirements: Agentic AI for Retail Supply Chain Operations
summary: Retail supply chain operations rely on coupled decision modules that must adapt as requirements evolve. LLMs offer a natural-language interface for this task, but existing methods primarily focus on individual optimization models. Extending them to heterogeneous decision pipelines is challenging because a requirement may admit multiple intervention paths with different downstream effects. We formulate requirement-driven adaptation as the joint selection of an intervention route and an admissible module-level change, and propose a graph-constrained agentic framework in which domain agents expose admissible reformulation interfaces and a central processor searches over bounded intervention paths. Candidates are validated and compared using downstream KPIs. In collaboration with a large retail partner, we evaluate 100 warehouse requirements elicited from practitioner interviews, with GPT, Qwen, and DeepSeek as base LLMs. Relative to direct LLM reformulation, our framework improves correctness and end-to-end success across all three models, raising end-to-end success from 72--76% to 79--83%.

AI.tldr: Jointly selecting intervention routes and admissible module-level changes via a graph-constrained agentic framework; improves end-to-end success in retail supply chain reformulations.
AI.motivation: Retail supply chains rely on heterogeneous, coupled decision modules; requirements can have multiple intervention paths; a mechanism is needed to explore paths while ensuring performance via KPIs.
AI.method: Domain agents expose reformulation interfaces; a central processor searches bounded intervention paths in a graph; candidates are validated against downstream KPIs; evaluation with 100 warehouse requirements elicited from practitioner interviews; base LLMs: GPT, Qwen, DeepSeek.
AI.result: Relative to direct LLM reformulation, improvements in correctness and end-to-end success across all three base models; end-to-end success rises from 72-76% to 79-83%.
AI.conclusion: Graph-constrained, agentic framework effectively coordinates heterogeneous modules for requirement-driven adaptation, yielding measurable gains in real-world retail settings.

title: TraveL: Transformer-based Multi-view Path Distributional Representation Learning
summary: Path representation learning (PRL) for road networks has received increasing research attention, due to various path-related applications. Existing works on PRL typically exploit the co-occurrence relationship among road segments and paths to learn a vector as the path representation, without exploring the varied traveler behaviors and the regional correlation on the path. In this work, we propose to learn distributional representations, which provide valuable information for use in path-related applications, by capturing the varied traveler behaviors as well as the various dependencies within regions of road segments. We propose a novel Transformer-based Multi-view Distributional Representation Learning (TraveL) framework to encode a path along with a travel starting time to a distributional representation, which can be used to decode possible samples of on-path traveler behavior. Moreover, by analyzing the regional correlation which reveals various road segment relationships, we propose a regional attention to encode these correlations in a path. Also, we explore the idea of Kolmogorov-Smirnov (K-S) test to compare the sampled traveler behavior against the collected ground truth to facilitate training. Experimental results show that the proposed TraveL model outperforms the state-of-the-art methods on both synthetic and real-world datasets, by 14.7% in Mean K-S distance for travel time distribution estimation, 16.7% in Mean Absolute Error (MAE) for path similarity prediction, and 3.97% in MAE for destination prediction.

AI.tldr: Transformer-based multi-view distributional representation learning (TraveL) for road networks that encodes a path and start time into a distributional path representation, employs regional attention to capture region dependencies, and uses KS-based training to align samples with ground-truth traveler behavior; shows improvements over SOTA on synthetic and real data across travel-time distribution, path similarity, and destination prediction.
AI.motivation: Existing PRL methods primarily leverage co-occurrence of road segments and paths, neglecting variability in traveler behavior and regional dependencies. A distributional representation can capture uncertainty and regional interactions to improve downstream tasks.
AI.method: TraveL uses a Transformer-based architecture to encode a path together with travel starting time into a distribution over traveler behaviors, from which samples can be decoded. A regional attention mechanism models correlations among road segments within regions. Training utilizes the Kolmogorov-Smirnov (K-S) test by comparing sampled behavior to ground-truth data to align the distributional representation with observed travel patterns.
AI.result: Experimental results on synthetic and real-world datasets show TraveL outperforms state-of-the-art methods: 14.7% improvement in Mean KS distance for travel time distribution estimation, 16.7% improvement in MAE for path similarity prediction, and 3.97% improvement in MAE for destination prediction.
AI.conclusion: TraveL yields distributional path representations that capture traveler behavior variability and regional road correlations, leading to superior performance across diverse path-related tasks. The time-aware encoding, regional attention, and KS-based training contribute to its effectiveness.

title: Understanding Autonomous Driving Datasets by Describing Differences between Image Subsets in Natural Language
comment: 9 pages, 5 figures, submitted to the IEEE Open Journal of Intelligent Transportation Systems (OJ-ITS), our implementation and benchmark dataset are available at https://github.com/KIT-MRT/AD-Diff
summary: Understanding the composition of large-scale autonomous driving datasets is essential for safety, robustness, and reliable operation across domains. For example, domain shift between locations could lead to the operating environment being misaligned with the training data, resulting in potentially dangerous performance degradation. Yet, existing data analysis pipelines largely rely on metadata, predefined labels, or manual inspection, which provide limited semantic insight or do not scale. This paper studies set difference captioning: given two subsets of images, the goal is to produce a natural-language hypothesis describing differences between the target and reference set. Building on a two-stage formulation, we adapt the method to autonomous driving by focusing on object-centric patches derived from object detection, which simplifies aggregation and enables attribution of differences to specific object instances or categories. To evaluate this setting in-domain, we introduce a new benchmark, AD-Diff Bench. Low-concentration experiments assess the suitability of set-difference-captioning approaches to sparse, real-world differences. We restrict our experiments to open-weight models to support reproducibility and ease of deployment. The proposed benchmark and analysis provide a step towards practical, human-interpretable dataset introspection for autonomous driving datasets. Our implementation and benchmark dataset are available at https://github.com/KIT-MRT/AD-Diff

AI.tldr: Introduces set-difference captioning for autonomous driving datasets, using object-centric patches from detections to describe differences between image subsets; presents AD-Diff Bench, evaluates with sparse differences, and emphasizes reproducibility via open-weight models.
AI.motivation: Need scalable, semantic analysis of large autonomous driving datasets beyond metadata or manual inspection. Domain shifts and dataset composition differences can degrade safety; a human-readable explanation of where and what differs aids robustness and validation.
AI.method: A two-stage set-difference captioning framework adapted to autonomous driving. It uses object-centric patches derived from object detection, enabling aggregation and attribution to specific object instances or categories. Builds a new in-domain benchmark (AD-Diff Bench) and conducts low-concentration (sparse) difference experiments using open-weight models for reproducibility.
AI.result: Introduces AD-Diff Bench and a reproducible evaluation protocol for set-difference captioning in autonomous driving. Demonstrates feasibility of producing human-interpretable hypotheses about differences between image subsets and provides baseline analyses under sparse/diffuse changes.
AI.conclusion: The approach enables practical, human-interpretable dataset introspection for autonomous driving datasets, with object-level attribution of differences and a benchmark to drive future analysis—supporting safety, robustness, and cross-domain validation.

title: FlashRender: Few-Step Generative Rendering via Camera-Controlled Video MeanFlow
summary: We present FlashRender, a few-step generative rendering framework that retakes a source video along a target camera trajectory in seconds. We identify sampling-step-dependent camera control as a prominent manifestation of discretization error in existing multi-step generative rendering models and show that resolving this inconsistency substantially lowers denoising trajectory curvature, facilitating subsequent step distillation. To this end, we introduce Representation Transformation and Alignment (RETA), which aligns hidden source-video representations with target-video features from a frozen visual geometry model. This directly encodes the geometric transformation within the source-video stream, enabling sampling-step-consistent camera control. We then fine-tune the model with the MeanFlow objective on the lower-curvature denoising trajectory induced by RETA, allowing the model to more effectively address discretization error. Finally, we apply on-policy flow map distillation to correct self-rollout errors under fixed few-step sampling. Extensive experiments show that RETA, MeanFlow, and on-policy flow map distillation play complementary roles in few-step generative rendering. Together, they enable our approach to match multi-step baselines in video quality and geometric consistency at 25x lower sampling cost while achieving superior camera controllability, even under out-of-distribution target camera trajectories.

AI.tldr: Fast few-step generative rendering framework achieving near multi-step baseline quality with 25x lower sampling cost via RETA, MeanFlow, and on-policy flow map distillation.
AI.motivation: Discretization error in multi-step generative rendering causes sampling-step-dependent camera control and denoising artifacts, hindering fast, controllable video retargeting.
AI.method: Introduce RETA to align hidden source-video representations with target-video features from a frozen geometry model, encoding geometric transformation in the source stream; fine-tune with MeanFlow on lower-curvature denoising trajectories; apply on-policy flow map distillation to correct self-rollout errors under fixed few-step sampling.
AI.result: Matches multi-step baselines in video quality and geometric consistency at 25x lower sampling cost; superior camera controllability and robustness to out-of-distribution target trajectories.
AI.conclusion: RETA, MeanFlow, and on-policy flow map distillation jointly address discretization error to enable fast, controllable, high-quality generative rendering, with potential applicability to diverse camera paths and content.

title: Bioinfoysis Technical Report
summary: Large language model agents have shown promise in bioinformatics, but most existing systems focus primarily on producing final answers, treating planning, tool use, and code execution as transient interactions. This design is poorly suited to long-horizon bioinformatics tasks, where conclusions must remain connected to the data, computations, and intermediate evidence that support them. We introduce \textbf{Bioinfoysis}, a multi-agent harness that represents each request as a persistent, artifact-grounded analysis run. Bioinfoysis combines global planning with step-wise, evidence-driven replanning: the planner maintains an executable checklist and revises pending steps using structured handoffs returned after each worker execution. These handoffs bind intermediate results to their responsible agent, checklist step, and plan generation, preventing stale evidence from being silently reused after replanning. A controlled runtime validates generated scripts, tables, and figures before they are used in downstream analysis or reporting, while role-specific context, persistent memory, and governed bioinformatics skills support reliable execution over long analysis trajectories. We evaluate Bioinfoysis on BixBench and two question-answering tracks of LAB-Bench 2. On BixBench, Bioinfoysis achieves state-of-the-art accuracy of 82.4\%. Across four underlying language models, Bioinfoysis increases average accuracy from 27.81\% to 64.13\% on SeqQA2 and from 3.13\% to 31.25\% on DbQA2. These results demonstrate that reliable bioinformatics automation depends not only on model capability, but also on the harness that governs planning, execution, memory, and evidence flow. We hope that the emergence of Bioinfoysis will play a driving and leading role in the development of the bioinformatics community. Our demo website can be seen in https://report.bioinfoysis.com/.

AI.tldr: A persistent, artifact-grounded multi-agent framework, Bioinfoysis, improves long-horizon bioinformatics analysis by maintaining a planner-driven executable checklist with evidence-based replanning and runtime validation, achieving strong accuracy gains on BixBench across multiple LLMs.
