Additionally, we propose a destination-based segmentation strategy to better model real-world communication structures in IoT traffic. Our framework is comprehensively evaluated on six distinct datasets spanning industrial, enterprise, general-purpose, smart home, and military automation domains across 44 transfer scenarios. Experimental results demonstrate strong zero-shot generalization in several cross-domain settings and competitive performance against a contrastive domain-adaptation baseline under realistic, heterogeneous, and privacy-constrained IoT conditions.

AI.tldr: A novel adversarial-contrastive VAE framework for multivariate time-series anomaly detection enabling zero-shot domain adaptation in IoT, with adaptor layers and destination-based segmentation, evaluated on six datasets across 44 transfer scenarios, achieving strong zero-shot generalization and competitive performance against a domain-adaptation baseline.
AI.motivation: IoT anomaly detection is challenged by device heterogeneity, limited labeled data, and domain shifts across environments. There is a need for zero-shot domain adaptation that preserves semantics and privacy, without raw feature transfer.
AI.method: A sequence-based Variational Autoencoder (VAE) augmented with adversarial learning and contrastive loss to learn domain-invariant latent representations and semantically structured embeddings. Introduces encoder/decoder adaptor layers to align feature distributions across domains while preserving contextual semantics, and a destination-based segmentation strategy to model IoT traffic structure. Evaluated across six diverse datasets with 44 transfer scenarios.
AI.result: The approach demonstrates strong zero-shot generalization in several cross-domain settings and competitive performance compared with a contrastive domain-adaptation baseline under realistic, heterogeneous, and privacy-constrained IoT conditions.
AI.conclusion: The framework effectively enables zero-shot cross-domain anomaly detection in IoT. Key contributions include adaptor layers for distribution alignment and a destination-based segmentation approach that captures domain-specific traffic structures, with broad cross-domain validation supporting its robustness. Future work could explore additional baselines, unseen artifact evaluation, and scalability to larger, streaming deployments.

title: Tree-Structured Vector Quantization For Efficient And Progressive Image Compression
summary: Vector-quantization based image compression has achieved strong rate--distortion performance, yet most of them still produce a separate compressed representation for each target bitrate. Such variable-rate behavior allows one model to operate at multiple rates, but it does not necessarily provide a progressive bitstream whose prefixes are themselves decodable and can be refined by appending additional bits. We propose \textbf{Tree-VQ}, a progressive tree-structured vector quantization framework for learned image compression. Tree-VQ organizes discrete codewords as a hierarchical binary tree and represents each latent token by a routed root-to-leaf path. Crucially, every prefix of this path corresponds to a valid quantized representation, so shallow internal nodes serve as coarse reconstruction codes and deeper nodes provide successive refinements. This allows a compressed image to be decoded from an early prefix and progressively improved as more branch symbols are received, rather than being re-encoded for different target rates. To make this structure practical for compression, we introduce a prefix-compatible tree entropy model that codes progressive continuation decisions and routed branch refinements using only causally available decoded contexts. We further use rate-aware refinement scheduling to decide which spatial blocks should receive additional tree bits under a given prefix budget, and hierarchical prefix supervision to ensure that internal nodes are directly decodable at low rates. Experiments show that Tree-VQ achieves a superior performance--efficiency trade-off, delivering the best perceptual compression results with much fewer parameters and lower latency than competing methods.

AI.tldr: Progressive, prefix-decodable tree-structured vector quantization (Tree-VQ) for learned image compression; enables progressive decoding via valid prefixes and achieves strong rate-distortion with fewer parameters and lower latency.
AI.motivation: Conventional vector-quantization-based methods yield single fixed-rate codebooks, lacking progressive bitstreams. There is a need for a single model that supports progressive refinement with decodable prefixes and rate-adaptive behavior.
AI.method: Organize discrete codewords into a binary tree; represent each latent token by a root-to-leaf path; ensure every prefix yields a valid reconstruction; introduce prefix-compatible entropy model using causally available context; rate-aware refinement scheduling; hierarchical prefix supervision.
AI.result: Experiments show Tree-VQ achieves superior performance-efficiency trade-off; best perceptual compression with far fewer parameters and lower latency than competing methods.
AI.conclusion: Tree-VQ enables progressive decoding with decodable prefixes and refined reconstructions through additional bits; improved rate-distortion performance with efficiency; practical progressive compression framework.

title: More Criticism Does Not Make a Better Review: EquiReview-R
summary: AI reviewers can now produce many specific criticisms, but more criticism is not necessarily a better review. A review may miss a consequential weakness or retain an allegation that available evidence does not support. These failures require opposite corrections, yet generation-oriented systems and aggregate measures obscure the distinction. We therefore recast AI-assisted review as evidence-guided refinement of a structured concern set, with omission and overcritique treated as separate risks. Building on this formulation, we introduce EquiReview-R, which resolves existing concerns against localized evidence, searches for missing issues from independent and review-conditioned perspectives, and returns stop, continue, or defer. To expose the failure mode that motivates this design, we construct an evidence-linked trajectory corpus. Its retrospective analysis shows why revision must precede further search: nearly all concerns in a high-recall review lack a definitive evidential disposition, while an earlier refinement mechanism cannot revise them. On a frozen cohort of previously unseen papers, EquiReview-R satisfies the prespecified non-inferiority criterion for major omission, reduces major overcritique from 15.5% to 8.1%, and attains a one-sided omission upper bound of 9.9% while stopping on 52.4% of papers. Computation-matched controls, controlled pairs, and ablations show that the gain comes from revision rather than extra inference or shorter output. We release the corpus as ReviewTrace, an evidence-linked resource for studying review revision, disagreement, and provenance.

AI.tldr: EquiReview-R reframes AI-assisted review as evidence-guided refinement of a structured concern set to reduce omission and overcritique, using an evidence-linked corpus ReviewTrace and a stop/continue/defer mechanism.
AI.motivation: Address that generation-focused reviews produce many criticisms but may miss consequential weaknesses or retain unsupported allegations; need to distinguish omission vs overcritique.
AI.method: Evidence-guided refinement of structured concern set; evidence-linked trajectory corpus; evaluation on frozen cohort; non-inferiority criterion; comparison to baselines; release ReviewTrace.
AI.result: On unseen papers, non-inferiority for major omission; major overcritique reduced from 15.5% to 8.1%; omission upper bound 9.9%; stop on 52.4% of papers; revision drives gains; corpus released.
AI.conclusion: Revision before further search is necessary; EquiReview-R shows benefits; ReviewTrace as resource for studying review revision, disagreement, provenance.

title: LongCounsel-8: A Benchmark Suite for Longitudinal Depression Tracking from Multi-Session Counseling Dialogues
summary: Tracking depression from multi-session counseling dialogues requires estimating both current symptom severity and how it changes across sessions. Yet progress on this task is constrained by the scarcity of longitudinal counseling data with standardized session-level depression labels. Existing resources typically provide either multi-session conversations without depression labels or labeled interviews in a single session. Building such a benchmark poses three challenges: maintaining longitudinal consistency and diversity, grounding symptom progression in empirical patterns, and expressing controlled depression states naturally without exposing target labels. To address these challenges, we introduce LongCounsel-8, a benchmark suite of three independently generated datasets totaling 7,749 five-session counseling trajectories, grounded in real-world client profiles, depression trajectories, symptom compositions, and counseling patterns. We combine profile-grounded simulation, empirically informed state construction, and indirect behavioral realization to address these challenges. Across the benchmark, simulated self-reports closely recover the controlled states, supporting label fidelity. Experiments on existing depression tracking methods reveal three key findings: (1) lower single-session score error does not guarantee accurate identification of trend, i.e., improvement or worsening; (2) existing methods are consistently less reliable on worsening trajectories; and (3) additional session history may reduce the accuracy of trend prediction. Together, these findings establish LongCounsel-8 as a foundation for advancing depression assessment from static, single-session prediction toward reliable longitudinal tracking of mental-health change.

AI.tldr: LongCounsel-8 provides a longitudinal benchmark for depression tracking across five-session counseling trajectories, using 3 datasets (7,749 trajectories) to study symptom states and their progression; key findings show that single-session accuracy does not guarantee correct trend detection, worsening trajectories are harder to identify, and longer histories may hurt trend prediction.
AI.motivation: There is a scarcity of longitudinal counseling data with standardized session-level depression labels. Existing resources typically offer multi-session conversations without labels or labeled single sessions, hampering consistent tracking of symptom progression across sessions. A benchmark is needed to (i) ensure longitudinal consistency and diversity, (ii) ground progression in empirically observed patterns, and (iii) express controlled depression states naturally without exposing explicit target labels.
AI.method: Three independently generated datasets totaling 7,749 five-session counseling trajectories are created under the LongCounsel-8 benchmark. The generation combines profile-grounded simulation, empirically informed state construction, and indirect behavioral realization, grounded in real-world client profiles, depression trajectories, symptom compositions, and counseling patterns. Simulated self-reports are used to recover the controlled states, providing label fidelity while avoiding explicit target-label exposure.
AI.result: Simulated self-reports closely recover the controlled states, supporting label fidelity. Experiments with existing depression-tracking methods reveal: (1) low single-session error does not guarantee correct trend identification; (2) worsening trajectories are less reliably tracked by current methods; (3) additional session history may reduce trend-prediction accuracy.
AI.conclusion: LongCounsel-8 establishes a robust foundation for moving depression assessment from static, single-session prediction toward reliable longitudinal tracking of mental-health change, enabling better benchmarking and development of methods that capture symptom progression across sessions.

title: PL-SCEA: Reconfiguring Pretrained Attention for Few-Shot Industrial Anomaly Detection
summary: Vision Foundation Models (VFMs) provide transferable patch representations for few-shot industrial anomaly detection, but their attention computation is typically inherited from pretraining objectives centered on semantic aggregation. This creates a potential mismatch: token relations that support semantic recognition may not adequately expose the localized texture and structural deviations required for anomaly localization. We therefore investigate the hypothesis that the attention computation of a frozen VFM can be reconfigured as a task-relevant component of anomaly detection. We instantiate this idea with Power-Law Self-Correlation Enhanced Attention (PL-SCEA), which retains the semantic context of pretrained query-key attention while constructing token-adaptive self-correlations over contextualized value features. Positive-correlation filtering and power-law reweighting then emphasize relations that are salient relative to each token's relational background, without introducing additional trainable attention projections. The resulting features are modeled by a lightweight variational autoencoder that provides a fixed-size reconstruction-based representation of category-specific normality. The two stages serve complementary roles: attention reconfiguration shapes how local relational deviations are represented, while reconstruction-based modeling converts deviations from learned normality into anomaly scores. Across MVTec AD and VisA, the complete framework achieves competitive image-level detection and consistently strong pixel-level localization across the evaluated few-shot settings. Ablations further show that PL-SCEA improves localization with either the VAE or a memory bank under the tested setting. These results support the view that task-aligned attention reconfiguration can improve the anomaly-localization capability of frozen pretrained representations.

AI.tldr: PL-SCEA reconfigures frozen vision foundation model attention for few-shot industrial anomaly detection, combining token-adaptive self-correlations with a lightweight VAE to achieve strong pixel-level localization and competitive image-level detection on MVTec AD and VisA.
AI.motivation: To address a potential mismatch in pretrained attention: semantic-focused token relations learned during pretraining may not expose localized texture and structural deviations needed for accurate anomaly localization when using frozen Vision Foundation Models for few-shot industrial anomaly detection.
AI.method: Introduce Power-Law Self-Correlation Enhanced Attention (PL-SCEA): preserve the semantic context of pretrained query-key attention while constructing token-adaptive self-correlations over contextualized value features. Apply positive-correlation filtering and power-law reweighting to emphasize relations salient to each token’s relational background, without adding trainable attention projections. Feed the resulting features into a lightweight variational autoencoder (VAE) to obtain a fixed-size reconstruction-based normality representation. Two-stage pipeline: attention reconfiguration shapes local relational deviations; reconstruction-based modeling converts deviations into anomaly scores. Evaluations include ablations and comparisons with a memory bank.
AI.result: On MVTec AD and VisA, the framework delivers competitive image-level anomaly detection and consistently strong pixel-level localization in few-shot regimes. Ablations indicate that PL-SCEA improves localization whether using the VAE or a memory bank.
AI.conclusion: Task-aligned attention reconfiguration can enhance the anomaly-localization capability of frozen pretrained representations.

title: FiMI Banking: A Sovereign Model for Indian Retail Banking
summary: Banks need conversational systems that can answer product questions, assist customers with account-related requests, and operate safely within strict operational and regulatory constraints. General-purpose language models do not reliably meet these requirements. They fall short when a task requires grounded information, correct tool use, or cautious handling of bank-specific sensitive situations. We introduce FiMI Banking, a controlled Indian retail-banking setting. We build it from vetted banking documents, structured ground truth, synthetic customer backgrounds, and banking tools. We evaluate two post-training approaches: preference optimization for response-level behavior, and reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards for multi-turn tool-use tasks. Preference optimization improves safe behavior substantially: out-of-scope refusal rises from 52% to 80%. Reinforcement learning improves edge-case performance from 0.509 to 0.718 and order-sensitive task performance from 0.590 to 0.679, while using 29% fewer generated tokens. These results show that preference optimization and verifiable-reward reinforcement learning address complementary requirements for reliable banking agents.

AI.tldr: FiMI Banking introduces a controlled Indian retail-banking evaluation setting and shows two post-training strategies—preference optimization for response safety and verifiable-reward RL for multi-turn tool usage—that together improve safety and task performance while reducing token usage.
AI.motivation: General-purpose LMs struggle with grounded information, correct tool use, and handling bank-specific sensitive situations under regulatory constraints. There is a need for controlled, auditable benchmarks and learning methods tuned for safe, compliant banking assistants.
AI.method: Construct FiMI Banking from vetted banking documents, structured ground truth, synthetic customer profiles, and banking tools. Evaluate two post-training approaches: (1) preference optimization to shape response-level behavior (safety/refusal patterns); (2) reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards to optimize multi-turn tool-use tasks. Compare to baseline LMs.
AI.result: Preference optimization raises out-of-scope refusals from 52% to 80%. Verifiable-reward RL improves edge-case performance from 0.509 to 0.718 and order-sensitive task performance from 0.590 to 0.679, while reducing generated tokens by 29%.
AI.conclusion: Preference optimization and verifiable-reward RL address complementary requirements for reliable banking agents, suggesting that a combination yields safer and more capable conversational banking systems.

title: LeanGRPO: Eliminating Redundant Recomputation in Diffusion RL
summary: Diffusion reinforcement learning (RL) has recently achieved significant success in post-training image and video generative models. However, most diffusion RL methods, including DanceGRPO and FlowGRPO, recompute selected timesteps with gradient tracking after rollout. Under on-policy training with the same backend for rollout and update, this recomputation is mathematically redundant. Intuitively, the rollout and policy update steps can reuse the same feed-forward backbone to avoid redundant computation, but doing so can incur a large memory overhead during rollout. To address the issue, we present LeanGRPO by restructuring the data-parallel layout and introducing two recompute-free training schedules for trajectory-logprob diffusion RL: (1) LeanGRPO-Retain enables gradient tracking during rollout and directly reuses the resulting computation graphs and saved activations for backward during update, requiring no recomputation; and (2) LeanGRPO-Reweight also enables gradients during rollout, but immediately backpropagates each selected step using a provisional advantage and delays gradient synchronization, then corrects the provisional gradients with the true advantage after the trajectory is completed. These schedules target different model scales and input sizes. Across FlowGRPO/DanceGRPO with FLUX.1-dev and Wan, LeanGRPO achieves up to 1.83x end-to-end speedup while preserving the original optimization objective.

AI.tldr: LeanGRPO introduces two recompute-free training schedules for trajectory-logprob diffusion RL to avoid redundant recomputation during rollout, yielding up to 1.83x end-to-end speedup.
AI.motivation: To eliminate redundant gradient-tracking recomputation in diffusion RL methods (e.g., DanceGRPO, FlowGRPO) that occurs when using the same backend for rollout and update in on-policy training, while managing memory overhead.
AI.method: Restructure data-parallel layout and propose two schedules: (1) LeanGRPO-Retain — gradient tracking during rollout with graph and activation reuse for backward without recomputation; (2) LeanGRPO-Reweight — gradient tracking during rollout using provisional advantages with delayed gradient synchronization, later corrected with true advantages after trajectory completion.
AI.result: Achieves up to 1.83x end-to-end speedup for FlowGRPO/DanceGRPO with FLUX.1-dev and Wan, while preserving the original optimization objective.
AI.conclusion: Offers recomputation-free training tailored to model scales and input sizes, balancing memory and compute; enables faster diffusion RL without altering the objective.

title: Rethinking 3D Noise: Learning 3D-Aware Video Priors via Optimization-Free Morphological Perturbations
summary: 3D scene representations like NeRF and 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) suffer severe artifacts in sparse-view settings. Recent generative 3D artifact fixers attempt to address this, but rely on paired corrupted and clean renders requiring costly, per-scene reconstructions across varying view configurations. While 2D image augmentations act as instant regularizers, no explicit equivalents exist for 3D representations to preserve spatial consistency across views, an essential property for 3D-aware training. We propose 3D Morphological Perturbations as an optimization-free regularizer that preserves spatial consistency. Leveraging explicit 3DGS, we treat each Gaussian as a fundamental building block - analogous to a 2D pixel - and apply perturbations across its morphological parameter space via scale, rotation, and pruning. Our method eliminates per-scene 3DGS optimization loops from dataset curation while enabling models to learn stronger geometric priors than sparse-view baselines in diagnostic ablations conducted on a lightweight video diffusion sandbox. Scaled to a 14B-parameter video model via ControlNet, our approach maintains visual fidelity while reducing mean depth error by 12.5% over state-of-the-art image-to-image 3D artifact refiners, ultimately boosting downstream robotics policy success rates by up to 8.0% across 3 of 4 manipulation tasks.

AI.tldr: Optimization-free 3D regularizer for 3D Gaussian Splatting that preserves view-consistency, reducing depth error and boosting robotics task success without per-scene 3DGS optimization, scalable to large video models.
AI.motivation: Sparse-view artifacts in 3D scene representations (e.g., NeRF, 3DGS) and lack of explicit 3D analogs to 2D augmentation. Existing 3D artifact fixers rely on costly per-scene reconstructions; there is a need for a spatially consistent, optimization-free regularizer for 3D representations.
AI.method: Model uses explicit 3DGS; treats each Gaussian as a fundamental building block; applies morphological perturbations over scale, rotation, and pruning to induce variability while preserving geometry; eliminates per-scene 3DGS optimization in data curation; validates via diagnostic ablations on a lightweight video diffusion sandbox; scales to a 14B-parameter video model via ControlNet.
AI.result: Mean depth error reduced by 12.5% compared to state-of-the-art image-to-image 3D artifact refiners; maintains visual fidelity; boosts downstream robotics policy success rates by up to 8.0% across 3 of 4 manipulation tasks.
AI.conclusion: 3D Morphological Perturbations provide an optimization-free, spatially consistent regularizer for 3DGS that enables stronger geometric priors in sparse-view settings, eliminates expensive per-scene optimization, and yields measurable gains in depth accuracy and robotics performance.

title: Interface-Induced Trajectory Censoring
comment: 39 pages, 14 pages main text. Code, data, and pre-registrations: https://github.com/nebula-1999/Interface-Induced-Trajectory-Censoring
summary:
Agent evaluations report a tool-call rate read off the serving stack. That number can be zero while the model is emitting well-formed calls: the interface censors the trajectory before anything downstream sees it.
  On BFCL v4's own data, executor and scorer, holding weights, cases, decoding and seeds fixed and changing only the serving adapter, the same model scores 0.00 or 0.96 / 0.19. A 2x2 over chat template and parser locates the effect exactly: both main effects are exactly zero and all of it sits in the interaction -- no component is defective, and repairing one side of the contract buys precisely nothing. On tau-bench's 115 interactive retail tasks the same swap moves server-parsed calls from 0 to 636 and tasks reaching any tool execution from 0 to 103. Our probe reproduces the funnel across a 21x scale range of Qwen2.5-Coder: the server parses 0/100 at every size while well-formed emitted calls rise to 80/100 at 32B (~72 after calibration against an adjudicated gold standard). Under a matched envelope, across a comparable scale span, the silent fraction stays at 0-2, a prediction committed to the repository before the run. Llama-3.1-8B's 23% rate of calling the task function itself as a tool falls to 0 under one strict:true flag.
  The mismatch reaches inside the training loop, and its consequence is scale-dependent: in verl's AgentLoop at 7B, 45 of 115 generations carry a complete call; 0 are accepted, 0 execute, 0 return an observation. At 1.5B the same zero is over-determined, so we report the two scales separately. At evaluation time, repairing the adapter restores the mechanism but not a significant outcome gain: parsing 0->84, rescues 0->9, pass rate 53->62 (n.s.). We release a 98-line preflight check that catches every silent failure here. The observed tool-call rate is not a property of the model alone; it is a property of the model-interface stack that measures it.

AI.tldr: Tool-call rates are driven by the model-interface stack, not solely by the model; interface silences and adapter behavior create scale-dependent tool usage that is invisible in some evaluations.
AI.motivation: To disentangle model-intrinsic tool-use propensity from artifacts of serving stacks and adapters by cross-model, scale-aware experiments.
AI.method: Fixed-base experiments across multiple models (BFCL v4, tau-bench, Qwen2.5-Coder, Llama-3.1-8B, Verl AgentLoop) varying only the serving adapter; measure emitted vs accepted tool calls, parsing, and task execution across scales; use 2x2 templates to identify main effects; calibrate against gold standard; introduce a 98-line preflight check to detect silent failures.
AI.result: Tool-call statistics depend on the interface; large parts of the observed calls come from interaction terms with the adapter. Repairs to the adapter can restore parsing but yield little/no improvement in outcomes. Silent failures are common at scale unless preflight checks catch them; silent fractions can be near-zero under certain controls but otherwise scale with size; the same model can show 0 vs high parsing depending on flags and envelope. The phenomenon is not a property of the model alone but of the entire stack.
AI.conclusion: Evaluations must account for the interface and pipeline; tool-use metrics can be misleading if judged on model output alone. Implementing preflight checks and reporting both emitted and parsed calls, along with scale-aware analyses, is essential to accurately characterize tool-driving behavior.

title: Coupled Scaling: A Representational Accessibility Framework for Neural Scaling Laws
comment: 35 pages, 2 figures. Code and reproducibility artifacts: https://github.com/quintonvina/coupled-scaling/tree/v1.0-reanalysis
summary: Existing theories derive neural scaling from data geometry or a specified data-model spectrum, but systems trained on the same data can scale differently when architecture or optimization changes the representations they can efficiently reach. We introduce Coupled Scaling, a task-conditioned framework in which finite-budget scaling depends on the relation between task structure and the geometry accessible to an architecture-optimization system. In a solvable mode-truncation model, loss separates into target energy outside architectural support and an unresolved supported tail. For an arbitrary priority order, the residual lies between the best-N supported tail and the tail beyond the largest completed high-value prefix. If the cumulative-tail and coverage log-rates are $γ_{A,T}$ and $ρ_{A,O,T}$, the residual exponent lies in $[ρ_{A,O,T}γ_{A,T},γ_{A,T}]$. Under bounded off-prefix gain, the completed prefix is rate-determining and $α_{A,O,T}=ρ_{A,O,T}γ_{A,T}$; for $a_{A,T,j}\asymp j^{-b_{A,T}}$, this gives $α_{A,O,T}=ρ_{A,O,T}(b_{A,T}-1)$. A fixed-kernel specialization derives the training-time exponent from the near-zero tail of a task-weighted spectral measure defined independently of the loss fit. The framework separates architectural support from finite-budget acquisition and motivates two tests: static task-relevant geometry should track loss at a common budget, while multiscale geometry should track coupling-specific exponent ordering, including reversal across contrasting tasks. An audit of released emergence trajectories identifies the controls needed for a direct factorial test that measures geometry separately from the scaling fit.

AI.tldr: Coupled Scaling introduces a task-conditioned framework where finite-budget scaling depends on the relation between task structure and the geometry accessible to an architecture-optimization system. Loss decomposes into target energy outside architectural support and an unresolved supported tail; for an arbitrary priority order, the residual lies between the best-N supported tail and the tail beyond the largest completed high-value prefix. If the cumulative-tail and coverage log-rates are γ_{A,T} and ρ_{A,O,T}, the residual exponent lies in [ρ_{A,O,T} γ_{A,T}, γ_{A,T}]. Under bounded off-prefix gain, the completed prefix is rate-determining and α_{A,O,T}=ρ_{A,O,T} γ_{A,T}; for a_{A,T,j} ~ j^{-b_{A,T}}, this gives α_{A,O,T}=ρ_{A,O,T}(b_{A,T}-1). A fixed-kernel specialization derives the training-time exponent from the near-zero tail of a task-weighted spectral measure defined independently of the loss fit. The framework separates architectural support from finite-budget acquisition and motivates two tests: static task-relevant geometry should track loss at a common budget, while multiscale geometry should track coupling-specific exponent ordering, including reversal across contrasting tasks. An audit of released emergence trajectories identifies the controls needed for a direct factorial test that measures geometry separately from the scaling fit.
AI.motivation: Existing theories derive neural scaling from data geometry or a specified data-model spectrum, but systems trained on the same data can scale differently when architecture or optimization changes the representations they can efficiently reach. There is a need for a task-conditioned framework that decouples architectural support from finite-budget scaling and provides testable predictions about geometry and exponent ordering.
AI.method: Solvable mode-truncation model with loss decomposed into target energy outside architectural support and an unresolved supported tail. For arbitrary priority orders, the residual is bounded between the best-N tail and the tail beyond the largest completed high-value prefix. Derivations yield residual exponent bounds [ρ γ, γ], and under bounded off-prefix gain α_{A,O,T}=ρ_{A,O,T} γ_{A,T}. For power-law tails a_{A,T,j} ~ j^{-b_{A,T}}, α_{A,O,T}=ρ_{A,O,T}(b_{A,T}-1). A fixed-kernel specialization links training-time exponent to near-zero tail of task-weighted spectral measure. The framework then motivates static geometry and multiscale geometry tests and proposes an audit of trajectories to enable factorial testing that separates geometry from scaling.
AI.result: Analytic bounds connect geometry exponents to observed scaling exponents. Specifically, α_{A,O,T} lies in [ρ_{A,O,T} γ_{A,T}, γ_{A,T}], and for power-law tails α_{A,O,T}=ρ_{A,O,T}(b_{A,T}-1). The fixed-kernel specialization yields a training-time exponent from the near-zero tail of the task-weighted spectrum. The framework predicts that geometry ordering can reverse across tasks under multiscale geometry, and that the proposed tests can validate geometry-agnostic vs geometry-dependent scaling.
AI.conclusion: The framework decouples architectural support from finite-budget acquisition, enabling two concrete tests to diagnose geometry relevance and coupling: static task-relevant geometry tracking loss at fixed budgets and multiscale geometry tracking coupling-specific exponent ordering. An audit of emergence trajectories guides a direct factorial test to measure geometry separately from scaling, and suggests conditions under which exponent orderings may reverse across tasks.

title: Cross-Dataset Transfer and Reliability of Explainable Artificial Intelligence for RhythmFormer Remote Photoplethysmography
summary: Background. Remote photoplethysmography estimates the cardiovascular pulse from facial video, and its explanations have rested on inspecting heatmaps rather than on quantitative evidence about where a model reads it. We quantified the explanations and asked whether such explanations transfer between datasets and track model performance. Method. We trained eight condition-specific RhythmFormer models on NCKU-rPPG, recorded under three illumination levels, speaking, rotation, and cycling, estimated one heart rate per 5.12-second clip, and set them beside a UBFC-rPPG reproduction. Raw attention, rollout, attention flow, and Beyond Intuition were assessed by skin coverage and the Salience-guided Faithfulness Coefficient (SaCo). Results. Beyond Intuition ranked highest on both datasets, at median coverage 0.789 and SaCo 0.837 on Static level 3 against 0.826 and 0.917 on UBFC-rPPG; lower ranks differed. Within one participant of one condition, neither measure was related to a clip's heart-rate error, waveform correlation, or signal-to-noise ratio on either dataset: 186 of the 252 coefficients fell below $|ρ|=0.10$ and 28 reached $p<0.05$ against the 13 expected by chance. Across the eight scenarios only Beyond Intuition's coverage followed the three performance measures, at $ρ=-0.43$, $+0.57$, and $+0.43$, while the attention-only methods' SaCo ran opposite to each. It failed at 40 lux alone, its median coverage falling to 0.180 and its median SaCo to $-0.178$, whereas motion degraded the estimates far more without such a drop. Conclusions. Skin coverage and SaCo carry information complementary to the performance measures rather than a proxy for them: attributing to the skin does not guarantee an accurate estimate. What an attribution reveals about a condition is where the model looks rather than how faithfully its map is ordered.

AI.tldr: Explores quantitative explanations for rPPG models (skin coverage, SaCo) and their transfer across datasets. Finds attribution to skin is not a reliable proxy for heart-rate accuracy; one method (Beyond Intuition) most aligned with performance, but overall explanations do not predict HR errors consistently.
AI.motivation: Quantify and validate explanations of deep learning models for remote photoplethysmography, and test whether explanations generalize across datasets and experimental conditions.
AI.method: Train eight condition-specific RhythmFormer models on NCKU-rPPG (three illumination levels; speaking, rotation, cycling) to estimate HR per 5.12-s clip; compare with UBFC-rPPG reproduction; evaluate explanations via skin coverage and the Salience-guided Faithfulness Coefficient (SaCo) across raw attention, rollout, attention flow, and Beyond Intuition.
AI.result: Beyond Intuition achieved the highest median skin coverage and SaCo on both datasets (e.g., Static level 3: 0.789 coverage and 0.837 SaCo; UBFC-rPPG: 0.826, 0.917). Within a participant/condition, most explanation–performance correlations were weak (186/252 |ρ|<0.10; 28 p<0.05 vs 13 by chance). Across eight scenarios, only Beyond Intuition's coverage tracked performance measures (ρ values around -0.43 to +0.57), while attention-only SaCo often moved opposite to performance. 40 lux caused a notable drop in SaCo and coverage; motion degraded HR estimates more than lighting.
AI.conclusion: Skin coverage and SaCo provide information complementary to performance metrics and are not proxies for accuracy. Attribution reveals where the model looks, not how faithfully its ranking of predictions matches the ground truth.

title: Common-Witness Certificates and Sharp Feature Bounds for Counterfactual Image Auditing
summary: An image editor may satisfy every regional plausibility constraint separately even when no single latent explanation fits the complete output. We formalize this local-to-global failure using a common witness grade and witness nerve. The framework separates auditing from causal identification: shared exogeneity alone allows every coupling of the regime marginals, whereas an externally justified witness relation yields sharp partial-identification bounds for prespecified image features. Helly-type arguments provide short incompatibility certificates for quasiconvex losses, heterogeneous action strata, and finite witness atlases; a blocker-hypergraph formula gives exact repair counts. Simultaneous confidence regions for the regime marginals give finite-sample outer coverage of the complete identified interval. Controlled MNIST, Morpho-MNIST, and smallNORB studies demonstrate the predicted local-global separation, while synthetic experiments test sharp bounds, certificate recovery, and structured computation. The method audits a declared feature relation and does not identify unrestricted pixel-level counterfactuals.

AI.tldr: A framework for auditing image-editing models via a witness-based local-to-global analysis. It separates auditing from causal identification, yields sharp partial-identification bounds for image features, and provides finite-sample coverage guarantees, validated on MNIST-like datasets.
AI.motivation: To diagnose when regional plausibility constraints can be satisfied by incompatible latent explanations and to formalize an auditing procedure that controls for exogenous factors while yielding rigorous bounds on prespecified features.
AI.method: Introduce a common witness grade and witness nerve to separate auditing from causal identification. Use externally justified witness relations to obtain sharp partial-identification bounds for prespecified image features. Apply Helly-type arguments to derive short incompatibility certificates for quasiconvex losses, heterogeneous action strata, and finite witness atlases, and use a blocker-hypergraph formula to compute exact repair counts. Develop simultaneous confidence regions for regime marginals to guarantee finite-sample outer coverage of the identified interval.
AI.result: Controlled MNIST, Morpho-MNIST, and smallNORB experiments demonstrate the predicted local-global separation; synthetic experiments validate sharp bounds, certificate recovery, and structured computation of repairs.
AI.conclusion: The method audits a declared feature relation rather than enabling unrestricted pixel-level counterfactuals, providing finite-sample outer coverage and exact repair counts. It offers a rigorous auditing pipeline for image-feature relations with practical validation, while acknowledging reliance on external witness structure.

title: WeatherNext 3: Increasing resolution and performance of global weather models with raw observations
summary: State-of-the-art AI weather models have shown impressive medium-range forecast skill and computational efficiency, but suffer two key shortcomings: their forecasts have lower spatial and temporal resolution than the best physics-based models and they are exclusively initialized with and trained on analysis data. As a result, they cannot directly make use of observations, and any biases in the analysis are inherited by the forecast. WeatherNext 3 addresses these shortcomings and establishes a new state-of-the-art for probabilistic medium-range forecasting skill. First, WeatherNext 3 generates new forecasts every hour (rather than every 6 hours like traditional global models) by ingesting low-latency geostationary satellite data. Second, WeatherNext 3's temporal and spatial resolution are on par with physics-based global models, with hourly time steps and 0.1 degree resolution for single-level variables, including solar radiation and cloud cover. Third, WeatherNext 3 moves beyond traditional analysis variables by learning to predict satellite-derived precipitation estimates, as well as tropical cyclone and station observations. Modelling sparse station data allows WeatherNext 3 to make 2m temperature and dewpoint predictions at any location and time, conditioned on local geographical features, with substantially lower error than competing global models, even when evaluated against unseen stations. Together, WeatherNext 3's capabilities move operational AI-based weather forecasting beyond emulating the traditionally distinct stages of data assimilation, forecasting and post-processing, which helps to further push the frontier of performance and granularity for global weather prediction.

AI.tldr: WeatherNext 3 delivers hourly, high-resolution probabilistic medium-range forecasts by ingesting low-latency satellite data and sparse station observations, surpassing AI models that rely on coarse updates and analysis data.
AI.motivation: To overcome core limitations of state-of-the-art AI weather models: lower spatial/temporal resolution and reliance on analysis data, which prevents direct use of observations and propagates analysis biases.
AI.method: Ingests low-latency geostationary satellite data to produce hourly forecasts at 0.1-degree resolution for single-level variables; predicts satellite-derived precipitation estimates and observations of tropical cyclones and weather stations; leverages sparse station data to predict 2 m temperature and dewpoint conditioned on local geography; enables location/time-specific forecasts.
AI.result: Establishes a new state-of-the-art for probabilistic medium-range forecasting with hourly updates and high spatial/temporal resolution, good performance on unseen stations, and an end-to-end capability that blends observation usage with forecasting.
AI.conclusion: Advances AI weather forecasting toward end-to-end operational systems that integrate observations, forecasting, and post-processing for improved global weather prediction.

title: ARCOS: Zero-shot Boundary Localization for Corneal Layer Segmentation Across Optical Coherence Tomography Devices
summary: Accurate segmentation of corneal layers in optical coherence tomography (OCT) is essential for quantitative assessment of corneal morphology, including layer thickness and structural changes associated with disease or surgery. However, automatic segmentation remains challenging because corneal interfaces are thin, affected by speckle noise, and variable across acquisition devices. In this work, we propose ARCOS, a patch-based zero-shot boundary localization framework for corneal layer segmentation in clinical anterior-segment OCT images. Rather than performing conventional region classification, the method predicts boundary heatmaps for the main corneal interfaces from overlapping native-resolution patches. Patch-level predictions are stitched across the full B-scan and converted into boundary locations to obtain continuous, anatomically ordered layer segmentations. The network combines multi-scale feature fusion with a self-conditioned refinement module that uses intermediate boundary information to improve local heatmap predictions while preserving spatial detail. The method was evaluated on clinical OCT images acquired from multiple devices and compared with representative segmentation baselines using boundary localization and derived thickness metrics. The proposed method achieved an off-by-one boundary localization accuracy of 95.1% and a mean absolute boundary error of 0.514 pixels on the matched-device test set. In zero-shot cross-device evaluation, it maintained an average off-by-one accuracy of 84.3% and a mean absolute boundary error of 0.855 pixels across unseen acquisition devices, outperforming the baseline models. Thickness estimates derived from the predicted boundaries showed low error across corneal regions, supporting the method's use for quantitative corneal OCT analysis.

AI.tldr: ARCOS is a patch-based, zero-shot boundary localization framework for corneal layer segmentation in anterior-segment OCT that predicts boundary heatmaps from overlapping patches, then stitches them into continuous, ordered layer boundaries with multi-scale fusion and a self-conditioned refinement module. It achieves high boundary localization accuracy on matched devices and strong cross-device generalization, with accurate thickness estimates.
AI.motivation: Automatic segmentation of corneal layers in OCT is critical for thickness and morphology assessment but is challenging due to thin interfaces, speckle noise, and cross-device variability; a zero-shot, patch-based approach could improve generalization without extensive labeled data.
AI.method: ARCOS predicts boundary heatmaps for the main corneal interfaces from overlapping native-resolution patches. Patch predictions are stitched across the B-scan and converted into continuous, anatomically ordered boundary lines. The network employs multi-scale feature fusion and a self-conditioned refinement module that uses intermediate boundary information to refine local heatmaps while preserving spatial detail.
AI.result: On a matched-device test set, off-by-one boundary localization accuracy = 95.1%; mean absolute boundary error = 0.514 pixels. In zero-shot cross-device tests across unseen devices, accuracy = 84.3%; MAE = 0.855 pixels. Thickness estimates derived from these boundaries show low error across corneal regions, indicating reliable quantitative analysis.
AI.conclusion: ARCOS demonstrates accurate, device-robust corneal layer segmentation with reliable thickness metrics and strong cross-device generalization, supporting its potential for clinical quantitative OCT analysis.

title: The Dually Flat Geometry of Planning as Inference
summary: We present an alternative characterization of the occupancy measure of reinforcement learning, obtained by embedding the planning criterion into the dynamics through a resetting planning process. Its stationary measure, which we term visitation measure, is the object on which the information geometry of decision making is most naturally expressed. The achievable visitation measures form a dually flat statistical manifold whose two affine charts are the visitation probabilities and the log-policies, dual under the conditional entropy. This structure makes planning-as-inference generalize from linear rewards to nonlinear functionals of the visitation, each iterate solved by one natural-gradient step, and gives the temporal-difference error the interpretation of a marginal-utility estimate. We develop the geometry and its consequences for reinforcement learning and theoretical neuroscience.

AI.tldr: A visitation measure from a resetting planning process forms a dually flat information-geometric framework for planning-as-inference, enabling nonlinear objectives and natural-gradient updates, with TD error as marginal-utility.
AI.motivation: Cast the RL occupancy concept into an information-geometric setting to support nonlinear functionals, unify planning with inference, and provide a bridge to theoretical neuroscience.
AI.method: Embed planning in the dynamics via a resetting process to obtain a stationary visitation measure; show the achievable visitation measures form a dually flat manifold with affine charts in visitation probabilities and log-policies, dual under conditional entropy; derive natural-gradient iterations; interpret TD error as a marginal-utility estimate.
AI.result: Establishes a dually flat statistical manifold of visitation measures; generalizes planning-as-inference to nonlinear functionals; provides natural-gradient iteration steps; reinterprets TD error as a marginal-utility signal; discusses RL and neuroscience implications.
AI.conclusion: The information-geometric framework offers principled planning in RL for nonlinear objectives and provides a biologically interpretable link to TD error via marginal utility, with broad consequences for RL theory and neuroscience.

title: Neural-Network Maxent: a general extension with learned nonlinearity, applied to time-series for Desert Locust distribution modelling
summary: Species Distribution Modelling (SDM) is essential for understanding how environmental conditions shape biodiversity, particularly for destructive pests such as the Desert Locust (Schistocerca gregaria), whose breeding dynamics are tightly coupled to rapidly evolving environmental conditions. Maxent has become the dominant method for presence-only data, but its reliance on a linear combination of hand chosen feature transforms limits its ability to capture the nonlinear, temporal relationships common in ecological monitoring, where covariates such as precipitation, soil moisture, and vegetation indices evolve meaningfully over time. Standard implementations flatten time-series covariates into independent features, discarding sequential structure that carries critical signal. We introduce RNN Maxent, an extension of the Maxent framework that replaces the fixed feature dictionary with a neural network, specifically a Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU), trained end to end via backpropagation. The approach preserves Maxent's presence only statistical foundations, background normalization, and probability calibration, differing only in that the nonlinearity is learned from data rather than fixed in advance. We apply RNN Maxent to map suitable habitat for the Desert Locust using 50 day environmental time series derived from ERA5 Land, MODIS, and Sentinel 3, maintaining a 7 day gap between covariates and presence records to yield forecasting behavior. Compared against standard Maxent, RNN Maxent improves performance across metrics (ROC AUC 0.862 std 0.036 vs. 0.792; F1 0.671 std 0.056 vs. 0.590).

AI.tldr: RNN Maxent extends Maxent with a GRU-based nonlinear feature learner for presence-only SDM, capturing temporal covariate dynamics to predict Desert Locust habitat; yields ROC AUC 0.862 and F1 0.671, outperforming standard Maxent (0.792 AUC, 0.590 F1).
AI.motivation: Address Maxent's fixed feature transforms that inadequately capture temporal structure in time-series covariates used for SDM, aiming to improve forecasting and predictive performance for environmentally driven pests.
AI.method: Replace the fixed feature dictionary in Maxent with a GRU neural network trained end-to-end, preserving presence-only framework, background normalization, and probability calibration. Use 50-day environmental time series from ERA5 Land, MODIS, and Sentinel 3 with a 7-day lag between covariates and presence records, and compare to standard Maxent.
AI.result: The GRU-based nonlinear feature learner improves predictive performance over standard Maxent, achieving ROC AUC 0.862 (std 0.036) vs 0.792 and F1 0.671 (std 0.056) vs 0.590, indicating better capture of temporal dynamics and forecasting capability.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating learned temporal representations via GRU within a presence-only SDM framework preserves Maxent foundations while enhancing flexibility and performance; demonstrates the value of temporal modeling for ecological monitoring and pest habitat mapping.

title: Do Video Generators Track the World Across Segments? A Benchmark and Method for World-State Reasoning in Video Continuation
summary: Video generators build long videos by composing shorter parts, either by generating segments one after another or by autoregressively extending chunks. Each new part usually depends on memories of historical observations, such as recent frames, selected key frames, memory banks, or cached features. These memories preserve visible evidence from the past, but current generators do not reliably turn such evidence into a world-state interface: what holds in the video world after previous actions and how it should change under the next prompt. A past frame remains valid history, but it may not describe the state needed by the next segment; some states must instead be inferred from occluded or implicit changes rather than copied from a directly observed frame. This creates a simple but overlooked question for video continuation: given a previous video, its prompt, and a new prompt, can a model generate a continuation that reflects the state determined by both the historical video and the new prompt? To answer this question, we introduce Statebench, a benchmark that targets this gap by testing continuations over three state categories: past-visible states, occluded-process states, and complex-transition states. We further propose Stateagent, which explicitly maintains an entity-state representation, updates it under the new prompt, grounds the predicted post-action state as a future end frame, and renders the next video. Experiments show that our method improves controlled video continuation by raising the all-case state score (SCS-All) from 45.2 to 69.3, and also benefits story generation at the one-minute scale. Code is avaliable at https://github.com/AMAP-ML/StateAgent.

AI.tldr: Statebench and Stateagent address a gap in long video generation: maintaining and utilizing an explicit world-state during continuation. Statebench tests continuations across three state categories (past-visible, occluded-process, complex-transition); Stateagent maintains an entity-state, updates it with the new prompt, grounds the predicted post-action state as a future end frame, and renders the next video. Empirical results show substantial gains in controlled video continuation (SCS-All: 45.2 -> 69.3) and benefits to one-minute-scale story generation. Code available at GitHub.
AI.motivation: Current video generators rely on memories (frames, features, caches) but seldom infer the underlying world-state transitions required by a new prompt. This mismatch can produce continuations that misalign with both history and the new instruction. There is a need for a benchmark to evaluate state-consistency and a modeling approach that explicitly reasons about state.
AI.method: Introduce Statebench, a benchmark that targets three state categories (past-visible, occluded-process, complex-transition). Propose Stateagent, which maintains an explicit entity-state representation, updates it under the new prompt, grounds the predicted post-action state as a future end frame, and renders the next video.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation shows substantial improvement in controlled video continuation, with SCS-All rising from 45.2 to 69.3; additional improvements observed in one-minute-scale story generation. Code is available at the provided GitHub repository.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly modeling and grounding world-state within video generation improves continuation quality and consistency across tasks, validated by the Statebench benchmark and the Stateagent model; the work provides practical tooling and code for future research.

title: LLM4CKD: Large Language Models for Early Stage Chronic Kidney Disease Screening
summary: Early screening of chronic kidney disease (CKD) is critical for timely intervention, yet most machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) approaches require labeled data and model training, limiting their use in real-world screening settings. This study evaluates the effectiveness of large language models (LLMs) for CKD screening under zero-shot and few-shot in-context learning settings and compares them with traditional ML and DL methods. We propose a framework that uses clinically selected tabular features and structured prompt templates to enable LLM-based inference without task-specific training. LLM performance is evaluated across multiple prompt styles, feature configurations, and data settings, and compared with standard ML, DL, and tabular foundation model (TFM) baselines, and existing CKD screening tools. The results show that LLMs can achieve competitive performance using only a small number of examples, often matching or outperforming traditional approaches in low-data settings. However, their performance remains model-dependent and less stable as input complexity increases. In contrast, ML, DL, and TFM models show more consistent improvement with larger training data. Overall, the findings highlight a trade-off between data efficiency and stability, suggesting that LLMs may serve as a flexible complementary approach for CKD screening when labeled data are limited.

AI.tldr: LLMs enable data-efficient CKD screening via zero-/few-shot in-context learning with structured prompts, achieving competitive performance in low-data settings, but with less stability as input complexity grows; traditional ML/DL/TFM methods improve more consistently with more labeled data.
AI.motivation: To explore whether large language models can perform CKD screening without task-specific training and to compare their data efficiency and robustness against traditional ML/DL methods and tabular foundation models.
AI.method: Framework using clinically selected tabular features and structured prompt templates to enable LLM-based inference in zero-/few-shot settings. Systematic evaluation across prompt styles, feature configurations, and data settings, compared against standard ML, DL, TFM baselines and existing CKD screening tools.
AI.result: LLMs achieve competitive performance with only a small number of examples, often matching or outperforming traditional approaches in low-data settings. Performance is model-dependent and less stable as input complexity increases. ML/DL/TFM models show more consistent improvement with larger training data.
AI.conclusion: LLMs can serve as a flexible, data-efficient complementary tool for CKD screening when labeled data are scarce, though they trade stability with complexity and rely on model choice; they are best used alongside traditional methods rather than as a sole replacement.

title: On the Interaction Between Model Compression and Test-Time Adaptation
summary: Deep neural networks deployed in the wild must be both efficient and adaptable, requiring model compression and test-time adaptation (TTA). While both are well studied in isolation, their interaction remains poorly understood. We systematically analyze how structured compression affects a model's ability to adapt under distribution shift. Using ResNet-18 and ViT-Base on CIFAR-10-C and ImageNet-C, we evaluate multiple compression methods combined with standard TTA techniques. We introduce a diagnostic framework that examines representational expressivity and adaptation subspace compatibility. Our results reveal a consistent gap: although compressed models retain high accuracy under supervised adaptation, their TTA performance degrades significantly with increasing compression. We show that this stems from reduced representational diversity and structural constraints that limit recoverability. These effects strongly depend on the compression method, highlighting the need to design compression strategies that preserve adaptability.

AI.tldr: Compression preserves supervised accuracy but reduces test-time adaptation under distribution shift; adaptability loss stems from reduced representational diversity and subspace constraints, varying by compression method.
AI.motivation: To understand how structured model compression interacts with test-time adaptation (TTA) under distribution shift, bridging gaps between compression literature and TTA performance.
AI.method: Empirical study using ResNet-18 and ViT-Base on CIFAR-10-C and ImageNet-C. Apply multiple structured compression methods in combination with standard TTA techniques. Introduce a diagnostic framework to evaluate representational expressivity and adaptation subspace compatibility.
AI.result: Compressed models retain high accuracy under supervised adaptation but show significant TTA degradation as compression increases. The degradation is linked to reduced representational diversity and structural constraints that limit recoverability; effects depend strongly on the compression method.
AI.conclusion: Design compression strategies that preserve adaptability and subspace compatibility; consider TTA-aware compression and develop methods to maintain expressivity under compression to sustain TTA performance.

title: CoFiE: Coarse-to-Fine Evidence Selection for Efficient Streaming Video Understanding
summary: Streaming video understanding requires Vision Language Models (VLLMs) to process growing video streams and answer user questions under tight latency constraints. Existing methods improve efficiency through token pruning and memory-bank schemes, but mainly reduce visual tokens after visual encoding. Consequently, downstream token pruning alone cannot substantially reduce end-to-end latency because the expensive frame encoding cost has already been incurred. We propose CoFiE, a Coarse-to-Fine Evidence Selection framework that decouples evidence selection into a coarse, query-agnostic filtering stage before the vision encoder and a fine, query-specific refinement stage during LLM prefill. CoFiE introduces Novelty-Guided Frame Filtering to retain visually distinctive candidate frames and Query-Specific Evidence Refinement to select the frames most relevant to the user query. This design removes substantial redundancy before frame encoding while preserving query-specific refinement once semantic information becomes available. Experiments show that CoFiE establishes a new state-of-the-art accuracy-efficiency trade-off across multiple video understanding benchmarks, reaching 78.86% accuracy on StreamingBench and 68.72% on OvO-Bench, with improvements of up to 3.15% over prior methods. Even with up to 80% evidence-frame filtering, CoFiE outperforms strong open-source multimodal models while improving end-to-end inference latency by up to 2.54 times.

AI.tldr: CoFiE introduces a coarse-to-fine evidence selection for streaming video understanding that decouples frame filtering before encoding and query-specific refinement during LLM prefill, enabling strong accuracy-efficiency trade-offs with substantial end-to-end latency reduction.
AI.motivation: End-to-end latency in streaming video QA is dominated by frame encoding; existing token pruning acts post-encoding and cannot significantly reduce end-to-end latency.
AI.method: Two-stage evidence selection: (1) Novelty-Guided Frame Filtering to pre-filter visually distinctive frames before vision encoding; (2) Query-Specific Evidence Refinement during LLM prefill to select frames relevant to the user query; this decouples coarse, query-agnostic filtering from fine, query-specific refinement.
AI.result: State-of-the-art accuracy-efficiency trade-off across StreamingBench and OvO-Bench: 78.86% and 68.72% accuracy respectively, up to 3.15% improvement over prior work; up to 80% evidence-frame filtering with end-to-end latency improvements up to 2.54×; outperforms strong open-source multimodal models.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling evidence selection into a pre-vision-filtering stage and a post-filtering stage preserves query relevance while removing encoding redundancy, yielding substantial latency reductions without sacrificing accuracy.

title: InSituMeasure: Probing Situated Measurement Grounding in Industrial Scenes with Multimodal Large Language Models
summary: For trained operators, gauge reading requires little specialized knowledge, low cognitive effort, and high repeatability. Yet Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) remain unreliable in continuous-valued measurement despite strong results on general multimodal benchmarks. Existing benchmarks expose this weakness but isolate measurement from realistic, knowledge-grounded settings, with limited situated context, specialized instruments, real-world noise, and matched diagnostic annotations, reducing realism and constraining root-cause analysis. We introduce InSituMeasure to evaluate situated measurement grounding. It contains 2,922 real industrial monitoring scenes across eight functional categories of professional engineering instruments, with dense gauge-attribute annotations and noise tags for failure diagnosis. We define metrics for numerical accuracy under predefined tolerances and unit consistency, rejection of fake or unanswerable tasks, and alignment between model failures and annotated error factors. Across 24 state-of-the-art MLLMs, the best model reaches only 25.7\% joint value-unit accuracy and 51.8\% confidence-diagnosis F1, revealing a substantial gap between general multimodal competence and reliable situated measurement. Further analysis identifies failures from text-induced shortcuts, overconfident responses, and authentic industrial noise, including mixed disturbances, viewpoint deviation, occlusion, and environmental interference.

AI.tldr: Introduces InSituMeasure, a realism-focused benchmark for situated measurement grounding in Multimodal LLMs. It evaluates gauge-reading tasks in 2,922 real industrial scenes across eight instrument categories with dense annotations, focusing on numeric accuracy, unit consistency, rejection of unanswerable tasks, and error-factor alignment. Across 24 SOTA MLLMs, performance remains weak (best: 25.7% joint value-unit accuracy, 51.8% confidence-diagnosis F1). The study identifies failure modes: text shortcuts, overconfidence, and authentic industrial noise (disturbances, occlusion, viewpoint shifts, environment).
AI.motivation: Current MLLMs are unreliable for continuous-valued, real-world measurements in knowledge-grounded contexts; existing benchmarks lack situated realism (noise, instruments, diagnostics). There is a need for benchmarks that facilitate root-cause analysis of measurement grounding.
AI.method: Proposes InSituMeasure dataset with 2,922 real industrial monitoring scenes spanning eight instrument categories. Provides dense gauge-attribute annotations and noise tags for failure diagnosis. Defines metrics: numerical accuracy under tolerances, unit consistency, rejection of fake/unanswerable tasks, and alignment between model failures and annotated error factors. Evaluates 24 state-of-the-art MLLMs.
AI.result: The best model achieves 25.7% joint value-unit accuracy and 51.8% confidence-diagnosis F1, revealing a substantial gap between general multimodal competence and reliable situated measurement. Analysis attributes failures to text-induced shortcuts, overconfident responses, and authentic industrial noise (mixed disturbances, viewpoint deviation, occlusion, environmental interference).
AI.conclusion: The benchmark reveals significant gaps in MLLMs for situated measurement grounding and identifies concrete failure modes and noise factors to target for improvement; it enables root-cause analysis and realism-enhanced evaluation for pragmatic gauge-reading tasks.

title: Local Updates, Global Learning (LUGL): Playing Games with non-incremental Learners
summary: The dominance of Neural Networks (NNs) in RL is partially due to their incremental learning capability, which naturally suits the online, non-stationary nature of self-play training. However, gradient-boosted trees like LightGBM are widely recognised as the state of the art for tabular data in supervised learning, often outperforming NNs in accuracy and efficiency. Game states are inherently tabular---discrete actions, categorical card identities, structured board positions---which makes them an ideal candidate for tree-based methods. We introduce LUGL (Local Updates, Global Learning), a framework that decouples data collection from model fitting, enabling non-incremental learners such as GBTs to operate in RL settings where they would otherwise fail due to distributional shift. LUGL alternates between a local updates phase, where the agent plays self-play games and accumulates tabular updates (Q-values, V-values, policies, or regret values) in a finite table, and a global learning phase, where the table is used to train a function approximator that generalises to unseen states before the table is reset. We test our approach in four standard perfect-information games (Tic-tac-toe, Connect-4, Othello, and Hex) and five imperfect-information games (Kuhn's poker, Leduc Hold'em, Liar's Dice, Goofspiel, and Flop5 Hold'em), and show that our results are competitive with or superior to DQN and DeepCFR. Our experiments demonstrate that the community's strong bias towards NNs in game-playing may be unwarranted, since LightGBM-based agents achieve competitive or superior performance across all tested benchmarks.

AI.tldr: LUGL uses a decoupled data-collection and learning scheme with gradient-boosted trees to perform RL in tabular-game settings, achieving competitive or superior results to NN-based baselines.
AI.motivation: To challenge the prevailing reliance on neural networks in RL for structured, discrete-state games by showing that gradient-boosted trees can perform as well or better if data collection and learning are appropriately separated.
AI.method: Local Updates, Global Learning (LUGL): during a local phase, accumulate tabular updates (Q/V/policies/regret) from self-play in a finite table; during a global phase, train a function approximator (LightGBM GBT) on the collected updates to generalize to unseen states, then reset the table. Evaluate on four perfect-information games (Tic-tac-toe, Connect-4, Othello, Hex) and five imperfect-information games (Kuhn poker, Leduc Hold’em, Liar’s Dice, Goofspiel, Flop5 Hold’em). Compare to DQN and DeepCFR.
AI.result: LUGL-based agents achieve competitive or superior performance relative to DQN and DeepCFR across all tested benchmarks, indicating LightGBM can be effective for game-playing tasks.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling data collection from learning enables non-incremental learners like gradient-boosted trees to succeed in RL settings with distributional shift; challenges the notion that neural networks are universally superior for game-playing, at least in tabular/discrete domains.

title: FLY-EVAL++: An Evidence-Driven Evaluation Protocol for Safety-Constrained Flight Prediction with Large Language Models
comment: Published as a conference paper at COLM 2026
summary: Evaluating large language models (LLMs) in safety-critical, physics-governed environments requires more than accuracy-based metrics, because predictions that are numerically close to the ground truth can still violate operational constraints, combine fields in physically inconsistent ways, or fail to produce usable structured outputs. Existing evaluation protocols do not measure these failure modes reliably. We propose FLY-EVAL++, an evidence-driven evaluation protocol that combines deterministic verification of protocol compliance, physical feasibility, and safety constraints with fixed rubric-guided aggregation into interpretable multi-dimensional scores. We instantiate FLY-EVAL++ for Flight Trajectory and Attitude Prediction (FTAP) by extending the PilotBench setting with history-conditioned and multi-step prediction tasks. Across 66 LLMs, safety compliance is the most discriminative dimension of model behavior: models with comparable predictive performance differ by more than 28 points in safety score, and we observe recurrent failures including safety violations under physically plausible predictions and instability in multi-step rollouts. These results show that evaluation in safety-critical domains should measure constraint satisfaction and structured validity explicitly rather than rely on accuracy-centric reporting alone.

AI.tldr: Proposes FLY-EVAL++ to evaluate LLM safety and feasibility in physics-guided environments by combining deterministic checks with rubric-based scores; demonstrates in FTAP that safety is a stronger discriminator than accuracy across 66 LLMs.
AI.motivation: Accuracy alone overlooks constraint violations and unsound outputs in safety-critical, physics-governed settings; there is a need for evaluation that enforces protocol compliance, physical feasibility, and safety.
AI.method: An evidence-driven evaluation protocol that deterministically verifies protocol compliance, physical feasibility, and safety constraints, then aggregates results with a fixed rubric into interpretable multi-dimensional scores. Instantiated for Flight Trajectory and Attitude Prediction (FTAP) by extending PilotBench with history-conditioned and multi-step prediction tasks.
AI.result: Across 66 LLMs, safety compliance is the most discriminative dimension; models with similar predictive performance can differ by more than 28 points in safety. Observed recurrent failures include safety violations under plausible predictions and instability in multi-step rollouts.
AI.conclusion: Evaluation in safety-critical domains should explicitly measure constraint satisfaction and structured validity, not rely solely on accuracy-based reporting.

title: Extracting Forgotten Prompts from Targeted Unlearned Models
summary: Recent unlearning methods (e.g. NPO, DPO, LUNAR) make use of refusal alignment to suppress forgotten data. However, it has been shown that refusal responses might leave traces of unlearning, and recent attacks have been able to successfully recover some of the unlearned knowledge. In this paper, we uncover a new vulnerability. Existing attacks typically assume that the forgotten prompts are already known to the adversary and focus on recovering their answers. However, we show that the forgotten prompts themselves can be extracted by using the retained data and black-box access to the model. Our attack, Targeted Active Search (TAS), first identifies the forgotten entities by constructing canonical templates and entity pool, and selectively querying the model using the most informative template-entity pair under a limited query budget. Once the entities are identified, TAS instantiates prompt templates with those entities to probe the unlearned model and reconstruct the forgotten prompts. Experiments across three unlearning methods with three datasets and three LLMs shows that TAS recovers the forgotten entity with $100\%$ accuracy and reconstructs up to $95\%$ of forgotten prompts, all while using up to $99.7\%$ fewer queries than naive probing.

AI.tldr: Introduces Targeted Active Search (TAS) to extract forgotten prompts from unlearned models, showing that privacy leaks persist despite refusal-based unlearning; TAS reconstructs forgotten prompts with high accuracy while using far fewer queries.
AI.motivation: Addresses a vulnerability in modern unlearning methods that rely on refusal alignment, demonstrating that forgotten prompts can be inferred from retained data and black-box access to the model; motivates stronger defenses for model unlearning.
AI.method: Construct canonical templates and an entity pool to identify forgotten entities; perform selective, budget-constrained queries to test template–entity pairs and identify forgotten entities; instantiate prompt templates with identified entities and probe the unlearned model to reconstruct forgotten prompts.
AI.result: TAS recovers forgotten entities with 100% accuracy and reconstructs up to 95% of forgotten prompts across three unlearning methods, three datasets, and three LLMs, using up to 99.7% fewer queries than naive probing.
AI.conclusion: Reveals a new vulnerability in unlearning via prompt extraction; implies the need for defenses beyond refusal-based methods and calls for robust evaluation of unlearning security, including mitigation of prompt leakage and resistance to targeted probing.

title: Instruction Duplication as an Inference-Time Control Primitive
comment: 7 pages, 2 tables. Code and frozen reproduction artifacts: https://github.com/victorlavrenko/answer-engineering/releases/tag/instruction-duplication-arxiv-v1
summary: Procedural instruction following is a basic requirement for controllable language-model systems, especially when generated trajectories are inspected or repaired downstream. We introduce instruction duplication, a minimal black-box inference-time control that repeats only the procedural instruction, without retraining or decoding changes. Across seven instruction-tuned models, 300 medical multiple-choice questions, eight placement conditions, and 16,800 scheduled generations, moving from one to two copies raises the deterministic All-8 diagnostic--responses passing all eight observable tests--from 90.22% to 93.17% (+2.95 percentage points), eliminating 30.2% of the failures remaining after one copy. Pre-provisional TF-IDF recall rises from 73.44% to 74.81% (+1.38 points; Holm-adjusted p < .001), while final-answer accuracy remains exactly 60.21%. Premature commitment increases from 1.52% to 2.30% (p_Holm = .00536). A blinded challenge audit yields 10/30 directional confirmations, 20/30 perceptual ties, and no reversals; its prespecified 28/30 confirmation criterion is not met. Yet this distinction can matter operationally when a downstream system acts on the generated trajectory. In Answer Engineering (AE), where explicit trajectory state determines local repair, the published reason-first no-editing SSNHL endpoint was 25.1%; system-only AE was later reproduced at 84.2%, and the same trailing duplicate raised it to 97.1%. For conductive diagnostic branch preservation, the corresponding values are 58.9% published without editing, 78.6% with reproduced AE, and 73.8% with AE plus duplication--a within-AE decrease, but still 14.9 points above the no-editing baseline. Instruction duplication is therefore a low-complexity, placement-sensitive control whose practical value can emerge through the downstream system that consumes the exposed trajectory.

AI.tldr: Instruction duplication—repeating the procedural instruction at inference time without retraining—modestly improves deterministic adherence to eight-test criteria across models and settings, with mixed downstream effects; final-answer accuracy unchanged; potential operational value via downstream systems.
AI.motivation: Evaluate a lightweight black-box control (instruction duplication) to enforce procedural instruction following and assess its downstream impact on generated trajectories.
AI.method: Assess seven instruction-tuned models over 300 medical MCQs, eight placement conditions, and 16,800 scheduled generations, comparing one vs two copies of the procedural instruction. Key metrics: All-8 test pass rate, TF-IDF recall, final-answer accuracy, premature commitment, blinded challenge audit; include Answer Engineering (AE) endpoints to examine trajectory-level effects.
AI.result: All-8 pass rate increases from 90.22% to 93.17% (+2.95 pp). TF-IDF recall rises 73.44%→74.81% (+1.38 pp). Final-answer accuracy unchanged at 60.21%.
