Premature commitment increases 1.52%→2.30%. Blinded audit yields 10/30 directional confirmations, 20/30 ties, no reversals; prespecified criterion (28/30) not met. AE endpoints show large gains with duplication (e.g., reason-first no-editing SSNHL from 25.1% to 97.1% under AE with duplication after reproduction). Overall, instruction duplication is a low-complexity, placement-sensitive control with potential downstream operational value, though benefits are metric-dependent and not universal.
AI.conclusion: Instruction duplication can be a practical, minimal-control method to influence generated trajectories, especially in systems that consume and repair trajectories downstream; its benefits depend on the downstream pipeline and evaluation metrics, offering meaningful gains in some contexts but not universal improvements in final accuracy.

title: Out-of-Distribution Generalisation with Sequence Models in Offline Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
summary: Generalising to unseen tasks remains a fundamental challenge in offline multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL). In this work, we present a principled analysis of zero-shot task generalisation in the offline setting and conduct an extensive empirical investigation into the scaling behaviour governing task diversity, dataset size, and network capacity. To facilitate this study, we extend offline sequence modelling architectures to handle multi-task observation and action spaces alongside variable agent counts across tasks. Our primary finding is that scaling task diversity---rather than sheer dataset size is the dominant factor in achieving robust zero-shot transfer. Through large-scale experiments across four challenging environments (Connector, RWARE, SMAX, and LBF), we demonstrate that our multi-task approach achieves a mean improvement of 3.2x on held-out test tasks compared to single-task models and consistently outperforms strong behaviour cloning baselines. These results suggest that the development of generalisable MARL agents should prioritise the diversity of the training distribution with varying numbers of agents, providing a roadmap for scaling offline MARL effectively.

AI.tldr: Zero-shot generalisation in offline MARL is driven by task diversity, not simply dataset size; a multi-task sequence model across heterogeneous tasks with varying agent counts yields large gains over single-task models and BC baselines.
AI.motivation: Tackle the core challenge of generalising to unseen tasks in offline MARL and understand how factors like task diversity, dataset size, and model capacity influence zero-shot transfer.
AI.method: Extend offline sequence modelling architectures to handle multi-task observation/action spaces and variable agent counts. Conduct large-scale experiments across four environments (Connector, RWARE, SMAX, LBF) comparing a multi-task model to single-task baselines and behavioural cloning (BC).
AI.result: Scaling task diversity is the dominant driver of robust zero-shot transfer. The multi-task model achieves a mean 3.2x improvement on held-out tasks over single-task models and consistently outperforms BC baselines across four environments.
AI.conclusion: Prioritize diversity in the training distribution—including varying numbers of agents—to enable scalable offline MARL. The results provide a practical roadmap for building generalisable MARL agents via diverse, multi-task training regimes.

title: ToPO: Token-Conditioned Preference Routing for Attention-Based Latent Diffusion Models
summary: Pairwise preference labels rank complete images, yet Diffusion-DPO applies their effect over many spatial and denoising-time coordinates. For attention-based, noise-prediction latent diffusion, ToPO (Token-Oriented Preference Optimization) constructs a per-minibatch, detached, separable spatial-temporal route from branchwise squared-residual contrast in a frozen reference denoiser. Preferred-branch cross-attention uses content tokens to modulate the spatial factor, and an auxiliary pixel-midpoint ordering term is added without local labels or a learned reward model. In matched three-seed retrainings with a shared update schedule, ToPO has higher endpoint estimates than Diffusion-DPO on all five reported SD-1.5 metrics and on HPSv2, ImageReward, and CLIP for SDXL. It also receives larger raw win shares in an aggregate blind SDXL A/B study. These findings are scoped to the reported equal-update U-Net protocols rather than an equal-compute comparison.

AI.tldr: ToPO improves pairwise-preference optimization in diffusion-based image generation by building a per-minibatch spatial-temporal path from a frozen denoiser's residuals, using prioritized cross-attention and a label-free pixel-midpoint term; in matched retrains, ToPO outperforms Diffusion-DPO across SD-1.5 metrics and SDXL-related rewards, under equal-update U-Net protocols.
AI.motivation: Enhance alignment with pairwise preferences across spatial and denoising-time coordinates without requiring learned reward models or local labels.
AI.method: Construct a per-minibatch detached, separable spatial-temporal route from branchwise squared-residual contrast in a frozen reference denoiser; apply preferred-branch cross-attention with content tokens; add an auxiliary pixel-midpoint ordering term; retrain with shared update schedule across seeds; compare under equal-update U-Net protocols; not an equal-compute comparison.
AI.result: Higher endpoint estimates than Diffusion-DPO on five SD-1.5 metrics and on HPSv2, ImageReward, CLIP for SDXL; larger raw win shares in blind SDXL A/B; results scoped to reported equal-update U-Net protocols.
AI.conclusion: ToPO yields consistent improvements over Diffusion-DPO in the reported settings, but conclusions are limited to equal-update-U-Net protocols; no insight about compute-efficiency or generalization beyond tested metrics.

title: IRWOZ 2.0: A Large Language Model-driven Dialogue Dataset for Industrial Robot Conversations
summary: IRWOZ has improved industrial human-robot interaction (HRI) dialogue systems through domain-specific annotations. However, its initial version contains substantial noise in dialogue states and utterances, limiting state-tracking accuracy. We introduce IRWOZ 2.0, which addresses these limitations through large language model (LLM) enhanced generation (Mistral/Claude-3.5) and quality refinements. Our improved dataset expands to 390 dialogues across 4 industrial domains (Assembly, Delivery, Position, Relocation), featuring manual corrections and automated typo removal. Benchmark experiments on dialogue state tracking demonstrate significant improvements, with GPT-2's BLEU-4 score increasing from 0.1651 to 0.5604 compared to original IRWOZ. To support industrial HRI research, we publicly released IRWOZ 2.0 dataset at https://ieee-dataport.org/documents/irwoz-20-large-language-model-driven-dialogue-dataset-industrial-robot-conversations

AI.tldr: IRWOZ 2.0 uses LLM-driven generation and data cleaning to enhance industrial HRI dialogue state tracking, expanding to 390 dialogues across four domains, with notable BLEU-4 gains for GPT-2, and public dataset release.
AI.motivation: Original IRWOZ contained substantial noise in dialogue states and utterances, which degraded state-tracking accuracy; there is a need for higher-quality, more diverse industrial dialogue data to improve DST.
AI.method: LLM-enhanced generation using Mistral and Claude-3.5 coupled with quality refinements including manual corrections and automated typo removal; dataset expanded to 390 dialogues across four domains: Assembly, Delivery, Position, Relocation.
AI.result: Significant improvement in dialogue state tracking metrics; GPT-2 BLEU-4 score increased from 0.1651 (IRWOZ) to 0.5604 (IRWOZ 2.0).
AI.conclusion: IRWOZ 2.0 delivers higher-quality industrial HRI dialogue data and improves state-tracking performance; dataset is publicly released at the provided IEEE Dataport link.

title: Resolution-Aware Experimental Design under Partial Identifiability
summary: Experimental design is commonly framed as choosing the experiment expected to provide the most information. Under partial identifiability however, persistent nuisance uncertainty can make the same observation carry different structural meanings. We introduce Resolution-Aware Experimental Design (RAED), which selects an experiment by the smallest expected nonempty structural candidate set achievable subject to false-exclusion control. We prove an exact cross-nuisance aliasing separation: an experiment can be preferred by structural and full-latent information gain, average classification, and nuisance-marginalized informativeness while having arbitrarily poorer valid structural resolution. RAED nevertheless preserves the expected ordering under a genuine composite Blackwell comparison. To make this criterion operational, we develop a learned score-based implementation with finite-sample nuisance-average and positive-tail calibration, and characterize a rare-tail sample-complexity obstruction. Under constrained sensing, two subsurface-flow benchmarks exhibit genuine RAED--expected-information-gain (EIG) experiment-selection disagreements, with the clearest and largest held-out resolution differences in WCA. In a fluvial benchmark, tail protection changes the selected physical experiment and replaces hard-region false exclusions primarily with explicit ambiguity. In a mechanistic methane-oxidation benchmark, a prospectively specified 5\% false-exclusion tolerance also yields a nontrivial finite-sample population guarantee for tail-sensitive nuisance risk, with 95\% joint confidence across all three structural families.

AI.tldr: Resolution-Aware Experimental Design (RAED) selects experiments by minimizing the expected nonempty structural candidate set under false-exclusion control, addressing partial identifiability and nuisance uncertainty; it includes theory of cross-nuisance aliasing, a learned score-based implementation, and empirical benchmarks showing RAED-EIG disagreements and tail-risk considerations.
AI.motivation: Under partial identifiability, nuisance uncertainty makes observations carry different structural meanings; traditional information-gain criteria can misalign with the actual resolution of structural inference. RAED motivates a design criterion that explicitly accounts for the smallest nonempty structural candidate set (resolution) while controlling false exclusions.
AI.method: Define the RAED criterion as selecting experiments achieving the smallest expected nonempty structural candidate set, with a false-exclusion constraint. Prove exact cross-nuisance aliasing separation: an experiment can be preferred by multiple information-measure criteria yet have poorer valid structural resolution. Show that RAED preserves ordering under a genuine composite Blackwell comparison. Develop a learned score-based implementation with finite-sample nuisance-average calibration and positive-tail calibration; identify a rare-tail sample-complexity obstruction. Follow-up methods to operationalize RAED via finite-sample estimation.
AI.result: RAED can diverge from traditional expected-information-gain (EIG) selections in the presence of nuisance structure; an experiment favorable under EIG may have poorer structural resolution. In constrained-sensing tests, two subsurface-flow benchmarks show genuine RAED–EIG disagreements; WCA exhibits the clearest resolution differences. In a fluvial benchmark, tail protection shifts the selected experiment and replaces hard-region exclusions with explicit ambiguity. In a methane-oxidation benchmark, a 5% false-exclusion tolerance yields a finite-sample tail-risk guarantee with 95% joint confidence across all three structural families.
AI.conclusion: RAED provides a resolution-aware alternative to purely information-gain–driven designs, reconciling information content with structural identifiability. The approach yields distinct experimental choices in practical benchmarks and offers finite-sample guarantees for tail-sensitive nuisance risk, albeit with calibration and sample-complexity considerations.

title: Semantic-Aware Subgraph State Space Model for WSI Classification in Histopathology
summary: Histopathological subtyping relies on the recognition of characteristic histological patterns. These patterns may be expressed by individual tissue structures or by the spatial distribution and co-occurrence of multiple structures, and they often span irregularly shaped tissue regions, termed semantic units in this work. However, conventional patch-based representations may fragment such units and fail to explicitly preserve their internal spatial organization, while efficiently modeling relationships among numerous spatially separated units remains challenging. To address these limitations, we propose the Semantic-Aware Subgraph State Space Model (SASG-SSM), a flexible and efficient framework for whole slide image (WSI) classification. Semantic-Aware Subgraphs (SASGs) first approximate irregularly shaped semantic units by adaptively grouping spatially connected patches guided by class-agnostic visual-semantic priors. By representing patches as graph nodes with adjacency edges, SASGs preserve their internal spatial organization rather than treating them as an unordered set. A Subgraph State Space Module (SG-SSM) subsequently combines a graph neural network encoder for intra-subgraph topology encoding with a Mamba-based state space encoder for efficient contextualization across large numbers of subgraphs. This module integrates local structural information within semantic units with global contextual information arising from their distribution and co-occurrence across the WSI, while efficiently modeling a large number of spatially distributed regions. Extensive experiments across four WSI subtyping datasets demonstrate consistent advantages over representative state-of-the-art methods. Further evaluations under small-cohort and few-shot settings demonstrate robustness and data efficiency under limited training data. Code will be released at https://github.com/HLSvois/SASG-SSM.

AI.tldr: A framework SASG-SSM for WSI classification that preserves irregular semantic units as adaptive subgraphs and fuses local topology with global context via a GNN encoder and a Mamba-based state-space encoder, achieving strong performance and data efficiency across four datasets.
AI.motivation: Conventional patch-based WSI representations fragment irregular semantic units and fail to preserve internal spatial organization, while modeling relations among many dispersed units remains computationally challenging.
AI.method: Construct Semantic-Aware Subgraphs (SASGs) by adaptively grouping spatially connected patches using class-agnostic visual-semantic priors. Represent patches as graph nodes with edges to preserve intra-unit spatial structure. Use a Subgraph State Space Module (SG-SSM) that combines a graph neural network encoder for intra-subgraph topology with a Mamba-based state-space encoder for scalable cross-subgraph contextualization across many subgraphs.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on four WSI subtyping datasets show consistent advantages over representative state-of-the-art methods; robust and data-efficient under small-cohort and few-shot settings.
AI.conclusion: SASG-SSM effectively integrates local structural information within semantic units with global contextual information, enabling accurate WSI classification with improved data efficiency; code will be released.

title: Spurious Advantage Hidden in GRPO
summary: Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) is widely studied for reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, where its advantage estimator assigns each rollout a magnitude from within-group reward statistics. In the common case, this magnitude rewards rollouts that reach the correct answer through reasoning. Yet, an overlooked case shares the same surface: a rollout may land on it by guessing, and the formula still assigns a high magnitude, which we identify as the spurious advantage. This arises in three cases: bounded-answer tasks with a small candidate set; open-answer sets hosting bounded sub-cases; and search agents whose budget opens many paths to the same answer. In all three, this misleads the policy toward guess-like behaviors. We propose SIGNBALANCE, whose magnitude is composition-free: it keeps the verifier sign, uses a global scale, and restores zero-mean balance via a stop-gradient per-class rescaling. Across math and search agent benchmarks at different scales, SIGNBALANCE matches GRPO on open-answer math and improves on bounded-answer math and search agents. Code will be released.

AI.tldr: SIGNBALANCE fixes a spurious advantage in Group Relative Policy Optimization by using a composition-free magnitude with a global scale and per-class stop-gradient rescaling, yielding robust performance across math and search benchmarks while matching or surpassing GRPO in several settings.
AI.motivation: GRPO's advantage estimator can reward guess-like rollouts in bounded/open-ended contexts, creating spurious advantages that bias policies toward guessing; a magnitude robust to surface similarities and sub-cases is needed.
AI.method: Propose SIGNBALANCE: a composition-free magnitude that preserves verifier sign, applies a single global scale, and restores zero-mean balance across classes via stop-gradient per-class rescaling. Evaluation across math and search benchmarks at multiple scales.
AI.result: SIGNBALANCE matches GRPO on open-answer math tasks and outperforms GRPO on bounded-answer math and search-agent tasks, demonstrating reduced spurious guidance and improved robustness.
AI.conclusion: SIGNBALANCE provides a practical, composition-free magnitude for policy evaluation that mitigates spurious advantages while maintaining performance; code will be released.

title: Federated Causal Discovery via Regression-Directed Cumulants
comment: Accepted at the 12th International Conference on Probabilistic Graphical Models (PGM 2026)
summary:
In this paper we study linear non-Gaussian acyclic models (LiNGAM) when used in federated environments. These causal models allow one to go beyond Markov equivalence. However, in many domains data are scarce, and increasing the sample size by centralising data from different clients is not advisable due to regulations such as the GDPR. The federated environment offers an attractive option to balance privacy and causal discovery accuracy. Unfortunately, the standard centralised estimator in the LiNGAM setting, i.e., DirectLiNGAM, cannot be straightforwardly federated. Higher-order cumulant tensors offer a way around this obstacle: they depend only on the joint distribution of the variables involved and add exactly across independent sample groups, so a single communication round suffices in horizontal, vertical, and hybrid partitions.
  However, FedISHC, i.e., the current federated method along these lines, breaks down under near-symmetric noise. To overcome the above limitation, we introduce the FedRCD family of causal discovery algorithms, and investigate three variants that trade off communication rounds against algebraic noise; two of them are exact federated counterparts of the centralised high-order cumulant (HC) and HC-LiNGAM algorithms, and the single-round variants further effectively support exact unlearning at any granularity, from a single observation to a whole client. Numerical experiments show that at sample sizes typical of real deployments, the entire cumulant-based federated family does not actually rank variables by the population asymmetry that the scores encode at zero. It ranks them by a variance ladder induced by the DAG along its directed paths, the cumulant counterpart of varsortability. Marginal standardisation collapses every cumulant method to near-random ordering, while scale-invariant DirectLiNGAM, not federable under this protocol, is unaffected.

AI.tldr: FedRCD extends LiNGAM to federated settings using high-order cumulants, enabling single-round aggregation and unlearning, but empirical rankings align with a DAG-induced variance ladder rather than true population asymmetry; marginal standardisation harms performance, while scale-invariant DirectLiNGAM remains unaffected but non-federable under this protocol.
AI.motivation: Regulatory constraints (GDPR) impede data centralisation for causal discovery. Federated learning offers privacy-preserving collaboration. Existing FedISHC fails under near-symmetric noise; a federated LiNGAM method with controlled communication and unlearning is sought.
AI.method: Introduce the FedRCD family of causal discovery algorithms leveraging higher-order cumulants that add across independent sample groups, enabling one-round federation across horizontal, vertical, and hybrid partitions. Develop three variants, including exact federated counterparts of HC and HC-LiNGAM; single-round variants support exact unlearning from single observations to an entire client. Analyze the impact of marginal standardisation and provide comparisons to scale-invariant DirectLiNGAM.
AI.result: Empirical findings show cumulant-based federated methods do not accurately rank variables by the population asymmetry encoded at zero; ranking is driven by a variance ladder along the DAG's directed paths (varsortability). Marginal standardisation collapses cumulant methods to near-random ordering. Scale-invariant DirectLiNGAM is unaffected by these issues but is not federable under the proposed protocol.
AI.conclusion: Cumulant-based federated LiNGAM achieves privacy-preserving, single-round aggregation and unlearning but sacrifices asymmetry-based ranking fidelity. Standardisation choices critically affect performance. Further work is needed to recover population-asymmetry rankings or develop alternative federated strategies that preserve causal directionality signals.

title: MetaStructAtlas: A Grounded 3D Vision-Language Dataset and Benchmark for Functional and Structural Reasoning in Whole-Body PET/CT
summary: The joint interpretation of metabolic function and anatomical structure is essential for clinical diagnosis in whole-body PET/CT. Although recent advances in 3D medical vision-language models have demonstrated remarkable progress, current efforts are limited to regional CT imaging, leaving a critical void in comprehensive whole-body PET/CT analysis. In this work, we introduce MetaStructAtlas, a large-scale dataset for grounded whole-body PET/CT interpretation that synthesizes multimodal imaging with integrated anatomical, metabolic, and semantic annotations. MetaStructAtlas provides 490 co-registered 3D PET and CT volumes with 50,470 organ-level segmentation masks and grounded radiology reports. To facilitate interactive reasoning, we further developed MetaStructVQA, a standardized 3D grounded visual question-answering benchmark containing 100,565 QA pairs. This framework explicitly links diagnostic queries to visual evidence across modalities, encompassing anatomical, morphological, and metabolic characteristics. Finally, we evaluate state-of-the-art 3D medical VLMs on MetaStructVQA, establishing a robust foundation for multimodal representation learning and integrated whole-body reasoning in nuclear medicine.

AI.tldr: Introduces MetaStructAtlas and MetaStructVQA for grounded whole-body PET/CT interpretation, enabling multimodal, anatomically and metabolically grounded reasoning; evaluates 3D medical VLMs on the benchmark.
AI.motivation: Addresses the lack of comprehensive whole-body PET/CT analysis in current 3D vision-language research, which mainly focuses on regional CT segments; aims to unify anatomical, metabolic, and semantic understanding.
AI.method: Assembles a large-scale dataset: 490 co-registered PET/CT volumes with 50,470 organ-level segmentation masks and grounded reports; creates a 3D grounded VQA benchmark with 100,565 QA pairs; assesses state-of-the-art 3D medical VLMs on the benchmark.
AI.result: Provides a robust foundation for multimodal representation learning and integrated whole-body reasoning in nuclear medicine; baseline results reveal challenges and establish a reference for future methods.
AI.conclusion: MetaStructAtlas and MetaStructVQA enable comprehensive, multimodal whole-body PET/CT interpretation and set the stage for future research in grounded, cross-modality medical AI.

title: DRACO: Fine-Grained Credit Assignment with Dynamic Rubrics for Long-Horizon Agent Training
summary: Reinforcement Learning from Verifiable Rewards works well when a task has a programmatic checker, but most long-horizon agent domains have none. We work in the outcome-blind setting, where ground-truth success signals are not available. Multi-criteria rubrics are a popular way to supply such a reward; they are scored once per trajectory, but a single scalar is a poor signal across tens of steps. We propose DRACO: Distributing Rubric-based Advantage for Credit Optimization. It generates rubrics dynamically during training to track the policy's evolving capability, scores those rubrics once per completed trajectory, and redistributes that judgment over the steps responsible for annotated rubrics to produce differentiated per-step advantages in GRPO. The redistribution is closed-form and does not introduce any trained attribution module. On AppWorld, DRACO gains 15.9 points over the base model and 5.3 points over GRPO trained with a sparse ground-truth reward, despite not using any verifiers itself. On out-of-domain Tau-Bench, it gains 5.3 points over the base model even without a frontier judge, beating both ground-truth-reward training and other rubric-based training settings. The code for DRACO is available at https://github.com/IBM/draco.

AI.tldr: DRACO distributes rubric-based credit to individual steps by dynamically generating rubrics during training and redistributing trajectory-level rubric scores in closed-form, improving long-horizon RL without verifiers.
AI.motivation: In outcome-blind settings lacking ground-truth success signals, rubric-based rewards are common but scalar per-trajectory scores are sparse and provide weak credit signals over long horizons; DRACO aims to provide fine-grained per-step credit assignment without learned attribution modules.
AI.method: Dynamically generate rubrics during training; score each complete trajectory with these rubrics; redistribute the trajectory score across the steps that contribute to annotated rubrics in closed-form, yielding differentiated per-step advantages for GRPO; no trained attribution module is used.
AI.result: AppWorld: DRACO improves by 15.9 points over the base model and 5.3 points over GRPO trained with sparse ground-truth reward, without using verifiers. Tau-Bench: +5.3 points over the base model even without a frontier judge, outperforming ground-truth-reward training and other rubric-based methods; code available at the provided GitHub link.
AI.conclusion: DRACO provides an effective, simple, closed-form credit redistribution mechanism that enables per-step advantage signals in rubric-based reinforcement learning without verifiers, yielding performance gains on long-horizon tasks.

title: Projected Riemannian Gradient Descent for the Bures-Wasserstein Barycenter: Dimension-Independent Linear Convergence at Unit Step Size
summary: The computation of the Bures-Wasserstein (BW) barycenter of an ensemble of positive definite matrices arises throughout machine learning, optimal transport, and quantum information. Riemannian gradient descent (RGD) at unit step size -- the fixed-point iteration used in practice -- converges rapidly, yet existing analyses present a dichotomy: unit-step guarantees carry worst-case exponential dependence on the dimension, while dimension-independent guarantees require small step sizes that forfeit the empirical speed. We resolve this dichotomy, not by improving the guarantees for unit-step RGD, but by proposing a Projected RGD algorithm that achieves dimension-independent linear convergence at unit step size. The achieved rate, $(1 - κ^{-3/2})$, where $κ$ is the condition number of the ensemble, also polynomially improves on the best small-step guarantee ($κ^{3/2}$ versus $κ^{5/2}$ iteration complexity). The crux is a novel Projection Lemma: clipping the eigenvalues of a positive matrix to an interval $[α, β]$ is the closed-form, non-expansive (1-Lipschitz) BW-metric projection onto the set $\{S : αI \leq S \leq βI\}$ -- a statement which, unlike its known one-sided counterpart, does not follow from convexity. The projection is moreover free: it reuses an eigendecomposition the next iteration must perform in any case, so the projected and unprojected iterations cost the same per step. The same analysis covers the invariant matrix projection problem of Brahmachari et al. (2025), whose fixed-point algorithm we identify as unit-step RGD on a totally geodesic submanifold, thereby extending the dimension-independent guarantee to that setting verbatim.

AI.tldr: Introduces Projected Riemannian Gradient Descent (PRGD) for the Bures-Wasserstein barycenter that achieves dimension-independent linear convergence at unit step size, via a closed-form BW-projection onto eigenvalue-bounded matrices. The key tool is a Projection Lemma: clipping eigenvalues to [α,β] yields a 1-Lipschitz BW projection, enabling per-iteration cost unchanged. The approach also improves iteration complexity compared with small-step analyses (κ^{-3/2} rate vs κ^{ -5/2}) and extends verbatim to Brahmachari et al.'s invariant matrix projection problem on a totally geodesic submanifold.
AI.motivation: The BW barycenter of PD matrices is central in ML, OT, and quantum information. Unit-step RGD is fast in practice but its worst-case analysis ties dimension to the convergence; conversely, small-step analyses are dimension-independent but slow. A method achieving dimension-independent convergence at unit step is highly desirable.
AI.method: Propose Projected RGD that, at each iteration, projects onto the set {S : αI ≤ S ≤ βI} by clippping eigenvalues of the current iterate. Prove that this eigenvalue clipping is the closed-form, non-expansive (1-Lipschitz) BW projection onto the constraint set. Reuse the current eigen-decomposition to perform projection without extra cost. Establish linear convergence at unit step with rate (1 − κ^{−3/2}) where κ is the condition number of the ensemble. Compare to small-step guarantees (κ^{−5/2} iteration complexity) and show polynomial improvement. Extend the same analysis to the invariant matrix projection problem of Brahmachari et al. (2025), by viewing it as unit-step RGD on a totally geodesic submanifold.
AI.result: The PRGD algorithm attains dimension-independent linear convergence at unit step, with rate (1 − κ^{−3/2}); per-iteration cost matches unprojected RGD due to reuse of eigen-decomposition; the projection is a free BW-projection onto eigenvalue-bounded sets. The framework also provides a direct analysis for the invariant projection problem of Brahmachari et al. (2025) by interpreting it as unit-step RGD on a totally geodesic submanifold.
AI.conclusion: A Projection Lemma for BW geometry—eigenvalue clipping is the exact, 1-Lipschitz BW-projection onto eigenvalue-bounded matrices—enables a simple, efficient PRGD scheme with dimension-independent linear convergence at unit step. The approach yields faster iteration complexity and extends to related invariant projection problems on totally geodesic submanifolds.

title: Observation-Conditioned Latent Energy Priors for Sparse Implicit Neural Shape Completion
comment: Accepted for publication in the MICCAI 2026 Workshop Proceedings (LNCS) as part of Off-Grid, the 1st Workshop on Continuous Representations and Grid-Free Methods in Medical Imaging. 12 pages, 4 figures, 3 tables
summary: Implicit neural representations (INRs) can model continuous 3D shapes with a shared coordinate decoder and per-instance latent codes. At test time, autodecoder-style models commonly freeze the decoder and optimize a new latent code from sparse off-grid SDF samples. When these samples underconstrain inference, the latent can drift toward regions that fit the observations but decode implausible unobserved geometry. We propose a post-hoc observation-conditioned latent energy prior for frozen INR decoders. The energy scores standardized latents conditioned on a permutation-invariant encoding of the sparse observation set and is used as a residual expert alongside an L2 latent prior selected on validation data. We evaluate on a controlled cell-nucleus SDF dataset and a public MedShapeNet-derived SDF completion dataset. The proposed L2 objective augmented with conditional energy improves consistently over a validation-selected L2 baseline in the sparsest cell-nucleus regimes and, on MedShapeNet, outperforms both L2 and a six-component GMM latent-density prior across all reported readouts. A shuffled-context ablation is consistently weaker than matched context, supporting an observation-specific contribution. These results suggest that lightweight conditional energies can make pretrained INR decoders more observation-aware without retraining.

AI.tldr: Introduce a post-hoc observation-conditioned latent energy prior to guide frozen INR decoders, improving 3D shape completion under sparse observations.
AI.motivation: Autodecoder-style INRs with a frozen decoder freeze inference; sparse off-grid SDF samples underconstrain latent codes, leading to latent drift and implausible unobserved geometry.
AI.method: Define a conditional energy score on latents using a permutation-invariant encoding of the sparse observation set; apply as a residual to an L2 latent prior chosen via validation. No decoder retraining. Evaluate on a controlled cell-nucleus SDF dataset and a MedShapeNet-derived SDF completion dataset. Compare against a validation-selected L2 baseline and a six-component GMM prior; include a shuffled-context ablation.
AI.result: The L2 objective augmented with conditional energy improves consistently over the L2 baseline in the sparsest regimes (cell-nucleus). On MedShapeNet, it outperforms both L2 and GMM latent priors across reported readouts. Shuffled-context ablation is weaker than matched context, indicating observation-specific contribution.
AI.conclusion: Lightweight conditional energies can render pretrained INR decoders more observation-aware without retraining, improving robustness to sparse observations.

title: Why Gated DeltaNet Survives 4-Bit Quantization: NVFP4 W4A4 for the Recurrent Half of a Hybrid 27B LLM
summary: Hybrid LLMs pair softmax attention with linear-attention layers such as Gated DeltaNet (GDN), whose recurrent state summarizes the context in fixed size. Early community 4-bit quantizations of Qwen3.8-27B (48 GDN layers, 16 attention layers) left the GDN block in 8- or 16-bit precision -- especially its decay and write-strength gates -- on the intuition that errors in a recurrence accumulate over long contexts. We test that intuition by building Minima: NVFP4 W4A4 on all 496 linear layers, GDN included. Across perplexity at 4K/32K, MMLU-Pro, GSM8K, AIME'25, GPQA-Diamond, LiveCodeBench, and RULER retrieval to 64K, Minima matches BF16 within seed noise (5-task average -0.52) while being the smallest (17.5 GiB) and fastest-prefill (+14-19%) recipe we compare, and its 32K perplexity gap shrinks with position. A four-part mechanism study explains why: (i) NVFP4's 16-element block scaling localizes the residual stream's extreme outliers, equalizing activation error across layer roles; (ii) the supposedly fragile gate projections are the least sensitive -- softplus/exponential and sigmoid parameterizations compress ~11% GEMM error to ~2% output error; (iii) the delta-rule recurrence holds injected noise at a flat plateau over 32K tokens and forgets a state impulse within hundreds of steps, because each write overwrites the state along the current key direction; (iv) the per-token quantization cost washes out with context instead of compounding. We also repair a global-scale mismatch that arises when per-module-calibrated NVFP4 checkpoints are served by kernels that fuse those modules into one GEMM, and show calibrated FP8 KV-cache scales are performance-free. The result: a practical recipe -- quantize everything, ship KV scales -- and a mechanistic account of why the recurrent half of a hybrid LLM is the easy half to quantize. Checkpoint: https://huggingface.co/minima-ai/mnma_qwen3.8_27b_nvfp4

AI.tldr: Quantizing the recurrent GDN component in a hybrid LLM (Qwen3.8-27B) to NVFP4 W4A4 across all 496 linear layers yields parity with BF16 within seed noise across long-context benchmarks, while achieving the smallest model size (17.5 GiB) and faster prefill. A four-part mechanism explains robustness of the recurrence to 4-bit quantization, and a practical recipe (quantize everything with KV caches) is proposed.
AI.motivation: To test whether the 4‑bit quantization of the recurrent, delta-rule based GDN blocks in hybrid LLMs degrades long-context performance, challenging the intuition that recurrence accumulates quantization errors over long sequences.
AI.method: Quantize all linear layers, including GDN, to NVFP4 with W4A4. Evaluate on perplexity at 4K/32K, MMLU-Pro, GSM8K, AIME’25, GPQA-Diamond, LiveCodeBench, and RULER retrieval to 64K. Address a global-scale mismatch from kernel fusion, calibrate FP8 KV-cache scales, and perform a four-part mechanism analysis explaining error localization, gate robustness, recurrence dynamics under injected noise, and context-dependent quantization costs.
AI.result: Minima matches BF16 within seed noise (5-task average −0.52) while being the smallest (17.5 GiB) and fastest-prefill (+14–19%). The 32K perplexity gap shrinks with position. A four-part mechanism explains resilience: (i) 16-element block scaling localizes residual outliers; (ii) gate projections are surprisingly robust to quantization; (iii) the delta-rule recurrence absorbs noise at a flat plateau and forgets impulses quickly; (iv) per-token quantization cost does not accumulate with context. Calibrated FP8 KV-cache scales are performance-free.
AI.conclusion: A practical recipe—quantize everything, ship KV scales—paired with a mechanistic account of why the recurrent half of a hybrid LLM is easier to quantize. This supports aggressive 4-bit quantization of recurrent blocks in hybrid LLMs and provides actionable steps for deployment.

title: From Nowcasting to Forecasting: Adapting a Reanalysis-Trained
summary: Accurate cloud-cover forecasts are important for temperature prediction, radiation forecasting, and solar-power operations. Short-range forecasting methods can preserve observed cloud placement during the first forecast hours, but their skill decreases when cloud fields evolve through formation, dissipation and deformation. Longer lead times require accounting for atmospheric evolution, but operational numerical weather prediction (NWP) forecasts may not accurately represent the satellite-observed cloud state at initialization. We develop CloudCast v2, a machine-learning model for 12-hour cloud-cover forecasting from observation-based initial conditions. The model is first trained on the Copernicus European Regional Reanalysis (Ridal2024) to learn cloud-evolution dynamics, and is then adapted to satellite-derived cloud fields using conditional flow matching (Lipman2023), a generative method that transforms noise into cloud-cover forecasts conditioned on the observed initial cloud fields and NWP inputs. CloudCast v2 reduces mean absolute error by 10% relative to its predecessor, CloudCast v1 (Partio2025), over the 1-12 h range. It also overtakes CloudCast v1 in fractions skill score, a neighborhood-based measure of spatial agreement, after approximately 3-6 h, depending on the cloudiness category. These results show that observation-initialized machine-learning forecasts can extend beyond the usual 1-3-hour nowcasting range while retaining spatial detail from satellite cloud fields.

AI.tldr: CloudCast v2 uses observation-initialized ML with conditional flow matching to forecast 12-hour cloud cover, improving MAE by 10% and FSS after a few hours versus CloudCast v1; trained on reanalysis and adapted to satellite-cloud inputs to extend nowcasting into longer lead times while preserving spatial detail.
AI.motivation: Accurate cloud-cover forecasts are crucial for temperature/radiation applications and solar power. Short-range models retain structure but degrade as clouds evolve; longer forecasts require evolution-aware approaches, and initialization from satellite data often mismatches NWP states.
AI.method: Pre-train on Copernicus European Regional Reanalysis to learn cloud-evolution; adapt to satellite cloud fields using conditional flow matching, a conditional generative method that creates forecasts from noise conditioned on observed initial fields and NWP inputs.
AI.result: MAE reduced by ~10% over 1-12 h relative to CloudCast v1; fractions skill score (FSS) surpasses v1 after about 3–6 h, varying with cloudiness category.
AI.conclusion: Observation-initialized ML forecasts can extend the usable forecast horizon beyond typical 1–3 h nowcasting while maintaining spatial detail from satellite observations.
